Arthur Saxe Crites
Grand Master, 1923-1924

'S ?-H1HJ.H'V
Our fifty-seventh Grand Master, Arthur Saxe Crites, was born on
Bear mountain in Kern county, California, February 4, 1879. His
father, Angus M., was a stock raiser and a pioneer of this· State, and
altl1ough not blessed with what the world is pleased to call material
wealth, the parents were able to give the boy Arthur a sound training
in all that goes tu make for the best manhood. He was schooled in
the arts of the great out-doors, keeping his heart and sympathies near
to mo.ther earth and to the people who make for the stability of our
governmental institutions. He attended a country grammar school
during five short summer terms, and later became a student at the Kern
county high school, graduating therefrom at the. age of sixteen.
Before he had attained his majority, Arthur enlisted as a private
in G company, Sixth California U. S. Volunteers, for service in the
Spanish-American war. He sailed with his regiment to the Philippines
in the spring of 1898, and was soon promoted, first to the rank of Corporal, then Sergeant, and Quartermaster Sergeant, with which rank he
was mustered out of the service December 15, 1898. He maintained
his connection with the military service by serving as private, First
Sergeant, Second Lieutenant, Captain, Major and Lieutenant Colonel
in the Sixth Infantry and Second Infantry of the California National
Guard from 1898 until 1916, when he was mustered out with the full
rank of Colonel.
In business life, Brother Crites has been active and useful. He
became a bookkeeper in 1899 with the packing department of the Kern
County Land Company, and in 1900 started his career as a banker by
holding with satisfaction the job of general errand boy for the Kern
Valley Bank. In 1903 he was made assistant cashier of that bank,
which place he held until 1905, when he resigned to take over the
office of cashier of the First Bank of Kern, holding such position until
1915. In 1916, first as Vice President and soon thereafter as President,
which office he yet holds, he assumed the management of the Security
Trust Company of Bakersfield in 1915, and built that institution from
third place to first place in the banking houses of the county. Always
active in all work which tended to build up the community in which
he lived, Brother Crites, in addition to his banking interests has been
Secretary and Manager of the Kern County Mutual Building and Loan
Association since May, 1905, and has through this association been
inRtrumental in the building of many homes at Bakersfield. In addition
to this association work, he assisted in the organization in 1921 of
the Bakersfield Horne Building Company, of which he is Vice President.
Indeed, he has been actively connected with nearly every financial and
community enterprise in Kern County.

Politically, Brother Crites is a Republican, and has served many
terms as a member of his county central committee, never, however,
seeking public office.
He is an active member of the Bakersfield Civic Association, and
of the Rotary Club.
The Masonic record of Brother Crites comprises the whole gamut
of degrees. He received his first degree in Bakersfield Lodge No. 224,
December 20, 1900; second degree, January 3, 1901; third degree,
February 21, 1901. Was Marshal of his Lodge in 1902-3; Junior
Warden 1905; Senior Warden 1906; Master 1907; Treasurer 1908, and
again 1915 to date. Was Inspector of the Bakersfie\d <listrict 1909 to
1915.
The degrees of Capitnlar Masonry were conferred upon him in
Kern Valley Chapter No. 75, R. A. M.: M.". M." ., September 21, 1904;
P.". M.". and M.". E.". M." ., October 19, 1904; R.". A."., October 26,
1904. Held. the office·of Treasurer of his Chapter, 1908 to 1912; King,
1912 to 1915; High Priest, 1916; Treasurer, 1918 to date. Was anointed
in the Order of High Priesthood in April, 1916.
The Cryptic degrees were conferred in Fresno Council No. 11,
Royal and Select Masters, April 25, 1917; S.". E.". M.'. degree in Grand
Council, April 15, 1918. Assisted in the organization of Bakersfield
Council, March 12, 1919, and was its first Tllustrious Master; Treasurer,
1921 until now.
The Orders of Knighthood were conferred in Bakersfield Commandery No. 39, K. T.: Red Cross, July 13, 1906; Order of the Temple
and Knight of Malta, November 2, 1906. He held the office of Sentinel,
1907; Captain General, 1908-9-10; Prelate, 1910-11-12; Generalissimo,
1915; Commander, 1916.
Brother Crites received his Scottish Rite degrees in Los Angeles
Consistory No. 3: The 14th, May 29; 18th, September 9; 30th to 32d,
September 11, all in 1915.
He organized the San Joaquin Valley Past Masters Association in
1914, and served as its President for seven years.
In Grand Lodge, Brother Crites served a number of terms on the
important Committee on Finance, and in 1920 was elevated to the
station of Junior Grand Warden; Senior Grand Warden, 1921 ; Deputy
Grand Master, 1922, and in October of 1923, he was· elected and installed as Grand Master.
On the 16th of November, 1904, our retirfng Grand Master took
unto himself a wife in the person of Nellie Lenora Duncan, a lovely
woman who has proved to be truly a helpmate and wise counselor.
Three children have been born to them: Emma Catherine, Arthur
Saxe Junior (who died September 21, 1915), and Angus Duncan.
The best wishes of the writer and of all the Craft go with Brother
Crites in his new relation as Past Grand Master, and to his family.

MESSAGE OF GRAND MASTER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of the
Jurisdiction of California.

MY DEAR BRl('rHRJ(N:
We are met today in our Diamond Jubilee Anniversary. This
means that there is three-quarters of a century of completed Masonic
history in this Jurisdiction. What a splendid record it has been! No
:Mason can give consideration to that record but with a feeling of great
pride. Those who established Masonry upon this coast during the
turbulent days of the gold rush builded far better than they knew.
The heritage is all ours. But with that heritage goes a trust-a trust
to do even a tide better than any of our predecessors. Need I say
that we will be faithful to that trust? With seventy-four years of
completed Masonic history behind us, but with our eyes resolutely on
the future; with seventy-four years of well-charted course behind us,
and with the real ideals of the Fraternity steadfastly before us, we
will be faithful to that trust and carry the standard of Masonry even
a little farther forward, and write the name of Masonry even a little
brighter upon the scroll of time.
It is my privilege to be before you today and to render an account
of the year which has just gone by. And what a wondrous year it
has been! A strenuous year-yes, the most strenuous year in a life
made up of strenuous years; but a year full of labor for, and service
to, the Fraternity I love. \Vhatever labor and service I have performed
has been only an exemplification of the labor and service I found
everywhere throughout the State. The one factor most impressed
upon my mind is the attachment to, and regard for, the Fraternity
manifested by our members on every hand, and the great work and
service being performed by the Inspectors and the officers of the
Lodges. They are the ones who are building the Fraternity and to
them should go the credit.
Succinctly, the various functions performed by me during the
year were:
The constitution of each of the thirty-nine Lodges to which char·
ters were granted at the last session of the Grand Lodge;

10

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The granting of twenty-one dispensations for the formation of
new Lodges;
The institution of five Lodges under dispensations;
The installation of the officers of sixty Lodges;
The laying of the cornerstones of three Masonic Temples;
The laying of the cornerstones of eight school buildings;
The laying of the cornerstone of the Courts and Library building
at Sacramento;
The laying of the cornerstone of the Scottish Rite Cathedral, at
San Jose;
The dedication of six new Masonic Temples;
The dedication of the new buildings at the Decoto Masonic Home;
The dedication of the University Masonic Club House at Berkeley;
The visitation of Lodges in all Inspectorial Districts in the State,
including the five special districts and the Territorv of Hawaii· and
The visitation of nineteen individual Lodges. ,~ll which is lntended
to convey the story that I have been in personal touch with each of
the 505 Lodges in our jurisdiction.

It has been my privilege to meet with the Educational Committee
many times during the year, as well as to be in touch and to advise
with the General Chairman and Executive Secretary continuously. It
would be unfair were I not to testify to the time and care given by
every member of this Committee to the work, and particularly to the
services of the General Chairman of the Committee, Adolphus E.
Graupner. He is entitled to special commendation.

In addition to the above, I was present at many committee meetings, a number of Masters and \Vardens Association meetings, and
many minor functions,-the year being devoted, as promised at the
outset, to the performance of the duties and responsibilities of the
office.
In performing these various duties, a distance in excess of 38,000
miles was traveled. I traveled the entire jurisdiction up and down,
crossing and recrossing. I have been in every county in the jurisdiction with the exception of two, and in every community of any size,
and in many of such communities several times.
Educational Committee
One of the very
and one of the most important duties necessary to perform, was the appointment of an Executive Secretary to
the Educational Committee. After consulting with a number of Past
Grand Masters, as well as with the present Grand Officers, Max A.
Plumb, Past Master of Charter Rock Lodge, of Berkeley, was appointed at a salary of $4,000 per year. As he was at the time e~ployed
as a teacher in one of the schools in San Francisco, it was necessary
for him to give notice of the giving up of his school position, so he
was not able to devote much time as Executive Secretary until January
1, 1924, thus making only nine months' complete service in the position.
There has been much organization and preliminary work to do; nevertheless, I believe the report which is being presented by this committee
jtlstifies the retention of a paid Secretary an<l the expenses incident to
a thorough Educational Department in this Grand Lodge.

11

Masonic Service Association
It will be recalled that this Grand body at its last communication
voted to continue its membership in the Masonic Service Association,
notwithstanding the recommendation by the Grand Master that we
withdraw therefrom. I wish to renew that recommendation. After a
full vear of consultation with Masons throughout the jurisdiction, my
conclusion is that nowhere near adequate results are being obtained
for the money expended. It is costing this body in excess of $5,000
annually for this membership. My judgment is that much better results can be obtained by expending this money in paying the expenses
of speakers to visit the Lodges, particularly the smaller Lodges in
outlying communities, to discuss with them their various problems and
to speak to them on Masonic subjects. It is difficult for any printed
article,-no matter how meritorious-to be read effectively by one
unfamiliar with it, whereas the spoken message reaches its auditors
much more effectively. I am somewhat of the opinion that the representatives at our last communication labored under the impression that
they were to receive Bulletins for a great number of their members.
The terms of our membership provide for only one of each Bulletin
issued, to be forwarded to each Lodge. That there might be no complaint as to these Bulletins being properly mailed, immediately upon
my installation as Grand Master, I requested the Grand Secretary to
forward to the Association a complete list of names and addresses of
all Secretaries of Lodges. I also reqnestcd a new list to be certified
and forwarded as soon as the new names of Secretaries were available
after the elections in December. Although a request was made of the
Association for an itemized account of expenses, no such account was
ever received. I, therefore, recommend that a resolution be passed
cancelling our membership, and that the amount heretofore expended
for this membership be utilized in paying the necessary expenses of
speakers to our Lodges and in furthering the efforts of our own
educ<ttional program.
George Wash'.ngton Memorial
During the year, the corncr:;tone of the C<"orge Washington
2\1emorial was laid, the ceremony occurring on October 31, 1923. The
Association extended an invitation to representatives of this jurisdiction

12

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

to participate. After making an effort to secure the presence at the
ceremony of Past Grand Master Filmer, and upon his inability, of
Past Grand Master Keesling, both of whom were in the East at about
that time, and failing, I delegated my own brother, George S. Crites,
a member of my own Lodge, Bakersfield Lodge No. 224, to be present
and represent this jurisdiction. He was present as a representative
and assisted in the ceremonies. Masons from almost every jurisdiction
in the world assisted. It may well be considered one of the most
significant Masonic events ever occurring in this country. The project
largely had its inception with a Past Grand Master of this jurisdiction,
Brother Oscar Lawler. It is planned to have it financed by all the
Masons in the United States, the plan being that each jurisdiction shall
raise a quota of one dollar per member. Considerable correspondence
passed between the President of the Association, Brother Louis A.
Watres, Past Grand Master of Pennsylvania, and myself about the
quota still due from this jurisdiction. According to our present membership, our· quota should be approximately $107,000, of which we
have paid $5,200. I refused to authorize a drive among the membership
to raise the remainder; nevertheless, I am of the opinion that California
should lay out a plan so that our full share of the undertaking will be
paid within a reasonable time. To this end, I have referred the various
correspondence to the Finance Committee, with a request that they
study the entire situation and submit a report. Whatever plan may
be adopted, I am of the opinion that it should bear equally upon all
of our members.

manner he found necessary. Brother Seale is deserving of commendation for the time and care he has exercised.
Subsequently, the Masters and Wardens Association of San Francisco felt this was a problem in which they could render service, and
T requested their assistance and set aside $300 for their use in connection therewith. This association is also deserving of commendation
for the spirit it has displayed.

Warren G. Harding Memorial
During the year, a movement was started to erect a memorial to
our late President and Brother, ·warren G. Harding. A request was
made to have a drive made among our membership for the purpose of
ass1stmg. I believe this to be a very commendable movement, one
that the Masons of this State should encourage by individual subscriptions, but believing it to be a bad precedent to establish, I refused to
authorize a drive among the membership for funds, but did permit the
literature to be sent to the various Lodges.

Base Hospital
Early in the year, my attention was called to the Base Hospital of
the United States Government near Palo Alto, and that a number of
the Fraternity were confined there, with but little attention being given
to them by our members. The situation confronting these unfortunates
was such that little could be done, but I felt that whatever could be

Public Schools Week
Pursuant to the custom established by Past Grand Master Adams
and followed by his successors, I requested the craft to set apart the
week of March 24 to 29 as Public Schools Week. It was observed by
nearly all of the Lodges and in most instances resulted in good meetings. There is evidence that the efforts being put forth in this regard
are bringing splendid results and increasing general interest in our
public schools. In this connection, there is one observation I wish to
make: Most of the information obtained was either by, or through,
our public school officials. This is well enough, but I believe it is
now time to study our school problems from angles outside the schools.
My experience emboldens me to suggest to the incoming Grand Master
that, should he decide on a similar observance, to endeavor to have
information sought from sources outside the schools themselves.
It is only fair to mention the splendid work done by the Grand
Lodge committee, and especially the Chairman thereof, Brother Irving
Magnes. Brother Magnes devoted much time and effort, did quite a
little traveling at his own expense, and bas gathered and compiled
much information pertaining to the meetings which is sure to be
valuable for the use of future committees.

Hawaiian Masonry
On April 30th, I, with Mrs. Crites and our son Angus, accompanied
by the Grand Organist, Brother George H. Taylor, sailed for a visit
to the Masons of the Islands called the Paradise of the Pacific-and
rather inadequately named at that. There followed two weeks of
Masonic visitations and social activity that will always remain a
pleasant memory and bright spot in not only my year as Grand Master,
but in my life. The charm of the Islands must be experienced to be
comprehended. The great beauty and superb charm, however, are
exceeded by the graciousness of its Masons and their wives. We
wished that all we met there might know how they won our hearts,
and how we enjoyed our stay and appreciated their many courtesies.
I found Masonry on the Islands in splendid condition. It is commanding the attention and service of the very best and most prominent
men there. On every hand was evidenced their great interest in the

14

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Fraternity and its welfare. The Inspector, Brother Lester Petrie, is
deserving of special mention and praise. He is a man of poise and
judgment and universally loved. His main concern in life seems to be
the advancement of Masonry. The Masons of California should feel
proud that the Islands are a part of the jurisdiction and that Masonry
there is in such splendid shape and in such competent hands.
I visited the four principal Islands of the group and every Lodge.
On the Island of Maui, I was received by Maui Lodge No. 472, with a
full-blood Chinese, Brother Apau Paul Low, presiding as Master.
This I considered almost unique and a real distinction, for it demonstrates the universality of Masonry, and that it is "the inward qualifications" that Masonry considers. He, a man of splendid character,
with a charming wife, is the Civil Engineer for the county, and is
highly respected and esteemed by all who know him.
I also visited Kauai, the western-most Island of the group, and
had the pleasure of granting a dispensation and instituting a new •
Lodge there. Heretofore, there had not been a Lodge, although the
Island is of considerable importance and with some sixty Masons
permanently residing there. I was most pleased with the showing
made and interest displayed, and predict a strong Lodge with much
possibilities for good.
.
At the time of my reception by the three Lodges in Honolulu on
May 7th, I convened Grand Lodge and officially installed the Grand
Standard Bearer, Brother Lester Petrie, in his o.fficial station.
Our Grand Organist, Brother George H. Taylor, made the journey
at his own expense, was present at every meeting, and materially
assisted in making the visitations pleasant and profitable, as well as
assisting in making the trip more pleasant.
Heretofore, this Grand Lodge has not allowed the traveling expenses of the representatives of the Lodges from the Islands when
attending the annual communications. This expense is borne by the
local Lodges. The burden necessarily falls heavily upon the individual
Lodges and cuts down the representation from there and to some
extent prevents the touch these brethren should have with the Grand
Lodge. I believe this should be changed, and that all Lodges of the
jurisdiction should be put upon an equal basis as to pay of representatives. Too much praise cannot be given for the work the Masons are
doing there. Much relief work is being done, with rarely a call upon
Grand Lodge for any reimbursement. They should be in better touch
with Grand Lodge and the work Masonry is doing on the mainland.
I therefore recommend that a<lequate legislation be passed by this
Grand Body, allowing the same rate of pay for the representatives
of these Lodges as· of the Lodges in California, and that this pay be
allowed to those present at this session.

The Other Bodies
During the year I have received many courtesies at the hands of
the other Bodies in Masonry. On every hand has been shown their
interest in Craft Masonry, and the guiding spirits in every one were
ever ready to serve and assist me and advance the interests of the
symbolic degrees. One of the most pleasant and memorable events
of the year was a reception tendered me in my home town on March 8
by our own Senior Grand Warden, Brother Albert E. Boynton, then
Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery of Knights Templar.
It was a meeting more largely attended by Grand Commandery Officers-every one but two being present-than was ever before held
outside of an annual conclave of the Grand Commandery. It was a
splendid event in every sense. The personal touch to the meetinga reception by friends I so admire, as well as by Masons I so esteem
-made it particularly memorable to me.
There have been criticisms of these other Bodies in the past. It is
probable those criticisms, at least in part, have been justified. Personally, I have found much inspiration in both the Scottish Rite and
York Rite. I believe there are real elements for good in the Sciots.
The Shrine is performing a most praiseworthy service to humanity in
its work for crippled children. On the other hand, I believe there is
a certain element of weakness, as well as of danger, in too many
organizations basing their membership upon the craft degrees.
There was one incident during the year resulting from.the activities
of such a body that was most regretable. It is true that the end sought
was commendablc,-the assistance of needy children. Nevertheless,
Masons must always remember there is never sufficient excuse to do
those things which the law forbids. Furthermore, Masons must always
remember that no matter in what capacity they may act, whether as
members of other bodies, or as individuals, or as citizens, if things
be done on which the world frowns, the reputation of our beloved
Institution will suffer.
During the year a number of the subordinate organizations of
one of such bodies sponsored various circuses, carnivals or similar
forms of amusement. In some, at least, games of chance and raffles
and kindred forms of diversion were employed in entertaining and
raising funds. It is doubtful if the results obtained are ever satisfactory, but whether they are or not, such means must not be employed by
Masons acting in any guise or for any purpose.
In reading the correspondence reports it will be seen that there
is a growing uneasiness concerning the activities-and particularly
of this nature-of those side orders which have some Masonic connection prerequisite to membership. It has never been the policy
of this Grand Lodge to attempt to dictate the activities of its mem-

16

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

hers in other lines, yet I believe it is safe to say that there is a
certain danger to Masonry on account of the questionable zeal of
such side orders. I therefore believe this body should now go on
record as opposed to the formation of any further orders which
makes any Masonic connection a prerequisite for membership, without first obtaining consent from this Grand body.

It would be difficult and undoubtedly would be unwise to establish any arbitrary limit. The larger Lodges must be permitted to
grow, remain healthy apd be prepared to meet all obligations that
may fall upon them. On the other hand, I believe it would be well
for this Grand body to now go on record as favoring Lodges of
a reasonable membership-say, of not ov.er four hundred. A Lodge
of this size would have sufficient income to maintain itself, would
permit its membership to become better acquainted, and instead of
devoting all its time to conferring degrees, would be able to give
more attention to the conveying of the real ideals of Masonry to
its members.

Aprons for Grand Lodge Officers
There were times while I was a subordinate Grand Lodge officer
had I been afforded the opportunity of appearing in my proper
regalia it would have assisted the occasion and have afforded me
real pleasure. No such aprons, however, were provided, and besides,
heretofore, it has seemed to be considered the . prerogative of the
Grand Master only to appear in· the Masonic clothing of his office.
I believed this was lacking in consideration of the positions held
by the other Grand Lodge officers, so planned on purchasing with
my own funds such regalia, but after discussing it with several of
the present Grand officers and Past Grand Masters, authorized the
purchase of collars and aprons for all officers, and caused to be
forwarded to· each officer his proper regalia, with the suggestion
that he wear the same upon fitting occasions, but with the request
that it be returned ·to the Grand Secretary before the session of
Grand Lodge, and also with the understanding it was not to be
considered a precedent for other Grand Masters to foilow unless
they so chose.
I am sure the privilege to appear in the official clothing of their
positions has met a very responsive chord in every Grand Lodge
officer, and has been received with favor by the membership in
general. The cost of the regalia was $853.88, which I authorized
paid from the general fund.

Size of Lodges
For some time Masonry has been concerned with the size of
Lodges and with the great number of applications for degrees that
were being received, and a continued fear expressed that there might
be a certain danger to Masonry from lack of assimilation of the
new material.
The Grand Lodge roster shows Lodges with memberships ail
the way from 12 to 1430. I have found in both large and small
Lodges a true Masonic spirit, and no motives actuating but the best
interests of the Craft; yet I think it safe to say that the members
get closer together, get more out of Masonry as a whole, understand
its principles better, where the membership is within smaller bounds,

Masonic Temples
It has been my privilege to lay the cornerstones of three Masonic
temples. I find that most of the Lodges throughout the jurisdiction
meet in Temples owned either by the Lodges or by Masonic Temple
Associations. Some of these are now inadequate. A number of
Lodges are meeting in halls either privately owned or owned by
some other fraternal organization. Most of these are very inconveniently arranged for Masonic purposes.
I believe it is a splendid monument to Masonry and its enterprise to have Masonic halls owned by Masonic organizations. I also
believe there is nothing more conducive to good meetings and a
proper Masonic spirit than a proper place to meet, and consider it
would be a forward step if this Grand body would find some means
of encouraging the building of Masonic halls. For the past ten
years there has been invested in the stock of the temple in San
Francisco considerable sums of money. This· has been done largely
for the purpose of paying off the then existing debt. This investment has little prospect of ever paying more than 3 per cent. No
criticism, however, should be offered to such an investment, as

The Inspectors are the men who are largely building Masonrv

Order of Jean d'Arc
There is an Order under the name of Jean d' Arc being formed
in the State. It is aimed to be for the daughters of Masons what
the Order of De Molay is for the sons. Its constitution, together
with its aims and principles, were submitted to me and examined
with interest. There was also submitted to me a resolution for the
subordinate Lodges to pass indorsing this organization. In answer
thereto I felt it necessary to advise that it had always been the
policy of Masonry in general as well as of the Grand Lodge of
California, to avoid any seeming connection with .or ;sp9nsoring
of outside organizations or movements, that I felt such policy was
still sound and the wisest one to pursue, and that until Grand Lodge
had spoken on the matter I would have to advise against subordinate
Lodges passing such resolution. And while passing, although it
may not be pertinent to my report to this Grand body, yet I cannot
refrain from remarking, that irrespective of how praiseworthy this
movement may be and however helpful its principles may proveand I believe all of this can be said of it-yet I believe there is a
serious question of its propriety, for there are, in my judgment,
already too many activities inclined to divert the attention of our
children from their school work and other duties. I speak from
close observation in this regard.

De Molay
This Grand body by appropriate resolution, at its annual communication in 1922, indorsed the Order of DeMolay for boys. This
Order has continued to grow and may he counted a splendid influence
for good. It was organized to teach the boy between the ages of
sixteen and twenty-one devotion to duty, filial love, patriotism, reverence, clean living and good citizenship. It is designed to make
better boys today and better men and better citizens tomorrow. I
find many ;\fasons throughout the State greatly interested in the
movei11e11t. Many times during the year I have been requested to
speak in its behalf. It is a constructive movrmcnt and can well
claim our active interest.
Dnriug the year I was requested to rule on the question of
whether a Lodge could "sponsor'' a chapter of this Order. It was

20

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

submitted to me by Needles Lodge No. 326. According to the rules
of the Order it is necessary for a Masonic body to "sponsor." There
was no other Masonic body available and it was a case where such
a Chapter could have been of inestimable benefit to the boys in that
community. The opportunity for clean amusement was very limited
and the other kind plentiful. I should have been most pleased to
have aided in the organization of a Chapter there, but after reading over
the resolution and having in mind the traditional policy of Masonry,
I ruled that the Lodge did not have the authority to "sponsor" such
a Chapter.
I subsequently learned of another Chapter that was "sponsored"
by a Lodge and requested the Inspector of that District to arrange
for the Lodge to withdraw its "sponsorship." I have recently learned
that there are now in this State twenty-four Chapters of this Order
sponsored by symbolic Lodges.
I am of the opinion that this Grand body should give serious
consideration to taking over the responsibility for this movement.
I recognize this is departing from the traditional policy of Masonry.
I also recognize that having once departed from that policy it is
difficult to predict where it may lead. I, too, recognize that it may
be construed as an effort to establish a recruiting ground for the
Fraternity. These are all objections worthy of much consideration.
But the Order is already established. It is being sponsored by other
bodies composed of ~fasons. The world is not going to differentiate.
So far as the world is concerned the responsibility of it is Masonry's
whether it be sponsored by other bodies or by this. Grand Lodge.
If this Grand body accepts the responsibility we can the better control
the activities.
The movement must be closely supervised. Great care must
be exercised in the selection of advisers. Boys' work should be closely
and continuously directed. Otherwise, it may degenerate and become
a source of mischief. High ideals of conduct must constantly be
before them and the initiatory ceremonies must never be permitted
to descend to the mock initiations practised by some boys' fraternities.
And whether this Grand Lodge accepts the responsibility for the
mov!!ment or continues it where it now rests, I wish to advise the
necessity of continuously keeping before the boys, before Masons,
before the world, that this DeMolay organization is not an adjunct
of Masonry nor a recruiting ground for Masonry. I have found an
inclination to overiook this, and too frequently to refer to the boys
as "Junior Masons." It must be continuously kept in mind, must
be made plain to our members and to the world that our only interest
is in making better boys, better men, better citizens.

Decisions
There has been much correspondence during the year; in fact,
it has been surprisingly extensive. Most of it, however, has been
on matters on which the Masters or Inspectors have wanted explanations or elucidations. I have endeavored to write a personal answer
to each letter received and have always received the requests with
pleasure and replied gladly, as it all shows the interest and loyalty
the officers have in our great Fraternity and their desire to follow
established principles. In most every instance it was only necessary
to apply existing regulations. There were some decisions made
however, which, in my judgment, should be reviewed by Grami
Lodge. I have elsewhere mentioned three: The question of subordinate Lodges sponsoring Chapters of the Order of De Molay,
of the indorsement of the Order of Jeanne d' Arc, and that the
necessary expenses of Masters and Wardens Associations are just
charges upon the Lodges whose officers are participating therein.
In addition to these there are two others which I feel should
be submitted to and passed on by this body.
Petaluma Case: I received a letter from a Past Master of Petaluma Lodge No. 180 advising that objection had been entered to a
Fellow Craft being further advanced; that the Master had submitted
the objection to the Lodge; a committee had been appointed; the
committee reported adversely to the objection, but the Lodge failed
by a two-thirds vote in sustaining the committee's report, and that
the Lodge was considering re-opening the case,
I ruled that the Lodge, having failed by a two-thirds vote to
sustain the report of the Committee, in effect sustained the objection
and that this decision was final and the Lodge could not reopen
the case.
Subsequently I received a letter from a member of the investigation committee, giving me a full history of the case. I then requested the Secretary of the Lodge to certify the case to me. This
he did. It developed that the objection made was that the Fellow
Craft was not under the tongue of good report, but no reason was
'given or evidence offered either to the Master, to the committee,
or to the Lodge, to sustain the objection. I thereupon ruled that
the Master had erred in submitting the question to the Lodge without
sufficient reason being given; that, although no requirement of the
Constitution provided that any evidence should be presented, yet

The Biggest Mason
The year has been replete with memorable events, with high lights
in Masonry as well as in my own career. It would be very difficult
to say that any one event stands out more prominently than all other
events, but at least among those that will always remain as outstanding was the raising by me, on July 14th, for Highland Park Lodge
No. 382, of the "Biggest Mason in the World," John Aasen. Brother
Aasen is eight feet nine and one-quarter inches tall and weighs five
hundred and sixteen pounds. The raising took p)ace in the spacious
Lodge room of Hollenbeck temple. It was estimated that fourteen
hundred Masons witnessed the ceremony and that over one thousand
more had to be turned away for lack of room to accommodate them.
Brother Aasen proved to he a very receptive candidate, and the
degree was voted to be as impressive an event as ever witnessed.

Pay of Members Fund
It has been the policy of this Grand Lodge to lay a tax on the
subordinate Lodges to create a fund for the pay of the Representatives of Lodges who attend its annual communications. At the
present time this tax is 12 cents for each member borne on the roll.
Undoubtedly this tax was levied at a time when all the resources
and income of the Grand Lodge were strained to meet the ordinary
expenses and provide the necessary emergency fund. The situation
is now changed. An emergency reserve is already on hand, and
after paying all expenses for the present year, including the added
expenses required for this communication, there will still remain a
surplus of approximately $40,000. It is fair to assume that the increase in expenses in the future will not be out of proportion to the
increase in our income. I am of the opinion that the emergency reserve should not be built beyond the hounds of reasonable requirements. I can see no necessity for providing a separate fund for the
pay of Representatives. I would, therefore, recommend that the
Lodges be relieved of this tax and that hereafter such expenses be
provided for out of the General Fund. This will still leave a surplus
.in excess of $25,000.

no pay is now being allowed the Representatives who attend our

Peter Lassen
At our last annual communication the Grand Master recommended the ai;quirement of the land where the grave of this pioneer
of Masonry in California is located. The Grand Lodge orally referred
this recommendation to the. incoming Grand Master with power to
act. At the time of my visit to Susanville it was my privilege to
visit the site of his grave. At the foot of an enormous yellow pine
tree, the outstanding tree of a grove of some one hundred trees,
it surely is a fitting resting place for this pioneer Californian and
good Mason.
I was accompanied on this visit by Judge Harry D. Burroughs,
who has been selected by the Grand Commandery of the State as
a committee on the same matter, and by Brother James A. Nutting,
who has been selected by the Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons
of California for the same purpose. It was thought .that three acres
should be acquired. This would include all the trees in ·the grove
and would give access to the county road. The grove is situated
in the edge of a field used for cattle grazing purposes and has an
irrigation ditch running through it, which would supply water were
it needed. We then visited the family owning the land. We found
it to be a Masonic family. The father, now deceased, was a Mason,
and two of the sons are Masons. They expressed a willingness to
sell to the Grand Lodge the necessary site, but were unprepared to
name a price. I left the matter with Judge Burroughs to follow up,
but at the time of writing this report no results have been attained,
although I was quite desirous of completing the matter during the
year. I recommend the same to the consideration of the incoming
Grand Master.

Hiram Lodge No. 43
On September 17, 1923, a disastrous fire visited the town of
~l Dorado in El Dorado county, and destroyed every business building
m the town. The Masonic temple was one of the buildings destroyed.
This left Hiram Lodge No. 43 without a place to meet. The indomitable spirit of the miners who established this I,odge in the early
fifties still prevailed. The twenty-four members of the Lodge determined that they would not permit the surrender of their charter. They
arranged the transfer of their meeting place to Diamond, a distance of
twelve miles and immediately commenced considering plans for rebuilding. The outlook was most gloomy. The Lodge finally submitted
a request to me to be permitted to submit to the Lodges throughout
the jurisdiction their plight and ask for assistance.
After determining that the prospect for the continual maintenance
of the Lodge was good, providing its hall could be rebuilt and believing that wherever possible these old Lodges, which have ~vritten so
much int.o the history of Masonry of this State, should be preserved,
I authorized such a letter to be sent out. The response was mQst
gratifying. Two hundred and three Lodges and eleven individual members have answered its distress signal, and a total of $6,061.30 has been
contributed. Each and every member of the Lodge is most grateful
for the response. The new temple is now well under way, and it will
not be long now before these indomitable spirits are rewarded with a
fine home of their own and free from debt.

During the year it has been necessary for me to write many
letters on this subject. From this correspondence and from my contact with certain Lodges in the j ttrisdiction, there is indisputable
evidence that certain Klan members are endeavoring to mix the affairs
of Masonry with those of the Klan, thereby causing discord and confusion in the Craft, and also creating in the mind of the public as well
as in the minds of some of our members a wrong impression as to the
actual standing of Masonry in this regard. It must be understood
that such action is most objectionable. No discord or confusion must
be permitted to enter the Craft, and any acts which may have such
tendency must be summarily dealt with. The interest of Masonry lies
in every member avoiding every possible occurrence which might give
color to any relationship between the Masonic Fraternity and this other
organization. In all of the letters which it has been necessary to write
on the subject, I have stressed this necessity.

Letters
I, al~o, feel that at this time it might be desirable to again quote
Masonic standing on matters of toleration. This may seem superfluous,
as Masonry's standing in this is so well known; is older than Grand
Lodges; is one of the landmarks of the Order; and yet I believe that
whatever ear may have been given by any Masori to the teachings of
the other organization is due to the lack of comprehension of Masonry's
standing on this question. It is surprising that this should be the
situation, because from the very first degree to the very last we are
taught the necessity of toleration; that Masonry's teaching is largely
based upon toleration; that the very origin of our Institution is largely
due to a demand for toleration; that the necessity of toleration was
written by members of this Order in the Constitution of this country.
Our stand on religious toleration was well defined by Grand Lodge at
its annual session in 1894. That all may understand the full purport
of the decision, I quote the same in full:
Objection was made to the advancement of an Entered
Apprentice. A committee reported that the cause of the object-

tion was alleged membership in a certain church, and that the
objection was not a valid Masonic one. A ballot was had on
the report, and the report was rejected. The Master declared
the objection to be sustained, and ordered the fee for the
remaining degrees to be returned. The Grand Master ruled
that the objection was not a valid Masonic objection; that the
report of the committee should not have been put to ballot;
that, other than a belief in a Supreme Being, there is no religious qualifications for membership in a Lodge; that it was
not an objection that could be entertained; and that the brother
was entitled to be advanced. The Committee on Jurisprudence
approved the ruling, stating that "it is fundamental law and a
part of the 'body of Masonry' that no man can lawfully be
made a Mason who does not unequivocally declare at the
threshold his belief in God and a future existence and that
no _inquiry can be made of him as to the creed, ~r sect, or
society, or people to which he belongs or with which he
affiliates." That law is older than Grand Lodges, and is a
landmark which no man or body of men has power to change.
In recognition of that law we have declared the rule to be
inflexible that this Grand Lodge will not interfere with religious or political matters or controversies of any kind. The
Master was directed to proceed with the remaining degrees.

Necrology
Although the year has been such a splendid one for Masonry, and
that we can all feel proud of Masonry's accomplishments during the
year and the position in which it stands at the close, yet there have
been some tears of sadness, because many good Masons and true have
answered the final summons. Not any more than ordinarily, in fact
the year has been singularly free from the loss of those prominent in
this Grand Lodge, for there has been the death of no Past Grand
Master, of no officer of the Grand Lodge, of no committeeman, and

"The last full measure of devotion,"
who
"Now rest beneath the low green tent
Whose curtain never outward swings,"
and it is only fitting that we should pause, if only for a moment, in
reverent remembrance of them.
The one Inspector whose .death we chronicle is Brother Francis
E. Irwin, Inspector of the 80th Masonic District at San Pedro.
Brother Irwin had been a Mason for 10 years, was very devoted to
the Fraternity, was most beloved by those who best knew him, and
was that kindly soul of which Masonry is so largely composed.
What is this mystery that men call death?
My friend before me lies; in all save breath
He seems the same as yesterday. His face
So like to life, so calm, bears not a trace
Of that great change which all of us so dread.
I gaze on him and say : "He is not dead,
But sleeps; and soon he will arise and take
Me by the hand. I know he will awake
And smile on me as he did yesterday;
And he will have some gentle word to say,
Some kindly deed to do; for loving thought
Was warp and woof of which his life was wrought.
He is not dead. Such souls forever live
In boundless measure of the love they give."

Grand Lodge, as well as all entertainments provided for your convenience and pleasure, are being provided by our good brethren south
of the Tehachapi without any expense to this body.

Appreciation
And now comes the most difficult task of all, that of attempting to
express the real appreciation I feel toward those who have rendered
Masonry such service and have showered me, as their Grand Master,
with so many courtesies. Everywhere I have gone I have been received
with the utmost courtesy and consideration. There has always been
shown more than a mere willingness to serve; there has always been
displayed an eagerness to do whatever I might suggest, and eagerness
to advance the cause of our Grand Institution. To one and all my heart
goes out in appreciation. I feel I must .not, in justice to all, attempt to
particularize, as it may not be the one who has done the most that is

Closing
And now I must bring this report to a close. I do it with some .
sense of relief, with some regrets. It has been a year of high .aspirations. Some have been fulfilled, some have not. I believe it can be said
that I have done the best I could, that I have devoted whatever time
and effort and ability I had to the cause. I am hoping· it can be said
it was worth the while that I passed by this way.
And so I close one of ·the happiest, one of the most strenuous,
one of the most fruitful .years of my life, with this quotation, a quotation that I have been pleased to use many times during the year :
An old man, going a lone highway,
Came at the evening, cold and grey,
To a chasm vast and deep and wide.
The old man crossed in the twilight dim,
The sullen stream had no fear for him;
But he turned when safe on the other side
And built a bridge to span the tide.
"Old man," said a fellow pilgrim near,
"You're wasting your strength with building here;
Your journey will end with the ending day,
You never again will pass this way.
You've crossed the chasm deep and wide,
Why build you this bridge at even-tide?"

Bulletin No. 1-My General Policies
The writing and publication of this Bulletin has been purposely
<ldayed, that the subject matter should reach the J..,odges for their
stated meetings of January. This has been so planned that the new
Masters might have information as to the policies of my administration
as they enter upon the duties of their office.
I desire at the outset to express to all the brethren my profound
:tppreciation of the great honor conferred upon me-the highest mark
of confidence and esteem that has ever come into my life. But with
appreciation of the honor comes also a sense of responsibility involved.
Jn proportion as honor is bestowed and confidence reposed so is responsihility placed and requirement made for labor answering to the trust.
This sense of responsibility on my part is deepened when I consider
the high character and outstanding qualities and attainments of the
ml'n who have preceded me in the high office of Grand Master of Masons.
Their efforts and abilities have brought the institution to a high place
in the estimation of the people, and it is for each succeeding occupant
of the Grand East to not only maintain the prestige of the fraternity
hut to insure its progress and to seek attainment of the higher good.
I am concerned that with the passing of my term of office the record of
California Masonrv shall show that gain has been made and that the
(~rand Lodge was Jnstilied in the choice made in my elevation.
To the end that the onerous duties of this place may be properly
and efficiently handled, it is my intention to consider this year closed to
my business career and interests. Thus I can devote to the Grand

Mastership whatever time and energy may be necessary to care for the
interests committed to my care. For me this will be a labor of love,
taken up earnestly and with sincerity, with a mind single to the benefit
of the Craft. No Lodge of all those within the jurisdiction will be so
small but that its welfare will be near to my heart. Nor will there be

Fraternity.
My general policies for the year to come may be announced under
four heads.
First, I would ask from the Craft and its every member a little
more loyalty to the Craft. Each one of us has in his time professed
to be of the Fraternity because of a high regard for the Masonic Institution. Such regard should be sustained and increased; it should be
jealously maintained. The reputation of the organization is in the
hands of its membership. By speech and action each brother will add
to or detract from the good opinion of the world without. The conduct of a Mason in his every relationship of life should be of such
a nature that it will reflect credit upon the Fraternity and insure confidence and regard for its principles and activities. A Mason's loyalty
should be : First, to his God; secondly, to his country; third, to his ·
family, and next, to his Masonry. Let me then plead for a little greater
loyalty, a little more thought given to the great Institution of our voluntary and loving adherence.
Secondly, let me plead for just a little greater harmony in. and for
Masonry. Past Grand Master Sherman's year in office was notable for
the splendid harmony that existed through all the Craft. It is my hope
and purpose to so labor that this may be continued, and even increased
and extended. It is a prime requisite that each one of us should fully
sense the fraternal relationship-a relationship that cannot be disturbed
by petty personal differences, nor suffered to become lax because of
varying opinions or temperamental clashes. Whatever may divide the
brethren should be adjusted in a truly fraternal spirit. Matters that
are of the individual life should never be permitted to bring discord
into the Lodge. Nor will any brother who has a right conception of
Masonry seek to use the Fraternity for personal business, social .or
political advantage. The mission of Masonry is service-service always
placed above self and self-interest. It is this great ideal, carried into
the daily life, that will promote and increase the fraternal regard that
should be paramount in every Lodge and in the consciousness of every
brother. It is the sincere wish of your Grand Master that the energies
of every Lodge and every Mason, collective and individual, shall be
devoted to the development of a true and abiding spirit of fraternity.
But upon no plea for harmony, nor other specious reasoning, can
there be compromise with wrong. The principles and ideals of the

Craft, the heritage received from the fathers, cannot be tampered with
or ignored for some fancied advantage of the moment. In every Lodge
there should be a clear vision of the right, an understanding of that
which is inherently righteous beyond question or sophistry. And for
the things that are of enduring good this Craft of ours should stand
firm, without equivocation or any reservation of mind. Likewise it is of
011r Masonic duties, implied or pronounced in every teaching of the
hrotherhood, that all things that are wrong should be opposed. We
m•t•<l more than ever before a fearless Masonry, and Masons who will
rnmhat evil, unafraid of adverse criticism or open opposition.
Third. There should be a greater. effort put forth by the officers,
that the initiates in our Lodges may the better grasp and retain and
111akc a part of their lives the great principles and ideals of Freemasonry. It is requisite that each neophyte shall be given a conception

and enforcement of the law of the land should be of concern to every
Mason. One cannot consider the existing disregard for law but with
apprehension and the sense of a growing danger. As citizens of a
democracy we have adopted and acquiesced in rule by the majority; the
law represents the rules of the game of_ life, by which we have tacitly
agreed to be bound while playing our little parts therein. The man
or woman who claims the privileges of the game, yet insists on playing
outside or in spite of the rules, can be regarded as neither a friend
worthy of confidence nor an antagonist who will go on fairly and
decently with the game. "The surest test of citizenship," says a recent
writer, "is the attitude of men toward laws they may personally dislike." To the Mason at heart all law will command obedience. This
whether it be the prohibition law, the traffic law, the game law, or the
police regulations of our home towns or cities-so long as these are of
the legal structure of our country, our commonwealth or our community. If the one hundi:ed thousand Masons of this Grand Jurisdiction will but observe the law for themselves, and will seek to aid in
securing its observance by others, then indeed will Masonry be a potent
force for good, lessening the existing danger to society and bringing
the people to a realization of their duties as citizens of the world's
greatest democracy, upon the stability of which the home of humanity
depends.

Bulletin No. 2-Public Schools Week
It has not been by chance nor happy inspiration that my immediate
predecessors as Grand Masters have taken up during their terms of
office the task of calling the attention of the Masons of this jurisdiction
to the need of supporting the public school system of the State and
Nation. The question has forced itself upon public attention; has revealed itself as among the matters most vital to our democracy. The
great institution of Freemasonry, which should be alert to all that is
involved in good citizenship, cannot remain inactive while such a question demands attention.
For several years a week has been set apart during which California Masons have been urged to gather, that they might become informed of the exact conditions of the schools of their localities and of
the State. To this end men fitted by experience and study have been
invited to address the brethren. Discussions have followed, covering
every phase of the subject, with the result that Masons have been the
better enabled to form intelligent judgments and to work effectively
with those concerned for the betterment of the school system.
The subject is not one of passing importance. As a matter of fact
it becomes with each passing year of greater significance. There are

influences that are consciously antagonistic to popular education.
There are others selfishly concerned to deny to the schools that gener1>11s support that must be accorded if they are to give the desired
results. There are new facts to be considered; new alignments of
forces that must be estimated; political and economic factors that require careful thought to properly measure. Then again the interest
already aroused must be sustained and intensified. The information
gained in other years is to be added and correlated. The young brothers
--those who have entered the fraternity since the last "School Week"11ced the instruction and inspiration that others have already gained.
The Fraternity in California cannot afford to rest on what may have
hccn accomplished. It must press forward to new and greater achieve1111·nts.
It is well within the truth to state that on no other matter demanding the attention of the American people has there been such unanimity
of sentiment among Masons, nor such widespread interest, as there is in
popular and State-controlled education. In this we but share in the
alll'l1tion given by the entire people of the United States. The Masonic
rnnccrn for education is not of recent growth or showing. It has but
d1•vcluped as the exigencies of the situation demanded a closer attentiou
and more emphatic expression. So long ago as 1847 there is this in the
proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Ohio to substantiate such statement:
"It shall be the duty, as no doubt it will be the pleasure,
of every Lodge in the State to have a list of all the Masons
and Masons' children living within its jurisdiction, and by its
own committees and officers to cause every child of a Mason,
especially the orphans and those of the poor and indigent, to
receive the benefits of a common school education."
The Nation and the Craft have gone far since that time. The
11101lest claims and very limited means of our brotherhood at the time
1111·11tioned went no farther than the effort to care for the education of
its own. Now the demand of a true Americanism and of an informed
Masonry is that every child within our national borders shall be given
th1• opportunity for an education to fit it for the duties and responsihilitics of future citizenship.
Until recent years it has been a boast of our people that the United
Stales was an example for other nations in the educational opportunity
ofTl'rcd freely to its children. With this went the conviction that nowhere else could be found such a low percentage of illiteracy. The
trsts of the World War and a consequent examination of census reports
hronght humiliation. We found that 5,000,000 illiterates were numlwn·cl among our population, representing, according to official explanation, "only those persons who have had no schooling whatsoever." Of
t11t•sc, 3,000,000 were American-born. In the draft it was found that

36

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

one out of every four of military age examined could not write a letter
home nor read a newspaper in English. Again, the census of 1920
showed that 1,437,000 children, from seven to ·thirteen years of age
"are not attending any kind of an educational institution. More than
1,000,000 children between the ages specified are classed as workers,
forced by untoward circumstances or parental necessities or indifference, to forego all privilege of education. The knowledge of these things
has silenced a former boastfulness and aroused a determination to correct the trouble and erase the blot from the Nation's record.
In many communities indifference or penuriousness has affected
the schools injuriously. It is stated on authority that during the past
year some 50,000 teachers, with no further equipment than a common
school training, were attempting the impossible task of properly preparing more than 1,000,000 children for the duties of life. To combat
such inefficiency becomes a duty. The remedy in sueh cases can only
be applied when the people are aroused and informed and determined
upon betterments.
We as Masons have a duty in this matter-a duty owed to ourselves, to the fraternity, to our communities, the State and the Nation.
Ours is a professed quest for knowledge-a knowledge that shall be
beneficial to ourselves and others. In no present way can we seek and
use knowledge to better advantage than in considering this question of
the public schools. To the end that information may be gained upon
which judgment may be based, I hereby call upon the Craft of Cali·
fornia to set apart the week beginning Monday, March 24, to be known
as "Public Schools Week." Within that time I ask that atl Lodges,
whether singly or in combination, as circumstances may dictate, meet
for the purpose of considering the situation. I suggest that all other
meetings be foregone and that speakers be chosen for familiarity with
the subject assigned, and that ample opportunity be given for discussion,
so that all phases of the general topic may be viewed and determined.
I would like to suggest further that discussions be had along at
least four lines :
First: That of efficiency in the schools;
Second : That of economy in their administration;
Third: As to whether or not the curriculum is too extensive; and
Fourth: ·About the extent to which social activities have been
. permitted.
To my mind these four questions are vital and are questions upon
which too much thought cannot be concentrated.
The Committee on Publie Schools Week will mail out further
suggestions for observances of the week.

Next, it should be emphatically impressed upon the mind of the
candidate that the Fraternity is never to be used in any way to further
personal, political or business interests. Any such attempt is certain
to bring discredit upon the individual who so far misapprehends the
purposes of the Institution. And in every case it brings reproach upon
the Craft. This is a matter that must be insisted upon. Too often it
occurs that brothers imagine they can gain a social or personal advantage, can aid themselves in business or promote their political ambitions
by means of Masonic affiliation. It will and must remain true that all
good Masons will condemn any such effort. Yet there are some who
hold out as an inducement to friends who have expressed a desire to
join the Fraternity that membership may aid them in their secular
activities. We must believe that they do this mistakenly and without
due thought. Their own Masonic education is incomplete. If proper
emphasis be given from the beginning to the fact that Masonry cannot
be thus used, and that any attempt to turn it to wrongful ends will
result in quick and stern condemnation, it would soon become unprofitable for anyone to trade upon the loyalty of the brothers. In this
connection I would call attention to the solicitation that is too frequently permitted within the precincts of the· Lodges in matters that
are semi-Masonic in their nature but that really pertain to business of
various kh1ds. Masters should particularly guard against such offenses,
for the Lodge becomes less attractive to the members if they are there
sttbjected to the appeals of those who would use Masonic affiliations to
further their own objects.
The education of the Mason covers a wide field of duties; these
extend to every relationship of life. Not one should fail in performance because careful instruction has been lacking. It requires no set
phrases to ground the initiate in his duty to the Fraternity, to his
brother and a brother's family-his wife, his mother, widow or daughter. It should be brought clearly to the young brother that in his
character as a Mason he has also taken on new duties as a citizen,
and that he owes more than before to alt humanity. That one who has
learned the lessons of Masonry, and gained their greater meaning, will

rerngnizc the brotherhood of man, and will in all things strive for the
betterment of his kind, as being children of the All-Father, in Whom
he has declared his belief and in Whom he puts his trust.
Secrecy should be enjoined; the initiate should be warned against
loose or careless speaking in matters wherein Masonry or the affairs
of the Lodge are involved. He should be informed of the nature of
Masonic offenses and the penalties for disobedience or wrong-doing.
11 c should be informed of the requirements for Masonic avouchment;
the right of visitation; Masonic etiquette, both in his own Lodge and as
a v1s1tor. He should know the duties of an investigating committee;
the qualities that are essential in one who would seek entrance to the
Fraternity. The methods and requirements of the examining commit1\'e should be made clear. It is pertinent to this last suggestion to
remind Masters that too frequently the examining committee is inclined
lo forget that its only duty is to ascertain whether the applying visitor
is a regular Mason, and in the shortest possible time and way to decide
·
whether he is entitled to enter the Lodge.
The information indicated, if properly conveyed to the young and
1·agcr brothers, will serve to equip them for active duty within the
Lodge. It will give them an abiding interest and the desire to constantly perfect themselves in Masonry. The officers can then rely upon
the continuing loyalty and willingness of the membership, and can call
upon any with confidence that the work required will be gladly and
dliciently performed.
These suggestions, made to the Masters and officers of our Lodges,
are intended only to start them upon thought for themselves upon like
lines. With consideration and experience they will, for themselves,
hring out new themes and thus the education of California Masons will
Iii' constantly improved. A Mason is not "made" by recitations and
<'l'rl'monies; these are means to an end, and not the end in themselves.
The true Master is that one who can truly "set the Craft to work
and give them proper instruction for their labor." It is for the indivirl11al Master or other officer to decide for himself how best he can
nmvcy such instruction for the greatest benefit of the learner. Some
111ay do this by means of a special coaching committee selected for the
purpose; others by arranging for the regular lecturing committee to
talk over the various matters essential to formation of the ::\fasonic
character; while again other :\fasters may by personal conversation and
1·011tact with the candidates achieve the best results. But that Master
fails utterly who ignores his duty in such matter, and whose "making
uf Masons" begins and ends with the perfunctory phrases of the ritual.
To the Masters of the jurisdiction I would say: "You have been highly
honored by the brethren; see to it that their confidence in you is not
misplaced."

GRAND LODGB OJ!' CALU'OHNIA

I am sure that the officers of our Lodges will gladly study these
problems for themselves; that they will seek to inform themselves and
thus be able to instruct the younger brothers. With this spirit prevailing throughout the jurisdiction there can be no reason for the pessimism sometimes expressed because of the great number of initiates
thronging at our doors. The keen and impressionable minds of the
young men who are entering the ranks of California Masonry can be
turned to work for good beyond our utmost wish. The lessons of the
ancient Craft are noble and inspiring; properly presented, they ean be
made lasting and of force in the daily life. The principles and ideals
of Masonry are based upon the eternal truth; their acceptance among
men would heal all bitterness and still all strife. 'It is our work to
bring these clearly to the consciousness and to make them part of the
lives of our own brethren, that so the leavening influence of Brotherly
Love, Relief and Truth may work more effectually in the world of
men. And so shall Masonry be free from any fear of danger within,
whence only injury can come.

Bulletin No. 4-Constitution Week.
The week of September 14-20 is hereby set aside as Constitution
Week. This is the same week the American Bar Association has
designated as such.
It is fitting that l\fasons should concern themselves in every movement calculated to advance the education of the people, or to increase
the prosperity, or insure the welfare of the Nation. That such movements occur frequently is a matter of encouragement to all good citizens. The forces of discontent and disruption are never idle. Even
in this great Republic there are elements seeking to spread the gospel
of hatred. There are those who are attempting to sow the seeds of suspicion and discord among their fellows. They would array class
against class with the intention, wholly avowed, to destroy all that the
toil of generations has built in the structure of our Government.
The naming of a week to be devoted to the consideration of the
Constitution of the United States is not intended to be a mere gesture.
It is not intended that there shall be empty repetitions of phrases taken
from the basic document of our American life. The occasion can mean
little or much, as it is given over to platitudinous utterances, or is
made an effort for real thought and reasoned conclusions. Rightly
considered, this movement is an attempt to define and make clear the
American attitude. It is a seeking for an understanding of the foundations upon which the structure of this Nation is built. We study the

41

great principles that were written into the charter of our Govern111cnt, with the idea that those principles shall not fail of understanding
or of practical application.
It is probably safe to say that the Constitution heretofore has
been too much considered a thing to worship-something to be referred
to with pride, and yet regarded as not coming within the practical view
of the average citizen. It has been for law-making bodies to consider,
or for courts to define, but not for men and women to understand as
au essential to their welfare or as a necessity to the permanence of
the l{cpublic. The setting aside of this week as Constitution Week
has, as a primary purpose, to bring the basic provisions and safeguards
of that Constitution, the basis of our freedom, within the knowledge
a1ul comprehension of all.
To the Masons of California I appeal with. confidence, that they
111akc of this week a time of value to themselves and to the craft. A
rnnsiderable portion of those who formed this Republic and gave sub~tance to its ideals were of our fraternity. It is safe to say that these
men brought to the councils that framed our Constitution the principles
tlwy had learned in Masonry. He that cannot see in the thoughts and
words expressed in the early life of this Republic the influence of
:\fasonry is poorly informed, indeed.
The time and the circumstances of the time demand from us a
s•Tious study of present-day conditions; let us, therefore, meet and
111;1kc this week a week of real benefit to ourselves, to our communities.
l therefore hope that every Lodge, either singly or in groups, or in
assisting some public meeting of the community, will enthusiastically
j .. in in the observance of this week. In our ranks are those who are
well informed on the subject-men who have given long and close study
10 the problems that confront the Nation. Let us requisition them for
thl' meeting. In this, as in any other work for the common good,
Masons must not fail nor fall behind.

At the beginning of our first quarter of a century of organization, October, 1874, we had 10,965 members; at the beginning of our
second quarter, October, 1899, we had 20,442 members.

Ratio of Losses to Gains
Too many Lodges do not appreciate the necessity of having a working committee on delinquent members, with the result that two-thirds
of the members who are suspended for non-payment of clues never
return to Masonry. Our losses from all causes per year are about
28 per cent of the gains. In the years 1913 to 1923 inclusive the
number of members suspended for non-payment of dues was 5,608,
and the number restored was 2,131, a net loss of something like
62 per cent. Some of the best Lodges in the jurisdiction never lose
a member by suspension except after a report of the committee
that suspension would be for the best interests of Masonry.

Duplicate Charter Issued
On the 7th of January, 1924, a duplicate charter was issued by
order of the Grand Master for Winnedumah Lodge No. 287, the
original having been destroyed by a fire which burned the Lodge
hall.
April 25, 1924, Dunsmuir Lodge No. 297 lost its hall and contents by fire, and by order of the Grand Master a duplicate charter
was issued. The Grand Master also gave permission to the Lodge
to meet at Sisson pending the construction of a new hall.
On the 16th of July, 1924, a duplicate charter was issued by
order of the Grand Master to Standard Lodge No. 440, to replace
the original one which had been partially destroyed.
An Echo of War Days
Under date of August 12, 1924, I received a letter from Brother
Edward Crolic, Past Master of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296, San
Diego, inclosing a check for one hundred dollars, the proceeds of
the sale of furniture which had been used in the Soldiers' and Sailors' Service Club during the late World War. This money was by me
deposited to the credit of the Emergency Relief Fund.
Degrees by Courtesy
The usual burden of courtesy work has been imposed upon our
Lodges, mainly at Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Pedro, San
Diego and Vallejo, the number being 23 first degrees, 281 second degrees, and 370 third degrees. Our Lodges have requested like favors from other jurisdictions to the number oi 5 first degrees, 24

second degrees, and 25 third degrees. I am still of the opm10n that
the Pennsylvania plan is sound, and does not lack in proper courtesy
or tend in any way to weaken the comity of jurisdictions.
