REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER

Called on the Grand Secretary, Brother Jesse, at St Louis, my
next stop.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:

61

I was not very fortunate in meeting many of the Grand Lecturers,
but those that I did meet were most courteous, and anxious to give
me information regarding their work.

In accordance with the Regulations, I herewith submit to you my
seventeenth annual report as Grand Lecturer, giving ai1 account of
rny stewardship for the past year.

Chicago was my next stop. I saw the third <legrec conferred, somewhat similar to our work.

Meeting as we are in this beautiful city of the Southland, and
celehrating the seventy-fifth anniversary of our Grand Lodge, causes
one to think of the vast amount of history that has been made during
these years, for the Nation, the State and for :\fasonry.

Next stopped at Indianapolis, where I met the Grand Se.cretar'.,
Brother Swintz. Saw the first degree conferred. The candidate 1s
presented with a Bible in this jurisdiction, with a short ceremony at·
tachcd to the presentation.

The old pioneers, and the brethren of the early days, were good
men and true, many of them ardent Masons who were always willing
and did go on foot· and out of their way to serve a worthy friend or
brother. .Masonry meant much to those brethren; in fact, it was a
good part of their lives, and worthy of imitation.

My next stop was at Cincinnati. The Grand Secretary, Brother
Bromwell, was at his home sick when called, and in fact was then
on his death-bed. He died shortly after I had gone. I visited a Lodge
there and saw the third degree conferred.
Washington, D. C., was visited next. Had a pleasant interview
with Brother Johnston, Grand Secretary, and also met Grand Master
Roberts and Past Grand Master Milans, and Brother Wo~fe, Grand
Lecturer. I saw the second degree conferred on 11 candH.lates-the
roup plan, and I am very frank to say that I was not greatly 1111pressed
:ith the degree. The Grand Lecturer kindly put Dll a Lodge of Instruction for my benefit while I was there.
Stopped at Baltimore and met the Grand Master, Brother Seipp.
Saw no work in ::Viaryland.
Arrived in Wilmington, Delaware, and met the Grand :Master,
Brother Cootch, and the Grand Secretary, Brother Robinson. Saw
the second degree conferred.
Philadelphia was the next place visited. Met the Grand Secretary,
Brother Perry, and the Grand Lecturer, Brother ~ oslyn. Witnessed
the conferring of the third degree. It was vastly different from anything I had seen.
Visited Trenton, N. J., where I met the Grand Secretary, Brother
Cherry. A very cordial reception at Jersey City, where the second
degree was conferred, was accorded me.
Arrived in New York City and called on the Grand ~ecretary,
Brother Kenworthy. Saw the third degree conferred on etght ca~­
didates. I also attended the Grand Lodge, which conveued while
I was there.
Hartford, Connecticut, was my next stop, where I met the Grand
Secretary, Brother Kies, but saw no work.
Arrived in Providence, Rhode Island, and saw the second degree
conferred by the group plan on five candidates. Met the Grand Sec-

At the last coinmnnication of the Grand Lodge, Grand :\faster
Sherman, in his message recommended that I he given a three months'
leave of absence for the purpose of visiting the Eastern jurisdictions,
and observing their rituals. This recommendation was concurred
in by Grand Lodge. I desire at this time to express my appreciation
and sincere thanks to Brother Sherman and the brethren of Grand
Lodge for their magnanimous recognition of my past services. J
assure you that I have been greatly benefited by the experiences
gained by these visits. I left San Francisco, accompanied by my good
wife, on April second. My first stop was at Salt Lake City, where
I met the Grand. Secretary, Brother Goodwin, and visited one of the
Lodges there that evening. Saw the third degree conferred, the work
being somewhat different in many respects. Also met the Grand
Lecturer, Brother Smith.
I next stopped at Denver, and had a very pleasant visit with the
Grand Secretary, Brother Cooper, who had been Grand Lecturer for
many years prior to his election as Grand Secretary. The Colorado
work is much like ours in the phrasing.
My next stop was at Topeka, Kansas, where I met Brother \Vilson,
Grand Secretary. Had a splendid visit with him and heard much of
the Grand Lodge working. Brother Wilson has the most complete
setting and system of any jurisdiction visited, and he is a very comteous gentleman. I saw the third degree conferred on several candidates that evening, with robes am! full form.
Kansas City was my next stop.
there.

Saw the second degree conferred

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

62

63

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

retary, Brother Williams. In Rhode Island the group plan does not
apply in the first degree. The limit in ·the first is five, and conferred
separately.
Boston was my next stop. Saw the first and second degrees conferred. Met the Grand Secretary, Brother IIamilton, and the Grand
Lecturer, Brother Smith.
Arrived in Portland, Maine, and met the Grand Secretary, Brother
Davis. None of the Lodges met while I was there.
Next stopped at Montreal, where I was greeted by the Grand
Secretary, Brother Williamson, and saw the first degree conferred.
Visited Buffalo and saw the third degree conferred by the group
plan. They use robes and 12 Fellow Crafts.
Arrived next in Detroit, where the third degree was conferred on
a large class, and I also saw the first degree conferred.
Visited the Lodge at Flint, Michigan, and saw the third degree
exemplified for the benefit of the Grand Lodge delegates.
Visited Cedar Rapids, Iowa, and called at the office of the Grand
Secretary, Brother Parvin, but he was at home sick. I did meet the
Master ·of one of the Lodges there, no Lodge being in session. The
work is somewhat similar to ours, but there is no limit to the number
of candidates in conferring degrees.
Stopped at Milwaukee, Wisconsin. No Lodges were meeting.
Called on the Grand Secretary, but failed to find him, he being out
of town.
Arrived in St. Paul and called on the Grand Secretary, but he had
gone to the Shrine meeting at Kansas City.
Passed through Vancouver and Victoria and on arrival in Seattle,
visited a Lodge there, where I saw the first degree. The wording of
the ritual is somewhat similar to our work.
Next visited Portland, Oregon, and attended their Grand Lodge,
which was in session; also saw the third degree conferred.
I had a most instructive and delightful trip, traveled about twelve
thousand miles and visited 26 jurisdictions, and met many splendid
Masons; also saw many varieties of work, but I can assure you,
Brethren, that I came back more deeply impressed with the simplicity
and beauty of our ritual than before I left, and I am thoroughly convinced that our ritual is hard to improve upon. We could, however,
if desired by the Brethren, adopt the form of closing by proclamation,
when going to examine candidates.
And also the shortening of the first and third degree lectures to
avoid repetitions, omitting portions of the Monitorial work. These

changes have been thoroughly considered by the Ritual Committee
and the changes will be presented by that committee for your approval.
All the jurisdictions visited desired me through their Grand Masters, to express to our Grand Master, and the brethren of the jurisdiction in general, their sincere fraternal greetings and best wishes
for the Grand Lodge of California.
I have visited all the districts of the State and held Lodges of
Instruction, both clay and night sessions, all being well attended by
the officers and brethren. The Lodges generally are in splendid condition in every way, peace and harmony prevailing throughout the
jurisdiction. I have accompanied the Most Worshipful Grand Master
on many of his visits. All tl10se meetings have been attended by large
gatherings, the Grand l\faster receiving a real Masonic welcome, and
his words of advice and instruction enthusiastically received by the
brethren. Reports have been received from all the Inspectors, each
giving an account of the condition of the Lodges under his supervision,
all of which have been most satisfactory. Of the new Lodges formed
this year, 21 in number, most of these arc in the southern part of the
state and several of them are composed almost entirely of brethren
fron: other states. It is gratifying that many of our sojourning
brethren are joining the new Lodges.
I would recommend that Section 56, "Duties of Inspectors," he
amended to read as follows: "And to report the working condition
of each Lodge in his district to the Grand Lecturer on or before the
first clay of May in each year." This will give both the Grand Master
and the Gram! Lecturer more time to look over the reports.
I desire to thank the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary for many
kindnesses extended to me in his office at all times.
Since last Grand Lodge death has callee! Brother Alvin F. E. Irwin,
Inspector of the 86th District, located at San Pedro. Brother Irwin
was a true and zealous Mason, and in his death the Grand Lodge has
lost a faithful officer, the community a good citizen, his family a
devoted husband, and his Lodge a very active memher.
In conclusion I am pleased to report that from my own ol1scrva1 ions, a.nrl the rcpo~ts of the Inspectors, the general condition of the
fraternity has manifestly improved during the year.
1\11 0 r wl1ich is respectfully suhmittecl.

Legal Aid Committee: This Committee, with John W. Kemp
as Chairman, has associated with it many of the leading lawyers,
members of the Los Angeles Bar, and have rendered legal service
to 248 cases which have been referred during the year covered by
this report.
Medical Aid Branch: This department has been operated throngh
the courtesy of several physicians belonging to the fratcrnitv and
many cases of illness have been cared for by these self-sacrificing
brethren.
General Remarks : It will be observed from the foregoing report, that the work of this Board of Relief is constantly increasing.
This is largely due to the great influx of brethren and their dependents from other jurisdictions, many of whom come here with the
expectation of obtaining employment immediately and with very
inadequate means of support in case they fail to obtain such
employment, or in case of illness. These brethren or their dependents must be cared for.
Invalids Coming to California: We desire to give a word of
warning to brethren contemplating coming to California in search
of health.
\Ve arc glad at all times to welcome brethren from other jurisdictions, BUT they should not attempt to come to California unless
they are amply provided for and unless they are sure of proper care;
ot.hcrwise it is mnch better for them to rt?main at home where they
will have the assistance of their friends and home surroundings.

San Francisco Board of Relief
While this report gives a complete resume of the financial transactions of the Board, it does not in any way report all the activities
in which we are engaged. It would be impossible to estimate the
amount of good it has accomplished outside of rendering monetary
assistance.
Our brethren of the medical profession are constantly serving in
a truly Masonic spirit, without any remuneration whatever. The entire
fraternity renders its thanks to Doctors: J. F. Cowan, Aaron S. Green,
Louis D. Green, Otto G. Freyermuth, James F. Pressley, William P.
Read, Jacob Schwarz, Alfred E. Meyers, Henry Silberman, Wilhelm
Wald eyer.
A great deal of legal work has been done for the Board free of
charge by Brothers: Charles Albert Adams, Arthnr Joel, Olin L. Berry,
to whom we are also greatly indebted.

85

In submitting a report of our activities for the past twelve months,
we do so with a feeling of pride and gratification in the results we have
accomplished.
The ligures do not mean much to the casual observer, but to those
who are in close touch with the employment situation, they are pregnant
with food for thought. The unemployment situation throughout the
U. S. during the past year has been critical, and thousands of men and
women troved West in the hope of better conditions. California, suffering at the time from a prolonged drought, and the usual results of a
Presidential Election, was overtaxed, and the man seeking employment
found here the same condition he had left behind. Skilled workers
were forced to take anything in the way of labor that happened along.
The large industrial plants in San Francisco have been operating on
two-thirds time basis, and the building trades have also found it difficult
to keep their full forces working, so in consequence, the Masonic Employment Bureau suffered and we found considerable trouble in placing
skilled help along these lines.
In the twelve months just passed, a total of 5,987 applications were
Ii led for positions, practically every recognized jurisdiction in the world
being represented, and only twenty per cent of the total were members
of California Lodges. At times the huge task confronting us seemed
hopeless, but the co-operation of the local Masters of Lodges in continually reminding their members of existing conditions, and the encouraging assistance rendered by local employers, were a continual
source of gratification to the few on whose shoulders the success of the
Employment Bureau depends.
In addition t~ securing employment for worthy Masons, our Bureau
also lists suitable living accommodations for the convenience of
strangers, and, further, we were fortunate during the ·year in securing
several boarding places for orphan children of Masons.
In all, we feel that the Masonic Employment Bureau has filled a
l<1ng-felt want, and there is no more practical application of brotherly
love ancl relief than the maintenance of these agencies by the Fraternity.
ln conclusion, in behalf of our great Fraternity, we wish to thank
all those who are responsible for our splendid showing, and may we
ask that this fraternal spirit will continue. When you are responsible
in seeming employment for a deserving M as011, yon trnly stretl'h forth
a helping hancl to raise a Brother.

Grand Lodge was called on at 2 :55 o'clock, the Grand

RELIEF AND EMPLOYMENT PROBLEMS
Past Grand ::Yfaster Sherman introduced the following:

w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, one of the principal activities of the fraternity is the
handling of relief and employment connected therewith; and
Whereas, this activity has grown to large proportions, and is bonnd
to increase and multiply; and
Whereas, the various Boards of Relief are conducted with-0ut any
specific rnles or regulations of this Grand Lodge, but depending upon
the Grand Lodge for their support; therefore, be it
Resolved, that the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee
of three to investigate this relief and employment matter, and report
at the next communication of this Grand Lodge their findings and
recommendations thereon.

To the M.« W.'. Grand LodKe of California:

PER DIEM FOR REPRESENTATIVES
Brother Gracey of Nevada Lodge No. 13 presented resolutions to amend Sections 6 and 70 of the Constitution, as
follows:
Sec. 6.-By inserting· after the words "meeting of the Grand Lodge
and back again" the following words: "and six dollars per diem during the duration of the Grand Lodge," and to eliminate the following
words: "viz. and unlimited first-class railroad fare, together with
cost of berth and sleeper when required." (The intention of this proposed amendment is tv give each representative the actual cost of his
railroad ticket, together with a per diem of six dollars.)
Sec. 70.-All Grand Lodge officers, except the Grand Master, all
Past Grand Masters, Chairmen of Standing ·Conimittees and members
of the Jurisprudence, Grievance, Policy and Purposes, Finance, Charters and By-laws, Pay of .l\fombers and Credentials Committees. shall
receive payment equal to the regular round trip ticket and $6.00 per
diem for every day of the duration of the Grand Lodge; but no Grand
officer, Past Grand officer, or member of Standing Committee shall
receive such payment in more than one of those capacities, nor shall
he receive it unless he shall be in attendance at such Communication
from the first to the last day thereof, inclusive, unless excused by the
Grand Lodge. The members of Standing Committees may receive the
above per diem for such number of days previous to and after the
closing of the Annual Communication as the Grand ;\faster may approve.

Brother D. S. \:V agstaff, Chairman of the Committee on

To the M.". IV.'. Grand I~odi;e of Califor11ia:

As Chairman of your Committee on Library, I have to rrport that
as no regular provision has been deemed necessary or advisable in
the past, looking to the establishment of a Grand Lodge library of
~ufficient diversity and size to take care of possible borrowers and
readers among the several Lodges of the State, 1 am unahlc to report
in detail anything of particular interest at this writing. \Ve now have
about six hundred volumes on our sh cl vcs, ranging from a littk light
Literature to quite a numher of the most vahtahle hooks owned hy any
organization. We have hut one volume each of this number. To
augment and therefore convert this fine nucleus into a workini.: force,

ordinarily involving the expenditure of considerable rnonev and a constant Stlpervision, I have a plan to propose which will pla~e the library
organization in a position to render efficient aid in research work and
provide educational advantages not heretofore enjoyed. This can be
accomplished at a minimum ·of expense, and allow us to use many
of the books we now have, to fill in here and there, which would
not be possible without having to restock our shelves at enormous

Brother Jesse M. \Vhited presented the following·
To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:

Whereas, at the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge of California, held in San Francisco in October, 1922, a resolution was
adopted that members of the Fraternity lend their moral and personal
support to Chapters of the Order of De Molay now established, or
that might hereafter be established, and
Whereas, under said resolution twenty-four Lodges have "sponsored" Chapters of the Order of De Molay, which said "sponsoring"
consists of appointing a committee of nine or more Master Masons
to act as an Advisory Council for a Chapter making application fur
Letters Temporary for a Chapter to the Grand Council of the Order
of De Molay, and thereafter lending their moral and personal support
to the Chapter so established. Now, therefore, be it
Resolved, that the sponsoring of such Chapters already established
or that may hereafter be requested shall be deemed to be within the
terms of the said resolution of 1922, and the legislative powers of a
Lodge as set forth in Section 77 of the Constitution of the Grand
Lodge of California.

Referred to the Committee on General Policy and
Purposes.
Brothers Henry B. Phillips and John McEwing presented the following:
Whereas, it is today recognized that our most important civic duty
in perpetuating the blessings of our government, is the spiritual, moral,
mental and physical development of the youth of our country, they
who are to be the future parents of our people, and
Whereas, we believe that young girls and boys between the ages of
14 and 21 years specially require support and direction along such
desirable lines, and
Whereas, any instrument or organization that devotes itself solely
to such purposes ought to be encouraged, and
Whereas, the Order of De Molay for hoys is now firmly estahlished under the direction of Master l\fasons, and
Whereas, it is the deliberate judgment of this hody that the Order
of De Molay is a distinct aid to the cause of Education, of Morality,
of Patriotism and Good Citizenship, and will be of real service in the
communities of this State; therefore be it

Resolved, that this grand body lend its approval and moral support
to this organization so long as it remains under the direction of Master Masons.

Brothers Henry B. Phillips and John McEwing introduced the following:
Whereas, it is today recognized that our most important civic duty

REPORT OF TRUSTEES, MASONIC HOMES
To the J1. W. Grand Lodge of California:

\Ve submit herewith our annual report for the year 1923-24,
together with reports from the Secretary and the Superintendents
of the two homes, and the itemized statement of receipts and expenditures.
As required by the Constitution, the Board, immediately after
the close of Grand Lodge in October, 1923, organized hy the clectio11
of officers. Brother James H. Gist, whose term had expired, was

102

l' H:OGH:h:DINGS OF' 'J'Hh:

reappointed by the Grand Master, and Brother George L. Jones,
the newly-elected Junior Grand Warden, appeared and was seated
as a member ex ofllcio. Brothers Charles M. Wollenberg and
Jam es B. Gist were elected President and Vice President respectively.

Finances
The financial affairs of the homes are in excellent condition,
notwithstanding the necessity of having to borrow heavily to complete the building program. The income in the next year will be
sufficient to properly cover regular maintenance changes and will
also probably pay the amounts borrowed and leave some surplus for
additional improvements which arc urgently needed.
It may be well at this point to review briefly the sources of
income for the homes in order that the members of Grand Lodge
may be advised how little the individual Mason contributes to the
support of the two institutions:
The major source of income is derived from the twenty-dollar
contribution required by the Constitution to be paid by petitioner~
for the degrees and by applicants for affiliation from outside jurisdictions. The gross sum paid from this source in the last twelve
months amounted to $185,180. The Constitution provides a per
capita tax on the membership of SO cents for the benefit of the
building fund, and 25 cents for the maintenance account, a total
tax on the Lodges of 75 cents a year per member. Our membership is now more than one hundred thousand, and this tax thus
produces now in excess of $75,000 a year. The members of the
Lodges contribute nothing toward the support of the homes except
as it may be indirectly so considered by coming from the Lodge
treasuries. It is true that a few brethren do annually contribute
directly, but the membership generally do not appear to be imbued
with the pleasure which would accrue to them by regular yearly
gifts of money. The cost of food, clothing, medical attention,
schooling, nurses, superintendence, and the innumerable items which
go to make up the aggregate cost of caring for more than three
hundred wards of the fraternity in California is about $130,000 a year,
and the rapid growth of the membership in the jurisdiction admonishes your Board that further provision must be made for additional cost for maintenance and for the housing of the applicants
whose numbers are rapidly increasing. The demands upon the
homes appear to be growing in about the same ratio as the increase
in membership of the Lodges.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

103

Building Program
We are pleased to be able to report the completion of the
buildings at the Decato Home, and of two additional dormitory
buildings at the home for children at Covina.
At the Decato Home we have caused to be erected a building
for men containing one hundred rooms, a building for women containing fifty rooms, two wings to the hospital providing fifty additional beds, and a domestic building containing a spacious dining
room and modern kitchen on the main floor, with an auditorium
having a seating capacity of three hundred on the second floor.
The assembly room has been equipped with folding-seat chairs, a
stage for use of the family when concerts and other diversions are
presented, a concert grand Knabe piano and a complete moving
picture outfit-the two latter being the gift of the members of all
the Lodges in San Francisco.
In the basement of the domestic building are an ice plant, sewing
room, drug store, and rooms for storage of supplies.
All the buildings arc connected by inclosed corridors, and the
residents are not required to go out of doors when going to and
from meals or attending functions in the auditorium.
The total expenditures at the Decato Home for the new structures and their equipment to September 3, 1924, have been $729,391.18.
At the Covina Home, after careful study of the growing wants
of that institution, your trustees have caused to be erected two new
buildings of the same general exterior design as the original group,
but with many changes in their interior arrangements. These
buildings, having a capacity for caring for forty-live bovs and a
like number of girls, comprise fifteen bedrooms in each ho.use, with
three beds to the room. They are equipped with necessary lavatories of the most complete and sanitary construction. Jn addition, there is provided in each of the buildings adequate quarters
for the house mother, living room, library, study room, music room,
isolation ward, sewing and linen rooms.
These all have been
designed for their special uses and will not only acid to the efficiency
of the management, but as well to the happiness and wellbeing of
the children.
Further improvements should he made at hoth homes, and it is
the purpose of your Board to provide them as rapidly as funds
will justify. Those who have visited the home at Decato know the
unsatisfactory condition of the roads lcacling to and immccliatcly
around the buildings, they being too narrow and having sharp
right-angle turns. A study is now being made of the driveway

104

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

from the main entrance to the administration building, and new
and better roadways may be made possible during the coming year.
In the early months of the year, the State Board of Health
served notice on the Trustees that our sewage was a menace to the
health of people who occupied lands adjoining on the west ana
south. Believing that we have an obligation to the neighbors
which should not be neglected, the Board employed Professor J.
Gilman Hyde, in charge of the division of sanitary engineering of
the University of California, to study this problem, and as soon as
his report is received his recommendations will be carried out.
The farm buildings, now twenty-five years old and in poor con.
dition, should be replaced at an early day by sanitary structures.
The construction work which has been going on for nearly
three years at Decoto has necessitated a new layout of roads around
the buildings and the destruction of some oi the garden and flower
plots, and inasmuch as the home will be visited by a larger number
of members of the Lodges each year, we believe it should not only
be a comfortable home, but a place of beauty. It is therefore our
intention to have the grounds immediately adjacent to the building~
surveyed and laid out by a competent landscape gardener. After
this initial work shall have been done, the employes and residents
of the home can care for this embellishment.
The children at the Covina Home-now numbering one hundred and thirty-admonish the Board that in the very near future
it w.ill be necessary to enlarge the dining room and kitchen. The
net additions in the number of children in the last four years has
been forty.

Hospital at the Covina Home
At the last annual conclave of the Grand Commandery of
Knights Templar of California, Grand Commander Albert E. Boynton recommended that that body donate the sum of ten thousand
dollars as a nucleus to a hospital fund for the benefit of the children. The members of that body generously and promptly adopted
the recommendation by an appropriation in the amount suggested.
An epidemic of mumps during the past year, and three cases of
appendicitis at one time had very pointedly suggested to the Trus·
tees the necessity of providing a hospital building at the Covina
Home. The present administration building contains two small hos·
pita! wards, but they are located immediately above the assembly hall
where the children gather frequently for their social affairs and
their Sunday services. The unavoidable noises in the lower hall
tends to ret~rd quick recoveries of children isolated in these hospi·
ta! wards. The gift of the Knights Templar was therefore accepted
with much satisfaction, and your Trustees are now working out
plans for a building that will meet the requirements ·of the home
for isolation and hospital uses.
Water Supply at Covina
The unusual deficiency of rainfall this year, amottnting virtually
to a drouth, rendered it necessary to provide additional facilities
for water to care for the orchard at the Covina Home. The Board
was fortunate in having the friendly interest of Mr. \Villiam Bowring, manager of the Irwin-Downey Corporation Rancho, and
through him the home purchased twenty shares of stock of the
La Verne Mutual \Vater Company. By courtesy of Mr. John H.
Lascelles, chairman of the advisory board of the Irwin-Downev
Corporation, who resides at Buffalo, New York, the home wa.s
granted the free use of a pipe line through the property of the
rancho. The orchard is now assured of a plentiful supply of water
for irrigation purposes. The Trustees desire to here publicly thank
Mr. Lascelles and Mr. Bowring (as they have already done pri·
vately) for their kindly interest in the home in the respect men·
tioned.

Scholarships
The Trustees are quite concerned in the education of .those of
our children who are mentally worthy of schooling beyond the
curriculum of the high school, and the funds for such schooling
can only come from donations of friends of the homes. So far,
funds have been forthcoming in amounts sufficient to cover the
expenses of the children who have been sent to vocational schools
and the universities, but if the requirements should increase, as
they undoubtedly will, more money would be needed in the very
near future. In the last year the Board has received donations to
the amount of $1800, the detail of which appears below. One girl
finished a course in practical office work this year, and she is now
gainfully employed. One boy is attending the dental department
of the University of Southern California, and is making splendid
progress in his studies. One boy will matriculate in the department
of architecture at the University this fall. One boy is taking a special
course in automobile mechanics at Los Angeles.
One ambitious girl is attending the southern branch of the
University of California, preparing to be a teacher of English and
dramatics, with a hope also of becoming a writer. All these students bid fair to become real ornaments to society, and their success will be due to the thoughtful generosity of the men and
women and Masonic bodies who 11ave been contributing to the
scholarsbip account.
One thoughtful and appreciated gift was liy Brother A. Gaylord Beaman, on behalf of the Masonic Digest of Los Angeles, who
tendered to the Trustees seven scholarships in the Mackay Business
College. These scholarships were donated primarily for the benefit
of boys and girls from the home, with the understanding that they
might also he available to other worthy children upon the recommendation of the Board of Trustees.

devolved the entire charge of the grounds as well as the farm, amt
in fact from all the employes of the home. Indeed we believe the
Fraternity should count itself fortunate in having been able to secure the type of men and women who are assisting in carrying out
the great work in which we are engaged.
In closing this report, your Trustees would impress upon you
that part of tomorrow has been set apart for your visit to the home
for children at Covina. \Ve hope you will all take advantage of the
opportunity. \Ve want you to inspect this property, which is ·your
property, in which you have a moral liability, so that you may have
a personal knowledge of what your agents are trying to do for you
and in your name, that you may realize in greater measure the constructive good your money is accomplishing, and there see with
your own eyes the living stones you are helping to shape for the
foundation of our citizenship.
We recommend that the per capita tax for the ensuing fiscal
year be fixed at twenty-five cents.
CHAS. M. WOLLENBERG,
President
JAMES B. GIST,
Vice President
SAMUEL E. BURKE.
CHAS. ALBERT ADA.MS,
DA VTD J. REESE,
ALBERT E. BOYNTON,
GEORGE L. JONES,
Trustees.

Report of Superintendent, Decato Home
To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California:
I herewith present for your consideration my fifteenth annual report
as Superintendent of the Masonic Horne at Decoto California for the
year ending September 15, 1924.
' .
'
The past year has been one of great interest in the history of the
Decoto Horne. The additional room now provided by the completion of
the new buildings has made it possible to care for all who have heretofore been _on the ';~iting Ii.st, and the increased comforts afforded by the
new hospital additions, kitchen, pantry and dining rooms men's club
room, ladies' social room and Assembly Hall have enabled 'the management to render a higher standard of service in meeting the needs of the
members of our large family.
!here are now at the Home, 187 residents, 106 men and 81 women.
Durmg the year there have been admitted 33 men and 18 women.
. The general health of the Horne has been normal with the except10n of those who are infirm and feeble, owing to advancing years. Our
enlarged hospital department, is now thoroughly equipped with all
sanitary appliances, enabling our physician and nurses to give to those
who are ill every care and attention. Day and night nurses are in constant attendance. There are at the present time 38 members of the
Home being cared for in the hospital.
A number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare of the
Horne by their labors in the carpenter and paint shops the care of the
garage, mail, passenger and express seryice, kitchen, ;antry, vegetable
room, laundry, chores, care of flower beds and lawns and light work in
a general way.
.
The. ladies of the Home attend to the making, marking and rnendmg of lmen, sheets, table cloths, pillow slips, etc. They also assist in
pre?aring fruit, work in the pantry and dining rooms and take care of
their rooms, halls, etc., and general light household duties.
At this season of the year, when the natural supply of water is
lowest, there seems to be no decrease in the service given by the deep
well pump. Our reservoirs are full at all times and equal to any demand
made upon them. The two large reservoirs, with a capacity of 650,000
~allons, have been cleaned out, the walls put in repair and new valves
mstalled to regulate the flow of water to the buildings fire hydrants
and for irrigation purposes.
'
·
.
. The greater part of the hill ranch has, as heretofore, been leased
e1t~er on shares or for cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of
frmt for table use, the surplus being dried and stored for future use.
The hay crop has been light owing to the dry season. The garden has

furnished vegetables for table use and plenty of greens. The chicken
ranch has supplied all eggs for table use, and all over and above our
needs has been sold in the San Francisco market. The orchard planted
several years ago is doing well.
The generous gift of the Grand Chapter, Order of the Eastern
Star, has provided a completely furnished social room in the new
Women's building and also a completely furnished club room in the
new Men's building. The class of furnishings placed in these rooms
are of pleasing design, selected for practical use. These rooms are for
the use of the members of our family where they may spend their
leisure hours in comfort. An itemized list of the furniture installed is
given under the head "Donations."
The combination billiard and pool table, a gift of the members of
Starr King Lodge No. 344 has been placed in the new men's club room.
The steady growth of the library continues, there being at this time
4,000 volumes on the shelves. Plans are now being made to open branch
libraries in the hospital department, and in the club, social and reading
rooms. In addition to this we are the recipients, through members of
the fraternity, of daily papers, magazines and periodicals.
Our new Assembly Hall has been fitted up with a completely
equipped stage with red, white and green lighting effects. The stage is
hung with draperies and the hall furnished with comfortable folding
chairs. The hall proper will seat 500 persons. Visiting Lodges and
friends are now enabled to present plays and literary and musical programs from time to time for the amusement and entertainment of the
members of the Home.
The San Francisco Lodges, through the Masters and Wardens
Association, have furnished the Hall with a Simplex Moving Picture
Machine, a spot light and a stereopticon. These have been installed in
a well-appointed projection room. A large silver moving picture screen
has been lmilt on the rear wall of the stage. A Knabe concert grand
piano has been placed on the floor of Assembly Hall. With the furnishings mentioned ahove, we are now enabled to give moving picture and
stereopticon exhihitions and to arrange evenings of entertainment
through committees made up of members of the Home.
The Thursday evening social, games and dances, also our Friday
evening song practice, have been regularly held. The usual services
are held on Sunday afternoon, after which a few musical numhers are
given hy the Home orchestra. All of these gatherings are well attended.
ArrangenH·nts have been rna<lc wherchy the rnernhers of the family,
a few at a tirn<', can visit Alarne<la Lorlgc No. 167, F. & A. M. and

A large delegation of members of the Grand Lodge arrived at the
Home, October 11th, 1923, and inspected the building operations, and
on May 30th the formal opening exercises were held in the new assembly
hall to commemorate the completion of the new buildings. The exercises were attended by the officers of the Grand Lodge, The Board of
Trustees and many members of the fraternity from Lodges throughout
the jurisdiction.
Many entertainments have been given for the pleasure and benefit
of the family by I.edges, members of Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters
and friends, and also at times by members of the Home. Following is
a list of the events which have contributed to our happiness:
September 27th. Members of the Guild to the Ladies Auxiliary,
California Commandery No. I, K. T., visited the Home in the afternoon,
October 7th. 45 members of the choir of the First Methodist
Episcopal church of Oakland, accompanied by the Rev. James Stephens,
attended our Sunday services.
October 10th. Members of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M., arrived
in the afternoon. After a tour of inspection of the Home they visited
points of interest in and around Santa Clara valley.
November Sth.
Sunday services.

December 22nd. 40 members of the Scottish Rite choir of San
Jose entertained the family with a program of Christmas carols and
brought a good donation of fruit, candy and cakes.
December 23rd. Washington Township Community Chorus visited
the Home and gave a program of Christmas music. A good time was
enjoyed by all.
February 22nd. California Chapter, Order of DeMolay, of San
Francisco, paid a visit to the .Home and conferred the initiatory degree
in the Temple, after which an exhibition of fencing, followed by a band
concert, took place on the grounds of the Home.
March 8th. Amity Lodge No. 370 visited the Home and entertained the family with a minstrel show. A very pleasing program.
April 12th. Choir of St. Stephens .tvI. E. Church gave a song
recital at our Sunday services.
May 20th. Members of the Ladies Auxiliary of Berkeley Commandery No. 42, K. T., visited the Horne and spent a pleasant afternoon
with us.

May 20th. Plymouth Lodge No. 560 conferred a third degree in

May 22nd. Thirty memhers of the Home family attended the
Chautauqua at Centerville daily until its close on May 26.
May 29th. Annual visit of Jewel Lodge No. 374 to the Home.
Band concert on the grounds. A very enjoyable afternoon.
May 30th. Formal opening exercises to commemorate the completion of the new building. Officers of the Grand Lodge, Board of
Trustees and many members of the fraternity were present.
June 21st. Fruitvale Lodge No. 336, accompanied by their ladies,

June 29th. Speranza ltaliana Lodge No. 219 visited the Home and

July 13th. Mt. Oso Lodge No. 46o visited the Home.
July 19th. Golden Gate Chapter No. 303, 0. E. S., entertained the
members of the Home with a program of songs and recitations.
July 26th. Brooklyn Lodge No. 225 visited the Home, bringing a
picnic lunch. In the evening a very entertaining program was given
in the Assembly Hall.
August 9th. The members of Apollo Lodge No. 396 visited the
Home and entertained the family with a pleasing program of music
and songs.
August 22nd. University Chapter, Order of DeMolay, conferred
the initiatory and Order of DeMolay degrees, which were greatly appreciated by the brethren of the Home.
August 23rd. King Solomons Lodge No. 260 conferred a second
degree in the Temple, after which a social time was held in the Assembly
Hall. An informal program was given.
August 26th. Standard Lodge :'\ o. 440 con fer red a second degree
in the Temple. Ice cream and cake were served to all the members
of the Home.
September Sth. East Bay Matrons Association made their annual
visit. Dinner at the Horne. An intere,ting program in the Assembly
Hall in the afternoon.
Septemher 5th. The official visit of Grand Matron Maude Bigelow
Sihlev and Grand Patron Guy W. Brnndagc and officers of the Grand
Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star, took place in the
Assembly Hall, where they were received hy the officers and members
of Orient Chapter No. 177, Hayward Chapter No. 331 and Golden Wave

Chapter No. 103 of San Leandro. The ritualistic work by the officers
of the several Chapters and the talks given by the Grand officers were
greatly enjoyed by the Eastern Star members of the Home.
September 16th. Alameda Lodge No. 167, accompanied by their
ladies, visited the Horne. A second degree was conferred in the Temple,
after which all gathered in the Assembly Hall, where an interesting
program was given and light refreshments served.
All the holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises.
The specials were those which were held on New Years Day, Lincoln's
Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Easter, Memorial Day, Fourth of
July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.
Most Worshipful Grand Master Arthur S. Crites and other office.rs
of the Grand Lodge have made a number of visits to the Home and
many brethren of California Lodges and other jurisdictions have spent
pleasant hours with us.
All these gatherings together with the comforts afforded by our
splendidly-equipped Assembly and social halls, billiard rooms, music
and reading rooms, are factors in creating an atmosphere of peace and
contentment in all the departments of the Home.
I wish to extend my appreciation of the loyal services rendered by
the officers and employes throughout the year, and to express to the
Board of Trustees my sincere gratitude for the friendly advice and
support they have at all times given me.
Fraternally submitted,
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

Report of Superintendent, Covina Horne

At the Charter Oak grammar school, seven were graduated from
the eighth grade this year. The girls made all their own dresses worn
at commei1cement exercises, and they were as chic looking as any.
Sunday school services are as usual regularly held in the assembly
room. conducted by the cider children, and somewhat on the lines of a
Christian Endeavor meeting. These services are intensely interesting
to our visitors, and the children take a proper and intelligent interest
in them. They provide special music for each Sunday session, and
frequently deliver prayers that would do credit to older minds. I take
the liberty of quoting one such, prepared and delivered by a sixteenycar-old girl of the Home, who was the class leader for the day. I am
sure the members of our Lodges will appreciate it:
"Our Heavenly Father, we come into Thy presence at this time,
thanking Thee for this opportunity to study Thy word. \Ve thank Thee
for the blessings we enjoy each day,-the blessings of health, the comforts of life, and all of the privileges and opportunities that come to us
daily. We ask that Thou wilt help us in our daily lives to follow the
example of all that is g;ood, and show onr gratitude to Thee by making
the most of the advantages which have hccn given to us. Help us to
prepare oursel vcs to lie of service and a benefit to others. Let Thy
blessing rest on those who have made this Home possible. Help us to
keep true to ourselves' throughout this tlay and throughout our lives.
Amen."
Tn hccoming humility we commend this prayer to the Masonic
fraternity of California.
The piano pupils show special interest in their work, and marked
imprO\·emcnt is noted.
A number of good Ji.,oks have hcen addc(l to the libraries. A central library for special reference hooks and magazines would he most
welcome as a needed addition to the equipment of the Home.
The Hoy Scouts of the 1lome, nrnlcr the direction of Scout Master

To the Trustees of the Masonic llomcs:
The resignation of Leland S. Drew as superintendent became
effective January 1, 1924, aml you displayed a confidence in my ability
to conduct the Home by placing me in charge. I hope that confidence
has not Leen lessened and that my stewardship has proved as satisfactory to you as the work and responsibility have been pleasant to me.
No particular change has been made in the conduct of the Home,
except such changes as were made imperative by the large number of
children occujlying the quarters originally intended for half the mtmhcr. \Ve now have one hundred and thirty children in our care, and
as soon as the two new buildings are furnished, life at this Home will
speedily become normal.
The health of the children has generally been good, notwithstanding
an epidemic of mumps. No complications resulted, and the disease was
generally mild in form. The Home, as for many years past, has had
the services of Drs. \V. P. and Shaen Magan and H. C. Barron, of
Covina, at all needed times, and by their care and skill we have felt
secure against serious illness. A trained nurse is part of our fixed
staff; and in the hospital ward a radio set was placed through the
generous gift of tl1e J\fasonic Digest through its editor, A. Gaylord
Beaman. Tl1is set was the means of providing pleasing diversion for
our sick children, and really contributed much toward their quick recoveries.
The Home is indebtetl to Dr. Ralph Russell, a most skillful dentist
who is loved hy all the children, and who has been assisted in the work
of caring for their teeth hy the following able dentists: Drs. Leo Baughman, A. E. Sanders, C. M. Ileebe, Wm. K. Chambers, Maurice Smith,
A. R. Martin. David E. Jacohs, M. G. Samuels,
Van Buskirk, H. M.
Ilarnhart, Rollie E. Olsrn, J. I. Soister, all whom have donated their
services without fee, and to whom we puhlicly acknowledge a debt of
gratitude.
Dr. George E. Kress, a skillet! specialist in diseases of the eye,
nose <end throat, has taken, great interest in the children, and his services
were all rendered without any pay other than the thanks of the Home.
Reports from the schools indicate that our children have not been
idle and that they arc showing a proper interest in their school work.
Twenty-eight of the children atteml the high school at Covina, and
one of them, a girl, has been an honor student there for two years.
One. a boy, was graduated last June, and will enter University this fall,
thanks to the donors of the Scholarship fund.

have been made for the comfort of camp fife. Five lots across the
canal from the main camp were recently acquired by the Trustees,
including one small cottage; but with our growing family, more ground
is needed.
The life at Camp Tucker is not an idle one. It is true the children
play and romp in the sand, and swim in the canal, but they are taught
as well in some of the very practical things not always known to grownups. This summer the Life Guard at Balboa gave instruction to the
cbiklren on how to handle one who is made helpless in the water and
in danger of drowning. He organized two classes, one called Senior
and one called Junior class. The Juniors are those who are from 12
to 17 years of age, and the Seniors those who were over 17. The
Jenior class is given eleven tests and the Seniors are required to pass
twenty-five tests before they are rewarded by an emblem and pin. Here
are some of the tests : 1, undressing under water; 2, release of stranglehold : 3, cross-chest carrying; 4, head carry; 5, chin carry; 6, swim one
lrnrnlrecl yards; 7, recover a ten-ponnd weight at a fourteen-foot depth
fro:n a surface dive; 8, Shaffers method of respiration; 9, fireman's
'carry; 10, hair of head carry.
Ilrother l\fark Levy, of University Lodge No. 394, made the
children a present of a life boat. Many other donations were received
as will be noted below.
'
The health of the camp was good throt1ghout the season, and the
children returned brown and with appetites as keen as the proverbial
boy. ready for school again.

It may he of interest to the T ms tees and others to know that the
~avings accounts of the children, now in hank, aggregate over three

thousand dollars.

Report of Dentist, Covina Home
\
I was appointed by th~ Trustees on May 1, 1924, as chief of the
dental staff, that is serving 'the children of the Covina Home.
The following Saturday, \with the assistance of Mrs. S. Burgess,
nurse at the Home and my office assistant, we were able to examine
and record the condition of the teeth and surrounding tissues of 108
children. The remaining 19 were ill or absent, but were examined at
a later date.
Through the wonderful cooperation of the Covina staff and wi1ling
dentists, all necessary work was completed in the short time remaining
before vacation, July 9, 1924.
After a thorough prophylaxis in all cases where restorations were
needed, and where any stains or deposits were present, the following
service was rendered: Amalgams, 171 ; copper cements, 2; pulp capping, 6; cast gold base restorations, 2; gold inlays, 1 ; gold fillings, 2;
extractions, 64, principally decidttotts teeth.
To accomplish this work the dentist has a drive of twenty-four
miles from Los Angeles to the Covina Home, through congested
streets for several miles, then on a beautiful highway still congested,
hut with all the battle of traffic going and returning, I have yet to
hear of one assistant who would give his opportunity of serving the
children to some other dentist, and in all emergencies will postpone
office appointments to serve the children.
The dental office at the Horne is equipped with the latest improved appliances, and sanitation and sterilization are the best.
Tndividual reports from the dentists show that the behavior of
the children is far superior to that of the office child patient. They
manifest no fear of the dentist or office, are courteous, thoughtful
and patient, reflecting the wonderful supervision of :Vfrs. Maude E.
1\1 ill er and her a hie assistants.
The l10nse mothers teach the right method for using the toothhrnsh, also the care it must he given to maintain a clean brush that
will give the proper service, and due to this fact, we have found
many 111011! hs with perfect teeth and healthy surrounding tissues.
Now the children are hack from their vacations and the care
u f their teeth will continue.
Fraternally submitted,
RALPH vVANn Rnssl\T.T..

To the Board of Trustees, lv!asonic Hon~es California:
Orange and Lc11wn Grmic: The ora1 e and lemon trees of the
Home grove are in an excellent condition They are healthy, vigorous
and clean trees, showing a good color, are sending out a mass of
new growth and are setting 011 a very promising new crop for the
next season. The June drop in the grove has been very light-with
the acquisition of the extra twenty shares of water stock from the
La Verne Mutual Water Company ample water supply for irrigating purposes is assured.

So far no fertilizer had to he hought for the grove. The cow,
horse and chicken manure 11rorlueed at the farm has been sufficient
to fertilize the orange and lemon trees and will be amply sufficient
until the trees become a year or so older.
This season has been the first time that the orange trees have
produced more than was needed for Horne consumption.
The children of the Home have had all the oranges which they
could eat. During the last two to three months on an average of
250 oranges have been picked daily for rlistribution among the children.
Besides this Home consumption we have been able to sell to
the Charter Oak Packing House 155 field hoxes of Valencias. \Ve
expect to get a fair price, as our fruit was clean and of good size.
As to lemons, the trees have yielded heavily and we have had
several good pickings, but the market has heen very poor and the
returns from the crop have been rather discouraging.

Dain•: The Home llairy is now on a paying basis, and I wish
to give you some figures to suhstantiate this statement:
\Ve now have seven prot!ucing milch cows and three as yet 11011producing heifers-ten l1ead in all. The cost of maintenance and
caring for these ten head per month~in other words, the cost of

Vegetable Gardrn: The vegetahle garden has been greatly increased in area this year, and is in excellent condition. \Ve are producing not only all of the vegetables needed at the Home, but during
the summer months we are selling on an average of from $20 to $30
worth of vegetables on the outside. Our outside vegetable sales for
the month of June amounted to $28.70, for instance.
Poultrv: \Ve have now in the chicken yards 120 laying hens,
which we .raised last year from day-old chicks, and they have developed into very
layers. On the 24th of May another 300 day-old
chicks were added. I am glad to say that I have hcen very successful
with these also, having lost only 17 out of the lot of 300 chicks. The
little birds, now seven weeks old, are coming along fine, and I expect
to get about 150 layers out of the lot by fall. The remainder will
be cockerels that will be used on the table of the Home.
The 120 year-old layers now in the yards, and the 150 new layers
expected out of the new lot, should give us by next winter 270
laying hens.
I would suggest that we add 100 more layers to that, so that by
next winter we would have about 370 laying hens. That should be
sufficient to supply the Home with eggs and do away with the outside huying of eggs. lt is just as economical-in fact more so-to
feed and take care of 370 layers than it is of 150.
Rabbits: The rabbits arc doing well and are producing good.
Hogs: From the offal from the tables arnl kitchen of the Horne
we arc feeding on an average of from four to six hogs. The hogs
are bought at 50 to 60 pounds weight, and within two and a half
months are ready for the market.
Ilorscs: The two oh! stand-by horses of the farm are holding
their own am! are well deserving of their keeping.

Farm Buildings: During the last few yeaij the buildings of the
Ilomc farm have been greatly improved. <;Ow barns, horse barns,
hay mows, storage sheds and storage roo s, tool sheds and tool
houses, cow sheds, calf sheds, hog pens, c cken and brooder houses,
rabbit hutches, corrals, pasture fields a
fences, have been either
enlarged, extended or newly erected, up ii now they are forming an
efficient and complete unit, which, as/it stands today, should, with
the exception of some minor adjusiinents and repairs, answer the
needs of the Home farm for many years to come.
Roads: The roads leading into and about the farm are in excellent condition. During last
these roads have been raised,
graded, oiled and graveled, with the result that they are now free
from dust during the summer-a very desirable feature, and easily
accessible during the winter months.
Wal nut Trees: The seventeen walnut trees and five hazelnut
bushes, which have been ·planted in the filled ground of the southeast corner of the farm, are. branching out nicely and it will only be
a few years before these trees will form a fine background, as well
as become an ample source of supply of walnuts for the children
of the Fl ome.
Tractor: The tractor has proven a great asset in the working
of the ranch, and is in excellent working condition. This is the
second season that the tractor has been in use, and aside from having
had the valves ground it has not occasioned any repair work. It is
a good tractor.

Family Orchard: The family orchard of 170 deciduous fruit
trees, i. e., apricots, peaches, plums, apples, mulberries, figs and persimmons, which were planted three years ago on the side hill of the
lower farm, is doing very well, being not under irrigation. The
trees have been loaded with fruit, only the boys could not abide
their time to let the fruit get ripe, but have cleaned up a good portion
of the fruit before it was hardly half grown. But then, when you
and I were kids we were up to the same tricks.
Gentlemen, in closing this report, I wish to say that with the
Foot and Mouth Disease going through the country, and the threatening shortage of water and power, this has been a rather trying
year. But so far we have pulled through on the farm all right, and
I have no doubt that we shall come through the remainder of the
season in good shape.
Every effort will be made to keep the farm in tip-top shape, and
worthy of \he splendid institution of which it is a part.
Respectfully submitted,

M. G.

CRADLER.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
Drother ~Tax A. Plumb, Executive Secret;iry of the Committee on l\Iasonic Education, presented the following
report:
To the NJ.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:

The present Committee on l\Taso11ic Eclucation is the first to have
been granted an appropriation which permitted the employment of
an Executive Secretary, as well as the use of a lmdget for expenses.
l ts report, therefore, should be of interest to the members of the Craft.
Due to the difficulty of obtaining the services of a competent Secretary, there was some delay in organization aml it was not until
the middle of December of 1923 that definite work could be commencecl.
The Chairman and Secretary drafted a list of matters for consideration of the Committee and on January 19, 1924, tl1e Committee met
in conference with the Grand Master to discuss plans and policy, not
only for the year ensuing, but for the future.
Consideration of the problem of Masonic Education led the Committee to reali7-e that it was confronted with some very important and
difficult problems. The Committees that had l1een working <luring
the previous years had 1Jeen pursuing some plans which the present
Committee felt it could not afford to abandon, yet at the same time it
was realized that a great deal should be done toward stnclying the
work in other jurisdictions .and attempting to discover the ncecls of
our own jurisdiction.
The Committee was unanimous in agreeing tbat the work of
Masonic education could not lie carric(\ on unless it bad the interest,
support and co-operation of the constituent Lmlges. \N c found that
none of the plans adopted by the Grand Lodge had met with uniform
acceptance by the subordinate Lodges, and that neither the Grand Lodge
nor the previous Committees had any definite knowledge of what the
Lodges had been doing. It therefore became necessary to investigate
the character of work clone within tl1c Lodges and also to get an
expression of opinion as to what the Lodges believed to be of the
greatest importance in the educational work. A questionnaire was
sent out to each Master. Out of approximately five hundred sent,
replies were received from only one hundred and sixty-six. This does
not show a proper consideration of the work nor a sufficient interest
on the part of the subordinate Lodges. The Committee emleavore(I
to deterrnine how many educational meetings had been held am! the

GUAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

171

names and addresses of the speakers. Masters were asked to suggest
topics which they belieYed would be of interest in their particular
Lodges or localities. While the questionnaire gave a great deal of
useful information, it left us to surmise a great deal more. There
was so little definite information given that a careful analysis of the
situation was impossible.
At the meeting of the Committee on January 19th, it was determined to publish a second edition of the roster of speakers in order
to provide some source from which ambitious masters could draw
names, addresses and topics to aid them in making up their monthly
programs. The Committee believes that there should be some degree
of uniformity in the educational program and at the same time that
the Lodges should be allowed a wide latitude in order that they might
avail themselves of speakers and topics that would appeal particularly
to their members. It was realized that the roster was merely a makeshift and would constitute hut a small part of a program which would
be really helpful to the Lodges, particularly those in the outlying sections. Jn other wonls, it was realized that the roster was merely a
stop-gap to permit the Lodges to fnnction while the Committee was
making a serious study of the conduct of eclucational programs in
other jmisdictions an(! re;icl1ing a conclusion as to what elements
should be included in the term "Masonic Fducation" as it was used
by the Grand Lodge of California in carrying out its work. Jn this
revision of the roster, the Committee was firmly of the opinion that
only men of education, who coul(l properly present their subjects and
who were intellectually and morally fit in every sense would he recommended by it to the Lo(lgcs.
The revision of t11e roster l1as heen carefully ma(le and it is now
in the hands of all l\lasters. Six months have lieen sprnt in listing
names and ,carefully scrutinizing personnel, arnl this Committee believes that its present roster is deserving of the confidence of every
Lodge. From time to time as the n<tlllL'S of additional speakers are
secured, supplemental lists will be sent out, and on exhaustion of the
issue a new edition will he publishe(l.
The Committee, umler the liclid that l\Tasonic education should
commence with tl1e newly initiate(! can(lidate, revised the booklet,
"Freemasonry, Tts Origin and Purposes," and sent copies of it to all
the Lodges, with the re(jllcst that they he given to each candidate as
lie was raisvd lo t11c degree of 1\lastcr l\1asn11. The <lcmarnl for these
booklets in some nf the Lodges l1as ""ceedcd all c"pcctations, hut
most of till' T,odgcs have not gin·n any indication lo the Committee
as lo their attitudL~ toward the h""klct or the manner in which it
was distributed. This booklet is a simple exposition of the funda-

newly initiated members, if not all of the members of the Craft in

While the Executive Secretary has worked hard during the present
year, he has not been able, even with the assistance of the Committee,
to approximate the desires of the Committee. It might here be said
that a program of Masonic education is one which should be prepared
with great care and gradually developed so that the Lodges can absorb
the program without detriment to the ritualistic and business work
and also so that there may be a degree of uniformity of educational
instruction carried on throughout the entire jurisdiction;

172

At the January meeting, the Committee decided that certain topics
would be presented to the Lodges in the form of bulletins am! it was
thought that the following might be given preference: To instruct
committees on examination of visitors; to instruct committees in
proper methocls of investigating petitioners; to advise the petitioner
as to what he should expect to give Masonry and what its principles,
objects and obligations are; to advise coaching committees as to proper
explanation of the work when instructing candidates; to suggest to
l\Tasters the best ways of co-operating with this Committee and in
making the educational work somewhat uniform in its application; to
suggest topics for presentation to the Loclges; suggestions_ to Masters
on how to conduct meetings at which special addresses are to be made.
The Committee has issued the first two, both of which have been
well received by the members and extra copies have been requested by
l\Tasters of many Lodg·es, about 75DO of "The Visitor at Our Door"
having been distributed, and about 11,500 of "To Members Appointed
on Investigating Committees." \Vhen these were sent out, fonr 'copies
were sent to each Master, and the subsequent demands of the various
:\Tasters have l1een met. These lmlletins mark the first of a series
dealing with the simplest elements of Masonry, and particularly the
mutual duties of the Lodge and its members toward each other. It
is the idea of the Committee that the fundamentals should be thoronghly nnclerstood before we seek to climb to the more ambitious
heights of symbolism and philosophy.
Certain other topics, such as instruction of new members in Masonic customs and usages and certain points of onr law were to l1e
presented in pamphlet form for distribution among o'.der members
as well as the newly raised. This has been done and the booklet,
":\.1asonic Law and Custom; a :\.Tanual for the Individual Mas·on," has
been distributed. Further copies may be had hy :\Tasters of Lodges
and any Mason may liave the booklet or a copy of any of our bulletins
free l1y sending a request to the Executive Secretary of the Committee.
Steps were also to be taken to outline and roughly to prepare
addresses on other topics dealing with the elemental history and procedure of the Fraternity.
The accomplishments of the year ha1·e not been proportionate to
t11c energy expended, hnt as state(! ahove, before the Committee could
mm·e with any degree of intelligence it was necessary that they gain
information as to what had been accomplished l1y the Lmlges. Furthermore, it was necessary to make some stncly as to what couhl be done
for the Lodges in the smaller communities and in the remote sections.

The Executive Secretary has corresponded with all the other
Grand jurisdictions in an endeavor to ohtain information regarding
their experiences in Masonic education. Much information has been
received, some of which is of value and which can well be adapted
or modified to suit the needs of this jurisdiction.
The members of the Committee, and particularly the Executive
Secretary, have been called upon by many of the Masters for speakers,
particularly in and about the Bay Region. These calls have been responded to in the best manner possible, although it is difficult to
carry on development and research and at the same time operate a
speakers' bureau.
This Committee has co-operated in every possible way with the
Public Schools Week Committee in getting out form letters and visiting
meetings of Masters to advise them as to publicity and plans for their
meetings during Public Schools Week and in furnishing ~peakers
wherever possible. As the Puhlic Schools VV eek Committee had no
appropriation made them hy the Grand Lo(lge last year, all their expenses were home by the Committee on Education.
Advice and suggestions were sent out hy the Execntive Secretary
to aid in tl1e comluct of meetings for Constitution Week. These accompanied Bulletin No. 4 hy the Grand Master on Constitution Week, but
as the latter was not received from the printer until the third week in
August, it is doubtful if the meetings held were as successful as they
might have been. These suggestions were hased on the experiences
of the Puhlic Schools Week meetings.
Beginning in March, the Executive Secretary visited and addressed
on the work of our Committee. the following Masters and Wardens
Associations or Masonic Officers Associations, as they are variously
termed:

He also visited informally the Masters Clnhs of Oakland and San

Two new l\fasonic Officers Associations 11ave been formed during
the year. The Masonic Officers Association of Siskiyou County was
formed with the help of Inspector G. A. H utaff on June 26th and the
Masonic Officers Association of the 65th Masonic District was organized
on August 4th with the assistance of Inspector W. D. Adriance. On
June 27th the officers of the 6th District having been convened by Inspector Otto Trautz, were acldrcssecl hy the Executive Secretary on the
advantages of such an association to l11cir Lodges ancl themselves, but
the conditions were not favorable at that time for the formation of such
an association. A similar meeting of the offi.ccrs of the 5lst and 52nd
Districts was arranged by Inspectors T. M. Wright and C. A. English
of San Jose hut, as the officers wished to discuss the matter further no
association was formed at the time. It is quite likely that associations
will be formed in these districts in the near future.
The formation and continuance of these Masters and Wardens or
Ma sonic Officers Associations should be fostered and encouraged in
every way possible. They form the best and first line of contact between
this Committee am! Grand Lodge and the subordinate Lodges, excepting only the communication of the Grand Lodge itself. They not only
develop personal acquaintances ;me! friendships among the officers of
Lodges, but the officers of the Lodges arc able to discuss with others
their particular problems as well as those affecting all Lodges in the
District. The Loclges can co-operate more effectively in problems which
nmtually concern them by this means.

For the Future
We now have a number of speakers on our list who have signified
their willingness to prepare new addresses. Most of these belong to
the city Lodges and others must be found for the smaller districts to
effectivdy carry out the program. The Committee on Education shoulcl
suggest topics to these speakers ancl the Fxecntive Secretary shoulcl
assist in evl'ry possible way to prepare these talks, after whicl1 the
Executive Secretary should hold meetings with the Masonic Officers
Associations to outline the program and induce them to have these
speakers present the prepared talks to Lodges. These talks thus pre-

GHAND LOlJGl<J O!<' CALIFORNIA

175

pared should be given before the Lodges in the speaker's own neighborhood so that his expenses which are borne by the Lodge before
which he speaks, may be kept as small as possible.
Every Lodge ought to own a Masonic Library, even if only a small
one. This will be of great help to those who volunteer to prepare
addresses under the direction of the Executive Secretary, as well as
for the assistance of the Masonic student working in other directions.
Eight or ten suitable books can be put in a strong wooden case with a
padlocked door ready to be sent to any Lodge that wishes one. The
Lodge may keep the library for a given period, paying the transportation
charges one or both ways, lending the books to its members in the
same way as in a public library. Such a set woukl cost from $25.00 to
$35.00. The Committee should prepare a ntunher of these traveling
libraries and assist and encourage the Lodges to buy Masonic books.
While the bulletins already publishccl hy the Committee have been
well received, it is thought best not to hurclen the Loclges with too many
of them so that thl'y will not intcrferl' with the bulletins sent out by the
Grand Master. Bulletins similar to these already printecl may be occasionally sent out by the Committee in those months when the Grand
Master has no special message, hut the chief dependence of the Committee for its program of education will he in the present roster of
speakers am! those to be developccl in the Loclges of the outlying districts. As a result of our study of the California situation during the
past ten months, we make the following recommcmlations:
One of the greatest prolilems con fronting the Committee is that of
rendering service to the Loclgc in the small isolated town. In such
Lodges there is a comparatively small amount of clegrce work and
much time is a vailahle for educational programs. On the other hand
the treasury of such Lodge is not such as can bear the traveling expenses for speakers to come from long distances and their membership
is perhaps scatterctl tlironghout the snrroumling country. It is believed
that these Lodges woulcl welcome a carefully prepared sketch of lectures
on Masonic and general topics, hut it .will be necessary to develop a
scheme which can be aclaptcd to local talent. This has been given considerable thought, but no complete outline is rcacly as yet for presentation.

Recommendations
1. The Committee has observed the activities of the Masonic Service Association of the Unitccl States ancl has paid particular attention to
their "Short Talk Bulletins." As far as information will enable it to
express an opinion, these Short Talk Bulletins arc not read in any of
the city Lodges and only. infrequently in the country Lodges. It was
the unanimous opinion of the Committee at its meeting in January that

176

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the benefits received from the Masonic Service Association were not
commensurate with the expense of membership. It was further the
opinion of the Committee that the Short Talk Bulletins which were
sent out to the various Lodges of this jurisdiction contained nothing
that was of any distinct aid or assistance to a carefully planned program
of Masonic education. The Committee believes that a properly constituted Committee on Masonic Education within this jurisdiction is
capable of devising a program far better suited to our local conditions
than is the Masonic Service Association. It is therefore recommended
that the membership of this jurisdiction in the Masonic Service Association of the United States be terminated and that the funds thus saved
be made available to a greater development .of the work of the Committee of this jurisdiction:
2. That the present form of the Committee be continued but with
the addition of an Executive Council of five (5), which shall include
the Chairman and the Executive Secretary.
3. That the Masonic Officers Associations already formed, be
visited at least once a year by the Executive Secretary to present and
explain the program of the Committee and to present information for
their benefit obtained from other associations and other sources and
that the formation of Masonic Officers Associations be continued with
the help of the Inspectors and the Executive Secretary.
4. That an attempt be made to develop speakers on Masonic subjects in the Lodges themselves and to take advantage of the ability that
has not been touched and to find a way to bring out this latent talent
for the benefit of the program ·of this Committee.
5. That Lodges be encouraged in every way to acquire Masonic
Libraries; that a number of traveling libraries be prepared to send
to Lodges on request so that the brethren may see the books before
purchasing.
6. That the membership of this Grand Lodge in the Masonic
Service Association of the United States be withdrawn and the S cents
per capita now paid for this purpose be given to the uses of this Committee.
7. That the appropriation of 1923 for this Committee be continued,
and that the 5 cents per capita heretofore paid for membership in the
Masonic Service Association of the United States be added to the
above appropriation for the use of the Committee on ~fasonic Education, all stuns to be paid upon the authorization by the Grand Master.

The report was adopted as read with the exception of
the recommendations contained therein, which were referred to the Committees on General Policy and Purposes
and Finance.

which was adopted as read:
To the M.'. if'.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns has pleasure in reporting that most
of the Lodges sent in their reports promptly and correctly.
:\fany Lodges sent in their reports promptly, hut they were incorrect and had to he sent back for correction. And some of them had
to be returned more than once. Our Very W·orshipful Grand Secretary
has made the forms as simple as possible. He tried to make them
narrcn-frei. It cannot he done. There is always the personal equation.
While there is one way to make ont the returns correctly there are innumerable ways of making out the returns incorrectly, and it is astonishing how so many Secretaries find so many different ways to have
incorrect reports. All this imposes a great amount of extra work for
the Grand Secretary's office and entails a needless amount of correspondence.

is a matter for congratulation. In fact your Committee believes that
every <lay, in every way, the Masonic Fraternity in California is getting
better and better.

PROG.EEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODG.E OF CALIFORNIA

Names of Proposed Lodges

The Grand Master appointed Frank M. Angellotti, John D. Murphey
and John Whicher as s.uch Committee.
This Committee consulted with many eminent members of Grand
Lodge, suggesting tD them that it would be helpful to the Committee
if brethren who have a working knowledge of the Constitution would
co-operate in the proposed revision to the extent of sending in suggestions as to changes desired, both as respects form and matter.
We found a general expression that the Constitution should be revised, but did not find therefrom any concrete plan or scope of the
proposed work.
While it is probably true that the Constitution could he revised and
made what it should be, viz.; more of a statement of basic law with
many of the small details now included eliminated, we doubt the advisability of attempting any work of so great importance and magnitude
unless the same be absolutely necessary. This we do not think is the
situation. We are, therefore, of the opinion that no changes in. the
Constitution proper should be proposed by us. Certain changes, however, in our judgment, should be made in the form of the book, and
we recommend as follows:
L That the Digest of Decisions and Regulations now appearing
in the book of Constitution and Ceremonies as footnotes and annotations
be arranged under topical headings and indexed, and printed as an
appendix to the book of Constitution.
2. That the book of Constitution should contain only
a. The Constitution of this Grand Lodge, with index;
b. The Digest of Decisions, including regulations, with an
index;
c. The Uniform Code of By-Laws;
cl. The Fotmdations of Masonic Law;
e. Form for Consolidation of Lodges.
3. That all public and other ceremonial rituals be printed and
bound within one cover, but not with the Constitution.
Your Committee has prepared copy for the Digest of Decisions
with Topical headings, which may be scrutinized hy members of Grand
Lodge. The copy may be seen at the rooms of the Committee.

Your Committee on Charters submits the following resolution and
recommends its adoption .
Resolved, That hereafter no dispensation shall be granted on a
petition for a new Lodge with a name similar to a Lodge already existing; which name has for its purpose the memorializing of a particular
person, place or event.

Referred to the Committee on General Policy and
Purposes.
