REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF THE
CONSTITUTION
To the M:. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
At the Annual Communication of Grand Lorlge in 1923, the following report of the Committee on Policy and General Pnrposcs was
unanimously adopted :
"Your Committee on Policy and General Pnrposes has had under
consideration the recommendation of the Grand Master that the
Grand Secretary be directed to revise the Constitution.
"This matter has been the subject of comment for several years,
and some of the criticisms of our present hook of Constitution are
justified. The subject, however, is one of as much difficulty as importance, and should receive more careful and deliberate consideration
than can he given during the few days of a Grand Lodge session.
Your Committee, therefore, recommends that the Grand Master appoint
a Committee of three to consider the subject of the revision .of the
hook of Constitution and report their recommendations at the next
annual communication of the Grand Lodge."

Brother Thomas Ingram, Past Master of Madison Lodge
No. 23, presented the following:
To the M.'. W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
The seventy-fifth Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, held in
the citv of Los Angeles, will go down in our history as notable for
many ~ccomplishments beneficial to the craft. Those who were fortunate enough to be in attendance, however, will never forget the gracious
manner and open handed hospitality of the members of the craft in
Los Angeles and vicinity. The fraternal spirit which they have displayed is as warm as the hearts which beat beneath their breasts and
as gracious and free as any offering that could be given.
To the Grand Lodge Week Activities Committee is special recognition due for the complete and painstaking manner in which they have
arranged for every comfort, and provided for the entertainment of the
visiting delegates. Their entire program has been of becoming dignity,
as well as affording that relaxation which has been enjoyable to the
fullest.
Therefore Be It Resolved by this Grand Lodge, that we extend our
heartiest thanks and appreciation to the Grand Lodge Week Activities
Committee and members of the Craft in Los Angeles and vicinity for
the splendid care they have taken of the delerates to this session of
Grand Lodge, for the splendid manifestation of fellowship and fraternal
spirit, and the true and genuine hospitality that has been displayed
everywhere.

Adopted by a rising unanimous vote.

REPORT OF MASONIC TEMPLE ASSOCIATION
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The Directors of the Masonic Temple Association of California are
again privileged to report a year of satisfactory financial results.
In 1906 Most Worshipful Motley H. Flint, then Grand Master of
Masons in the jurisdiction of California, called to the attention of the

197

members of Grand L?dge the fact that the old Temple at Post and
lVIontgomery streets was destroyed by the fire wliich devastated a larg~
portion. of the city of San Francisco, and suggested that Grand Lodge
dcternunc what action, if any, should he taken as to rchuilding the
Temple.
At that Communication Grand Lodge ordered a committee of seven
to he appoined by the Grand Master to consider the proposition. This
committee reported at the same Communication, recommending a plan
whereb~ a new organization should be established for the purpose of
'.iur~hasmg new property anti erecting a Temple thereon, which organ1zatton should be under. the control of this "Grand Lodge and other
.\fasonic Associations of California" and that the "Directorate be made
large enough to permit a representation of all l\fasonic bodies who mav
snbscrihe to stock." The Grand Lodge pledged the sum of two lnmdre;I
and ten tlmusand dollars for the purpose. At several subsequent ComllJtmications Grand Lodge pledged itself to such additional sums as
would eventually free the Temple from debt.
The Temple was first occupied in l\ngust, 1913, and dedicated at
the Annual Communication in Octohcr.
Now, after eleven years, we are pleased to report that the iinances
of the Temple Association are in such condition that we hope no
further assistance from Grand Lodge may he necessary.
The demand for accommodations from Lodges has been such that
we deemed it necessary to provide another Lodge room in the Temple,
and t~1is was accomplished during the year at a cost of about $10,000.
Had 1t not been for this and other 11m1sual expenses incurred during
the past year, our linancial statement would indicate absolnte freedom
from indebtedness.
The Directors, representing 111any Masonic organizations owning
large blocks of stock in the Temple, most gTatcfull v express the thanks
of the various Masonic bodies concerned for the g~nerous subscriptions
from Grand Lodge made from time to time which have enabled m to
retire the mortgaged indebtedness and hopefully look forward to the
time, which we believe is not far distant, when we· may he en a hied to
declare dividends.

It may he of interest to Grand Lodge to know that our stock hook
reveals the fact that stock in the Temple Association to the amount
of some $90,000.00 stands in the name of individuals and that it has
heen deemed advisahlc that all issued stock should he held hy Masonic
organizations, am! that an effort is now being madt' by the dircctm·s to
divert the stock from individual to organization ownership.

and use of the building. The large lounging-room, library, and
billiard-room occupy the greater portion of the main floor. The
large social hall, equipped with a commodious stage, occupies the
rear portion of the structure. At the front, and opposite the secretary's office, are the parlor and rest-rooms for the women, while the
smoking-room and hat-room for the man adjoin the billiard-room.
In the rear, and adjoining the social hall, is a completely equipped
modern kitchen. The basement contains the heating plant and
large banquet hall. Several study-rooms and quarters for the resident hostess occupy the mezzanine floor, which extends across the
front of the building. The furniture throughout was specially designed to harmonize with the architectural features, and in keeping
with the interior finish of the building.
All doubt about the use of the club house by the students at
the University has been clispellecl by what has actually taken place
since the completion of the building. It is daily used by large numbers of men and women who find occasion to avail themselves of
its privileges, and, in a larger sense, the need of such a structure
has been demonstrated by the meetings and social gatherings which
are regularly held by the various Masonic activities at the University. The initial "smoker" by the Masonic CltJb, the afternoon tea
and reception to new students by the Women's Masonic Club, and
the De Molay rally during the opening days of the fall semester
were largely attended, and served to acquaint the students of Masonic affiliation with the advantages of the club house. More than
two hundred young men and women, and several members of the
faculty and their wives attendee! the first Sunday evening "fireside
meeting."
The Board of Trustees believes that it was exceedingly fortunate
in securing Mrs. Sallie M. Pease to be the resident hostess for the
club house. The controlling factors which led to her selection for
this important post are that, although herself the mother of a
student at the University, she is but a recent graduate of that institution, and has for several years last past been intimately associated with various student activities on the campus. She
was the unanimous selection of the students for the place. The
club house is .at all times under direct personal supervision hy
.Mrs. Pease, or someone in her place if she be absent, and all
the actiYities of . a social nature which function there are guid,~d
and counseled by her. The Masonic Council is very largely
responsible for the conduct of all events of puhlic and social nature.
This body is composed of representatives from the Masonic
Club, the ·women's Masonic Cluh, De Molay, and Henry
Morse Stephens Lodge. The fact that this Lodge, composed as
it is of members of the faculty and older students at the Uni-

versity, is a member of the Masonic Council insures at all times
the restraining influence of mature judgment and advice in the
c~nduct of, the club. house affairs. It will be the policy of the
hoard of 1 rustces, m so far as is consistent with that absolute
control and management of the club house which, in the last
analysis, rests with your Board, to permit this self-constituted
body of control to conduct and regulate the activities for which
the club house has been erected.

The M. W. Grand Master, Brother Arthur S. Crites, was
present at the formal dedication of the club house on Saturday,. September twenty-seventh. He was accompanied by Brother
David J. Reese, Deputy Grand Master; Brother Albert E. Boynton,
Grand Senior Warden; Brother George L. Jones, Grand Junior
\Varden; Brother John Whicher, Grand Secretary, and other Grand
Officers, members of various committees of the Grand Lodge, a
number of Inspectors, and visiting brethren from many parts of the
State. The remarks of the Grand Master, the words of greeting
from Miss Stella Linscott, Past Grand Matron, on behalf of the
Grand Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star, and the dedicatorv address of Brother Past Grand Master Charles A. Adams will- long
be remembered by the large number of persons who were so fortunate as to .hear the~. Another outstanding feature of the day
was the official greetmg on behalf of the University. Dr. Paul
~adman, speaking on behalf of President Campbell, declared that the
mfluence of the Masonic activities on the campus, materially represented by the erection of the club house, had come to be recognized
as 0~1e of the pronounced factors for good at the University of Ca!ifor111a.

It~ the evening, following the dedicatory exercises which were
held in the afternoon, the Masonic Council tendered the M.
\V. Grand Master and Mrs. Crites a dinner and reception in the
banq net hall. More than three hundred men and women of
the student body and a large number of inviter! guests sat down
to a fine dinner entirely planned and served hy the students
th?mselves. It was a typical student affair, and was thoroughly
e111oycd by the Grand Master, his good wife, and all others present. It >vould be hard to find a liner body of young men and
women than those members of the student body who were present on that occasion.
It was necessary, in order to make final payinents on contracts for the constrnction of the building and to provide neces;ary fonds for the purchase of furniture and equipment, for the
Trustees to borrow $15,000 from one of the local hanks. In addition to this amount, about $1.500 will be re([tlired for additional

The question of the maintenance of the club house at the University has been an ever-present proh lcm since the inception of the
enterprise. It must he admittecl that it was first contemplated
that a very small :.md inexpensive venture should be undertaken.
Later it was thought that the duh house might he made very nearly
self-sustaining through the erection of a much larger structure, costing perhaps twice as much as the present building, and devoted
largely to the housing of students on the dormitory plan. While that
plan seems to have worked in other jurisdictions, it did not appeal to
your Board of Trustees as answl'ring the conditions at the University of California, where th('re arc more than ten thousand
:;tmlents, many lnrndreds of t h('m ht'ing equally entitkd to recognition as having mor<' or Jes.' intimate J.fasonic affiliations. Neither
was it possible to carry ont any intelligent plan whereby such a
large numher of students with such affiliation, as there are at Berkeley, could receive any material benefit unless the project was

enlarged to its present dimensions. The records of the young men
and the young women at the University whom this club house is
to serve show that a surprisingly large number of them are actually paying all, or the major part, of their expenses while attending
college. Many of them are denied even the simplest of privileges
and social activities which add anything to the burden of their expense. It is utterly impossible to think that our students at the

These estimates are submitted only after a most careful investigation of the actual needs of the institution, and a comparison with
other institutions. The item of $900 for interest charges will be decreased as the various Lodges and individual Masons continue their
voluntary contributions. Grand Lodge could well afford, out of its
funds not appropriated, to absorb the amount required to pay the
outstanding note and the amount necessary to complete the furnishing of the club house, the advance thus made to be reimbursed
as unpaid quotas from Lodges are received.
So far as the operating and maintenance expenses for one year
are concerned, it will re<JUire only an amount of eight cents per
member for the more than one hundred thousand Masons borne on
the rolls of Grand Lodge. No better use of the funds of this Grand
Body can be made than to invest that amount in the welfare of the
several hundred students of Masonic affiliation at the University.
Your Board of Trustees recommends that both courses be
pursued.

To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred the several
trial records, reported through the office of the Grand Secretary, begs
leave to report as follows:
Trial Record No. 393, from Hawaiian Lodge No. 21. Your Committee offers the following resolution: Resolved, That the judgment in
this case be reversed without prej l!(lice to a new trial upon a proper
charge if one be filed against the accused.
Trial Record No. 397, appealed by the accused from the judgment
of Sacramento Lodge No. 40. Your Committee recommends the adoption of the following: Resolved, That the action of the trial commissioners in this case be and the same is hereby affirmed.
Trial Record No. 410. from Inglewood Lodge No. 421. Your Committee frel that a proper trial on proper charges has not been had and
the case should be remanded for a new trial on amended specifications,
setting out the offenses charged with particularity so that the accused
may know with reasonable certainty with what he is charged, should
the accuser desire to press the matter further. We recommend the
adoption of the following·: Resolved, That the action of the trial commissioners in case No. 410 in finding the accused guilty and sentencing
him to expulsion he reversed, and that the case he remanded to Inglewood Lodge No. 421 for a new trial upon amended specifications setting
out the offenses charged with particularity in plain, concise language,
if the accuser desires to further prosecute the matter, an<! that the
summons, if issued, state the exact time and place when and where the
accused is to appear.
Trial Record No. 383, concerning a member of Crockett Lodge No.
139, tried by Occidental Lodge No. 22, on appeal from a judgment of
reprimand. We are of the opinion that the accused is clearly out of
place in our fraternity and is entitled to no consideration whatsoever,
and therefore, offer the following resolution: Resolved, That the decision of the Trial Commission he and the same is hereby sustained, but
the penalty he modified, and the penalty he and the same is hereby fixed
at expulsion.
Trial Record No. 390, relating to a memher of Center Loclg·c No.
465, triecl by Las Palmas Lodge No. 3t6. Tn this case the T1·ial Commission found the accused guilty of embezzlement of public funds and
fixed the punishment at suspension. One of the highest honors that can

same is hereby reversed.
Trial Record No. 403, from Anaheim LOllge No. 207. In this case
the accused is alleged to he "a Mason now residing in the State of
Kansas, at Leavenworth." The minutes of the Lodge show that at the
meeting at which the Trial Commission was elected, the Master asked
the Commissioners elected to meet "with him in the Lodge room at the
close of this meeting." The minutes of the meeting of the Commissioners show this meeting to ha vc been held on the same date as the
election of the Commissioners.

209

PROCEEDINGS 01'' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALJFOR='<IA

Section 198 of the Constitution requires that after the election of
Commissioners, and at the same meeting, the Master shall name the
time and place for the first meeting of the Commissioners, keeping in
view the time allowed to the accused for appearance; and Section 199
provides that if the accused be without the State and his residence be
known that time shall not be less than ninety clays. The action of the
Commission having been taken immediately on its election, it affirmatively appears that the Commission was without jurisdiction to act,
and in the opinion of your Committee the judgment of the Commission
must be reversed and the same remanded for a new trial on the ground
that jurisdiction was not obtained in the manner provided by our Constitution.
The charge of unmasonic conduct is defined in the specification as
follows: "That on or ahout the 27th day of December, 1923, he did
violate Sections 194 and 189 of the Federal penal code." The Commission lli1d accused guilty on this specification but fail to find on whether
or not he is guilty of unmasonic conduct. Though it cannot be ascertained from the record whether or not the accused is charged with or
found guilty of conclnct that would constitute a Mawnic offense, we
may infer from his residence in Leavenworth, Kansas, coupled with
the charge of his alleged violation of certain sections of the Federal
penal code th at charges should be preferred against accused on account
of matters involved in the conviction of some crime involving moral
turpitude. If such is the case and a new trial of accused is had, it
may be helpful in a new trial of the matters that may be herein involved
to point out other serious errors in their record.
•
First. The record fails to show that notice of the special meeting
to elect commissioners had been given as required in Section 242 of the
Constitution. This notice is held jurisdictional in Section 194.
Second. The minutes of the meeting at which the Commissioners
were elected fail to show how many members of the Lodge were
present at that meeting.
Third. The specification does not set forth the matters involved in
the offense complained of.
Fourth. The :\faster failed to have summons issued or served on
accused.
Fifth. Though the accuser is shown by the minutes to be present,
the ::\faster does not call on him to present his case, but the Master himself becomes the prosecutor instead of the presiding officer, as required
of him in Section 200 of the Constitution.
Sixth. The Master failed to present the question and the Commissioners failed to !ind on the question of unmasonic conduct, as is required by the Constitution.

Seventh. The minutes do not show that the record of trial bas
been recorded as the judgment of the Lodge.
Your Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption:
Resolved, That the judgment in the case covered by Trial Record
No. 403 he, an cl the same is hereby reversed, and the case remanded
for new trial.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON GENERAL POLICY
AND PURPOSES
Masonic Service Association of the United States
To the lvJ:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

This Grand Lodge is now a member of the Masonic Service Association of the United States and the Grand Master recommends a withdrawal of this Grand Lodge therefrom. At the last annual comnmnication of this Grand Lodge your committee fully considered the subject of the Masonic Service Association and, at that time, approved a
withdrawal therefrom. The Grand Lodge, however, continued the
membership during the current year.
This committee, after a further consideration of the subject, is
of the opinion that, under present circumstances and prevailing conditions, and in view of the educational work inaugurated and now being.
carried on by this Grand Lodge, it would be wise to withdraw from
the Association and to concentrate its efforts and expenditures upon
the educational program of this Grand Lodge. Therefore, your committee recommends the adoption of the following:
Resolved, that this Grand Lodge withdraw as a member of the
Masonic Service Association and that the Grand Secretary be, and
hereby is, authorized to give to said Association a proper notice of
such withdrawal.

Per Diem for Representatives
Your Committee has also considered the resolution introduced by
Brother Gracey of N eva<la Lodge No. 13, proposing amendments to
Sections 6 and 70 of the Constitution, providing for the payment of
$6.00 per diem, during the duration of Grand Lodge, to Grand officers,
officers and representatives of Lodges, etc., in addition to a payment
equal to a regular round-trip ticket from the home of the attendant
to the place of meeting of the Crand Lodge, and also providing for
the same payments to members of committees as those embodied in
Brother Sherman's resolution a hove referred to. Your committee is
informed of the arguments whieh ran be advanced in support of this
resolution and is conscious of the defects in the present law, yet it is
unable to find any improvement in the proposed amendment over the
present law. Yom committee believes that this subject is entitled to
greater consideration than can he given to it during this session of
Grand Lodge and that a proper determination of a better policy will
require a careful examination of the financial condition involved in
the proposed legislation. This examination your committee has been
unable to make. The payment for Masonic services to members of
Grand Lodge is such a radical change in our policy that it should
not he reeommended until after the fullest consideration. Your committee, therefore, recommends that the resolution he not adopted.

Heport adopted.

Pay of Members of Standing Committees
Past Grand Master \Villiam A. Sherman proposed an amendment
to Section 71 of the Constitution to provide that, in addition to certain
officers aml committeemen named in said section, that members of
standing committees shall receive payment for their necessary expenditures for transportation to and from each Annual Comnmnication
of the Grand Lodge, in the same manner as ordered for the officers
of Lodges. Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes has
considered the proposed amendment and believes that, as a matter
of policy, the same should be adopted, and that the proposed amendment be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence for its consideration and report.

and complications. The apportionment of the loanable funds in this Grand
jurisdiction would be a task requiring unusual wisdom and delicacy
and, no matter how justly or carefully performed, would engender illfeeling and dissatisfaction. Local communities possess a commendable
local pride in Masonic Temple projects, without the use of Grand
Lodge funds, but often involve Lodges and Masonic communities in
an unwarranted burden of debt. This Grand Lodge should not assume
to direct and guide those who are expending the money of their Lodges
and members in the erection of buildings which seem to them suited
to their requirements and creditable to their communities. Moreover,
it is a safe business rule not to lend money to relatives or intimate

Adopted.
Other Bodies of Masonry
Your committee has considered and warmly commends tbe statements of the Grand Master relative to the "elements of weakness as
well as the danger in too many organizations basing their membership
upon the Craft degrees." Your committee is of the opinion that it
is regrettable that a policy was not adopted by this Grand Lodge, many
years ago, forbidding the exploitation, by Master Masons, of societies
and organizations requiring, as a prerequisite to their membership
that a candidate be a Master Mason. The Grand Master clearly and
concisely states the dangers which arise from the existence of these
side orders, but it is doubtful if the best interests of the Craft would
be served by drastic action taken at this time to destroy existing societies, and it is equally doubtful that it would be wise, at this time, to
attempt to dictate the activities of Master Masons in connection with
their associations and societies. Your committee believes that it is
apparent to all that Craft Masonry suffers by reason of these organizations, and that a repetition of the abuses called to our attention by
the Grand Master will finally result in disciplinary action bv this Grand
Lodge. Although this Grand Lodge has no connection ~ith or control over, such associations, it will not tolerate the fair name o/ Masonry
to be tarnished by its members, although operating outside its pale.
It seems to your committee that at the present time the comments of
the Grand Master are a sufficient warning to the existing organizations
as well as to those which may hereafter be formed.

friends.

Adopted.
Concurrent Jurisdiction
H. C. Sutton, Master of Paso Robles Lodge No. 286, offered the
following resolution:
"Resolved, that all Lodges within the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of California shall have concurrent jurisdiction."
Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes has carefully
considered the proposed resolution and recommends that it be not
adopted. Your committee believes that the evils, if any, proposed to
he corrected by the adoption of the resolution, are not so great as
those that would follow as the result of its adoption. In the opinion
of your committee the present law relative to exclusive jurisdiction
and concurrent jurisdiction has been tested by time and has proven
adequate to the needs of the Fraternity. A State-wide concurrent
jurisdiction might lead to abuses, and the adoption of such a policy
would be abandoning a practice approved by experience and justified
by results, to experiment with a new and untried scheme of j urisdiction.

Adopted.

Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes, to which was
referred that portion of the Grand Master's report relating to De Malay
and to which was also referred the resolution introduced by Past
Master Jesse M. Whited, relating to sponsoring of De Malay Chapters
by Grand Lodge, and another introduced hy Past Master Henry Byron
Phillips and Past Master John M. Ewing, relating to approval and
moral support by this Grand body of such De Molay Chapters, has
had the same under careful and deliberate consideration, and beg to
report as follows :

218

PROCJJ]EDINGS OF THE

Collectively and individually, the members of your committee are
in entire accord and sympathy with the attitude of the Grand Master
concerning this splendid work among boys. This Grand Lodge has
already expressed itself on this matter. At the seventy-third Annual
Communication held two years ago, Grand Lodge, by proper resolution, approved the ideals, aims and purposes .of the Order of De Molay,
and the members of this fraternity were requested to lend their moral
and personal support to any chapters of the Order of De ::Ylolay then
organized in their city or community or that might thereafter be
organized, "as a method of carrying out the ideals embodied in the
teachings of the Order."
It is the opinion of your Committee that Grand Lodge should do
no more than was done two years ago. The Order of De Molay,
as the Grand Master has said, will "grow and may be counted a,
splendid influence for good. * * * It is a constructive movement
and can well claim our active interest."
The committee deems it important that Masons throughout the
State continue to interest themselves in the movement, but we do not
feel that this Grand body should take over the direct responsibility
for the movement, splendid and helpful as it is. It has already been
given a deserved and an unqualified endorsement as to its ideals, aims
and purposes, and, so far as your Committee can observe, nothing has
occurred to suggest, or lead to a desire, that a single thing be retracted
or withdrawn from that endorsement. But De Molay is not a Masonic
institution. The Grand Master has clearly pointed that out. It is in
no sense allied with, nor can it become a part of Masonry. As such
distinct and separate organization, it is subject and subordinate to its
own parent organization. For this last reason, if for no other, and
others might he suggested, Grand Lodge can exercise no degree or
direct control or supervision bver the movement.
Your committee believes it would be just as much a departure from
the ancient landmarks of the craft for this Grand Lodge to assume
direct responsibility in any sense for sponsoring De Molay as it would
be to assume such responsibility for other organizations which claim
to he allied with Masonry. We also believe that to legislate to the
extent of directly permitting the subordinate Lodges throughout the
jurisdiction to sponsor chapters by Lodges, such action would have the
effect of committing this Crancl Lodge to a policy which it has never
departed from, and which just at the present moment, it is earnestly
seeking to follow. TJ1e action taken two years ago was dear, simple
and exclusive. To do more than was implied by the resolution then
adopted and which ca1led upon the indi'l1idual members of the fraternity
to lend their moral and personal support to the movement, would be,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

219

as stated by the Grand Master, "departing from the traditional policy
of Masonry" in this jurisdiction. We commend the zeal and interest
of the brethren who introdnced these resolutions, and all those interested
in the great work done by De J\folay among boys. \Ve are sympathetic
with the suggestions of the Grand Master that this great movement
should be carefully safeguarded, but we feel that it is a matter which
must rest with the individual members of the Craft.
We, therefore, advise that the resolutions referred to be not adopted
and that no legislation on the subject be enacted at this time.

The report was adopted.

Courtesy Degrees
The recommendation of the Grand Secretary on the subject of
"Degrees by Courtesy" was referred to your Committee on General
Policy and Purposes for consideration, and your committee respectfully reports that the present law appears to adequately meet the situation and that no change therein is required at the present time.
At the last communication this committee considered the same subject
matter and at that time expressed a hope that the situation might soon
be ameliorated, but this hope has not been justified by the experience
of the past year. The problem presented by the Grand Secretary is
a serious one, and unless a substantial improvement is experienced
during the next year or two it may be desirable to adopt the Pennsylvania plan or some other method to lessen the burden now being
imposed upon our Lodges.

Adopted.
Ku Klux Klan
Your Committee on General Policy and Purposes, to whom was
referred that portion of the Grand Master's address entitled "The
One lintoward Condition,'' has been considering the utterances of the,
Grand Master on the subject of the Ku Klux Klan, and the same
have the unqualified approval and commendation of your committee.
The Grand Master correctly states that Masonry has no connection
whatsoever with that organization and that Masonry in California will
not tolerate any act which may have a tendency to give color to any
seeming connection therewith. He further states the traditional policy
of this Grand Lodge "never to mingle in the affairs of other organizations and also never to permit other organizations to mingle in its
affairs."
In view of the fact that the Klan has no association or connection
with Masonry and that its reputed purposes and methods are totally
different from those of Freemasonry, it is deplorable to learn that
certain Klan members are causing discord and confusion in the Craft
and creating in the minds of some of our members a false impression
respecting the attitude of Masonry. No 1'1ason in this jurisdiction
should be so little versed in the principles and tenets of our institution
that he could be misled or mistaken in this matter. As the Grand
Master pertinently says, "that Masonry's teaching is largely based upon

toleration; that the very origin of our institution i_s largely d~1e to a

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON REPORT OF GRAND
LECTURER
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:

Your committee to which was referred the report of the Very
Worshipful Grand Lecturer begs leave to report as follows:
We have studied with great interest the Grand Lecturer's account
of his travels, which, during the year, have placed him in touch with
the ritualistic work of twenty-six jurisdictions, as well as with all the
Inspectoral districts in this jurisdiction. We would be pleased to comment at length with respect to the observations made by Brother Baker,
but realizing that the Grand Lodge must accomplish a great deal within
a very limited time, will refrain therefrom. Suffice it to say that the
narrative placed before us in the Grand Lecturer's report but emphasizes
the thoroughness, loyalty and devotion so characteristic of our Grand
Lecturer.
The ritualistic revision referred to in the report has been exemplified for the benefit of the brethren of Grand Lodge and will be brought
before this body formally for its action. We believe that there is a
general desire for the elimination from the ritual of repetitions, and
we are sure that the changes proposed will receive your most earnest
attention.
Your committee heartily concurs in the recommendation for the
amendment of Section 56 of the Constitution, providing that reports
from Inspectors shall be returned on or before the first day of May
in each year. This change will, as pofoted out, give much more time
for the study of such reports by Grand Masters. We therefore refer
the proposed amendment to Section 56 to the Committee on J urisprudence, with the request that it report same back to Grand Lodge for
final action.
Fraternally submitted,
WrLL H. Frscm\R,

J. B. McLl\l\s,
IRVING MAGNES,

Committee.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
Decisions of Grand Master
To thr At:. w:. Grand I,odgc of Califor11fo:

Your Committl'c on J nrisprudencc makes the following- report:
\Vith reference to the decisions of the Grand Master, reported in
his address, we believe that all of the same are in accord with our
law, as the same is now written.

264

PROCEEDINGS 01<' THE

Upon the question of subordinate Lodges "sponsoring" chapters of
the Order of De Molay or indorsing the Order of Jeanne d' Arc, it is
unnecessary. to add to the expressions of the Grand Master in his
Address.
Upon the question of payment by a Lodge of the necessary expenses
of Masters and \Vardens Associations, we understand that it meant
simply that a Lodge may, if it sees fit, expend money in defraying such
necessary expenses, as a necessary expense of the Lodge, on the theory
that the same is for a strictly Masonic purpose, and of benefit to the
Lodge. Of course the provisions of Section 88 of the Constitution
are controlling in such matters. \Ve see no reason to differ with the
Grand M;.,ster in this conclusion.
The Grand Master's decision with relation to the insufficiency of
the objection made to the advancement of a Fellow Craft in Petaluma
Lodge No. 180 was clearly right: In order that an objection may
suffice to ·bar the adv;,ncement of one who has been made a Mason it is
essential that it be a valid Masonic objection, and, in the nature of
things it is clear that a more general statement that one is "not under
good report" is entirely insufficient. One who has been made a :Mason
occupies an entirely different position from one not yet initiated. He is
entitled to certain rights and privileges, including the right to be advanced in the absence of sufficient cause to the contrary. '.fhe cause
assigned should cert.::inly be specific in nature, showing something done
or omitted to be done by him, which goes to his character or fitness.
And when any such objection is made it should be fully investigated
and appropriate action taken.
The objection here really amounted to no more than this Fellow
Craft Mason was not highly regarded by some person, or persons.
The Grand Master properly held that the Trustees of a Lodge have
only such power, with relation to the funds and property of the Lodge,
as are given them by the Lodge.
We recommend that all of the ;lecisions of the Grand Master above
referred to be approved by the Grand Lodge.

Report \Vas adopted.
The Grand Master has submitted to us for consideration his ruling
to the effect that if a member affiliating with one of our Lodges from
a Lodge of a jurisdiction other than California, paying, in addition to

GHAND LODGE 01~ CALIFORNIA

265

other sums requisite, the $20 required by sub-paragraph 1st of Section
41 of the Constitution, for the use and benefit of the Masonic Homes
of California, subsequently dimits and becomes a member of a Lodge
of another jurisdiction, and thereafter seeks again to become a member
of a Lodge in this jurisdiction upon a <limit or certificate of standing
or withdrawal from such Lodge of such other jurisdiction, he must
again comply with the provisions of said sub-paragraph 1st of Section
41, hy paying again said sum of $20.
Although the statement of the question seems a little complicated,
there can be no doubt that the Grand ~faster could have made no
different ruling.
We recommend that the decision of the Grand Master be approved.

Report was adopted.
Pay of Representatives from Hawaiian Islands
The Grand Master recommended that adequate legislation be enacted under which representatives attending annual communications of
the Grand Lodge from the Territory of Hawaii he allowed the same
rate of pay as is allowed representatives of Lodges located in the State
of California. At present such pay is restricted to officers and representatives of Lodges in this State, and to Inspectors so located.
This Committee, with the Committee on General Policy and Pur·
poses and the Finance Committee, have conferred with the represent;J.tives in attendance from the Territory of Hawaii. 'We all feel that
some provision of this general character should be made, though not
inclined to go to the full length suggested by the Grand Master. By
agreement of all such committees, entirely satisfactory to the representatives from Hawaii, it was decided to present the following resolution for adoption by Grand Lodge. It may be aclded that the expenses
of the representatives in attendance at this communication will be provided for in the report of the Finance Committee.
We recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
At each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge there shall be
appropriated a sum, not to exceed fifteen hundred dollars, for the pay
of one officer or representative of each Lodge located in the Territory
of Hawaii in attendance at such meeting, and also the Inspectors
therefrom in such attendance, the same to be apportioned by the Committee on Pay of Members on the basis provided for pay of members
in Section six of the Constitution. Provided, that no such officer or

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

266

267

representative or Inspector shall be paid a smn larger than the aetual
cost of transportation from the place of his residence to and from the
place of meeting of the Grand Lodge.

Report, together with recommendations, was adopted.
Amendments to Constitution
Certain proposed amendments of our Constitution have been introduced by the Masters' and ·wardens' Club of the East Bay cities,
through a committee directed by the Club.
\Ve have considered their propositions and report thereon as
follows:
!st. It is proposed to amend Sections 101 and 104 of the Constitution so that the same shall definitely determine when an application
shall be deemed received, permit the withdrawal of the application
when after reference t0 a Committee the petitioner leaves our j urisdiction, and permit an objection to be foterposed to a petitioner hefore
ballot.
Your Committee is entirely in accord with all these purposes, a
majority thereof believing also that withdrawal of an application should
be allowed when the petitioner, after reference of his application to a
committee leaves the jurisdiction of the subordinate Lodge.
ft further is satisfied that all these purposes can he accomplishe<l
by amending Section 101 only.

It is proposed to amend Section 206 of the Constitution by providing that a sentence of reprimand shall be carried into effect by the
Master of the Lodge which tried the case, in the Lodge of which the
accused is a member, unless the trial commission shall otherwise direct.
As the law now stands such reprimand is administered by the Master
of the Lodge which tried the case, but in the Lodge in which the trial
is had. The matter is of importance only where the party is tried in
a Lodge other than that of which he is a member. We can see no
advantage to be gained by the proposed change, and some disadvantage.
We can see that it is desirable that the Master of the Lodge in which
the trial is had should be the one to administer the reprimand, in view
of his superior knowledge with relation to the case. This, it is admitted, should continue to be the law. If he is to act in the matter,
his own Lodge would seem to be the proper place in which to act. He
there speaks with all the authority of the Master of a Lodge. Why
should he be compelled to journey, perhaps a long distance to the
Lodge in which the convicted party holds membership, for the purpose
of administering this reprimand, when the natural course would seem
to be to require the convicted party to appear before the Lodge in
which the conviction is had, there to receive his punishment. The proposed amendment makes the Lodge of which the accused is a member
the place where the reprimand is to be inflicted, entirely regardless of
whether such party resides within the jurisdiction of that Lodge or n.ot.
He may reside within the jurisdiction of the Lodge which tried him,
indeed the charges may have been originally filed therein, and his own
Lodge may be at the other end of the State, or for that matter in some
other State, thousands of miles away. Should the Master of the
trial Lodge be required in -such a case to journey to the Lodge of which
the convicted person is a member in order to administer the reprimand?
~or docs the proposed amendment make any provision for the payment
of the expense of the trial Master in making this journey. Ts the trial
Lodge to be compelled to pay this expense? ft is manifest that there
are cases in which it would he unjust to require the Lodge of which
the accused is a member to pay the same, and other cases, such as those

/
'270

where members11ip of the accused is in another 'State, in which this
jurisdiction could not compel such payment. ·
We think the proposed amendment unwis.e. and recommend that it
·
be not adopted.

The Report was adopted.

It is proposed to amend Section 165 of the Constitution which
covers the matter of non-affiliates residing in this State who have
neglected for a specified time to apply for membership in some Lodge
herein. The existing section is the result of long and careful study of
the subject by this committee, and has been in force for eight years.
Although necessarily long, and somewhat involved, in view of the
nature of the subject matter we do not see how it can be made more
clear. \Ve think it prescribes a fair and decent rule with regard to nonaffiliates, and covers every branch of the subject. \Ve see no reason for
a change therein, and do not believe in changing the Constitution unless
it appears that some advantage is to be obtained thereby. We, therefore, recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

The report was adopted.

Ni:ither Culver City nor Belvedere Lodge evinces any desire to surrender any jurisdiction in Culver City or Belvedere, or to give the
Los Angeles city Lodges concurrent jurisdiction thereover. The law
does not authorize the invasion of the jurisdiction of the Los Angeles
city Lodges involved in such request.
Section 92a, we think, gives to the utmost limit compatible with
fairness in the matter of prescribing special jurisdiction, and we know
of no way in which it can be remedied to advantage. We think
that upon analysis it will be found to provide as complete a remedy as
can be provided without undue injury to other Lodges for any situation
that absolutely requires exception to the ordinary rules of jurisdiction.
For instance, if not improper under the circumstances, exclusive jurisdiction of a part of Los Angeles city territory could be given to a Lodge
adjacent to the city. In fact this very thing was done in the case of
San Fernando Lodge No. 343, when it was given such jurisdiction over
certain territory in the city of Los Angeles, of which it had been deprived by annexation proceedings.
We recommend that the action of the Grand Master be approved.
In this connection we have to report that Bellflower Lodge No. 523
has asked that it be given concurrent jurisdiction with the Lodges in
the city of Long Beach. The opinion of your committee as to this is
covered by our report on Culver City and Belvedere Lodges.
FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,

Jurisdiction of Culver City Lodge No. 467
Culver City Lodge No. 467, the charter of which designates the
municipality of Culver City as its meeting place, requested the recommendation of the Grand Master to the effect that it be given concurrent
jurisdiction with the Lodges of the city of Los Angeles over all territory embraced in the city of Los Angeles, as to portions of which
Culver City is adjacent. Belvedere Lodge No. 539, located in Belvedere, Los Angeles county, made a similar request for itself. Objection
to any such conferring of jurisdiction was made by certain Los Angeles
city Lodges. The Grand Master very properly ruled that under the
provisions of our Constitution as they now exist, such concurrent jurisdiction could not be granted in either case. Section 92a provides a
method under which, where special circumstances require, exclusive
jurisdiction over certain prescribed territory may be given one or more
Lodges, such territory removed from the ordinary rules prescribing
jurisdiction and confined to the special rules provided therefor, and the
Lodges given jurisdiction thereover, exclusive from any jurisdiction
over any other territory. Such a course was not the desire here.

The Masonic Club of the University of California
The Masonic Club House at the University of California at Berkeley has been built and substantially furnished at a total cost of $158,080.26. The building fund has been raised by contributions from members of Masonic Lodges and other Masonic bodies within the State,
including two prior appropriations of Grand Lodge. The sums so
provided have been adequate with the exception of $15,000, which the
trustees of the club have borrowed from a Berkeley bank in order
to make possible the dedication and opening of the building this semester. In ·order to liquidate the indebtedness of $15,000 for construction and furnishings, it is recommended that the trustees of the club
endeavor to raise that sum from the Masons of the State, particularly
from the membership of such Lodges as may not have heretofore raised
their quotas for that purpose. It is the committee's belief that this
sum will be promptly provided when the need therefor is squarely
presented to the officers and members of such subordinate Lodges.
The tide to the building is in a corporation, similar to that of
the ~fasonic Homes, and the Trustees are elected from nominations
made by the Grand Master. The articles and by-laws ,of the corporation provide that the building shall always be operated under rules
and regulations agreeable to Grand Lodge, and in furtherance of the
trust of providing a meeting place and social club for Master Masons
and their sons and daughters at the University of California.
For the maintenance of the Club, it is estimated that $8000 will be
required for the current year over and above such contributions as
may be received from student Masonic organizations.
,
\Vhile the institution is still in a formative stage, the present indications are that the Club will more than realize the hope of Grand
Lodge, and a most salutary influence for moral and social betterment
will be afforded by it to the young people of Masonic ties who are
attending the University.

Summary-Grand Lodge Tax
In the year 1898 and prior thereto the tax on the subordinate
Lodges was $1.00 for each member.
In 1898 a tax of $1.00 was levied in addition thereto for the support
of the Masonic Home, thereby increasing the tax to $2.00.
At that time the Representative Fund was reduced from 25 cents
to 20 cents, which made the tax $1.95 up to and including 1912.
At the annual communication in 1912, a SO-cent building tax was
levied and has remained a Constitutional enactment ever since so
that between 1912 and 1920 the tax remained at $2.45 per member.'
After the enactment of the $20.00 tax on initiates and affiliates
the tax for the maintenance of the H omc was cut to 25. cents pe;
annum, and the tax for pay of representatives was reduced at various
times until at last its present point of 12 cents per member was reached.
After the close of the present session the tax will be $1.50 per member, which means that the levy on the subordinate Lodges has been
reduced 95 cents on each member borne on the roll by subordinate
Lodges during the last few years, and is the lowest at any time since

1899.
The difference between what the subordinate Lodges would have
had to pay had the tax remained at $2.45 and what they are now paying would amount to more than $100,000 annually.

Grand Master and Afe111bers of the (;rand Lodge of California:
I appreciate the important place that is accorded to the Grand
Orator ~f t~e Grand Lodge in directing him to deliver, at each annual
~ommumcat1on of the Grand Lodge, an address on matters appertainmg ~o the craft. But I cannot believe that the Grand Master of Caliform~, .who~e rr.iost. con.spicuous quality, among his many strong charactenstlcs, is l11s kmdlmess, would have laid upon me this burden if

of Masonic character and Masonic influence in California during the

But the humility I feel in the presence of such earnest authorities
on Masonry as Past Grand Masters Keesling and Hunter and Bledsoe
and Hervey, fades away in your presence. I feel that I am one with

GRAND LODGE 01'' CALIFORNIA

you, in membership of the Grand Lodge, and that on this level of
Masonic interest and . Masonic experience I may, with you, discuss
for these few minutes, questions appertaining to the activity and the
purposes which we, in our conduct here and at home may exemplify.
I do feel, as no doubt each of you do, a deep respect to the Grand
Lodge as such, for it is the sole fount of authority for us as Masons
raised in and responsible alone to the Masonic authority of the
Lodges subordinate to the Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction. Owing
fealty as we do, as well as respect to the Landmarks of Free Masonry,
and owing brotherly kindliness to ·Masons in good standing whithersoever dispersed around the globe, it is this Grand Lodge alone which
can define for us the terms of Masonry, and can direct for us our
future Masonic growth. There is no supreme Grand Lodge to ordain
for us, no other Masonic jurisdiction that can take precedence over
this body. So I am humble in offering to make suggestions about
what the Masonry of California should do.
But it is vitally necessary that we, as members of this Grand
Lodge, in our annual communications, do take stock of ourselves, with
an eye upon this grave responsibility. There are now something over
a hundred· thousand of us, in something like five hundred lodges.
Each of these hundred thousand of us was at one time outside the
door of Freemasonry. We had gathered from our friends and fellow
citizens a respect, perhaps an awe, for the reputation of this venerable Institution. We had felt that its ancient character gave assurance of its capacity to serve men and that it might, with our humble
assistance, serve ourselves as well as others. We knocked and were
admitted. Each of us at the altar took the obligations of Brotherly
Love, Relief and Truth. Each of us .came to share personally in the
noble record of what had been done by our ancient brethren. Each
of us entered with fervency into the enthusiastic service of the order.
And then each of us, in the course of a few months settled down into
the commonplace routine of life. A few of us, called by the wishes
of our brethren and perhaps our own talents and energy to hold office,
stepped into the path of Lodge service and of honorable preferment.
Rut for the great mass of Masons, there has come the satisfaction of
"being" without in any notable degree, the call for "doing." It has
been noted already in the reports in this Grand Lodge that there is
a percentage of failures to keep up dues, in the Lodges-not a great
per<.'entage-but a notable one. You and I may each of us know that
a part of these failures to maintain standing in the Lodges is not
due either to poverty or to lack of appreciation of membership in
the Lodrre. It is due definitely to a lack of interest in the runnin<?;
facts of. Lodge membership. There is a failure to find "purpose" in
Lodge membership. Men who should be ardently occupied, year in
and year out in maintaining their "standing," fail to do so because

for some lack they find in the Lodge work as it operates-a "purpose"
that they perhaps unconsciously demand, and which has not been, by
the Lodge processes, supplied t.o them.
It is, to be sure, no new discovery of mine that everv institution,
no matter how venerable, how highly placed in the respe;t of its own
members or of men without its limits must. have "purpose." An institution, like a man, must have a soul, and no soul is possible without
a goal. There must be a reaching out for the future, there must be a
flame to guide, a gleam of hope to pursue. Even if never grasped,
it arms the sririt for the deerer discharge of daily tasks; it wires
away the cornmonplaeeness, the drudgery of daily tasks. It makes
life worth living. Of course, Masons have wanted a purpose. But
they have not agreed on this purpose,
Our past history as an Institution gives striking illustration of this
search for a purpose. Arising in the somewhat limited needs of operative l\fasonry, with the reaching out into the wide possihilities of
speculative Masonry, the division in objective came early, and acutely.
New degrees were added, in great number. And some of these were
squeezed out, some were forgotten, some were made rather permanent additions to the body of Masonry. Some became the brilliant
if complicated bases of the various "Rites." Most of them have been
shunted off, in one direction or another, until today the Grand Lodge
of California, as the official ruler of l\fasonrv in this State is verv
nearly, in its official utterances, purely "Sre;ulative," in th; earlie;t.
sense, a reflection of the primitive virtues of the operative Masons
of our ancestry, worshiping God each according to his own conscience,
binding himself simrly but with a whole heart, in workmanlike fellowship to all men of goocl w_ill, particularly our brethren in Freemasonry.
Then there have been other efforts toward making a formal "purpose" in Freemasonry. There has heen the purpose to make the
Lodge a mutual benefit association. There have heen attemrts, mostly
unsuccessful, to commit it to the formality of insurance relationship
to the practical affairs of life. There has been the attempt to assure,
between Masons, the mutual obligations of trade and ratronage. There
has been the demand that Masons support each other in political or
other public aspirations. There have been proposals that J\fasons
commit themselves to definite political aims and associate themselves
in the campaigns that might accomplish political results either for
personal aggrandizement or for the imposition on the government
of certain policies in alignment with actual or snpposed Masonic
objectives.
Each of these efforts has
for the great body of Masonry,
a failure. Each of these efforts, while it may have at certain times

and places shown success, has not impinged upon the body of Masonic
theory or of practice. Masons have rejected the call upon them to
make their Masonic membership a preliminary to force them into a
.Masonic communism, either of industry or trade; of rublic policies;
or of intellect; or of religion.
There has arisen, however, in the last few years, a new sort uf
·'purpose" which must l:e regarded with deep respect, and yet whose
weaknesses must be recognized. This is illustrated among us here in
California by the Grand Lodge policies of promoting "Constitution
\Veek" and "Public School Week." These are made the practical
objectives of acti\'ity by Grand and Subordinate Lodges. Tl1ey appeal
to our instinct as Masons because they are in line with our attitude
of mind toward public questions generally. \Ve are earnest and intelligent supporters of our government, and therefore encourage study
of the Constitution. \V c believe in the liberty of thought and action
that comes from wide knowledge and of a trained understanding and
so we are for the public schools.
And vet in this, we face a danger of falling into the rut of our
past, rati1er than in developing a living, doing purpose. The W0fk
of our recent Grand Masters and our subordinate Lodges in promothrg
these public interests has heen wonderful. Hut just as uur Lodge
activitv tends to become woodenk "ritualistic," so is there a danger
that ~ur observance of these "~eeks" shall hecomc formalistic, repeated year after year with the shell of respect and without the purpose of making these anniversaries productive of new service to ourselves and our fellowmen.
The failure at one time or another of the rroposed "'purposes" of
those who with eager intent hut with an enthusiasm and a judgment
which did not accord with the feelings of their fellow Masons, in
the course of time ha« produced a defoiite "conservative" hocly within
our Masonic numbers. It is a hody suspicious of any proposals whatevn to vitalize the outward aspect of Masonry. It finds its sufficient
apology for heing l\Iasonic within the ritual of the Order. These
conservative Masons perhaps protest that they are not purely ritualistic.
But they do find the entire scope of Masonry as they would have it
within the ritual. They ask if there is any authority for some proposed action in the ritual. Ancl any attempt to change the ritual is
viewed not merely with regard tn its practical dfcct, hut also as a
possible hlow upon the "authorizt'd version" of what Masonry is,
a hlow at the "apostolic succession" within thl' fraternity.
\Vorthy as has hcen !he sentiment of the intellic;cnt su;lportfrs
of this view of Masonry, it has prodnccd, among the rank and file
of Masons a suggestion of despair. It has been a hasis for reactionism, a gospel of negation in Masonic thinking. It has produced an

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

impression both within and without the fraternity that members of
our Order are brought together purely to revere symbols, to go
through ceremonies honored in the past, but not understood in the
present. It has been a smart saying outside of the Craft that Masons
never do anything except attend funerals. Observing the remarkable
growth of Masonic membership, some Masons and many non-Masons
have realized that it is impossible for a personal relationship of
brotherlv affection to exist between Masons as such. With fraternity
formali;tic, with the history of the Order an obscure science, with
the thinkers of the brotherhood amusing themselves with Isis and
Osiris, a1'd excited about the digging up of the treasures of Tutankhamen, what wonder that at the period of its greatest extent, men
should wonder whether there was a dry rot setting in at the roots
of this great Order.
A part of the reason for the tendency toward extreme conservatism in Masonic thinking has been due to this same intimate knowledge of the past. It has been a knowledge that has failed to ·recognize
that all that was great in the past was creative, and in that sense was
new. Christ, who rebuked the Sadducees for their undue respect for
the formalities of the past, was a creative force in the world, even
when He declared that He came to fulfil, not to destroy the law. Our
Masonic forefathers, I make bold to declare, gained the glory that is
theirs in our eyes, alwa}'s, because they manifested in their own con·
duct the vitality needed at those times. When we read of ~fasonic
exploits in renascent Europe, when we tell of the Masonic influences
that were so potent in the Revolutionary period in the United States,
when we learn of the men who owed allegiance to our Order who
broke their way into the Western frontier of our country and on to
the Pacific slope-we find that each of these generations of Masons
builded anew for themselves and their families and fellow citizens.
They were not satisfied with worshiping in faded shrines of old
memories, kneeling in deathless dust to pay reverence to a Great
Architect of the Universe whose work was done. They found the
opportunity of the time, they searched out stones to cut and timbers
to hew. And if it be said that these men worked in these matters not
as workmen but as citizens, I say to you that it is as citizens, then,
that we honor them, even though we recall with pride the fact that
they were :Masons.
Do not imagine for a moment that in this I am urging that the
Grand Lodge of California gird itself up for some outbreak of propaganda. I do not ask even that we be "progressive," whether that word
be now under suspicion or have the courageous value that it once had.
All that I ask is that we as Masons refuse to permit ourselves to be
used for the forces of social reaction, that we properly classify our

own respect for the past so that it will not be used by weaklings or
scoundrels as a cloak for new villainies under old privileges. I believe with that flaming voice of the American Revolution that we
"have no lamp by which our feet are guided, except the lamp of ex·
perience." But I also notice that the feet of our Revolutionary forefathers moved forward, with the aid of that lamp. They did not
mark time.

288

289

'What is the purpose that we can find in our Masonic outlook,
which will be consonant with our Order's history, which can vitalize
our membership, which will aid the normally wholesome impulses of
ourselves and our fellows as citizens of this as well as of other lands?
I find that purpose in Masonry itself.
I do not believe that it is necessary to go outside of the scope laid
down in our Masonic tenets, to give a living vitality to our Masonic
experience, to enable us to give to the Entered Apprentice a satisfac·
tion in Masonic membership that will keep him going not for months,
but for years, as a Master Mason.
It would be vain to take up your time in a detail of these mainsprings of this Masonic purpose that we finfl in our Masonic teaching,
but I do. want to emphasize a few striking points.
First: Our Masonry must appeal, ever anew, to youth. We fall
too easily into the habit of thinking ourselves as having eternal youth,
when in fact each of us is aging, much too fast. We fail to make our
Order, as a human institution, appeal, with new force year by year to
the young men entering our ranks. The most of you doubtless still
think of yourselves as "young men," as I do. \Ve must remember
that to the man of 30, the man of 40 is old, to the man of 25, the
man of 30 has a character that is matured, to the lad just qualified to
enter our doors, at 21, the man of 25 is experienced. We slide into
middle and old age with an ease that is terrifying to us. It is still
more terrifying to the young man, who we demand shall be respectful
of our whims and fantasies, as well as our wisdom and experience.
We must keep our Order young in its sympathies and its outlook,
no matter how many years we stay in it, or the young men will take
our obligations, walk out of our halls and never darken them again,
no matter how long they may continue to pay dues.
Secondly: We must make our Order work. Surely there could
be nothing more fitting than that our fraternity, founded on the mutual
interest of builders in their means of livelihoocl, and symboled with
the tools of their handicraft, should honor the value of1 labor in deed
as well as in word. We have grown too used to regarding our responsibilities as members of an institution as "symbolical" rather than
actual. There is no other Order in the world which gets along so
well with as big a proportion of inactive members as the Masonic

290

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Order. If St. Paul in declaring that "faith without works is dead"
expressed a truth of primitive Christianity, we may well declare of
our own humanity, that it cannot be true to any prim:iples if it does
not with hand and heart as well as with tongue and brain, conform
daily.
It will not he easy, this proposal, either for ourselves as an Institution, or for the men that we ex"pect to make better Masons as well
as better men. There cannot any great good come without a rigor
of soul, and of body.
"Who never ate with tears his bread
"And through the long-drawn, midnight hours
"Sat weeping on his lonely bed,
"He knows you not, ye heavenly powers."
Thirdly: We must make our Order love. Much maudlin talk
has been spent upon the quality of friendship, upon the scope of
brotherly love. We have been doing too little practically to make our
Institution a means for promoting true friendship among men. We
may give with some freedom to Masonic charity. We may in an illguided moment make a loan or sign a note. What we don't do is
to so know the Masons within our reach that we may love them, and
what is important, that we may have the affection for them that is
fitting to them and to us as neighbors and fellow citizens with the same
decent public purposes and communal relations. One of the most
forceful things that has been said in this Grand Lodge session was
that no man could love a "name in a roster." Our Lodges are so
large that our friendship is a thin film of sloppy sentimentality, expressed on very rare occasions and having little relation to our working lives.
I confess that while I have pride in the fact that there are a
hundred thousand fellow Masons of mine in California, I have no
interest in it, and I would be very shallow if I were to declare that
I love them. I don't, and there is no need for me to love them. Those
that I should love are the Masons of my own Lodge, of my own
acquaintance, in my own community, the men whose intercourse with
me puts a debt of fellow sympathy upon me. And do I love them
·as I should? Does my Lodge help me to know them and to love
them, each the other as we ought? The answer, given by too many
intelligent Masons, to this question, is that we give a wonderful
·foundation at our Masonic altar for this friendship. We do not
provide in our Lodge's working relations for a building and a strengthening of it.
This friendship must be real. It must have substance. It must
be understanding and constructive. It must be personal.

291

"Sometimes, when shadows cross my path, as shadows sometimes do,
"I reach a hand across the mists, and touch the hand of you.
"I know the sun is overhead, I know true love is true ·
"B ut what a comfort in the dark, to touch the hand of' you."
And finally, my brethren, our Order must produce leadership. It
must do this, fully conscious of the limitation that is upon us that our
Order is not conduct-controlling, but character-forming.
'
We cannot tell our members what they shall do. We cannot
dictate how they shall think, nor talk, nor act. If we have selected
them c~r.efu~ly and have ~nitiated, passed and raised them as a living
exemphf1cat10n of our ritual impels, their conduct will be decent,
beyond any need for our reprimand. But our members will not be
the men that we expect them to be, they will not have justified our
training, if they be but decent citizens. They must afford somethina
more to us and to their community than this bare return for th~
nourishment of body and soul that they get.
And this greater return will come from them to us and to our
state and nation in the leadership they afford to our communities.
It is an opportunity, the fulfillment of which is sadly needed. I
think I· am not pessimistic in declaring that, no matter what may have
been the fact in previous generations, the great lack at present is for
men who can supply leadership to their cities, their states and their
country. Everywhere men and women are calling for leadership for
constructive visions of public needs, for management of public affairs
that will satisfy natural conditions and human inclinations alike.
Everywhere there is this demand. Too feeble is the response. \Ve
:ind plen~y who offer, but few that can make good. They fail in
mtellect, m breadth of human understanding and sympathy in energy
in adaptability.
'
'
Ours is the great democratic Order. It is composed of men who
are indifferent to race, to sect, to creed. It is based upon common
human qualities. It knows all men. But it should have no limit on
the capacities of its leaders. And it should, through its good offices
t~rough it~ training in liberty of thought, in respect for human rights:
give to this country of ours, in which Masonry has had its greatest
growth and its greatest opportunity, a service in leadership.

REPORT
of the

Committee on Correspondence
October, 1924

By JESSE M. WHITED
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
I submit herewith my fifth report on Foreign Correspondence.
As in the past the same is along the lines known as "topical."
At the suggestion of one of the members of the Committee the
arrangement is somewhat different.
The opinions, as usual, contained in the following paragraphs
are expressions of opinion only of the Chairman.
A review of the Proceedings of the sister Grand Lodges show
that practically the same conditions exist as heretofore and the
attitude of the various Grand Lodges remain the same. No revolutionary ideas having been advanced or been put into force.
"Peace and harmony prevail" with the exception of the difference between the Grand Lodges of New Hampshire and Kansas
over the question as to whether "visitation" is a "right" or "a
privilege."
There has been an approximate. gain in membership in the
United States of over 150,000 according to the latest figures available.
Borrowing from the report of the Chairman of the Correspondence Committee, Ralph C. McAllaster, P. G. M. of Washington,
which we have always remembered, we are "lifting" from his report
of 1922 the following:
"Harmony is the strength and· support of all institutions, and
Masonry, especially, is dependent thereon for her perpetuity and her
usefulness. Yet that harmony is rapidly being destroyed in the race
to commit Masonry to a multitude of things wherein harmony is an
impossibility. Plans and policies wherein men of the best intentions
differ; purposes of the very highest, wherein there is no difference
of opinion whatever as to their advisability and propriety, but concerning which the methods of accomplishment leave very large
opportunity for difference, are being foisted upon Masonry for her
endorsement.

2

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE
REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE!

"We proudly proclaim that Masonry is in no sense a political
institution; yet Grand Lodges, one after another, are endorsing certain political measures; while thousands of Masons are advertising
their Masonic affiliations as vote-catchers in the political campaigns.
"We proclaim the equality of all men within the brotherhood;
yet the Ku Klux Klan ga;ns such foothold within our ranks that
it is in places taken for a Masonic institution.
"We are fostering within our ranks a large and growing opposition to a group of citizens on account of their religion, and yet
there is not a th:ng in our declaration of principles which renders
them ineligible to membership in our Fraternity.
"We declare that Masonry is a system of morality; yet we sit
supinely by while groups of Masons, under certain distinguishing
titles, exist for 'entertainment,' and carry on projects for the raising
of funds which violate every law of morality.
"We have read page after page of calls upon Masonry to do
something to justify herself; to take this or that stand that will
show to the world where we stand on all these great questions. We
have read many sarcastic references to the Mason who refuses to
allow himself to be drawn into these problems under the banner of
Masonry, with the idea that Masonry is united and can be counted
upon to support unitedly any project which a Grand Lodge endorses,
and we invariably find the proponents of these measures oppose the
pet projects of some other brother.
"It may be a reflection on our intelligence, but we have gone
over in our minds the various degrees through which we have
passed, and we fail to recall anything, any place, which looks toward
anything but the development of the individual. To give him
strength of mind and heart to meet the problems of daily life for
himself; to enable him to differ with his brother man and yet to
grant that brother man credit for equal sincerity with himself; to
differ with his Brother Mason in the affairs of the world, but to
leave those differences outside the door of the Lodge and meet him
upon the level inside the tiled recesses; these and only these things
can conciliate true friendship among those who would otherwise
remain perpetually at a distance."
Acknowledgment is again made of the obligation we are under
to the Secretaries of the Grand Lodges and several Grand Bodies
of the United States, the Editors of Masonic publ!cations and other
writers who have materially added to whatever value this report
may have.
ATTENDANCE
The lack of attendance at Blue Lodge meetings is shown by the
attention that is being given it in the Annual Addresses of a number

3

of Grand Masters. The cause depends, of course, upon the viewpoint of the party discussing it. It is variously ascribed to lack of
interest, as the Blue Lodge is becoming in a large number of cases
merely "a degree mill," effect of the so-called "higher degrees" or
co-ordinate Masonic Bodies, large Lodges where members find it
impossible to become acquainted, and the general change in the
ideals and amusements of the present.
We have always held to the belief that. if the average Blue
Lodge would take a leaf from past history and supply the demand
of the individual member along fraternal, ritualistic, social and educational lines the cause for non-attendance would be removed. When
an institution specializes on one of these particular lines, from the
Masonic standpoint it ceases to serve the purpose through which the
Fraternity has developed.
It has been estimated that the average Masonic life of a member is seven years. As a matter of fact it will be shorter, unless
as an organization we can supply a continuous program along various lines that will entertain and instruct. This statement, of course
eliminates those that have become members through curiosity or fo~
financial gain.
LAMBSKIN APRON
The rituals of some jurisdictions allow the Master to use either
a long or short form in presenting the Lambskin Apron. That recently adopted by Indiana has found favor with a number of Ritual
Committees.
As "variety is the spice of Life,'' we believe California could
make use of this classic. We have a precedent as our Ritual
allows the u.se of two different forms of prayers.
BALLOT
Many of the difficulties of the average Lodge from the standpoint of finances, attendance or trials can be traced to the unintelligent use of the white or black ball. This does not refer to one who
uses the black ball for purely personal reasons or spite. In a number of cases the average member perhaps considers the casting of
a.b~llo~ ~urely a perfunctorr matter rather than a duty, not only to
hfs 10d1v1dual Lodge but to the Fraternity in general.
The education of the members to the intelligent performance of
this duty would be of benefit. It has often been stated, and perhaps
truthfully that at the present time it is impossible for an applicant
who has attained prominence either in civic, political or intellectual
affairs to become a member, solely by reason of his activities and not
for personal reasons.
