BOUQUETS AND BRICKBATS
As customary, when the Report of any jurisdiction is received
by a Grand Master, Officer or Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, he first turns to the review of his State to see
what has been written.
In the numerous Proceedings reviewed it is gratifying to find
that the work of Masonry in California, whether carried on collectively or individually, has been generously treated.
We cannot all think alike. Where there has been a difference
of opinion the criticism has been fair. The idea can perhaps best be
expressed by the following from a popular author:
"This world we're living in
Is mighty hard to beat,
We get a Thorn with every Rose,
But ain't the Roses sweet."
BURIAL SERVICES
A number of the jurisdictions have revised their burial service,
making it more in accord with the ideas of the present time than
the orthodox one that prevailed during the early existence of the
Fraternity.
There is no question but that this has been an improvement.
Some still in vogue are more appropriate to a particular religion
rather than for an order that "unites men of every country, sect and
opinion."
CLUBS
The principal objece.on, and which is more apparent than. real,
to Masonic Clubs composed entirely of Masons, is the use of the
word "Masonic." It does not seem entirely just that such a Club,
performing only the social work that unites members of all different
Lodges of a jurisdiction into an organizat:.on that does what we are
taught in our Blue Lodges should be prevented from identifying
themselves with the Fraternity.
If organized for private gain the objection is perfectly proper.
A Masonic Club, whether soclal 'or otherwise, that does not
carry out Masonic ideals in every respect should, of course, be suppressed regardless of its name.
CORRESPONDENCE REPORTS
As usual the "topical form" of Correspondence Report comes in
for its share of criticism. Some six or seven years ago this form
was a rarity. It is a source of satisfaction to those who have adopted

HEPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

5

the plan to know that others are adopting it. We have always
maintained that the Correspondence Report is a matter for "home
consumption." The "golden age" for a Correspondence Committee will be when some form of report can be devised that will
present, not only to the members of their jurisdiction the Masonic
thought of the day on matters interesting the Fraternity but what
has actually been done throughout the world other than the mere
recitation of facts interesting only to a particular jurisdiction.
Greater than all of this though will be some way to make the
result of the labors of the Committees available to every Mason
whethersoever dispersed.
There are Chairmen who have served for years in this field. It
is a pleasure to review their writings. Their names are legion, and
to recite them would be to call the roll of some of the brainiest men
in Masonry.
We have received the Correspondence Committee Report of J.
Edward Allen, North Carolina, for 1924. We are making special
mention of him as this is his first effort. He is to be congratulated,
not only on account of his report as to the individual States but
particularly on the statistics that he has compiled. We regret that
lack of space prevents them from be:ng embodied in this report.
CRIMES AND CRIMINALS
One of the disagreeable sections of the Proceedings of a Grand
Lodge is the space used for telling the results of Masonic trials. In
some jurisdictions the names, details and results are set forth at
length. Continued criticism by Correspondence Committees, who
have been in service for years, seems to be having an effect and
some Jurisdictions are giving only a skeleton detail rather than
a typical reproduction of the front page of a "yellow journal."
The idea that Masons as individuals are bound to respect each
and every law now on our Statute Books, whether popular or unpopular, in force or allowed to slumber by the authorities, and the
result of the law to them if enforced, is continuously being stressed
by Grand Masters and Correspondence Committees. It is a matter of
education and it will only be by continuous reference to the matter
that practical results can be secured.
There can be no argument along th;,s line. The necessity for
continually calling attention to the matter may perhaps be due more
to the policy of attempting to legislate for "everything under the
sun" rather than the inclination or desire in Masonic or profane to
disobey the law.

EDU CATI ON-MASONIC

there might be established a clearing house for ideas of the various
jurisdictions to secure uniformity in procedure connected with standard matters.

A politician in referring to his opponent stated that "the gentleman in question knows less about more subjects than any man in
the United States." While this may not be true as to Masons regarding the history, law and purposes of the Fraternity, still as a matter
of fact such a condition exists among the members of the Craft in
general.
Education along purely Masonic lines is distinct from civic or
political matters, and in order to be of use must be put within the
reach of all those seeking "light" and in such a form as will be
practical. A well edited Masonic publication devoted to this idea
and sent to all members would accomplish more than perhaps
the work of brilliant speakers, pa:d lecturers and Masonic Education
Committees.
The average person derives a large part of his information and
pleasure from reading scare head lines, epigrams or thrilling articles.
If some system could be inaugurated to present Masonic education
along this line we believe it would prove acceptable and productive
of results.
GAMBLING
A cloud no larger than a man's hand appears on the Masonic
horizon. This is the practice of not only some Blue Lodges, but
also some of the co-ordinate Bodies, to finance themselves through
methods where "the element of chance" predominates. Several
Grand Lodges have prohibited this custom in Blue Lodges. One
Grand Lodge extended it to include some of the "Play Grounds of
Masonry."
The cause of th'.s is due pr;marily, we believe, to the small initiation fees and dues. To carry out plans requiring large financial
expenditures an organization must necessarily resort to some way
of securing "easy money." Perhaps the most effective curb would
be to establish, through a Grand Lodge law, such initiation fees and
dues as would be adequate to enable an organization to carry on the
work for wh:ch they are organized. This would prevent the necessity for securing funds through means that might be open to criticism.
GRAND LODGES
Throughout the Proceedings, both in the Annual Messages of
the Grand Masters and Committee Reports, is the thought that there
is too much Grand Lodge Legislation as far as the individual Lodge
is concerned. Also that some method should be devised whereby

7

We do not believe that the general Grand Lodge will ever be
possible, but there certainly should be some way whereby certain
standards could be adopted (either expressly or impliedly) that
could meet with the approval of every Jurisdiction.
The regretable breach between New Hampshire and Kansas
furnishes an example.
If each Grand Lodge would adopt a certain form of receipt, uniform method of procedure, and communication between the -various
Grand Lodges, etc., a part of the difficulty would be removed.

GEORGE WASHINGTON MEMORIAL ASSOCIATION
When this idea was first suggested the plan was to have a
Temple at Alexandria, Va., sufficient to protect and preserve the
mementos of George Washington and Alexandria Lodge. In the
Correspondence Committee Report for 1919 the following statement
was made:
"We yield to no one in our respect for George Washington,
but we do believe that if these relics are so valuable, they could
doubtless be located in a place where they would be more accessible
to the world in general, and, furthermore, that the money could be
better employed for the ultimate good of Washington's memory and
the Craft in general."
Developments since then have not caused us to change our
opinion. We believe that the statements made by Brother Goodwin
of ~tab and Brother Jenks of Wisconsin, included in this report, are
particularly apropos:
"George Washington was a believer in education. Wou1d not a
great national university, as planned by him, endowed, established
and supported by the Fraternity and Masons be a greater memorial
than the one to be erected."
Disraeli, the great English statesman of the last century, said:
"The youth of a Nation are the Trustees of Posterity."
A Congressman once said:
"Posterity has done nothing for us. Why should we worry
about them."
In this commercial age perhaps that thought is too commonWe as citizens ·and Masons should pay attention to the "Trustees of
Posterity."

REPORT ON COllRESPONDENCE

HISTORY
Napoleon said that "History was fiction on which liars agreed."
If a large amount of mis-information as to the Masonic standing and
activities of some of our prominent members, both past and present,
is to be accepted as truth (?), Masonic History has yet to be
written.
Perhaps the Masons as well as others want to believe what accords with their particular ideas. Research shows that a number
of statements, as far as the Masonic connections of some of our
Revolutionary forefathers is concerned, is "pure bunk." They cont:nue to be published and accepted as absolute facts.
If Grand Masters, Editors, Orators, Writers and all others would
first make an investigation and determine from responsible sources
whether their statements are true or not the condition would be
materially improved.

The ritual of the Order of the Eastern Star distinctly states
that it is not a Masonic organization. From the testimony of various
Grand Masters, and from practical results, there is no doubt but
what the organization is performing work in connection with Masonic Homes that cannot be reckoned in dollars and cents.
In France, perhaps with the natural gallantry of that Nation,
some confusion and criticism was occasioned through one of the
Grand Bodies of France suggesting that the "Rite of Adoption" be
recognized. We understand the matter has been satisfactorily adjusted and the mix-up was caused more by a literal translation of
the French language and lack of knowledge of the h:story and system in France Masonry rather than their desire to admit women.
In some of the other countries "Co-Masonry" has produced
regulations which have practically put that organization out of
business or caused a change in their program.

INVESTIGATION
A large amount of trouble both past, present and perhaps future
can and will be directly traced to the failure of an Investigating
Committee to faithfully and consc'entiously perform the duty assigned them. Too often that duty is not performed and as a result
unworthy applicants become members. This ultimately results in
suspension for non-payment of dues, dimits and work for the Committee on Grievances and Appeals.
A system adopted in several jurisdictions by legislation, and in
others by custom, is the establishment of an informal Committee
before whom the candidates must appear and be examined previous
to the presentation of his application to the Lodge. By this method
there are two investigations in place of one, with corresponding
beneficial result.
KU KLUX KLAN
The history of this organization, its objects and purposes,
whether known or unknown and their offenses whether real or supposed have been so well exploited through the daily press that comment is unnecessary. Practically every Grand Master and the Grand
Lodges have assumed the position that the Klan is not a Masonic
organization and therefore Masonry should refrain from criticising
or entering into any controversy. In a few instances wher:e a Grand
Lodge has legislated the result has not been satisfactory.

THE MASONIC SERVICE ASSOCIATION

8

THE LADIES
The comment and criticism caused by the edict of Grand Master
Sills of Pennsylvan:a a few years ago against the Order of Eastern
Star has practically ceased. Pennsylvania appears to be satisfied,
so that should end the matter.

9

Like all new movements this Associat;on has been open to
doubt, fear and criticism. Judgment can only be passed upon the
results accomplished in States where the Grand Lodge is a member.
In some States there is no doubt that it has served and accomplished
great good. In others the financial expenditure has not been justified based on results.
To make the Masonic Service Association program effect:ve in
a large jurisdiction requires the creation of an active working body
with sufficient enthusiasm and money. Where this has not been
done the Association has perhaps been unjustly criticized. A
decision either for or against the Association must necessarily be
based upon the conditions applicable to each Jurisdiction.
PAST MASTERS
Whether the "Past Master's Degree" should be a part of the
Blue Lodge system is a moot question. Histor:cally the matter
is interesting. From a practical viewpoint any attempt to now embody the Degree in the Blue Lodge ritual, or make it a requirement
before installation, will continue to produce much controversy. The
Jurisdictions officially recognizing the degree appear to be satisfied with it and little trouble has arisen.
The ceremony, whether obligatory or not, however, can be
made of value to an incoming Master.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
This question, "like the poor, is always with us." The summary
contained in another portion of this Report from various States is
only given for general information. Where trouble has arisen it
appears to be more the result of resolving physical disability in
favor of the individual rather than for the general good of the
Fraternhy.
"PLAY GROUNDS OF MASONRY"
If the statement in some of the Proceedings reflect the activities
of certain of these Organizations there should be drastic legislation
in those particular places. They have however been few and far
between.
If it can be brought home to every individual Mason that even
if he is a member of another organization, he is Mason first and
bis conduct and conversation must be based upon that, there might
perhaps be less cause for complaint.
Disciplinary action against an offender through his Blue Lodge,
with adequate punishment, might do more to settle the matter than
wholesale legislation.
RELIEF

The method of extending relief whether through the individual
Lodge, a general fund maintained by the Grand Lodge, or through
the establishment of Homes, is ever present in the various jurisdic~
tions.
The yearly increase in members, the growing popularity of the
Masonic Fraternity and the public idea that it is an institution of
fabulous wealth have a bearing upon this question.
Some of the difficulties might be overcome by higher initiation
fees and dues in indiv;dual Lodges and a stricter investigation as
to the physical and financial condition of an applicant. This should
be ncit only as to the applicant, but also as to his immediate family.

ROUGH AND PERFECT ASHLARS
Last year we designated this subdivision "Found in the Rubbish
of the Temple." It was· not intended to imply that the activities
and good deeds of the various Jurisdictions were "rubbish." It was
the valuable part of the work of each Jurisd:ction taken from the

laws and rules and other matters through which the Chairman of a
Committee on Foreign Correspondence must wade.
In this Report we have changed the title and commend to our
readers every excerpt printed.
If we were permitted to pick out a "perfect ashlar" in this subdivision it would be that set forth under the caption, NEW
SOUTH WALES (1922). It was the gift of $500,000 by a former
Pennsylvanian (now residing in New South Wales) to establish
.there by the Grand Lodge of that Jurisdic1ion a College for Boys
and the appropriation by the Grand Lodge itself of $100,000 to supplement this great gift. This is practical Masonry.
TEMPLES

Any attempt to link Masonry with Religion, either for or
against, should be frowned upon. We part;cularly commend,· under
this subdivision, the statements from NEW MEXICO and UTAH.

The question of the Grand Lodge giving approval to the l"rection of Temples by individual Lodges is receiving consideration. Too
often a Lodge with a small membership desires to build, either for
advertising or commercial purposes, and without being properly
financed. Th's, in the long run, means disaster. There should be
some force to curb enthusiasm and also act in an advisory capacity.
Perhaps the easiest solution would be to allow no Temple to be
erected un1il sufficient funds have been collected to entirely pay for
it. This might curtail building operations for a time. It would
elim:nate one of the things that commercializes Masonry.

Cahada ( 1924) :
1
A more constant attendance may be secured by the vital sparks
of the Master and \Vardens charging the atmosphere of the Lodge
meetings. Look well to the East, \Vest and South; the North
(where is the revealed· light) will then take care of itself. Unless
the Officers of a Lodge are men of light and leadership, full of
kindling power, the agenda will drag and there will be many empty
interstices of precious time. Masonry, like nature, abhors a vacuum.
Fill every minute with good Craftsmanship-draw out latent talentgenerously but discriminatingly divide the work. It may sound
heretical bnt I personally would like to see the opening formalities
of the several degrees much shortened, and the Junior \Varden's
lecture-that gymnastic test of mnemonics-considerably curtailed,
or divided as it is in other jurisdictions. Encourage your members
not to come to Lodge alone-always bring a neighboring brother-·
there is great joy as we walk and talk by the way and a pleasant
companion is as good as a coach. Rain or shine commence on time
and have all your members realize that at every regular meeting
one-half hour will be specially featured along educational or inspirational lines, led by brethren whose pride it will be to prepare
and share. The apprentices have covenanted to learn; we have
covenated to teach. To secure a good attendance it is not necessary
to have buffoonery or vaudeville at the refreshment tahlc. Do not
mistake vulgarity for vivacity, or excitement for refined and happy
pleasure. Do not go beyond the liounds of the Craft for "talent,"
except in those rare cases where an outstanding public man (who
may not be a Mason), may be desirous of propagating the knowledge of some subject of general interest which he has made peculiarly his own. Above all let your members go away satisfied
and feeling that they have been factors in the work and social
pleasure of the Lodge, and not spectators and side-henchers only.
The eyes and ears are the way to the heart.

THE LAMBSKIN APRON

Kentuc\y (1922):
It seems that the Elli tor of the Home Journal wrote an article
explaining how the Apron should be worn in the different degrees.
This caused quite a little flurry, and finally the Chairman of the
Jurisprudence Committee was asked to decide the point, he did so in
quite an exhaustive report:
"The apron is to be worn in full view, flowing freely, and as
follows: First Degree, bib ap; Second Degree, bib down: Third
Degree, bib down, except that when worn as a mark of distinction,
the lower corners should he tucked np."
In sup\Jort of this regulation he states:
"I find that the plates in the Freemasons' Monitor, printed by
Thomas Smith \Vehb, in 1858, show that the aprons were worn as
directed by Regulation 18 of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky.
"I also find a Masonic Text Hook published. in 1866, nncler the
authority of the Grand Lodge of Tennessee, accords with this Regulation of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky."
He also quotes from Mackey:
"In this country there arc no distinctive decorations for the
aprons of the different symbolic degrees. The only mark of distinction is in the mode of wearing, and this differs in the different
jurisdictions, some wearing the Master's apron turned up at the
corner, and others the Fellow Craft's. The authority of Cross conclusively shows that he taught the former method, although the latter is now the more common."

for nobler deeds, for higher thoughts, for greater achievements, and
when at last your weary feet shall have come to the end of their
toilsome journey and from your nerveless grasp shall drop forever
the working tools of life, may the record of your thoughts and actions be as pure and spotless as this fair emblem which I place
within your hands tonight.
"And when your spiritual body shall stand, naked and alone,
before the great white throne, may it be your portion to hear from
Him who sitteth as a Judge Supreme: 'Well done, good and faithful servant, enter thou into joys of thy Lord.'"

BALLOT
District of Columbia (1924):
It was called to my attention that several brethren of the jurisdiction and members of various Lodges had signified their deliberate
intention to prevent the operation of the collective ballot by casting a black-ball, not against any of the petitioners, but as an expression of opposition to the principle of the collective ballot. In
the Lodges where this disposition had been manifested, I admonished the brethren that such action on the part of any Mason would
be a wilful violation of the law of the Grand Lodge, and that any
brother so offending should be placed on trial and, if found guilty
punished accordingly. The proposition of any brother passing upon
and rendering nugatory a law of the Fraternity, under the pretext
of the exercise of the right to vote as he sees fit, is intolerable and
subversive of every Masonic principle.

Maine (1923):
A member of a Lodge is invested with the right of ballot as
a Masonic trust, and it is a privilege which should be used by him
only in the execution of that trust, and not for the purpose of enabling him to gratify any individual or personal grievance, real or
supposed. And it makes no difference whether that grievance is en-

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

17

endered by a feeling against the Lodge or against the candidate
o be balloted for. I have no hesitancy in saying that a violatio11
o that trust and the casting of a ballot by a member for the purp e of enabling him to satisfy any personal feeling, is un-Masonic
an if clearly provable against such offending member, would furnish good cause for filing charges against such member for unMasqiic conduct.
\

Utah (1924)
The black-ball comes up for attention regularly in all parts of
the world, it seems. That the ballot hox is made use of to give point
to petty spite cannot be successfully c1uestioned. Masonic Lodges
are made up of human beings, and some of these "critters" cannot
be reached by any sort of appeal or environment-they were built on
a 2x4 plan and that is all there is to it. Spite work will go on, and
always there will be these Masonic "no-see-urns," as Indians characterize the pestiferous infinitesimal gnats that do their stinging un ·
seen but not unfelt, in our Masonic Lodges, but this obvious fact
should not, in our judgment, lead to modification of the rule in
general use of a unanimous ballot. The peace and harmony of the
Lodge is of vital importance and this condition can obtain only
where each member has opportunity to say "Yes" or "No" to every
applicant. There is an honorable and important use of the black-ball,
and it is used oftener, we are confident, for the good than it is to
the harm of the Fraternity.

"BOUQUETS AND BRICKBATS"
George F. Rodden, Grand Master, 1921
Canada: The Grand oration was delivered by Brother Harvey
D. Loveland. It has seldom been our privilege to read so learned
and so eloquent an address on the principles and influence of Masonry. He chose for his text a definition of science as "knowledge
classified and made available in work, in life and in search for
truth." It is paraphrased "as the science of life or of living as the
Great Architect intended man should live as a free man, free in all
that term implies, and rich in that freedom, because of having earned
and not inherited it."
Saskatchewan: The Grand Master's address is long and exhaustive in its details covering some fifty-eight pages and embracing
almost every act and detail that occurred during his term of office.
Yet it is not in any way dull, but runs along quite easily and is full
of interest from beginning to finish.

Fraternity to American citizenship. It is thoughtful as well as
merely forensic, it touches in a deep and vital way on the profounder meanings and implications of Masonry and is replete with
historical and literary allusion to enforce the main thesis, and we
are not surprised to find that "the brethren sat spellbound throughout the delivery of our brother's eloquent oration." It has worked

Missouri (1923):
These clubs are multiplying rapidly and their advent into Freemasonry portend danger, especially those organized along national
lines. This is obviously a stricture on the National League of M asonk
Clubs bnt the Committee in its extended reports makes out a good
case for its contention by saying: "A good illustration of the evils
that may arise from snch cluhs is that of the National League at
its recent session in Boston. The transactions of the opening session,
was a contest between the K. K. K. and Freemasonry. On the
closing day of the session a big 'Masonic parade' was scheduled.
This consisted of Masonic Clubs, the DeMolay and the Eastern Star,
etc." Surely there is something wrong here, unless such parade
was held by dispensation of the Grand Master of Massachusetts, and
under the authority and permission of the Grand Lodge. Unless
this was done, there was unwarranted assumption of authority by
the officers of the National League of Masonic Clubs.
Virginia (1924):
Fort Bayard, N cw Mexico, is one of the largest tubercular hospitals for ex-serviee men in tlfr United States. Our brethren of the
Grand Lodge of New Mexico are doing a wonderful work among
our Masonic brethren whom ill health has made participants iu the
Governme11t's provision for their restoration and care. They have
organized and financed what is known as "The Sojourners Club"
at this military reservation, where the courtesies and interests of
home life and the principles of Masonry and brotherhood are made
possible. \Vhile the Grand Jurisdiction of New Mexico has a Masonic membership of less than six thousand, its contribution to this
work amounts to over $8,000, and it has assumed proportions far
beyond the ability of our New J\Iexican brethren to adequately perform. In our opinion, it is a wonderful work. To the credit of the
brethren of New Mexico, it may be said that not a single member
of their Grand Jurisdiction is a patient in this hospital, and the work
which they are doing is for the brethren of the other Grand Jurisdictions of the country.
West Virginia (1923):
The Grand Master (California) recommended the organization of
a Masonic Club at the University of California. It is stated that there
are over 500 students in the university who are Freemasons, and it is
for their convenience that the club is to be established. To my mind
this is a very doubtful experiment, and is too much of a risk to be
undertaken by a Grand Lodge. There is no telling what a bunch of
college students will do when banded together, and I do not regard

30

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

it a safe proposition to allow them to bandy the name of Masonry
as a college organization. But I am opposed to Masonic clubs of any
kind at any place, or under any conditions_, Lodges are the places
where Masons should meet for the transaction of Masonic business and
nothing should be transacted, or allowed, in the name of Freemas~nry,
that could not be transacted within the tiled precincts of a Masonic
Lodge.

CRIMES AND CRIMINALS
Alberta (1923):
I regret the necessity of referring to the fact that a few of our
brethren have lost touch with us through yielding either to temptation or the pressure of circumstances, and have fallen from the high
standard of integrity or morality our principles require. While
anxious that every brotheF should receive every assistance and comfort when in trouble or distress, yet I am firmly of the opinion that
Masonry cannot excuse grave offenses against the well-recognized
laws of God and man and should purge itself of such offenders.
Further, I endorse the views expressed by some of my predecessor,,
that dissolute living must be discountenanced, and if persisted in by
any of our brethren, they should be fully disciplined.

Arkansas (1923):
Resolved, That it shall be the duty of the Junior \Varden of
a Lodge, when notified or advised that a member of the Lodge has
been convicted in any court of competent jurisdiction, of the offense of having violated either the State or National prohibitioll
laws, to procure a certified copy of such conviction, and present
it at the first meeting of the Lodge, and thereupon it shall be the
duty of the Lodge to expel or indefinitely suspend such member.
The failure of the Junior Warden or the Lodge to act in accordance with this resolution shall subject them to such discipline
as the Grand Master may determine.

Indiana (1923):
It is my order that the Lodges of Indiana take cognizance of
all cases where strictly Lodge matters are divulged to persons not
members of the Order, apprehend the guilty brothers and bring
them to trial. If found guilty, there are cases where the highest
penalty known to Masonic law should be inflicted. Each case, however, should be judged on its merits and the penalty made to tit
the case. The end to be accomplished is to effectually stop loose
talk by members or to terminate their membership.

Iowa (1923):
Among the gloomy portents of the day, he (Arkansas) mentions
expressly the disobedience of children, the modern dance, the movie,
and the abuses of the automobile, saying of the latter:
"Someone has said the Eighteenth Amendment saved our boys
from the saloon; now we need something to save our girls from the
garage. It has come to the point where a young man can get a girl
to go with him in the car, who wouldn't allow him in her parlor.
It is not a question whether a young man has any character now;
the question is, has he a car?"
He also deplores the waning influence of the home, sensationalism in the pulpit, official graft and political indifference, unpunished
crime and political demagogy.
Then at last he emerges from the dark chamber and gives testimony to the light breaking through the dark clouds when he says:
"Whose pictures get on the front pages anyhow? It is the
Yates Standridges, the Henry Starrs, the Dave Lockharts, and the
Fatty Arbuckles. But while this bunch of criminals feature the
front pages it must be remembered that the decent, home-loving,
law-abiding, hard-working, God-fearing citizen, who remains at
home and attends to his business, and supports his family and reads
his Bible and says his prayers, does not break into print, and they
outnumber the other ten thousand to one.
"Where there are 2,000 bootleggers in Arkansas there are 1,500,000 other persons who are not bootleggers but who arc living upright, decent lives, and nothing is said of them."

Maine (1924):
A very interesting and human letter from a young brother, who
had heard the Grand Master (Massachusetts) speak, is printed
(without signature) and shows how a man's influence may count on
the right side in some moment when he least expects it. \Vould that
all our Masonic words could have a like result. The young man
wrote: "When you made this touching appeal to all members to be
upright and regular Masons, I was sitting there in my Mother
Lodge with a pair of dice in one pocket, and a box of Merry \Vidows
in another, and had been, for some months, traveling about all the
gaits. After hearing you that evening, as soon as I could find a
place to make disposal of such things, I cleaned my pockets of everythin&; that I would not have my mother or any one of my sisters
see, and henceforth began a general house-cleaning. The result is,
a Christian man is writing you tonight, so that you may know just
what you have helped to bring about in my life."
In our idea that beats Billy Sunday and his type of frenzied
fanatical dragooning into the Kingdom of Heaven. Masonry is a
sane, wholesome, livable reality and when it grips the deeper nature
of a man is apt to be far more constructive and permanent in its
results on character and conduct than the emotional appeal of the
professional evangelist. Surely this incident and letter may well
stand forth as one of the noblest Masonic labors of Grand Master
Paul Murphy, and deserves extended mention in this review as perhaps (and this is the highest praise of the other achievements of his
administration) the masterpiece of his Grand Mastership.

One of the most interesting functions of the Foreign Correspondence Committee, is to peruse the comments of reviewers of other
jurisdictions upon our own reports and the actions of our Grand

One who writes, must be both the ant, collecting what is around him,
and also the spider, spinning the silken threads that shall hold objects

Connecticut (1924):
On the well-timed warning of G. M. Prince (Massachusetts) of
the danger of dragging Masonry as an organization into endorsement
of public policies, he sanguinely fails to "sense any danger,'' and points
to what Massachusett's Masons did in promoting liberty just before
and during the Revolution: But the latter, which by the way rests upon
tradition, was done by individuals and not, so far as we know, by organized Masonry. The danger of discussing public questions in Lodge
lies in the fact that there are likely to be several differing shades of
opinion on such matters. And even a majority vote endorsing any
policy is of only academic effect, and will not influence the positive
opinion of a single brother. Further, such academic endorsement sometimes makes us appear ridiculous. Better leave all such matters to individual opinion and action. Past history shows that on an average
the individual Mason can be trusted to spontaneously live up to his
patriotic and civic duties. We believe public opinion, while a gradually
moving force, is ever accretive and in the last analysis can be trusted
to finally settle matters rightly.

Vermont (1924):
Brother Darrah does not believe in making comment or criticism and so avoids both. In this, we differ with him, feeling that
the real purpose of a correspondence report is not to be read by
the grand officers or grand correspondents of other jurisdictions,
not primarily to exchange quip, compliment, or badinage with the
other correspondents; but is rather to enlighten the Masons of one's
own jurisdiction not only as to the acts, but also as to the laws,
usages and ideas of the brethren of other Grand Lodges. In thb
service and from this point of view, it seems competent to call
the attention of our brethren to such differences as to usage or ideas
as we may note; not in any spirit of carping criticism or fraternal
advice to other jurisdictions, but with the aim of broadening the
vision of our brethren in our own jurisdiction.

Iowa (1922):
The mere conferring of degrees upon a man never yet made a
Mason. The making of a Mason is no swift and sudden process. You
can no more turn a profane into a Mason by having his take an obligation than you can turn a pumpkin into a peach by making faces at
it. The making of a Mason consists in a continued course of education,
of training, of character formation. While in one limited sense it may
be true that it is the obligation that makes one a Mason, yet in a truer
and better sense a man is never a Mason until he loyally lives up to his
obligation, and he can't do that until he understands it-comes to really
know its scope and meaning.

a month-whatever they might require in the way of reading matter for
their members. The time is long past when Masons are content to be

Quebec (1923):
There is a dangerous tendency for a Lodge to become a mere

turned out under the impression that he is a Mason. Nothing could
, be worse than that. It is not the mental possession of certain secrets
that constitute' a Mason, but the fact that these secrets have entered
into the character and form the controlling force of life. A Mason
is not the product of one evening's session of a Lodge, but is the fruit
that springs from the seed of Masonic truth sown in the hearts of
honest men and carefully nurtured in a healthy Masonic atmosphere

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

the use of punch boards for the distribution of prizes in connection with
and under the auspices of constituent Lodges, is a reflection on
Masonry and not in keeping with the principles of our great Fraternity,
I deem it my duty to issue this order prohibiting such practice by any

.
If there is any one thing that Masonry stands for it is the upholdmg of the laws of our Commonwealth, and I am sorry to say, many of
the things being practiced today are in direct violation of the law.

The office of Grand Master existed long before there were any
Grand Lodges, which are of comparatively recent origin. Thev are
the successors of the General Assemblies, which prior to 1717. were
the whole body of the Craft meeting in annual session. At these assembly meetings a Grand Master was elected, and he retained the
office until the next General Assembly meeting. In the interval his
authority in the government of the Craft was unlimited. Hence grew·
up the rights and prerogatives which are considered inherent in the
office. These powers were never taken away from the office and cannot be taken away today by any modern legislation. He was elected
by the Craft and became its absolute ruler, being limited onlv in
power by the customs, usages and landmarks of the Fraternity. ·Out
of this grew the rights and powers inherent in his office.

New Jersey (1924):
The use of devices of questionable nature by members of the
Craft, in campaigns for raising of funds for purposes supposedly incidental to Lodges, has become a matter for serious consideration and
thought.
In December I received in every mail numerous protests from
brethren and Lodges against the activities of a certain Masonic Club
in a campaign to raise funds for the Masonic Home at Burlington. '
The device used was a punch card, and was in substance a game
of chance. In my opinion, a gambling device, pure and simple.
Campaigns of this or similar nature, conducted by Masons, are
conducive of inestimable injury to the Fraternity, and evidence but one
conclusion, that those responsible have failed to realize the ideals, purposes and great objects of the Institution.

Connecticut (1924):

District of Columbia (1924):
We recognize it as a landmark of the Craft that the Grand Master
has the right to preside over every assembly of the Craft wheresoever and whensoever held, and concomitant with this right is that of
visitation, which :Mackey says is the "right to enter any Lodge to inspect its proceedings, and to correct its errors. * * * Th~ right
is specifically recognized in the Regulations of 1721, but it is also an
inherent prerogative; for the Grand Master is, virtute officii, the head
of the whole Fraternity, and is not only entitled, but bound, in the
faithful discharge of his duty, to superintend the transactions of the
Craft, and to interfere in all congregations ot Masons to prevent the
commission of wrong, and to see that the landmarks and usages of
antiquity, and the constitutions and laws of the Grand Lodge, and of
every Lodge in the jurisdiction, are preserved and obeyed."

Illinois (1923):
If there is one thing which Freemasonry needs today more than anvthing else it is a universal platform embodying certain essential pri~­
ciples. For instance, the Grand Lodges of the United States should be
tmited upon the fundamentals necessary for the recognition of foreign
Grand Lodges. There should be uniform rules relating to the rejection
of candidates transfer of membership from oni; jurisdiction to another
without the taking of a dimit and other equally important matters,
concerning which there is at the present time such a diversity of opinion
and procedure. It would not hurt any Grand Lodge to surrender some
of its so-called inalienable rights and unite with other Grand Lodges
upon a universal platform to which all might agree. If this could be
accomplished, no harm would be done to any one. 'Whether it can be
hrought ahout remains to be seen. No doubt, an extensive campaign
of education would be necessary to bring the Grand Lodges of the
United States to a point where they would consent to a conference to
consider these matters. Even a conference when called would have a
vhy ·difficult time in getting a respectable bearing. A universal platform of Masonic principles would in no wise interfere with the idea
of a State Masonic sovereignty and would have not even a suggestion of national Grand Lodge, and there would be no national
president, national secretary, nor any other of the appurtenances
which belong to national organizations. All that would be necessary would be for the several Grand Jurisdictio11s to send representatives to a central point, let these representatives come to an agreement upon some of these questions and it would then be in order
for the several Grand Lodges to ratify what had been done. Each
Grand Lodge would necessarily have to make concessions. There
could be nothing in the way of domination. It would have to be
a game of give and take. Whether or not this can be accomplished

42

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

remains to be seen. It is a serious question whether the Craft have
advanced sufficiently far in their evolution as to make a universal
platform of principles. This writer believes it will come in time.
It is true that it is needed now, but only through education and
a spirit of forbearance will it be accomplished.

decisions, edicts, rulings, dispensations and other judicial acts of
the Grand Master to be referred to said board for consideration
and review, the decision of a majority to be final, and no_t subject
to review by Grand Lodge. So the Grand Lodge will not be
supreme, it has delegated its authority to a board within itself.
Utah (1924):
For some reason the report of the Committee on Grievances
and Appeals is given in full-names of the offenders, character of
the offense and all-why, we do not know, and always feel that
such a course is detrimental to the Craft. There will always be
dirty linen to wash, for Masons are just human beings, but we
might avoid flaunting this soiled stuff in the face of the public.
Now that the war is passed, it does seem as though the "speed
bug" might be eliminated along with cholera, typhoid, mosquitos
and other pestiferous and deadly scourges which produce such disastrous results. In this connection attention may well be directed
to the fact that the Committee on Appeals had fourteen cases
refe~red to it for consideration. The connection between this and
the "emergency" contagion may not be recognized, but we suspect
that they are closely tied together.

Washington ( 1923) :
The Grand Lodge of Michigan declined to pass an amendment
stipulating a minimum sum to be charged by the Lodges as dues.
The Jurisprudence Committee said:
"\Vhile it is true that many of the constituent Lodges in this
state fix the annual dues to be paid by the members at a ridiculously
small sum, and many of them at a sum which will not properly
pay the running expenses and maintenance of the Lodge, yet that
is a matter under the law which is exclusively for the Lodge to
decide. \Ve do not believe it is a reason why the right of each
constituent Lodge to make its own by-laws should be taken away."
In the matter of fees for the degrees they take a different stand.
"The fees for conferring the degrees should," they say, "according
to Masonic law, be used for Masonic charity, and it is upon this
ground that the Grand Lodge has a right to say what fees shall be
charged by a constituent Lodge for the degrees."
\Ve cannot quite see the point. In either case, it seems
to us it 1s the Lodge's business, so long as it violates
no law of Grand Lodge. If it really is Masonic law that the fee~
for the degrees be used for charity, why permit them to be used
for anything else? No doubt these Lodges which charge ridiculously small dues figure to recoup themselves out of the fees fo,the degrees. Thus the Grand Lodge of Michigan permits them
to violate Masonic law, but it regulates the charge for fees to
enable them to be charitable, whether they want to or not.
Many thoughtful brethren are coming to the opinion that we
are over-legislated. The constituent Lodge is more and more
being "managed" with a minutiae of direction that is taking away
from it all personality. It may be trite, and we have said this
before, but we shall keep on saying as long as we write or speak
on these lines, that a Masonic Lodge is a body of men, and should
be treated as such even hy its own representatives in Grand Lodge
assembled.
There has for a long while been quietly going on assumption of
power on the part of Grand Masters and Grand Lodges, plainly
speaking-usurpation. Grand Lodges and Grand Masters have no
powers except such as is delegated to them by the constituent
Lodges. Grand Lodges of bodies of limited and delegated powers
all original Masonic powers are, ex necessitate rei, visited in the
constituent Lodges, and Grand Lodges, and their presiding officers,

One phase comands our admiration, and that is the habit of
plain speech which seems to be such a feature of the Grand Lodge
(New York) methods. If the brethren are laggard, well they are
told of the fact, and this without any circumlocution at all. \Ve
sometimes wish they would use more of this method when they
find themselves launched on the usual cry which can be best
summed up in the American colloquialism: "God's own country."
No doubt the Great Architect of the Universe may act as a special
.Providence to the American nation, but surely the Creator also has
certain other little jobs to look after in regard to Freemasonry in
other quarters of the globe.

Illino:s (1924):
The writer attended the first meeting of this association and
remembers the modest plans which were in the minds of its promoters at that tlme. The plan was to erect a building in Alexandria that would be monumental in character and would contain
a room in which the trophies and relics of \Vashington might be
kept. In this building was also to be a lodge room in which the
I .ocal T.odge could find a permanent home and become custodian
of the building. At the first meeting it was suggested that $200,000 would be sufficient to carry out the enterprise, but it would
seem that the idea has grown and today there is in process of con-

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

struction a building which is estimated will cost almost $4,000,000
when completed. It is evident that the builders propose to construct the building piecemeal. by that is meant a section at a time
or as fast as funds are received for the progress of the work. About
$750,000 has been collected to date and this it is estimated will be
satisfactory for the foundation and superstructure. Two Grand
Lodges have refused to in any way recognize the association or to
contribute to its cause. They are Ohio and Wisconsin. Pi::obably
the brethren of these jurisdictions have very good reason for devoting their funds to other purposes. It seems that in connection
with this enterprise a new thought has been launched and that is, it
would have been far better to have erected the monument to Washington in the form of a Masonic university where the sons aml
daughters of Masons might have education under Masonic atmosphere and environment. It has been suggested that a great monument of stone and mortar will only serve to please the eye whereas
the Grand Masonic University with an abfe faculty would have been
a monument to Freemasonry of far greater importance.

The work of transforming the. hill itself is practically completed,
and the broad grass-covered terraces extending from top to bottom
of the hill, which are later to he artistically planted with trees and
shrubs, are now disclosed. The reinforced concrete foundation in
a solid mass lying over the entire top of the hill, covered by the
building, and which the engineers considered necessary to carry the
weight of so great a structure is finished, and upon this has been
erected a granite base course, 13 feet 2 1-4 inches high. This, with
its concrete backing, forms a wall 40 inches thick around the entire structure. The main entrance steps, up to. and including the
floor of the memorial hall, the administration rooms and the assembly room, arc all included in this base course as are also the
stage and amphitheatre of the auditorium.
The assembly hall takes up the center of this base course. On
each side of this assembly hall are four huge column 4 feet 6 inches
in diameter and 18 feet high. Each is cut from a single block of
green Conway granite, perfectly matched in color, without cracl<
or blemish. and most beautifully polished. Each of the 8 columns
weighs 20 . tons. They will support the columns of the memorial
hall directly above and serve as a foundation for the tower.
At this stage in the construction of the memorial one can hegin
to get an idea of its noble proportions. Standing 011 the now completed floor of the entrance porch, one is exactly on a level with the
balcony surrounding the dome of the Capitol Building over in the
City of Washington. The light which will top the tower of the memorial will be just 333 feet above the floor of this porch. This
light will not only add to the architcctual beauty of the memorial at
night, but by request of the United States Government, will be constructed so as to perform a practical service as a beacon and a
guide to aviators arriving and leaving the flying field at Fort Myer
nearby.
The cornerstone of the memorial was laid on November 1, 1923.
Amid a vast assemblage·, which has been called "the greatest gathering of Blue Lodge Masons as such since the world began," and in
the presence of the President of the United States, the Chief Justice
of the Supreme Court, Grand Masters and representatives from 49
Grand Jurisdictions of the United States, and many others.

Michigan (1923):
The world is full of memorials. Nature's memorials are seen in
mighty rivers, giant oaks and lofty mountains. There are memorials
of wa.r and peace, to victory and defeat, memorials of great joys
and bitter sorrows. There are the tombs of the great and the near
great. The Parthenon and the Pyramids.
At Bunker Hill and Lexington, and on a myriad of battlefields
a grateful country has sought to perpetuate in imperishable stone
the achievements of heroic sons.
At Arlington, the beautiful memorial theatre can be seen. where
slumber known, unknown, but honored dead of all our wars. Of
recent completion stands the Lincoln Memorial on the banks of the
Potomac, marble templed shrine, whose snow-white colonnades contain thirty-six Doric Columns, one for each State constituting the
Union at the time of Lincoln's death.

He invited attention to the grave of David Brearley, which had

Brearley was a general officer in the War of the Revolution and the

prayer book of the Church of England, which edition has been in
use ever since by the Episcopal Church here, and he did it so admirably that little room was left for extemporising, which has done
so much to preserve the purity of the Church.

Massachusetts (1922):
I quote from an incident, growing out of the anti-Masonic
Morgan excitement, when all Lodges were requested to surrender
their charters. The Charter of Jerusalem Lodge was bricked up in
a hole made for that purpose, by Major Wm. Parsons, in the great
chimney of his house. When the messenger of the Grand Lodge
demanded it he said he remembered having seen such a document,
but he had not seen it for a long time
If the messenger
would go to the house perhaps the women-folks could find it. He
himself had not seen it recently. Needless to say, the women-folks
could not find it.

Massachusetts (1922):
Brother Ferrell mentions an interesting "find." In an old inn
in the village of Cheshire, in an upper room, 15 by 30 feet, there
was found on its walls, painted in large circles, all the emblems of
our Craft. This room used to be the meeting place of Franklin
Lodge, chartered by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in 1794.
No mention of this Lodge is made in the records of the Grand
Lodge after 1829, so we guess it died a natural death about that
time. In the winter of 1921, while preparing to repaper the room,
the old emblems were discovered under four layers of wall paper.
The emblems have been carefully retouched, and it is hoped to
preserve this old Lodge Room as a memorial of the oldest Lodge
in Western Massachusetts.

* * * *
The Mason persecution arose out of the disappearance of one
William Morgan, which took place on September 12, 1826. How
one of Morgan's character was admitted to a Masonic body, if it
had been known at the time, is rather incomprehensible. He appears to have been of intemperate habits, envious, malicious, aml
vindictive in disposition. During the year 1825 serious difficulties
sprang up between Morgan and his Masonic brethren. He failed
to receive a contract to build a Masonic edifice at LeRoy, New
York, and further was not permitted to become a charter member
of a new Chapter at Batavia, New York. Soon after this he collaborated with one Miller, and published a so-called expose of Freemasonry. He was committed to Canandaigua jail on September 11
on a charge of petit larceny, and was released the next evening.
He left the jail with one Lawson with whom he appeared to be on
friendly terms. From that time nothing is known of him, except
that he disappeared. The Masonic Fraternity was charged with his
murder, which was of course ridiculous; if in any way true, it could
have only been the act of individuals, but there was no evidence of
even that. There is some evidence that he was bribed to leave the
country and that he was afterwards seen in foreign parts.

The Grand Secretary presented a memorandum showing that
neither John Adams or John Quincy Adams were ever members
of the Masonic Fraternity. While there was a John Adams who
took his degrees in a Lodge, it was not the John Adams who was
afterwards President of the United States.

Massachusetts (1924):
When George Washington was Commander-in-Chief of the
Continental Army, local history records that there was a meeting
of a Masonic Lodge on Cambridge Common, and one of the younger
privates, a farmer's boy who had joined the army, impelled by curiosity, peeped under the tent where this meeting of the Lodge was
being held, and there was the Commander-in-Chief of the American
Army sitting humbly among the brethren, while seated in the chair
of the Worshipful Master was a private of that army.
New Hampshire (1924):
President Franklin Pierce and our three signers of the Declaration are often named as having been of our Fraternity. After years
of effort to ascertain the truth, we can now say that only William
Whipple was a Mason.
New York (1923):
The idea that any woman should ever have been duly initiated
into the Society of Freemasonry has been poo-poohed by historians,
but Ireland, nevertheless, insists that one of her fair daughters was
duly initiated. The story goes that Elizabeth St. Leger, only
daughter of the first Viscount Doneraile, himself a Mason and
Grand Master in 1740, witnessed the proceedings of a Lodge, and
on revealing the fact to the Brethren, was promptly initiated in due
and ancient form to bind her to secrecy. This is supposed to have
happened about 1740. Later she became the Hon. Mrs. Aldworth.
Her Masonic apron is preserved at Newmarket House, in the County of Cork. A portrait showing her Masonic regalia is to be found
in many Irish Lodge Rooms. The lady is said to have been a member of Lodge No. 44, warranted in 1735, but the distinction is also
claimed for No. 95 and No. 150.

The Committee on Masonic History referred to the fact that

granted by the Grand Lodge of Missouri. The story continues:
On the very date that the Charter was received by the Worshipful Master the brethren opened a Lodge convened in the upper story
of a log building used ordinarily as a general store by the Senior
\.Varden, \Villiam T. Dougherty.
Necessarily the furnishings of the Lodge were crude, but they
filled the legal requirements. An improvised altar was made for the
time of a rough packing box. The record further points out that
the pertinent allusions of the Craft to the corn of nourishment, the
wine of refreshment, and the oil of joy, were not overlooked at
these pioneer proceedings, as the pedestal of the \Vorshipful Master was a flour barrel, the pedestal of the Senior \.Varden a barrel
of whiskey, and the Junior \.Varden a barrel uf pork.

Quebec (1923):
The discussion of something so abhorrent to the spirit of Freemasonry as we know it, as the idea of the admission of women !<J
the Lodges, lends a special interest to the following article contributed some time ago to the Philadelphia Public Ledger by the Marquise De FontC'noy:
Since the Paris "Ere ::\ouvelle" announces that the Grand Lodge
of France has declared itself by a majority in favor of the admission
of women to Freemasonry, it may be as well to recall the fact thac
this is no new departure. The popular heEef to the effect that Lord
Doneraile's daughter, the Hon. Elizabeth St. Leger, who died as
Mrs. Richard Aldworth, was the only woman Freemason is due to
a misapprehension. In the eighteenth century and in the early
years of the nineteenth century there were quite a large number of
Masonic Lodges in France, composed exclusively of women, practicing all the rites and initiated into all the secrets of the Craft.
In fact, in 1805 Empress Josephine was installed in office as
Grand Mistress of the Order of Women Freemasons of France. The
first feminine Lodge in France was founded in 1730, and had for its
Grand Mistress the Marquise de Courtehonne, and among its leading members the Comtesse <le Choiseul, the Comtesse de Polig-nac
and the Comtesse de Romane!, who sncceed~d Mme. de Chautcauroux as favorite of King Louis XV. In 1775 the Duchesse de

It is suggested that members of committees will do well to call
upon the applicant early in the progress of their investigation for
two reasons. First, to satisfy themselves as to his physical qualifications, for it may happen that the candidate will be found to be
disqualified in this respect, and the early discovery of this fact will
save much time and effort. Secondly, having met the applicant
they will appreciate more understandingly and be able to weigh
more intelligently what may be said to them concerning him than
would otherwise be the case.
A man may be better judged by his acts than by his words, and
some conclusions reached as to his character from the company he
keeps. Also the nature of his occupation will naturally have an
important bearing on the question of his desirability. Persons who
engage in any occupation that is subject to public criticism are .undesirable Masonic material.
Inquiry should be made as to the business standing of the applicant; whether he meets his obligations promptly; whether he has
a reputation for fair and honest dealing. If he is engaged in the
practice of a profession or calling inquiry as to his standing with
his fellows engaged in the same pursuits· will be likely to throw
considerable light upon his desirability.
Inquiry should be made as to the antecedents of the petitioner.
Inquiry as to his domestic relations should by no means be
neglected. If he is married, does he live with his wife and family?
What church, if any, does he or the members of his family attend?
If he has children, what schools or institutions do they attend?
If the applicant is past middle life, what explanation does he
give for having so long postponed knocking at our doors, and what
motive does he advance for the step he is now taking.
Regardless of the applicant's physical qualifications to comply
literally with the requirements imposed upon a candidate in the
degrees, what is the apparent condition of the applicant as to health?
Is there anything about his physical appearance to indicate the
probability of his becoming a charge upon the fraternity through ill
health? Is his sight or hearing defective?
Information as to membership in other fraternal organizations
may be enlightening as to his desirability as a member of our body,
as membership in certain organizations is at least pursuasive that
he is favorably regarded by his fellows.

Has he ever served in the Army or the Navy of the United
States, and if so, has he an honorable discharge?
What are his habits and appearance?
Bearing in mind the disastrous effects of introducing inharmonious or discordant elements into our Fraternity, inquiry should
be carefully made as to what manner of man the applicant is. Is
he a trouble maker? Is he contentious and disputatious? Is he
of the type which delights to array himself on the wrong side of
questions with no better purpose than to create a disturbance or to
be obstinate? Is there any stigma resting upon his past life which
would cause the public to misjudge our organization if he were admitted to membership? Masonry may and should forgive its erring
ones, and be charitable of their shortcomings; but it is no part of
its duty to admit to membership applicants for whom it would rteed
to apologize.

I kept a careful record of the answers given in response to my
questions, and hereby submit the rather startling results:
-Forty-six members were asked: "vVhy did you wish to become
a Mason?" Thirty-seven of these promptly replied that they wanted
to join for several reasons; that the Masons held a high standing in
their community, and that it was a good thing to belong; that they
wanted to be eligible to attend the Masonic dances and social functions; that they might go higher and be eligible for the good times
of the Shriners; that the Masonic pin was a valuable asset among
strangers, etc.
Qnly nine of the new members interviewed expressed themselves as having joined for the purpose of being of service to their
fellow man or for the good the knowledge they gained thereby
would do in upbuilding their own character and usefulness.
Only seventeen of the members interviewed had passed examination on the 3rd degree, although they had been members more
than six months-the time required by our by-laws for such examination.
My selection for Masons for this interview was made at random; taking the men as I chanced to meet them, so it would seem
that the situation is alarmingly typical, and gives one food for
serious thought.
Masonry cannot hope to build her rightful place in the world
if these conditions are allowed to prevail. There must be a remedy and it should be applied vigorously until the need has passed.

Massachusetts (1922):
Altogether too often a man is admitted because nothing ~an be
found against him. It is ·a question whether such a negative recommendation ought to open our doors. Rather, we ought to be able
to discover something in an applicant's character which will add
strength to the Institution.
It is rather startling to find that one-half of our membership
is made up of those who have been Masons less than seven years.
Here are 55,000 men who have not had the benefit of long Masonic
experience. They are men, who, with the proper schooling in the
principles, aims, and limitations of the Fraternity, will make Masonry strong and influential, but until this can be accomplished
should we not demand that men who seek admission to our Lodges
sihould be possessed of salient characteristics that will assure us,
at least potentially, of added strength.
Montana (1923):
Too many investigating committees see nothing for them to do

without investigation.
The result is there are too many who are members of the

During my administration as Grand Master, I undertook to
interview some of the new members of our Fraternity as to why
they sought membership in the order.

Saskatchewan (1922):

rejected, but, in my opinion, there is i1~measurably greater need for
a wholesome development in the Masonic knowledge and spirit of
our present membership than for numerical growth or the lure of
initiation fees.

KU KLUX KLAN
Alabama (1922)
I have been called on repeatedly from different periodicals over
the country to give an official expression relative to the Ku Klux
Klan. I replied to all such requests that I had neither commendation nor condemnation for this order and thought that I would
be overstepping the bounds of propriety to give an expression as
Grand Master; that so far as Alabama was concerned, Masonry
had no connection with this order, and that I refused to permit the
Grand Lodge of Alabama to become involved.
Arizona (1923):
During the year my attention has been called to the activities
thr~ughout the State of an organization known as the Ku Klux
Klan, and I have been asked to define the attitude of Masonry
toward the Klan as an organization as well as urged to take some
action as Grand Master to prevent members of the Masonic fraternity holding membership in the Klan. I have given the question
careful consideration and in my judgment the best policy seemed
to be one of passive resistance, or at least "hands off" until the socalled Klan had had an opportunity to demonstrate that it was
inimical to Masonry, or the fact that a Mason by reason of his
membership in the Klan, if such did exist, was thereby bringing
the Fraternity into disrepute. Masonry is constitutionally opposed
to mob violence or unlawful acts of any kind, and her attitude as
relates to law and order too well known to need defining; I could
therefore see no good reason why I should mix in the controversy
and place our Order in a questionable position by giving undue attention to an evident attempt to mix Masonry up with something in
which she has no interest.· Neither could I find any law or authority
by which I, as Grand Master, could forbid any member of the
Fraternity joining any other oganization if he so desired. The only
question to be decided was whether such membership brought the
Order into disrepute, and that could only be determined after said
membership had been acquired. Masonry, as I understand it, concedes to its members the right to freedom of thought and liberty
of action, holding them personally responsible for any discreditable
act that would reflect on the Fraternity.

Georgia (1922):
There has been more or less agitation over the Ku Klux Klan
throughout our country. Several of our Grand Masters have become
considerably exorcised over the matter, issuing pronouncements
against it. The question in my judgment· does not deserve consideration; Masonry has nothing to do with any clan, any society,
any organization, denominational or what not. Masonry stands
alone, fearless and unafraid, not courting any affiliation and denouncing no other organization. Masonry is founded on freedom of
thought and action; just so long as her membership live the lives
of good men and true; just so long as the principles of Masonry
are alive in our communities, just so long will we enjoy that freedom of speech and press that our fathers fought for, that freedom
which Masonry teaches, has taught for many centuries, and will
continue to teach in the centuries to come.
We know nothing of the Ku Klux Klan of the present day, but
any Southerner, whether a member or not a member of the organization, does know that existing conditions do not make it possible
for there to be any semblance of principle between that organiza··
tion and the original association of the days of reconstruction following the Civil War.

New South Wales (1923):
In the transactions of our sister Grand Jurisdictions of the
United States of America we find many references to this mysterious organization. Much has been written and more talked about it,
but comparatively little is known with certainty, probably because
those who are qualified to speak from personal knowledge are prevented by oath or secrecy from saying what they know. Much
of what is said is contradictory so it is evident that much of it is
untrue, but which is the true and which the false, and how much
there is of either, it is impossible for a non-member to say. Some
have indulged in extravagant laudation of the Klan, while others
have expressed themselves in terms of wholesale commendation.
Knowing, however, how much untruth is promulgated concerning
Freemasonry, we are unable to believe the best, and unwilling to
believe the worst that we hear about the Klan.
From impressions gathered during a recent trip through
America, the writer believes that the Ku Klux Klan was established when and where the law was particularly weak and inefficient,
and especially where the law had completely failed to protect
women and children, or to punish the perpetrators of a horrible
class of crime. It is said that the Klan succeeded in stamping out,
or at any rate greatly reducing, the number of crimes of this kind,
less by the barbarity of its punishments than by the psychological
effect of its methods.
The original reason for the organization of the Klan has almost passed away in America, yet that body grows in numbers anJ
in influence. What is its object? It is rumored that it has been
used to influence political elections by persuading (some say co··
ercing or intimidating) voters to- support the candidates approved by
the leaders of the Klan. Do we want that sort of thing in A ustralia?

Virginia (1923):
In the South, in reconstruction days, when fanaticism had put
the bottom rail on top, and when lawlessness was so rampant that
white people would have been massacred in large numbers, civilization required that there be an organization to enforce the law outside the pretended machinery of ludicrous pretences of courts.
The same was true in early days in many of the new Western
settlements in the days of the bad men. 'When these conditions
were corrected Vigilantes and Ku Klux Klan respectively disbanded.
Intolerance leads to anarchy. If Masonry does not influence its
votaries to live and let live in the American sense it has failed of
one of its chief missions. Membership in this foolish organization
should be a grave Masonic offense not to be tolerated.
Washington (1923):
Most Grand Masters and Grand Lodges have taken the stand
that it is none of our affairs so long as they go their own way, and
stand on their own bottom. In other words, we should mind our
own business so long as they do the same.
The writer Is unable to see how any man can be an honest
member of two institutions, one of which declares its purpose to
"unite men of every country, sect and opinion," while the other
definitely discriminates between peoples and sects. Several piece3
of literature have been put in our hands purporting to be issued

the principles of Masonry. One does. not need to go further than
their public declarations and printed matter to know that they are
not Masonic, and a Grand Lodge has a perfect right, if it so desires, to make all men choose between the two what membership
they will retain.

Human nature never changes. If you cannot ruin a man in any
other way you may do so by associating his name with a woman,
and no matter if it is the baldest calumny, the public will believe it.

It was brought to the notice of the board that a spurious and

Oklahoma (1923):
On the sixth day of April, 1922, there was born in the city of
McAlester an order for the daughters and sisters of Master Masons
and members of the Order of the Eastern Star, and for girls recommended by them, who are between the ages of fourteen and
eighteen years. It was named "Order of the Rainbow for Girls,"
and is fashioned after the Order of DeMolay for Boys. This new
order is the child of Right Worshipful Brother William Mark
Sexson, Grand Orator of this Grand Lodge. He, with the help
of some of his Masonic brethren and Eastern Star sisters, wrote
its constitution and ritual. It was made national in its scope,
and Supreme Council selected, with the home officers at McAlester,
in Oklahoma. The order is growing rapidly and now has assemblies, as its subordinate bodies ·are called, in nine States of the
Union, Oklahoma having forty-three.
The Order of DeMolay for Boys having been recognized as
worthy of the fostering care of the Masonic Service Association,
we believe the Order of the Rainbow for Girls to be also worthy,
for the girl question is just as great and just as important as the
boy question. The girls will be equal sharers in the burden of
citizenship, and deserve the same care and advice accorded the boys.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORHESPONDENCE

Among the notable things done by the Grand Master was to
issue a letter to the Lodges calling their attention to the necessity
of impressing upon the minds of our members the importance of
bridling their tongues and keeping the business of the Lodge more
secret. It is a fine precedent to be followed in most other jurisdictions. Among other instances, he cited the case of a brother
charged, tried and expelled from a Lodge. Before leaving the
building some of the brethren called their wives on the phone and
told them all about it. It reminds us of the cruel anecdote about
a little boy asking his father the meaning of "broadcasting." The
brute replied: "Son, it means telling a secret to one's wife!" It
is gossip (we distinctly disclaim authorship) that certain members
of a female near-Masonic organization have no difficulty in finding
out· what takes place in their husbands' Lodges, to the limit of
their curiosity.

It is natural for large Lodges to receive many petitions for
the degrees. In consequence of which, the Master and officers
arrange their trestle-board accordingly, thereby preventing confusion or delay, and thus avoid converting the Lodge into a mere
degree machine; in many instances the members are encouraged
to join in all its activities and assist the officers in conferring
the degrees.
The conditions here are somewhat different from those in
older Grand Jurisdictions, because the membership is not constant. We find that the non-resident membership of our Lodges is
about twenty-five per cent; a large number are life members;
quite a number are exempt from dues, and the losses by death and
dimission are many. As the membership grows older and more
scattered, the demands on the treasury become greater; hence,
it is necessary to recuperate by the only lawful process in order
to meet the necessities and retain undiminished interest. There
are various other details concerning this subject which we might
set forth, but as many of you are more or less familiar with
them, we deem it unnecessary at this time.
We have corresponded with the officers of several Grand
Jurisdictions who have had this subject under consideration for
many years; have read their interesting, exhaustive and admirable
committee reports, the earnest arguments advanced, the presentation of facts, and find they have aroused widespread interest and
comm~nt-both for and against the proposition.
Those of our brethren who desire further light on this question
are fraternally referred to the exhaustive reports in the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts for 1920-1921, Nebraska
1918, Ohio 1920, North Dakota 1922, and Utah 1921-1922.
In all our investigation we were unable to find a Grand Jurisdiction which had adopted a by-law limiting the size of Lodges,
or the number of candidates to be admitted during the Masonic
year, but many instances were noted where Grand Jurisdictions
adhered strictly to the observance of the general regulation of a
Lodge making· but five Master Masons in any one day.
After careful investigation, due deliberation and satisfying ourselves as to the condition of the membership in our larger Lodges,
and the future effect it would have financially in curtailing the
true Masonic work now being performed by them and eventually
placing limitations upon the growth, influence and power of our
great Fraternity, your committee is of the opinion that it would
be unwise to recommend the adoption of a by-law limiting the
membership of Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction.

LARGE LODGES
Colorado (1923):
The result of our investigation discloses that at the present
time our large Lodges are inculcating the true teachings of the
Craft, they observe the hours of labor and refreshment, and that
genuine fraternity exists. Frequently their time is employed in
the proper Masonic development of the brethren by instructive
lectures and discourses on Masonic subjects; occasionally social
family gatherings are held in the temples, so that no member
has cause to complain of not receiving brotherly and hospitable
attention. In cases of distress, illness or the passing on of a
brother, or member of his family, the sympathy and duties of
the Lodge are fully extended in the proper Masonic manner.

Nevada (1923):
The question is not so much the size of the Lodge as it is
whether the Lodge functions as a Masonic body should. We have
found some large Lodges doing a greater work than some small
ones.
New Hampshire (1924):
Finding a finer atmosphere in the Lodges of smaller membership than in the largest Lodges, the Grand Master asked the Grand
Lodge to consider the advisability of limiting Lodges to a membership not exceeding 500. We have known for many years that real
Freemasonry is existent in the small
but have not yet
been convinced that a Grand lodge should undertake to fix a
maximum in this respect. A good way .to accomplish it has not

New South Wales (1923):
One question which arises out of the great development which
is taking place in Freemasonry throughout the English-speaking
world is that of the increase in the size of Lodges. Several issues
are raised, one being the question as to how far the influx affects
the work carried out in Lodge, having in view the fact that a
great number of candidates connotes a great amount of time in the
carrying through of the work in the degrees. Of course one should
not object to sitting through the meetings so long as new and
properly accredited members are entering the Order, but it stands
to reason that the most enthusiastic brother will hardly find it
attractive to sit for hours, night after night, watching and hearing
the same. thing being done and said. Yet this is obviously what
must happen when the number of candidates reaches such dimensions as we find in some American Lodges, and even some Australian Lodges.

Illinois (1923):
The Masonic Service Association continues and is apparently

the organization and the general "feeling has been that the association is striving to do a good work and that it should be properly
encouraged. The Grand Master of one Grand Lodge stated that

practically no benefit whatsoever had been derived. He said this
was no fault of the association, but on the contrary was due to

offered. In other words the jurisdiction lacked internal organization which must co-operate with the efforts of the Masonic Service
Association in order to make them effective. There are some jurisdictions so thoroughly intrenched in their ideas of State sovereignty
that they will refuse to unite with any enterprise which they do
not initiate and sponsor. These Grand Lodges will hold aloof from
the Masonic Service Association and decline to give it any assistance whatsoever.
