MASONIC INTERNATIONAL ASSOCIATION
North Carolina (1924):
\Ve find in this volume (New York, 1923) first-hand information concerning the Masonic International Association. It was
held at Geneva, Switzerland, October 18-23, 1921. We quote the
following to show of whom it was composed and what it did:
"Eleven European Grand Jurisdictions were represented by delegates at this conference. New York was the only American jurisdiction present. As a result of this conference the Masonic International Association was organized, and a charter or declaration
of principles adopted, which charter was subscribed to and signed
without reservation by the representatives of all the jurisdictions
except New York and Holland, which signed subject to the ratification by their respective Grand Lodges.
"Upon its return to this country, your delegation to that conference under date of December 12, 1921, made a report of the
work of the conference, and of the part had therein by them, to
the Grand Master and which report contained a statement of the
delegation's view of the accomplishments of the conference as follows:
"1. The conference established an agency through which all
Grand Lodges are enabled to deal with one another in their efforts
to get at the truth concerning each other, this facilitating their
getting the facts upon which to base their several judgmen1' of

each other, instead of having to rely and act largely upon hearsay,
as has been the case in the past.
"2. Contact between jurisdictions is afforded without their being
in diplomatic relations with o.ne another, through their joint membership in the association. Recognition and diplomatic relations
will begin only when agreeable to those concerned.
"3. The membership of Grand Lodges belonging to the asso·
ciation must be composed of men exclusively. Thus woman Masonry, as a part of the Order, is disposed of.
"4. Members of the association respect the territorial integrity
and jurisdiction of each other member. Foreign Lodges within
our territory, chartered by legitimate Grand Lodges acting, however, in hostility to our claims of exclusive territorial jurisdiction,
will be eliminated.
"5. Grand Lodges maintain each its entire sovereign independence.
"6. The association has no concern with matters other than
those of its own organization and functioning.
New York controls the question of membership in the association so far as the United States are concerned and thereby is
in a position to eliminate recognition of clandestine bodies in the
United States which in Europe heretofore have often, through ignorance, been recognized, and thereby have been enabled by pointto such recognition to give themselves the semblance of legitimacy and use it to further their fraudulent schemes.

District of Col urnbia ( 1924) :
Resolved. "That it is the sense of the Grand Lodge that duly
installed Ma~ters of constituent Lodges in this jurisdiction are
entitled to sit in a Lodge of actual Past Masters."
The presentation of this resolution grew out of the refusal of
the Assistant Grand Lecturer to admit three of the Masters of Lodges
of this jurisdiction into an emergent Lodge of actual Past Masters
convened by direction of the Grand Mas'ter to confer the Past
Master's degree on Masters-elect, who were not already invested
with it, in a Lodge of actual Past Masters or in a Royal Arch
Chapter, the admission being denied on the ground that they had
not themselves been invested with the Past Master's degree in a
Lodge of actual Past Masters, and thus had not become actual
Past Masters, but only in a Royal Arch Chapter, and thus were
only nominal or virtual Past :\,fasters.
It is true that the practice has been in this jurisdiction for a
long period of years to recognize the Past Master's degree conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter for the purpose of installation requirements of the Master-elect of a Symbolic Lodge. A discussion
of whether that practice is right or wrong, or whether receiving the
degree in a Royal Arch Chapter entitles the recipient to sit in an
emergent Lodge of actual Past Masters, need not be entered upon
at this time, as these questions are not involved in the pending
resolution.
Mackey in his book on Masonic Jurisprudence says that the
Past Master's degree is conferred in a Symbolic Lodge as an honorarium upon a duly elected Master and as a part of the installation
ceremony. He also says that Past Masters and installed Masters,
although not having been twelve months in the chair, are in Masonic law identical, and that the Master of a Lodge becomes a Past
Master, for all legal purposes, as soon as he is installed.
We think with Mackey that they were Past Masters for legal
purposes pertaining to installation and were entitled to sit in the
emergent Lodge of actual Past Masters.

Alabama (1923):
We have constantly maintained that there should not be a
rush ~or "higher degrees" or "side shows" in Masonry, but, to save
our. hves, we cannot see in what respect an audience composed
entirely of 1fasons would desecrate a Masonic hall. We know
that it is an almost universal custom for Royal Arch Masons
Knights Templar and the Order of the Eastern Star to meet i~
Masonic halls, and we can see no reason why the Order of the
Grotto should not be accorded the same privilege.
We quite agree with the Grand Master that many young mer.
ioin the Masonic Fraternity in order to become "Shriners." We

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

77

would discourage this practice, but we cannot follow the Grand
Master in his remarks relative to the Shrine and Grotto when it
comes to a question of charity. Our observation and experience
has been that members of the Shrine and Grotto are much more
charitable than many Blue Lodge members who have not missed
a meeting for a quarter of a century and who hold in reverence and
veneration the walls and furniture of the Lodge above charity and
brotherly love. Our idea is that a Lodge is composed of men
and not mortar, brick and wood.

* * * *
Far be it from us to intimate that the "higher degrees" and
"side shows" should in any way supplant the Blue Lodge; the
Blue Lodge degrees comprise real Masonry and we think Master
Masons should "wait a time with patience" before applying for
"higher degrees" and that they should be thoroughly conversant
with the ritual and tenets of the Order before attempting to
advance to the so-called "higher degrees."

Manitoba (1922):
There are two clouds in the Masonic skies, one restricted
as yet to the United States, while the other is spreading and becoming more general. The first is the deviating from established
customs by a number of Grand Jurisdictions through the passing
by them of motions concerning legislation of a public nature being
dealt with by State or National legislatures.
Masons are all, or should be, vitally interested in educational
policies, but whether action should be taken by them in their
capacity as citizens or as a Masonic body is open to argument,
but the great danger as I see it is that if the latter policy was
agreed on, where do we draw the line?
The other cloud is the multiplying of orders requiring as a
pre-requisite for membership Masonic standing or relationship.
In addition to the well-known branches of the Scottish Rite,
Chapter, Council, Preceptory and Shrine, we find mention made of
The Mystic Order of the Veiled Prophets of the Enchanted Realm,
more familiarly known as The Grotto; The Tall Cedars of Lebanon;
The Order of the Pyramids; The Egyptian Mystics; The White
Shrine of Jerusalem; The Sciots; The Sons of Hiram; The Order
of the Eastern Star; The Order of Builders; The Order of the Rainbow; The Daughters of Job; The Order De Molay; and the end
is not yet. Even the Ku Klux Klan through its organizers is claiming Masonic affiliation.
To some this popularity of Masonry may appeal, but to me
it would look as though the superstructure was becoming top-

Alabama, Michigan and Vermont have abandoned the perfect

Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire an<l our own

West Australia (1923):
This question of physical perfection seems never to be absent
from the proceedings of some of the American Grand Lodges,
and whv it should :be so we are at a loss to understa,nd. Jn. the
old op;rative days it was necessary that an apprentice should

a man's limbs. The West Australian rule has justice and common
sense to recommend it-"That a candidate is eligible for initiation
who, although not perfect in his limbs, is able substantively to

Illino!s (1922):
It is just beginning to dawn upon members of the Craft that
Freemasonry is in a sense a sort of insurance which carries with
it the care of the member and his family in case of dire need. Now,
it is not supposed for one moment that the Fraternity is going
to take into its ranks anyone who is likely to become a burden
on it. In fact, most Lodges are very discriminating in this matter
,and take great pains in looking up a prospective candidate in order
to ascertain just what liability he is going to prove himself, but
that does not argue that every man who enters the Masonic Fraernity is going to be exempt from the need of help from his brethren.
The Masonic Fraternity is a guarantee that if a man loses
his fortune and becomes in need, or if through sickness he finds
himself reduced in circumstances, or if he passes on and his family
are left without proper means of support, then the Masonic Fraternity steps in and does its part in caring for those who are dependent.
Perhaps when the man joined the Masonic Fraternity he
was in splendid circumstances, but misfortune overtook him. When
a man takes out life insurance he is supposed to be in a perfect
condition of health, but the insurance company knows he is a
liability and do not know just how soon he will be dependent
upon it. While Freemasonry is not sold in the sense of being
life insurance, yet members of the Fraternity are commencing to
realize that the man who joins the Fraternity gets a sort of an
insurance.

The old charges required that the applicant should not only
have the physical qualifications imposed under our law, but should
have the financial ability to not only provide a good living for

day a gentle reminder can do no harm. In the Lodge room Masonry inculcates the principles of love and benevolence· too often

A delicate situation developed between the Grand Lodges of

from a local Lodge and, against the advice of her Masonic and

was derived therefrom.

South Australia (1924):
Of all the adjuncts in Freemasonry the Shriners have best justified their existence inasmuch as they have, with a membership
of over half a million in the United States and Canada, undertaken
to erect, equip and maintain a wheel or chain of hospitals for the
relief or care of crippled or deformed children. A million dollars
are furnished annually for the philanthropic work. Crippled or malformed children regardless of color or creed or nationality, lfasonically connected or otherwise are admitted and cared for or helped,
without cost or charge, the only restriction being that they b~
nnder fourteen years of age, and that their parents or guardians be
unable to pay for treatment in regular hospitals.

Connecticut (1924) :
A resolution declaring for reading the Bible in puhlic schools
was the subject of a favorable majority Committee report (Arizona)
and an adverse minority report. The resolution was finally tabled
after a lengthy discussion pro and con. The main opposition centered on a point made by a clergyman that any passage read, especially from psalms would inevitably arouse discussion. A brother
who had been a member of a school board asserted that it would
be seized upon as religious instruction. While your reporter believes in the Bible as the best book extant and crammed full of
sound philosophy and ethics, we feel that compulsory reading of
it in schools is a questionable expediency.

Our Government is not exclusively a white man's government,

in the sense that the liberties, privileges, opportunities, and all the
good things of the American Republic are for one class alone or
that one class or race or creed may dominate all others in respect of
their liberties, rights and privileges, and never will be such a government if the ideals and purposes of the patriot fathers, the founders of our republic, are perpetuated. Ours is a great democracy,

against Catholic, Jew against Gentile, the white man against the
black man, without inpairing the sta~ility and imperiling the perpetuity of our republic. Our democracy permanently endure unless
all classes, creeds and races are allowed to live and work and worship freely and peaceably under the equal protection of the law.

religious bigotry or class antagonisms or race prejudices will be deprecated and deplored by men who love theif' country and who
want to keep it noble and make its future greater.

South Carolina (1924):
As to confering degrees on Ministers of God free of charge, we
threshed this out with Brother Louis Block of Iowa in 1915, and
will quote one paragraph therefrom:
"Clergymen, as a rule, a,re by far the worst paid set of men we
have among us. They have litle or no chance of making more than
their meagre salaries, while the claims on their resources, from
their very calling, are far greater than those made on any other
class of men, leaving them, as a rule, barely sufficient to keep the
souls and bodies of their families together. Their presence, again
from their calling,. in any society of man, tend to keep conversation
within due bounds. As comparatively few could afford, with justice to their families, to pay for Masonic degrees, for the reasons
above stated, Lodges should be allowed to admit them to membership as an honor conferred on their profession."
According to authentic statistics, there are in this country 160,000 Protestant ministers who have charge of 207,000 churches,
with a membership of more than 25,000,000. Of these, perhaps 12,000,000 persons are regular and consistent attendants upon public
worship. On this basis each minister has the spiritual responsibility for the well-being of 150 persons, and the average salary paid him
is between fiv~ hundred and six hundred dollars, or from $12 to $15
a week.

Tasmania ( 1924)
My attention has lately been drawn to an objectionable practice
which has again made its appearance amongst the members of the
Craft. I allude to the matter of a chain prayer. Some years ago
this abuse became so flagrant that the Grand Lodge of England
condemned it, and the brethren were asked to abstain from circulating or signing any such documents, and in this connecti?n ~he
Grand Master of New South Wales, at the quarterly commu111cat1on

every Freemason, but this should be the fervent outpouring of th_e
heart of the humble supplicant, the creature in the presence of his
Divine Creator, for mercy, not only for ourselves, but for our
brethren all the world over. The chain prayer reminds one of the
custom of the ignorant, but pious people of Thibet, who pas~e a
few thousand written prayers within a revolving barrel, and consider
them duly recited when they have turned the barrel once or twice.
Moreover the appeal to that little vein of superstition by the veiled
threat of 'dire calamity to any individual breaking the chain is utterly unworthy of anyone professing adherence to our great and
heavenly-inspired system of morality."
I endorse those views, and sincerely trust that the chain prayer
will receive no encouragement from the members of any Lodge
in this jurisdiction.

Chaplain. Nevertheless, we do not think the theme chosen is one
that should be presented on such an occasion, where Jews and perhaps Mohammedans as well as Christians are present. It is introducing a question of controversial theology which our regulations
prohibit bringing forward in a Masonic Lodge.

Kansas (1924):

South Carolina (1924):
Almost every Mason writer since that time has either wholly
or partially agreed with Mackey's list of landmarks or taken exceptions to it, proving conclusively, at least to himself, its incorrectness and has ended by proposing a list of his own. Findel
mentions four, Crawley three, Simons fifteen, Morris seventeen,
Pound seven and many others, differing widely. This variance of
opinion, of course, is also found in the laws of our several Grand
Lodges.
Each Grand Lodge is sovereign in its own jurisdiction and may
define what it will recognize as landmarks. And so we find seven
in West Virginia, ten in New Jersey, thirty-one in New York,
thirty-nine in Nevada and fifty-four in Kentucky. Massachusetts
mentions seven but admits that number is not exclusive. Nine jurisdictions state the "Old Charges" contain the landmark but they
do not specifically enumerate them.
It is apparent that all of these Grand Lodges cannot be right,
yet each is conscientious and sincere in its own belief. We will

violates the landmarks of Freemasonry, and yet, we are in harmonious correspondence with all these jurisdictions.

Virginia (1924):
The Master's duties include more than conferring degrees, and
he should not confine himself exclusively to his sacred precincts in
the East. Wardens should be encouraged to do more degree work,
and the Master permitted to give more time to the supervision aild
direction of the Lodge's activities. No brother, however humble,
should fail to receive a word of greeting from the Master, and
Senior Deacons should put a proper emphasis on the importance
of the introduction and accommodations of visiting brethren. Opportunities for social intercourse should be given a place in the life
of the Lodge, and a roster of the widows and the orphans of our
deceased brethren kept so that they may not be overlooked.
And, lastly, all degree work should be done with dignity and
decorum, and made as impressive as possible. Candidates should
be courteously treated and not subjected to embarrassment or ridicule, or their minds filled with disturbing apprehensions.

(South Dakota) Resolved, That while we fully endorse the
protests and pronouncements against the circulation of so-called

Several Grand Lodges have tried expedients to gain the much
desired end of having the newly made Masons taught the Master's
Degree, for their own benefit, of course, but so far nothing seems
to succeed. A few of our city Lodges have resorted to the persuasive method. They appoint at each Communication two young

to exemplify the catechism of that degree. This, it is believed,
will spur them up to learn it and then two others will be selected
for next time. This looks promising. Competition is always a
stimulant and is better than imposing a penalty. Certainly the
plan of denying a right to vote or hold office until proficient seems
everywhere a failure.

but has great value in that it shows how great is the public appreciation of Masonry in the United States.

Many of the Lodges in Illinois hold their stated communications on some specified day of the week "on or before the full
moon of each month." It so happened that during the last Masonic
year there was no full moon during the month of December and
many of the Lodges were uncertain whether their annual meetings
could lawfully be held in December. The volume of correspondence became so great that it got on the nerves of the Grand
Master and to one inquirer he stated:
"I do not know whether the Egyptians in the time of Ptolemy
had discarded this antiquated and prehistoric system of calculating
time or not, but I thought they did soon afterward at least."

Washington (1923):
I like enthusiasm. It is the greatest motive power in the
world, but there are times when enthusiasm in the planning of
Masonic temples overshadows good business judgment, and the
success or failure reflects on Masonry in the community. Besides,
from an effort to carry overhead expenses, the Masonic hall is
rented for the purposes that are not altogether creditable to our Fraternity.
I therefore recommend that in the planning of Masonic temples
in the future, where the Lodge does not have the enterprise properly financed, the Grand Lodge require that plans and specifications be submitted to the Most Worshipful Grand Master for his
approval.

But I do not approve, I earnestly condemn, those so-called

An amendment covering all excrescent organizations W<\S submitted and carried in the following form:
"That as regards any organization, lodge or society unaffiliated
with, or not now recognized by Masonry in our jurisdiction, it
shall be and is hereby declared to be improper and unlawful for
any Freemason under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge to
become a member of such an organization, lodge or society, if
membership in the Craft is in any way or to any extent a prerequisite to membership therein, unless such organization, lodge or
society at the time has received and continues to possess the express recognition and approval of this Grand Lodge. In the event
of any question arising as to whether any particular organization,
lodge or society now in operation "requires the recognition and
approval of this Grand Lodge, the question shall be decided by
the Board of General Purposes,· subject to review hy this Grand

may call for Masonic recognition in this form; but temporary
gatherings of individuals, transient cullective interests social clubs
sections of associations, or mere personal friendships do not furnish
a sufficient cause.
No attempt should be made by any form of pressure to obtain
signatures to the petition, and a large number of signatures is not
to be aimed at. A sufficient total of qualified Masons prepared
to vouch the necessity for, and promise the performance of, the
proposed Lodge will carry more weight than a great many gathered
for the sake of demonstration. No brother who has not been a
Master Mason three years should sign; and it is undesirable that
any brother should do so who is not prepared actively to assist
in the conduct of the proposed Lodge. The Lodge which is asked
to endorse a petition should be made fully acquainted with the
reasons for its presentation, and should satisfy itself by inquiry
that these reasons are adequate. The endorsement should not be
regarded as a formal act, but as a deliberate approval, for which
full reason could be given.
The desired title should be simple and appropriate; and if
the proposed Lodge has a special character, this should be signified
by the name. A Lodge should not be named after any brother,
living or dead, unless he is, or has been, of the highest eminence
in the Craft; and, if a suggested title be of a professional nature,
it should be linked with such a limitation as not to embrace within
a local circle an influence or interest which is widespread. The
petitioners, moreover, must show that they can secure thoroughly
suitable accommodation for the proposed Lodge, but no arrangements for its consecration are to be made and no announcement
concerning it issued until the Petitioners receive an intimation
that a warrant has been granted.
In every case it should be clearly understood that no attempt
must be made to obtain signature to a petition by advertisement
or public announcement of any kind, and that in every case it
must be made evident that the Lodge is not to be used for professional advancement or commercial gain. No petition, indeed,
should be presented unless it ·can be shown that the proposed lodge
is not only desirable in the opinion of individuals, but is called
for in the interests of the Craft.

Chile (1923):
Freemasons are not permitted to own real estate in the Republic
of Chile. So Chileno citizens built the Club of the Republic, and
in that building the Masons hold their meetings in Santiago. The
club was wrecked in the fire, and $300,000 is wanted to rebuild.
District of Columbia (1923):
We would like to remind our readers that already 23 States
in the Union have legalized "Columbus Day" as a holiday. The
College of Cardinals has discussed making Columbus the patron
saint of all America, and effort has been made by the Knights of
Co1umbus to get an act of Congress to legalize the day in the
Territories and District of Columbia, but failed. They claim that
as Columbus discovered America he should be its saint. For a
fact his discoveries were limited to the Bahamas and Antilles, and
he never once set foot on the continent of North America, and
was a Jew.

Kansas (1924):
The practice of using the public press as a means of informing
the membership of the contemplated action of their Lodge, or
announcing official transactions of the same, has grown to such
an extent that some Grand Masters have found it necessary to
issue official communications and edicts forbidding the same.
This is in. keeping with the edict issued by our own Grand
Master during the year along the same lin~s, limiting the use of
the public press to that of funeral and other local Masonic notices.
We doubt not that the practice of publicity is prompted largely by
a desire on the part of many of our Symbolic Lodges to ape the
methods used in some of the other bodies.

Lodge of Kentucky.

Grand Lodge "sanctioned and approved" of the formation of

Maryland (1923):
This Lodge has organized its workers into a welfare committee,
which has classified its membership into districts and groups; lieutenants have been assigned to each group, so that within a few minutes any member of the Lodge can be reached either in person or by
phone. A personal canvass of the membership has been conducted
and the effect of this organized action has been remarkable. Men
have been to Lodge who have not been out in years; the forgotten
old and sick have been looked after, positions have been obtained
for the unemployed, and non-resident members have been communicated with and kept in touch with the activities of the Lodge.

All those hereafter initiated, passed and raised shall become
proficient in each degree and shall give proof thereof by examination in open lodge. After such examination the Master may, if
there is no objection made, declare the brother proficient. If objection i!\ made the Master shall put the question: "Is the brother
proficient?" and the question shall be decided by a majority vote
to the members present. The Secretary shall make a record that
the examination was had and the action of the Lodge upon the
same.
Examination of all those hereafter raised to the degree of Master Mason shall be had not later than ninety days following the
conferring of said degree, but the Lodge may for good cause shown
extend the time, but not for more than six months after the cjegree
is conferred; provided, that the Grand Master may extend the time
for good cause shown.
A brother refusing to qualify and pass an examination as providea by Section 65 renders himself liable to charges. No one hereafter made a Master Mason shall be entitled to demit, a diploma,
nor to hold an office in a Lodge, until he has complied with said
section.

New Jersey (1923):
The Grand Master reports that upon a careful investigation
of the doings of the Lodges, he finds that during the year almost
$150,000 was expended by the Lodges in entertainments and refreshments, while only about one-third of that amount was expended for charity. He reports that this is a serious wrong that
will soon work incalculable injury to the Fraternity.

Question: Last fall our Worshipful and four of the brethren
of "S" lodge No ......... , took a boy from the church house and had

the church what was up. Has he violated Masonic law and how

Answer: Yes. If the Master has been re-elected for the present

Michigan, on its petition for the degrees, provides for the rejection of candidates addicted to profanity.
We haven't seen a better thing in years than this. We do
not believe a Mason can be consistent and use the name of God
profanely. We think such as are addicted to this habit should be
kept out by ballot.
North Dakota (1923):
About two years ago there was appointed a Children's Code
Commission. The result of their labor in this connection was
enacted into statutory law by the last session of the Legislature
of this State. While this commission rendered valuable service
and received no reimbursement whatsoever for their labor, yet the
cost of preparing and circulating their report incurred an indebtedness of $1,200.00 which was personally assumed by the members
of the commission. There appears to be no way of defraying this
from public funds, and it has been suggested that the Masonic
bodies of this State donate one-half of this amount, and the commission will endeavor to collect the remaining amount from other
fraternal bodies .. This is undoubtedly a very worthy cause, as the
laws enacted are considered to be excellent, and this matter should
merit our consideration. The Grand Commandery of this State
has already contributed $100.00 and the Grand Chapter the sum
of $200.00, which leaves a balance of $300.00 of the amount to be
raised from Masonic bodies. I recommend, therefore, that the sum
of $300.00 be donated from the Relief fund to defray the expenses
of this commission. (Adopted.)

Philippine Islands (1924):
We have not examined all the constitutions of the variou~
States, but we doubt if even a respectable mino~ity have the "diploma" requirement which New Hampshire has.
At best a diploma guarantees the holder only on the date of
its issuance, whereas a receipt for dues, signed by the member,·
.signed by the secretary of his Lodge, and signed by the Grand
Secretary of the jurisdiction, would seem to be more of a guarantee
of Masonic fitness than all the bulky, or ornately inscribed and
sometimes antiquated diplomas in the world. We usually think
of a diploma, too, as something to be framed not carried in the
pocket with passports, letters of credit, travele;s' ch~cks and other
impediments when the Master Mason starts to "travel in foreign
couritties, work and receive a Master Mason's wages."
We were once refused examination in a Lodge of fine .fellows
in the biggest city in our "home state" when a committee of Past
Masters discovered that our only "document" was a little pasteboard about as big as a visiting card.
Not to be daunted, we went to their library, got out their
own Constitution, showed them that, our pasteboard fulfilled, tu
the letter, all their constitutional requirements; we were admitted
to examination as an humble Master Mason, soon convinced them

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

107

that we "knew," and then they asked us why -we hadn't told them
we were a Past Master and an officer of our Grand Lodge, before.
Our reply was, "I am not traveling on my reputation, but on my
ability as a Master Mason to work and receive wages."
We cannot see how a diploma assures against clandestine
Masons any more than we can that it consti_tutes incontrovertible
evidence that the holder is in good standing as a Mason. He may
even be expelled and still retain his diploma, he cannot be expelled
and retain his .current credentials, at least for any lengthy period.
Upon how many diplomas issued by Grand Lodges does the
seal of the subordinate Lodges appear, and how many subordinate
Lodges issue Master Masons diplomas?
Quebec (1924):
It is :a matter for sincere regret that the fraternal relations
hitherto existing bet:!'veen the Grand Lodges of New Hampshire
and Kansas have been severed by the latter because of the retusal
of a Lodge in New Hampshire to examine one seeking admission
as a visitor, who had no Master Mason's certificate, but claiming
to be a member of a regular Kansas Lodge. Lacking the diploma;
the official receipt for dues was exhibited, but the committee oi
examiners declined to accept it in lieu thereof, and to proceed with
the examination of the candidate, basing this refusal upon a regulation of 1903 of the Grand Lodge, stating explicitly that no visitor
to a Lodge shall be examined until he exhibits to the examining
committee the . diploma issued to him as a Master Mason under
the seal of his Lodge and of the Grand Lodge. The Grand Master
fully justified the action of the Lodge, and so did Grand Lodge .
This unfortunate incident surely points to the necessity for some
better understanding between Grand Lodges on subjects of this
nature.

Utah (1924):
Among recommendations made by the Grand Master (Texas)
was one to make it a Masonic offense to advertise one's Masonic
standing for political purposes. We believe in that thoroughly.
In connection with an election in Chicago, not so long ago, we
were regaled weekly with the pictures, and the full Masonic records of candidates for various offices, and this in the pages of a
Masonic publication.

* * * *

The following resolution was adopted by Utah :
Resolved, That no Master Mason raised in this jurisdiction after
January 17, 1923, shall be entitled to a certificate of membership, or a
receipt of dues, or a dimit, or to vote in the Lodge, until he shall have
been examined and found proficient in the catechism of the Master
Mason degree, but he shall be entitled to all other rights and privileges
of a Master Mason.
The above is along the lines most popular as a remedy for a lamentable condition, but we submit that it does not fill the bill. What will,
we are not prepared to say, nor does anyone, anywhere, seem to have
an idea what will accomplish the •h sired end. In olden times, when
men went little from home no such provision was necessary. Now
our Masons wander all over the land and many in foreign lands. They
want to visit and we all want them to visit Lodges. Take the case
of a commercial traveler. Practically he is in a new town each day.
\Vhen his day's work is over, supper eaten, the evening hours must be
passed somehow. If a Mason, his first thought will be to inquire if
there is a Lodge on that night. How often will he, if not well versed
in the work, remain away because he is ashamed to exhibit his ignorance
of what he should be perfectly familiar with? American Masonry
must devise a remedy. Documentary evidence alone will never do.
This very day we have the report of the Masonic Relief Board and
therein read several cases of frauds traveling with what might pass
for reliable papers, some of them were originally all right, but these
frauds were using them for their unholy purposes.

In some places it is quite customary for the enthusiastic brother,
anxious to increase the membership in other :VIasonic orders, to importune the newly admitted brother to sign an application, even before
he has left the building and thus divert his attention and interest away
from that which he has just received. How much more good could
these enthusiasts do for Masonry if they would endeavor to help the
brother to become thoroughly familiar with what he has received, and
make the foundation secure. While we may not be able to place a time
limit after one has become a member of a Blue Lodge before he can
apply to other orders, we can control the time between degrees.

West Australia (1923):
In Australia one would as soon think of smoking in church
as of smoking in Lodge. Surely there are times when even heavy
smokers like ourselves can refrain.

* * * *
Situated at this distance it is naturally rather difficult for us
to size up the position, but it appears that at the present time in
most jurisdictions in the United States candidates are pouring into
the Craft at such an enormous rate that, in say, 25 to 30 years,
when these young men grow old, the claims upon the Craft will be
more than they can bear, and there will have to be a tremendous
increase in the dues, or a great falling off in the relief afforded.

* * * *

According to Brother Herriman the E. A. and F. C. degrees
may not be conferred on more than five, and the M. M. degree on
more than three candidates at the one time, while there must be an
interval of two weeks at least between degrees. \Ve exercise greater
restriction in the number of candidates receiving a degree simultaneously, and place an interval of two months between degrees.
That a candidate may be initiated on the first of one month and be
a M. M. before the first of the succeeding month is not, in our
opinion, conducive to a sound education in Masonic principles on
the part of the candidate. Apart from that, rush work tends
towards inefficiency, and at the same time opens the gates to the
faetory system, not of making Masons but of making members.
If a candidate finds that his passage to the M .. M. degree will tah
a matter of months he is less likely to seek the privileges of Masonry frorn unworthy motives.

Montana (1922):
The following additions were made to the Code:
Every brother who has been raised to the degree of Master
Mason shall pass a satisfactory examination thereon in open Lodge
within six months after his raising, failing in which he shall be
deemed suspended until he shall pass such examination, unless for
good cause shown he be granted further time by the Lodge.
Resolved, that if any Master Mason shall be suspended for
failure to pass examination as to his proficiency in the lecture of
the third degree, any other Master Mason shall be permitted to instruct him in the work, and the brother so instructed may then
enter the Lodge for examination.
Nevada (1923):
The man who knocks at the door of the Masonic Lodge i11forms us that he was first prepared to be made a Mason in his
heart. By. that all-comprehensive statement is meant that he really
desires light, he really desires to be helpful to his fellowman, he
really desires to participate in the search for truth with an earnestness and a zealous inquiry true to the traditions of Masonry.
Those who seek the superficial honors and prestige, usually
evidence that fact by an expressed desire to hurry through the
degrees in order that they may wear some coveted emblem upon
the coat lapel at the end of their quest.
I therefore recommend, that to assist in the effort to admit
only those who are really prepared in the heart to be made Masons
this Grand Lodge adopt legislation requiring that at least fou~
months shall elapse between the conferring of the entered apprentice degree and the fellowcraft degree, and at least six months
shall elapse between the conferring of the fellowcraft degree and
Master Mason degree.

Pennsylvania (1923):
There appears to be a phase of this educational movement
that deserves consideration. We refer to laws and regulations
adopted by some Grand Lodges restricting the liberty of Master
Masons to seek so-called "higher degrees" for a certain period
after receiving the Craft degrees-the usual limit being one year.
Evidently this is intended to fix a time within which the newlymade Mason is expected to confine his thoughts to basic Masonry
and to acquire a sufficient knowledge therecf to develop the wellrounded member of the Craft. In our opmion this expedientstanding by itself-will fail of its purpose; and, further, it is but
a makeshift that is an unjust discrimination against the young
Mason in favor of bis older brethren who are not any better informed. It is also a plea of guilt that a duty to the members of
the Craft bas been sadly neglected. A child (the novice is but a
child in Masonry) will not acquire a sufficient education unless
he is furnished with a school and competent instructors. Lacking
such facilities, it is not strange that the average young Mason
finds the Lodge dull and unattractive-after the novelty is worn ·
off-and looks about for other sources of light and knowledge.
Men of this generation demand action; if they find inertia in a
movement with which they affiliate, it soon fails to hold their
interest; there must be "something doing." For obvious reasons,
when a man enters the door of Masonry he knows little or nothing
of what Masonry means; and he acquires little in the ceremonies
that follow his entrance. Immediately thereafter his mind is receptive and he wants to know what it is all about. Then is the
psychological moment to take him in band and meet his demand
for knowledge. To hold him in abeyance for a year, expecting
him during that period to become adequately self-taught, is futile.
At the expiration of that probation the so-called "higher bodies"
get him, a member of a Lodge, but not a Mason.

Oregon (1923):
No Master Mason under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge
shall petition for membership in any order or fraternal society,
the qualification of membership therein being that of Master Mason,
until after the expiration of one year from the date of bis having
been raised to the degree of Master Mason, nor until be shall have
shown suitable proficiency in the candidate's lecture of the Master
Mason degree by an examination in open Lodge satisfactory to
the Master of the Lodge. This section shall n.ot apply to college
fraternities having the approval of the faculty of the college, or to
the Order of Eastern· Star.

in seeking Masonic degrees, and in a number of Grand Lodges
legislation has been enacted making it un-Masonic conduct for a
Master Mason to petition for other Masonic degrees until he has
been a Master Mason for one year, in some cases for six months,
and in one or two cases for three m·onths. This character of legislation will retard the progress of some candidates in applying for
the degrees, but will it make them better Masons? Will it increase
the attendance in the Blue Lodges? You can lead a horse to water,

but you cannot make him drink. The Grand Lodge may require

Utah (1924):
In the reviewer's discussion of the subject of restrictions placed
on the advancement to other degrees of newly raised Masons,
he appears to be doubtful as to the value of such legislation. Utah
requires such a brother to wait twelve months before. rushing on
to something else, and further, that the catechism of the third
degree must be learned and examination had in the same before
application can be made. We believe this is a move in the right
direction. It may be true, as Brother Harvey implies, that some
at least will not be any better Masons for waiting-in such cases
the mistake lies, in our judgment, in their admission to the Blue
Lodge, but to many, our observation shows, this plan affords an
opportunity to gain some knowledge of Craft Masonry, and this
is a distinct gain, and at the worst those who receive nothing from
a year's contact with the work of a Blue Lodge will not be any
worse off and the sifting process carried on for twelve months
may rid the fraternity of some of the undesirables who use Masonry
only as a· means to reach a red fez-such are not Masons and
never will be. They are just ordinary, very ordinary barnacles;
the ship of the Craft will continue to plow the main, if you please,
in spite of them, though somewhat retarded by them. The i..ord
Himself cannot make over the sons of men, even those who are
enlisted under the banner of the church. Masonry can hardly do
more than He, for some of those on its rosters, but we believe the
legislation under consideration has served, and will continue to
serve a good purpose.

APPENDIX
AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction
is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter
and are the Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent
Master and the Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests
upon those who have been regularly elected to preside over a
Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular because
they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are c.alled Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandary and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight
Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take
the temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the 33rd,
inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States (which
includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the Mississippi River) th~ organization of the different bodies, and the degrees conferred by them are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to
30°; Consistory, 31 ° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all States north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River); the degrees
conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and
18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons-Commence their era with the creation
of the world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Scottish Rite-Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology is used. Anno Mundi (A M.), "in the year of the world."
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple was
commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno Inventionis. (A. Inv.), "in the
year of discovery."
Royal and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the
Temple of Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Pep.),
"in the year of the deposit."
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organization of
their order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of the blessing
of Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis
(A. B.), "in the year of the blessing."

David John Reese
Grand Master, 1924·1925

DAVID .JOHN REESE
·Grand l\lmder

IH25

David John Reese, our fifty-eighth Grand Master, received his
Craft degrees at a time when the total membership of the jurisdiction
was one hundred thousand less than it is now. He was initiated
March 30, passed April 13, and raised to the sublime degree of Master
Mason, April 27, 1897, in Santa Paula Lodge "'.'Jo. 291, and in February,
1901, affiliated with San Buenaventura Lodge No. 214. His active
interest in Masonry was contemporaneous with his membership, and
he served his mother Lodge as Senior Deacon, Junior and Senior
Warden. The year following his affiliation with the Lodge at Ventura
he was selected by his brethren to serve as Seni .. r Warden, and in
1903 and 1904 was Master.
In the allied Masonic bodies his record is: Royal Arch in Ventura
Chapter No. SO-Mark Master, August 27, 1901; Pa$t Master, September 24; Most Excellent Master, January 7, 1902; Royal Arch, January
21. Council degrees: Ventura Council Royal and Select 2\1asters,
2\farch, 1902, holding at different times all the offices, including that of
Illustrious Master in the years 1909, 1918, 1919. Orders of Knighthood:
Ventura Commandery, January, 1904, in which he served as Senior
vVarden, Captain General, Generalissimo, Recorder, and in 1912, 1913,
was Eminent Commander. Scottish Rite degrees : T.,os Angeles Consistory, November, 1919. He is also a member of Al Malaikah Temple,
A. A. 0. N. sf. S.; Past Patron of Ventura Chapter No. 79, Order
of the Eastern Star.
In Grand Lodge Brother Reese served as Junior Grand Deacon
in 1910; Grand Standard Bearer, 1915-16-17; Junior Grand Warden,
1921-22; Senior Grand Warden, 1922-23; Grand Master, 1924-25. During all the years from 1904 until 1922 he was Inspector of the :Masonic
district comprising the Lodges of Santa Barbara and Ventura counties.
He served in all the offices of the Grand Council, R. and S. M.,
and was elevated to the office of Grand Master in t:hat body in 1920.
In the Grand Chapter, R. A. M., he now holds the position of
Grand Scribe and following its regular procethtre Crand Chapter will
select him as Gram! High Priest in 1928.
Our retiring Crand Master is of good W"lsh stock, and was born
at Cold l-liJI, Nevada, August 22, 1871. 11 is father was a mining
engineer and a member of the Nevada legislature in 1883 and 1885.
The family removed to Sonoma county, California, in 1885, and in that

county Brother Rees,e received his education, graduating from the
Petaluma high school. He adopted the profession of school teacher,
his first experience in that work being in Sonoma county at the early
age of nineteen, and then in Ventura county, at Santa Paula and
Oxnard, in the last named city being the first school principal. In
1900 he removed to Ventura and engaged in the newspaper business,
and has published the Ventura Fr,ee Press since that time. He has
been a member of the executive committee of the California Pr,ess
Association since 1907.
Public service has engrossed much -0f his attention. For two years
he was a member of the Ventura County Board of Education, and for
four years was postmas.ter of his home city. In 1915 Governor Hiram
W. Johnson appointed him a member of the State Civil Service Commission, and he was reappointed by Governor William D. Stephens
the same year to serve four years. \Vhen the Civil Service Commission
was reorganized in 1921, Governor Stephens appointed him as president
and executive member ,of the commission for another four years' term.
The legislature of 1925, again reorganized the commission and Governor
Friend W. Richardson appointed Brother Reese as wle commissioner
for the term ending 1929.
At the International Assembly of Civil Service Commissioners
,held at Minneapolis in 1921, Brother Reese was elected president of
that body and in 1924 he was again chosen to lead the Assembly.
Probably the date holding the sweetest memories in the mind of
Brother Reese is June 27, 1894, when he was married at Petaluma
to Miss Julia Ormsby, who has proved a helpmate indeed, and with
their three daughters ,the 1home is one of which every Mason may he
proud. Two daughters are happily married; one to Louis C. Drapeau,
an attorney at Ventura, and is the mother of David Reese Drapeau;
the other daughter is the wife of Dr. R. B. Armistead of Oakland.
The husbands of the two daughters are members of our Fraternity.

Seventy-sixth Annual Communication
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and

REMARKS BY GRAND MASTER
Before proceeding with the roll call, my brethren, and while you
are all here with us, I am going to take advantage of this opportunity
to extend to you a most cordial, a most hearty good morning, 'an
affectionate greeting and a sincere welcome to this Grand Lodge. I am
turning the tables in a measure and am extending the right hand of
fellowship to you good men who have greet·ed me and so hospitably
welcomed me all over this great State. No man knows better than
I do the mingled feelings, the feelings of awe and wonder and strangeness that beset you this morning. More than fifty per cent of you
are strangers and have never sat in Grand Lodge before. But this is
your Grand Lodge, as much yours as it is that of the oldest battlescarred veteran in the line. And you are going to get out of this

MESSAGE OF ·GRAND MASTER
Introduction
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
MY BRl!THRl!N, MY FRIENDS:

"Masonry is friendship, to be friends with all men, however they may differ from us in creed or color or condition; to
filt every hu.man relation with the si>irit of friendship-is there
anything more or better than this that the wisest and best of
men can hope to do? Such is the spirit of Masonry; such is
its ideal, and if to realize it all at once is denied us, surely it
means much to see it, to live it; and to labor to make it come
true."
One year ago as I stood before this Grand Lodge, advanced by
you to the greatest honor that can come to a citi.zen of California, with
all the sincerity and earnestness in my being, I offered up to Almighty
God my fervent prayer that He in His Wisdom might guide and
direct me aright, in word, thought and deed to the end that there
might come to our Fraternity in this jurisdiction, peace and harmony
and happiness and prosperity ; that there might not occur anything to
bring discord and confusion into the Craft and that we might be
spared illness and death and disaster and that all things might work
together for the upbuilding of Masonry and for the Kingdom of God.
It seems but yesterday that I stood before you and yet the year
has come and gone. The days and weeks and months have succeeded
each other with almost unbelievable rapidity. The Great All-father has
been giood to us and has given us the most. wonderful year in all the
history ·Of Masonry in this jurisdiction. It is with the same deep
sense of gratitude, after the labors of a remarkable year, that we
again offer up to Almighty God our thanks for the year that is past
as wcl1 as our api>eal that this communication of the Grand Lodge,
in all its proceedings, in all its deliberations, may have His b~essing
and protecting care and that it may redoun<l to His glory and. to the
credit of the Craft.
The gratitude which I attempted to express to you one year ago
has been intensified as the months have gone by. That gratitude and
appreciation have been exceeded only by the deep sense of humility
awakened in my heart by the outlook of opportunity and responsibility
which yQur honors and favors imposed upon me.
I have not been unmin<lful at any time of the dignity and honor
of the Grand Mastership, and I have been conscious at all times of

my own short-comings, my own limitations, my lack of ability to deal
with the many problems which oonfnmt a Grand Master. But I have
ever had as a source of inspiration the splendid achievements of my
predeeessors, as well as their kindly counsel and advice. These with
the remarkable spirit of kindness, of cooperation and withal of charity
of the brethren throughout this jurisdictkm have made less difficult a
strenuous task, have enabled me to grope with and master many
entangled problems. The support I asked for in the beginning has
been accorded . in the. most gener·ous and heartening way and it has
made easy and pleasant my efforts to serve you. In fact, I do .n10t
hesitate to say that whatever achievement or success may have ~tte.nded
my administration, would have been impossible had it not be~n for
loyal assistance of the Craft, the cooperation 10f the District Inspectors,
the loyal service of my Grand Officers and the a-dvice and counsel of
Committeemen and Past Grand Masters.
And now the year of my trusteeship is in its closing hours. The
record of my year is written and I shall s•oon slip back inti) .the rank~
from which I sprung. To paraphrase that great and good man and
Mason, the late Thomas R. Marshall, "My retirement is not a demotion
to the ranks, because I have never rose above them." It is a comforting
th10ught indeed, that, though retired, I shall still be permitted to go
along with you and possibly in some humble capacity contribute to th~
work and welfare of this Gra,nd Lodge and of our great Fraternity.
As you have welcomed me to your hearts and your homes and your
Lodges during this year, so I now welcome you here to this seventy;:sixth annual communication of Grand Lodge as the delegates .of yiour
respective Lodges and hence as the representatives of the. Fraternity
at large. I welcome you because through yau the great hea~t of
Masonry comes here to express its needs and its desires and its purposes and to demand of the wisdom here congregate.4,,11~d aggregated
such llJiCasures as may tend to its larger development .. I wekomi: yoi1
because through you and your counsels and wisdom .we may krww
what is best to be done. I welcome you whether yau be ti).e aged

who now hesitatingly enters the councils of thLCraft. . And it .is my
hope that this meeting may in every respect bring such encouragement
to your labors, such enthusiasm and zeal, that yoi1 will not alone' carry
home to your respective Lodg.es an interest that ~illbe contaglously
fruitful, but also that you will be induc~d to ret.urn ~gain and again
to' this fountain of Masonic inspiration.
.
'· • , '"
Because our Constitution, our custom and precedent require, and
my desire and pleasure dictate, I ,now prese):lt to you a review of the
more important affairs of my adn1lnistratiori, a. rec,ord of my official

acts, together with my recomrnendations offered as suggestions to
make just a :little better and stronger and clearer some of our laws
and regulations, to eliminate some of those things that seem unnecessary
and to provide some things which appear to be needed.
At the outset may I convey to you the information which I know
can never be appreciated except by those who have actually discharged
the duties of this office. No greater h10nor can come to a citizen of this
Commonwealth than his selection as Grand Master of Masons. But
the Jurisdiction has grown so large, the Lodges have so increased in
numbers the executive and administrative duties of the office have
become ~'o great, the correspondence has become so voluminous, that
the day must come when it will be physically impossible for our Grand
Masters to "<iischarge the duties of the office as established by precedent
and under the present system. In fact, that day is here now. A Grand
Master cannot meet the demands of the brethren; he cannot attend to
the administrative duties of his office; he cannot give attention to his
correspondence, without untold personal sacrifice. It seems to me now,
and I offer it as a suggestion to Grand Lodge, that 10Ur Grand Masters
must soon have permanent secretarial assistance. Later on in this
message it is my purpose to suggest some measure of relief and
assistance for future Grand Masters.
In the vear's report which follows I have· endeavored to submit
to. you, und~r proper headings, a brief review of the various agencies
which have been adopted during the year to promote the interest and
welfare of the Fraternity and at the same time directing your attention
to the detailed reports of the various Grand Lodge committees.
It may be interesting for you to know in a general way, that which
will be presented to you later in detail by Grand Lodge officers and
committees, that 8,307 Master Masons have been raised this year; that
there has been a net gain of 7;319 members on the roster of this Grand
Jurisdiction and that our total membership is nearly 116,000 Master
Masons ; thwt 3() new Lodges have been instituted during the year ;
that the assets of the Grand Lodge exclusive of our Homes properties
now totals $688,474. But these are merely material things and have
no part in this presentation. Rather am .I concerned, rather are you
concerned in what has been accomplished by Grand Lodge and by
our constituent Lodges in the moral, social, intellectual betterment of
the members of the organization, of our communities, and of humanity.
Because, my brethren, this Fraternity of ours is being judged and will
take its place in this world; not by reason of the accuracy of any
designs upon a trestleboard ; not by the correctness of any ritual or
ceremony; not by the buttons which we wear in our lapels or ~he
charms on our watch chains; not by any names on ·a roster or dollars

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

'in a treasury; but only by the suocess which we attain in making these
things articulate in the lives of the membership of this Order. It is
gratifying indeed to note the wonderful griowth of California Masonry
and its material prosperity, but we must bear in mind that the power
of our Fraternity is not in its numbers or in its financial strength,
but rather in its record of good deeds accomplished. Unless the community in which we live is better and richer because of the truths we
teach; unless there is a greater sense of honor, a higher purity in
those who have participated in our ceremonies and those with whom
we come in contact, we have failed in our mission, and our professions
are as tinkling cymbals. The success of Masonry in this Commonwealth, aye in this world, does not depend upon the numbers we
initiate, but it does depend upon whether the lessons we communicate
to these members, the precepts we publish to the world, are making
for better citizens and better citizenship in the communities in which
they live.
Condition of the Craft

carrying 6n in an endeavor to bring about better education, higher
morals, better social conditions, and are exemplifying the teachings of
Freemasonry in their daily walk and life. And this is our work and
mission, brethren. If we can raise but one brother who is worthy
and well qualified, a credit to the Fraternit.y and an honor to ~he
Craft, we have accomplished more for humamty than rubber stampmg
a hundred and making them Masons in name only.
And after all, and notwithstanding all else, I am convinced that
Masonry in California will wield an abiding influence for good, for
fraternal and charitable assistance to the needy; for the fostering and
promoting of the public schools, for supporting every laudable plan for
the moral and physical welfare of our children; for the upli~ing of
humanity, and for the enlightenment of its own membership-all to
the end that it may confirm its creed of the Brotherhood of Man
under the Fatherhood of God.

It is customary to make use of that time honored phrase, "There
is peace and harmony and prosperity among the Craft." I presume
the expression is as true at this time, as it ever has been in our
Masonic history, and yet I frankly confess that there is not now and
has not been at any time during my administration absolute peace and
harmony. There is prosperity and I am not quite sure that there is
not too much prosperity. We have grown so fast: we have taken in
so many new and young members, that these members have failed to
grasp the vision and purpose of Masonry, have failed to understand
that Masonry is builded upon a foundation peculiar to itself. It should
be our purpose to· hold firm and true to our time honored standards.
It is not enough that a candidate bring no discredit upon this institution of ours; rather should we insist that he reflect credit upon our
Fraternity when we admit him to membership. With the great growth
of the Fraternity ·this year we have not had a oorresponding increase
in interest or in attendance. It is evident, grievously evident, that
hundreds, yes thousands of men who have petitioned for the degrees
have petitioned merely because they must have the prerequisite of
Masonic membership in order to reach ·the playground of Masonry.
Once there they are never heard of again save as dues payers and
as names on the roster of some Lodge. I am convinced that we cannot
make Masons too fast, but I am also convinced that we are making
members too fast. But notwhhstanding this rather discouraging aspect
of our present situation, notwithstanding a note of discord here and
there, it is pleasant to note that the great heart of Masonry is still
staunch and true; that good men and Masons all over this State are

My attention has been called frequently to the fact that members
of our Masonic Lodg.es are not only violating the laws of the land,
but that they have been arrested and convicted of such violations and
notwithstanding such convictions, they are permitted to retain their
membership in their Lodges without action on the part of said Lodges.
In every case where proof was given, I have directed that pmceedings
be ·taken, because, brethren, it is not conceivable that a Masonic Lodge
will harbor or encourage law breakers, whether they be bootleggers
or embezzlers.
The world judges Masonry by its least desirable member and if a
Lodge condones or overlooks the offenses of any one of its members,
so will the world judge the character or standing of that Lodge.
Masonry means good citizenship. Through all of its lessons and
obligations and charges winds the thread of loyalty to country;
obedience to law; support of constituted authority; good citizenship.
And I cannot conceive of a good Mason who is not first and above
all else a good citizen.
New Lodges

'3'60

Good Citizenship

Firm in my belief that more Lodges and smaller Lodges will in a
great measure solve the ever present problem of apathy, disinterestedness and nonattendance of Masons at Masonic meetings, I have signified
my assent to and agreement with the formation of new Lodges in
California during this year. I have not encouraged nor participated
in the organization of new Lodges, but as the proponents came to me
with their plans, I have with few exceptions, when convinced that the

I
362

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

proposed organization was for the best interests of Masonry, granted
a dispensation for the opening of a new Lodge. Nor was the dispensation granted without due and careful inquiry. Wherever possible
I have summoned the charter members of the new Lodge before granting the dispensation. I have made the most thorough inquiry into the
purpose of the p11oposed organization, as well as the purpose of the
organizers. I have referred the petition to an Inspector and directed
investigation by him and in every respect I have endeavored to be
fully informed before I have finally signed my name on the dotted line.
Thirty new Lodges have received dispensations this year. All are
prospering, all have executed satisfactory work, .all liave complied with
the terms of their probation, save in the single instance which we have
in this message represented.
The smaller Lodge of California is a thing of comfort and a joy
forever. It affords the largest opportunity for and the greatest promise
of future Masonic strength; it facilitates acquaintance, friendship,
brotherly love; it gives opportunity for most of its members to engage
in its activities, and thus encourages a greater p11oportion of attendance.
The large Lodges have become, because of their size and nature centralized business institutions. They are managed and controlled' in a
cold, unresponsive, unfriendly way; and they have to be. There is in
them the tendency to lay stress upon business affairs and ritualistic
work; friendship, fellowship, fraternity are forgotten, or have never
been thought of;. the administrative affairs, the ritualistic work crowd
all other conditions aside and the officers have no time, no opportunity
and no enthusiasm to perform the many duties for the advancement or
the education of the members which are equally or even more important
than either business or degree work.
I know that there are criticisms and objections to the large number
of new Lodges. I fully realize the dangers that confront a new Masonic
organization. I know the tendency and proclivities of certain Masons
to make increase of members the basis of success, but I am convinced,
too, that these new Lodges individually and collectively will be a credit
to Freemasonry in California.

Our Extraneous Organizations
And this brings me to the question of the extraneous organizations.
Sir Alfred Robbins on his return to England after his American Masonic
mission declared that the one great danger to American Masonry was
the existence of extraneous organizations or the so-called side degrees.
During this Masonic year I have had considerable correspondence
with the presiding officials of at least one of these extraneous 0 rgariiza-

\
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

363

tions. I have been given uniform courtesy and assurances of support
and cooperation as well as promises that these officers would do all in
their power to see that Mas·ons, members of this organization by reason
of the Masonic prerequisite, should observe their Masonic obligations.
I am convinced that these officers are honest and sincere and I deeply
appreciate their. efforts to help me in the great work I have been •trying
to do. And yet there percolates through the air, seemingly radioed from
some broadcasting station, the echoes of some celebrations, some picnic,
some dance, some ceremonial-the stories of Masons, members of this
organization of ours, who, with you and me have knelt at our sacred
altar and have assumed our obligations, who seem to believe that membership in this or that organization absolves them from any and all obligations to their mother Lodge, and who conduct themselves unbecoming
their professions as Masons.
I have no quarrel with any of these organizations, but I do believe
and it is not alone my recommendation but ·also my prayer, that this
Grand Lodge should make a solemn and unequivocal pronouncement on
this matter. This Grand Lodge is big enough, is powerful enough, is
influential enough to direct •that a man's standing in Masonry is dependent upon his loyalty to the institution, is dependent upon his obedience to its laws and regulations. Whatever else he may be in Masonry
or in any so-called side degree of Mas-onry, he is a Mason first and
above all else, and unless he conforms to every law and regulation his
membership in Masonry is jeopardized. This Grand Lodge should and
must take steps to prevent the establishment of other side degrees and
to provide regulating supervision for all such side degrees as may be
established. It should and must make known without any doubt of the
certainty of its pronouncement that the honor, the dignity, the prestige
of Masonry, aye even its Ancient Landmarks, are under its guardianship
and protection and that these things may not be defiled and trailed in
the dust by men, who as members of organizations dependent on
Masonry, will do the things that they would not dare to do as Masons
or in a Masonic Lodge.
It is quite evj.dent that the brethren who do these things are answerable as Masons for their conduct but it is evident, too, that these brethren have not the conception, the vision, of their rdations to their Lodge
and to this Grand Lodge. They do not understand that this Grand
Lodge still retains the power and authority to enforce obedience among
its members, of the Landmarks of Masonry. Action should be taken to
definitely settle this question here and now.

of Pennsylvania is apropos:

vania recognizes nothing but Ancient Freemasony. It does not countenance side degrees, nor will it permit organizations not Masonic, to use

its symmetry and pervert it from its original purpose. This is virtually
-in theory at least-the attitude of most American Grand Lodges; and
yet, the organfaations we are referring <to, while technically observing

Fur·ther, they appeal to the imagination of the Craft and bid for their

writers; they find a wealth of material in the forms and ceremonies of
Masonry from which to borrow, as well as its science and philosophy,

degrees. Instead of the constitutional committee of three, no one of
whom knows the other members of the committee, and none of whom
are known to any members of the Lodge except the Master and Secretary, Masters of Lodges are now using so-called advisory committees,
to which petitions are referred, and which advisory committees go
thoroughly into every phase of the petition, holding open meetings and

This may not be in accordance with our Constitution, but it is serving
as a means of preventing unfit and unworthy applicants to receive the
degrees in •our Lodges. The secret committee of three is not functioning
in very many of the Lodges. There is a situation which obtains with
such committees which is not satisfactory or advisable. We believe that
the section providing tha't the names of the members of the committee
shall not be made known except to the Master and the Secretary is not
necessary and is inadvisable, and, therefore, recommend that such provision be stricken from the Constitution, and that provision be made
for the appointment of advisory investigating committees as now
obtain in many of the large Lodges and in Lodges having concurent Jurisdiction in this State.

"No one will question that these various organizations-as well as
most all other fraternal societies-have merit in themselves; that truth
never suffers from frequent reiteration; >that the moral and social virtues cannot have too many advocates, individual or collective. But the
point we make is, that Masonry should not be directly or indirectly responsible for them; that they should not be allowed to threaten its
'symmetry', or divert it from its original purpose.
"At the inception of the Great War, when Germany was marching
through Belgium to enter France, the fictional (but none the less apt)
protest of Belgium was: 'This is a country, not a road!' Masonry was
never intended to be a road, or a stepping stone to other organizations
or instHutions. It has stood alone with .unparalleled grandeur and impr·essiveness through the centuries, pointing men to higher standards
of civilization; its tenet~ are sufficient for the highest moral development; its business is ·to make Masons, in all that the title implies. If it
can succeed in that, its votaries are not to be easily diverted by the
:lure of fancy, or recreation; if it fails in that mission the fault lies
within; it cannot profit by outside help; it must clean its own house."

Masonic Clubs and Regulation
Keeping pace with the great increase in the number of Masonic
Lodges and Ma&onic membership in California, numerous Masonic clubs
have been springing into existence, clubs of all sorts and wHh all kinds
of purposes, all of which demand as a prerequisite, membership in a
Masonic Lodg·e. There is no question but that these Masonic clubs
in general are working for the benefit of the Fraternity at large. The
names of many of these organizations do not indicate <that there is a
prerequisite requir·ement as to membership, and yet they are generally
known to be Masonic organizations, while others of them have names
which indicate to the general public that they are connected with
Masonry: The aggregate membership of these clubs reaches into the
thousands. They are not detrimental to our Fraternity or to our
organizations, but, in the main, are bringing credit to themselves and
to our membership. However, there have been complaints that the

and subject to the regulations of our Grand Lodge, that the Grand
Lodge of California should provide some regulatory supervision, and
that all such organizations hereafter formed should submit to the Grand
Master and Grand Lodge for approval a constitution and by-laws and a

Degree Teams
A few years ago there came into being certain organizations of
Masonic ritual enthusiasts, all of whom were employees or members
of the same industrial, professional, or public organizations, so-called
degree teams whose purpose originally was to confer the degrees of
Masonry upon candidates who were members of their said organizations.
The original plan of degree teams was undoubtedly rightly conceived
and well carried, out. There was a desire ori the part of the Brethren
who filled the official positions in these so-called degree teams not alone
to confer the degree upon their associate as a tribute to him but also
in such a manner as would bring credit to the Fraternity in the rendition
of accurate and perfect work. But in the past year or two degree teams
have sprung up like mushrooms after a spring rain, and every organization which can furnish an excuse for a degree team 'is now represented
in the field of Masonry. There are degree teams in every industrial
association, in every professional occupation, in every governmental and
public association. There are so many degree teams that Lodges, in
responding to requests for permission for these so-called degree teams
to confer the degrees, do not find opportunity i() have the degrees conferred by their own officers. In fact, degree teams have become so
common ithat more and more innovations have been introduced, each
degree team evidently trying to vie with other degree teams in attracting
attention to itself by means of the innovations which are introduced.
My attention has been called to the fact that these degn'e teams, in
many instances, have been cheapening ()tlr ritualistic work and have, in
fact, been making the conferring of degr.ees a matter of competition;
and while I verbally remonstrated upon· several occasions, I felt called

give formal approval to so radical a departure from our established procedure. Competition in the conferring of the Entered
Apprentice or any other degree of Masonry, in my opinion, is
unethical and is a departure from our Masonic ideals. Competition smacks of advertising and of undue and unethical notoriety, because it is evident, that without the publicity given by
the announcement Qf the proposed contest; of the progress and
the result thereof; and of the proffering and awarding of
trophies therefor; there would be no incentive whatever for
such competition.
"It is without question that the candidate for whom, and
upon whom, the degree is conferred, would be entirely lost sight
.of in this unseemly and un-Masonic scramble for a silver trophy.
A Masonic degree should be conferred for itself alone and
Masonry will be in a sorry plight when interest and loyalty and
devotion, when accuracy and perfection in the esoteric work
must be stimulated and kept alive by the introduction of rivalry
and competition in the conferring of degrees. To permit such
competition would tend to open the door for the injection of
doubtful oratory, or dramatical and theatrical effects, of jazz
music and other innovations in order to create impression upon
the minds of those who would act as judges in the decision of
such competitions.
"Competitiv·e contests would be a menace and a detriment
to, and an impairment cf, the ritualistic work cf the degrees of
Masonry.
"It is my order, therefore, that such competitive contests in
the conferring of the Entered Apprentice degree or any degree
of Masonry be not permitted or carried on in the Lodges of this
jurisdiction. You are respectively directed to communicate this
order to the Lodges in your District."
