Competition in Conferring Degrees
During the year there was submitted to me for my approval a plan
for competitive first degree work among the Lodg.es Qf San Francisco,
sponsored by a Masonic organization of that city. It was argued that
such competition would lend credit and dignity to the ritualistic work;
that it would encourage the idea among officers and members that the
first degree was the most important degree of the Blue Lodge; and
that it woul·d increa'se attendance at degree meetings. It was submitted,
too, that certain trophies had been presented as awards in the contest
and that the compefrtion altogether would work for the best interests
of Masonry in San Franci~co and over the state.
It was my belief that the competition or competitive contest was
Masonically unethical, and I so expressed myself to the Inspectors of
the San Francisco Districts, but there being an insistent demand for an
opinion from me on the question submitted, I finally issued the following
bulletin to the Inspectors of California:
"Dear Brother Inspector:
August 31, 1925.
"There has been submitted to me for consideration and
ruling the question of competition or competitive contests in
the conferring of the Entered Apprentice Degree of Masonry
by Lodges of this Jurisdiction. There is pending at this time
and awaiting approval, a proposed competition or competitive
contest among certain Lodges of San Francisco and in which
competitiQn a silver trophy cup and a gold gavel are to be
awarded to the ,Lodge or Lodges declared to be the winners in
said contes·t.
"A competitive contest in the conferring of degrees is an
innovadon in Masonic procedure and practice. If approved, it
will establish a new precedent in our j.urisdiction. W:hile I am
averse to having our Lodges held down by ancient precedent,

Using the Words Mason, Masonic or Masonry for Personal Gain
Protests innumerable have come to the Grand Master from Lodges
and brethren over the State concerning the misuse of the words "Mason,"
"Masonic" and "Masonry" for ·the purposes of personal gain. So-called
Masonic insurance companies have agents, representatives and solicitors
scattered over the State who pounce upon the Entered Apprentice as
soon as he .receives his degree and, in many cases, as a mattler of fact,
these solicitors have in some way ascertained !the names of petitioners
and have even solicited their business before they have been elected to
receive degrees of Masonry. Promoters of residence parks and real
estate subdivisions are using the names "Masonry' and "Masonic," as
well as the emblems of Masonry, to advertise and give publicity to
their propositions; salesmen for Masonic emblematic jewelry, metal
containers for lambskin aprons, and ·other knick-knacks, adv·ertising
their wares, write soliciting letters to Entered Apprentices in behalf of ·
their business. Protest is made that a Master of a Lodge in this Jurisdiction, representing an insurance company, sells insurance to his

Masonic Club at Berkeley
The Grand Lodge of California and the Masons of this Jurisdiction
builded better than they knew when they provided the funds and arranged for the erection of the Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley near
the campus of the University of California. The erection and furnishing
of the Masonic Clubhouse has been a very expensive undertaking. It
yet carries an indebtedttess of a considerable amount, but every dollar
that has been expended in the erection and furnishing of the building,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

every dollar that will be expended in paying off its indebtedness, will
be returned an hundredfold to the Masons of California. The Clubhouse
at Berkeley furnishes for the hundreds of students at the University of
California who have Masonic connections and relations at home and who
are ass-ociated with the various Masonic .organizations at the university
social entertainment, retirement and relaxation, and, more than all else,
it supplies, as near as humanly possible, the touch of home life and
home comforts that are so deplorably absent in a great institution of
more than ten thousand students. I have had opportunity, and rt has
been my pleasure, during the year, to visit on two or three occasions
the Clubhouse at Berkeley. It was a privilege to be present, just before
my administration began, at the formal dedication of the Clubhouse.
In April, Mrs. Reese and I were the guests -of the Masonic organizations of Berkeley at a reception given by them at the Clubhouse. On
two or three -0ther occasions, the opportunity has been afforded me to
pay a social visit there. On every occasion I have been charmed
and delighted with the atmosphere created among the students who
avail. themselves of the Clubhouse and its advantages. The Clubhouse is proving the center of social activities for the Masonic s·tudents
of the university. It furnishes them rooms for study and relaxation and,
under the able and kindly direction of a charming hostess and housemother, it is a real home for the young men and women who have come
from great distances in this state to attend the university. The Grand
Lodge Committee on Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley will, later during
this communication, present to you its annual report. This report will
give to you the activities of the Clubhouse, the facts in connection with
its maintenance, and its financial condition. The committee must come
to Grand Lodge with a request for an appropriation for the maintenance
and support of the institution during the ensuing year. The Masonic
Clubhouse at Berkeley is ours. It was conceived and established by
this Grand Lodge. It has depended, and must depend, upon Grand
Lodge for its support, and it is my urgent recommendation that the
appropriation which will be requested by the committee be approved
and granted by this Grand Lodge.

to the little children and the old of age; the comfort and satisfaction he
gives the Trustees, I most heartily commend our beloved brother, the
Very Worshipful John Whicher.

Our Masonic Homes
The bright stars in the crown of California Masonry are the Homes
at Covina and Decoto. As a matter of fact, the only real tangible
achievement of our Fraternity in this state, the one great monument
to which wi1th pride we can direct the attention of the world are these
splendid institutions. The outstanding feature of my four years in the
official line of the Grand Lodge of California, the greatest pleasure and
satisfaction of those four years, have been my membership on the Board

It was my privilege to reappoint M. W. Brother Samuel E. Burke
to succeed himself. I am proud indeed of my appointment. The report
of the Trustees hereafter to be presented will be a detailed review of
the physical and financial affairs of the Homes, and it is unnecessary
for any reference to these matters here. There are, however, certain
features to which I ask your privilege to refer.
'When I first became a member of the Trustees of the Homes, there
were 64 children at Covina. In four years the population at the Covina
Home has grown ·to 165, an increase of 158 per cent. To care for this
added growth, new buildings have been erected, additions to ki~chen
and dining room have been built and other necessary improvements
have been made, entailing an expenditure of more than $300,000.
If this has been the result of four years' growth; if the years that
are to come, with their promise of untold thousands added to the population of this state, will, as they must, bring proportionate increase in
our Homes, the problem of housing and caring for our dependent children will be indeed a most serious one. It may be advisable to meet
the problem as, and when it confronts us, but the suggestion is offered
at this time as one that deserves and demands serious consideration
by this Grand Lodge.
An outstanding feature in connection with the Covina Home this
year has been the wonderful work of improvement at Camp Tucker,
Balboa Island, the children's summer camp. Replacing the old unfitted,
unsuitable, unsanitary tent houses and shacks at the camp, there have
been erected frame buildings on concrete foundations; recreation hall,
dining room and kitchen, 1dormitories, all fitted with up to date plumbing; all electrically wired; all sanitary; convenient, livable and pleasant.
The property lines have been rearranged and the property centralized
and made more convenient of management. And this has been done,
not by Grand Lodge, not by the Trustees, but by the Masons and
Masonic Lodges of Southern California, under the -direction and leadership of our W. Brother Mervyn J. Newburg, a member of our Grand
Lodge Finance Committee. As Pr,esident of the Past Masters' Association of Southern California he has interested the Lodges and Masons
of Southern California in the Camp Tucker project, and these Lodges
have provided the funds, have actually assisted in the erection and
furnishing of the buildings. The brnthren of two of the neighboring
Lodges furnished all the wiring and fixtures, also the plumbing and
fixtures for the Camp and actually performed the work of installation.
Brother Newburg has given weeks and months to this work, remaining
at the Camp, negotiating for the exchange of property, attending to
street improvements, directing and actually performing manual labor.
His has been a labor of devotion; of loyalty; a service that can never

be repaid by this Grand Lodge. To him, to the Lodges and 1:-0 the
members who have aided in this great work, I have expressed my
personal appreciation as Grand Master. But this Grand Lodge should
make official acknowledgment of the great service rendered.
Nor can I leave this subject without expressing personal
tion of the services rendered by Brother Frank B. Hartman, Superintendent of the Decoto Home, and his able assistant, Mrs. Richardson;
by Mrs. Maude Miller, Superintendent of the Covina Home, and her
assistant, Mrs. Avery. All of these have been most courteous and kind·
to me during the year, but my acknowledgment to them is for their
unselfish, devoted, exceptional service to Masonry and to humanity.
One of the surprising but at the same time gratifying circumstances
of the year was the proffer to the Homes by the Grand Commandery
of Knights T,emplar of California of a gift of $40,000 of stock in ·t.ihe
Masonic Temple Association for the purpose of bui'.din:5 a hospital at
the Home at Covina. This offer supplemented a former gift of $10,000
in cash, which was made as a nucleus to the hospital fund. It was
accepted and the stock is now in the possession of the Trustees. I most
earnestly recommend to this Grand Lodge that if, and when, the funds
are sufficient for the purpose, the Grand Lodge purchase this stock;
first that the Trustees may have the available funds with which to
erect the hospital, and second that Grand Lodge may acquire possession
of the stock.

Our Inspectors
The remarkably able and efficient men who are serving this Grand
Lodge and the Grand Master as Inspectors of the respective districts
of California, have been a source of comfort and inspiration to your
Grand Master. Early in my administration, I arranged conference
with the Inspectors, north and south, and these early meetings called
for repeated sessions, in which with the utmost good feliowship, friendship and entire frankness, the welfare of Lodges, the vexatious problems,
the many troubles of the year have been discussed. For some reason,
probably because of these many meetings, there have been perhaps more
difficulties and problems than ever before, and while the assignment
of the Inspectors to investigate these matters have inconvenienced
them greatly, they have responded readily and willingly; their investigations have been prompt and effective and their reports have been
conclusive. The Inspectors of this jurisdiction have come very close
to my heart. The questionnaire sent QUt by me at the required time
brought to me most intelligent and carefully considered replies and
opinions and helped me greatly in my work as well as in my preparation of this report. I would that space might permit in order that
I might include here some of these very splendid and very original
ideas. No official of this Grand Lodge does more effective work and
receives less compensation, less real appreciation than does the Inspector
of a Masonic District, but I am on record here and now, that they
have been my most helpful assistants during the year and they have
my sincere gratitude and appreciation.

District Deputy Grand Masters
My travels through the Masonic Districts of California this year,
my contact with Lodges and brethren have convinced me that there
is a need for representatives of the Grand Master in various sections
of the State. Not to supplant the District Inspectors but to supplement
their activities and to aid and relieve the Grand Master.
In his message to Grand Lodge in 1920, Past Grand Master Adams
recommended the creation of District Deputy Grand Masters; that
such officers be appointed by and act as the representative of the
Grand Master; that they be responsible to the Grand Master, and
report to him.
In his recommendation Past Grand Master Adams said in part:
"The District Deputy Grand Master would have no concern with
the esoteric work ; but would discharge the other duties now devolving
upon the Inspectors.
"While many of those now serving as Inspectors would naturally
be appointed District Deputy Grand Masters (unless they had a prefer-

ence for the esoteric work) the creation of that office would make
available the services of some of the ablest and most influential Masons
in the State for whom there is no place under our present system."
And, furthermore, the Grand· Master recommended the appointment
. . .
of Deputy Grand Lecturers, saying in part:
"The Deputy Grand Lecturers could be appointed by the Grand
Lecturer, and might include any Master or Past Master who could

The recommendation was referred to the Committee on Policy

Santa Barbara Earthquake

This Masonic year has been marked by a great cataclysm of Nature
. which practically wrecked the entire business section of the city of
Santa Barbara and which, in recent years in this State, is only comparable with the great earthquake which wrought such great havoc in
the city of San Francisco. On the morning of June 30, 1925, a great
earthquake visited the city of Santa Barbara, wrecking and damaging
all public buildings and practically destroying all business houses 011
State street, the principal business street of the city.
The new Masonic Temple of Santa Barbara, erected after years of
effort by, the two Masonic Lodges and other coordinate bodies of that
• city, which had just been completed and accepted by the Masonic Temple
Association, and which had not y.et been occupied by the Masonic
bodies, was among the structures which suffered serious damage in the
earthquake.
On the day of the earthquake, with Worshipful Bro. Thomas J.
Baker, Grand Lecturer, I had been invited and had accepted the invitation. to officiate at the ceremonies of laying the corner stone of the new
Masonic Temple at Guerneville, Sonoma County. Shortly after the
ceremonies there, were completed the news was broadcasted through
the assemblage that the city of Santa Barbara had been destroyed, and
that other Southern California cities had suffered seriously as a result
of. the earthquake shock. Cancelling all of my Northern California
appointments for that week, I hastened south and was at Santa Barbara
·at six o'clock on the morning after the earthquake. After having conferred with Grand Officers and Past Grand Masters, I carried with me
·to Sarita Barbara a warrant for a sufficient sum to insure immediate
relid for earthquake sufferers, and on my arrival in the stricken city
. turned this sum over to Past Master Bro. George W. McComber to be
: used for immediate relief. I assisted in establishing Masonic relief
headquarters and an information bureau, insp·ected the damage wrought
in the new Masonic Temple, as well as in the Fithian building, which
. was jn use up. to that time as a Masonic Lodge room. The la'tter
. build_ing had collapsed, the roof falling in and carrying its weight to
the. ground _and with it the furniture, the regalia and the property of
alL,t)1e Masonic bodies of Santa Barbara.
The· new Masonic Temple had been erected at a total expenditure
of $225,000. Only a few days before the earthquake it had been
·accepted by the Masonic Temple Association from the contractors. ·No
earthquake insurance had been placed upon the building; as a matter of
fact, there was practically no earth,quake insurance in the city of Santa
Barbara. The Masonic Temple Association had incurred indebtedness

388

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

to the amount of $120,000 to· complete the building. The membership
had subscribed for stock practically to the limit of its ability. The
T.emple, while not in ruins, was in such s,hape that it was condemned
and could not be occupied. Masonry in Santa Barbara was without
a home, without means to secure a Temple, without means to repair
the damages wrought by the earthquake; the membership of the two
organizations who ha·d contributed to the extent of their means in the
purchase of stock were now in a position where most of them had
~uffered almost irreparable damage by the earthquake, and Masonry
m Santa Barbara was, indeed, in a most unfortunate and deplorable
condition.
·

Masonic Temple. The good Masons of that city had labored for years
to provide a home and domicile of their own; they had given until
they could give no more; they had sacrificed time and effort to erect a
building which was not alone an ornament to the city but a credit to
the Fraternity as well. Out of the unknown, unexpected, unheralded,
unwelcome, the earthquake came and wrecked their splendid edifice.
The cataclysm which wrecked the new Masonic Temple wrecked also
many a staunch Masonic heart. T,he Masons ·of Santa Barbara were
helpless and discouraged. In every great world call they had ever
responded generously. The time had come when relief must be furnished to them. The Grand Lodge of California had ample funds in
its treasury, funds which could be worthily bestowed in such a cause.
The Finance Committee realized the situation and responded. The
Grand Master heartily approved their a·ction. The Grand Lodge of
California is now asked to endorse the action of the Finance Committee
and of the Grand Master,
Almost immediately after the news of the Santa Barbara disaster
had been sent to the outsid1e world, there came to the Grand Master
telegrams from outside sources offering aid to the stricken Masons of
Santa Barbara. Notable among these were the messages from Most
Worshipful Morton S. Gregory, Grand Master of Masons of Washington; William A. Rowan, Grand Master of Masons of New York; and
Most Worshipful Andrew S. Randell, Executive Secretary of the
Masonic Service Association. To each and all of these your Grand
Master expressed his appreciation and gratitude and gave assurance
that so far as the Masons of California and Santa Barbara were concerned, our losses and relief could be easily taken care of by the
Masons of this jurisdiction.
During the month of March, while we were on our official visit
to the Hawaiian Islands, storms and floods wrought great havoc in
the State of Illinois. When the news reached us in Honolulu, we
promptly communicated with Deputy Grand Master Right Worshipful
Albert E. Boynton, and with Secretary Very Worshipful John Whicher,
authorizing the proffering of needed funds for the relief of any sufferers in the storm-swept region. The offer was immediately wired to
the Grand Master of Illinois, who informed us that the Grand Lodge
of IHinois could care for all relief and that our funds were not needed.

After conferring with the Masters of the Lodges, with the members
of the Masonic Temple Association, and with other prominent Masons
in the city, I decided to summon our Grand Lodge Finance Committee
in or·der that the damage might be surveyed and the conditions consider.ed, to the end that some relief might be extended the Masons of
Santa Barbara. Accordingly, at my request, the Finance Committee of
G1-and Lodge assembled in Santa Barbara on July 8, 1925. In the
meantime, at my request, engineers had made a survey of the building
and the loss, and their report was ready to be presented to the Financ~
Committee. It was early ·determined that some financial assistance must
be given the Masons of Santa Barbara, in order that the Temple might
be repaired and a meeting place provided for the Masonic bodies. The
engineers'. estimate showed that the damaged building could. be repaired
at a. max1?1um cost '?f $35,000, and the Finance Committee, after conferring with the engineers and with the Masonic leaders of Santa
Barbara, agreed to finance the work of restoring the Temple and
authorized the Masonic Temple Association to draw upon Grand Lodge
and t~ prese~~ itemized vouchers for the expenditures ·of all moneys
used m repamng and restoring the building. This action on the part
of the Finance Committee had the endorsement and approval of the
Grand Master, and it is submitted at this time for confirmation and
approval by this Grand Lodge.
Following the conference and the decision of the Finance Committee
to provide a suffici~t sum for the reconstruction of the building, your
G;and Master appomted a committee, composed of Bro. William P.
Filmer, Grand Treasurer, chairman, Bro. George W. McComber of
Santa Barbara and Bro. William P. Jeffries of Los Angeles to take
charge of the reconstruction work. A report in full is pre;ented by
the Santa Barbara Masonic Temple Association and this committee

Lassen Monument Site
Particularly interested fn and concurring with the recommendations
of Past Grand Master Sherman and Past Grand Master Crites that the
Grand Lodge of Masons of California should acquire, properly improve
and care for the tract of land on which is located the grav·e of Peter
Lassen I found opportunity, during the year, to visit the site of the
grave ~ear Susanville; to oonfer with t~ose inte.re:ted in. the preserva·
tion ofi the site in Susanville and to begm negotiat10ns with the owner
of the tract in order that Grand Lodge might acquire the same.
Peter Lassen brought the first Masonic Charter into the State of
California and at Benton City, near Redding, he opened and held the
first Mas~nic Lodge under that charter. The charter itself is now. t~e
proud possession of Western Star Lodge at Shasta. Peter Lassen, 1t js
said, was killed by the Indians, and his body was br?ught to a place
near Susanville for burial. Susanville Lodge has, at its own expense,
erected a suitable monument over the grave to replace an older monument whkh was disintegrating and weatherbeaten. The grave is· located
at the foot of an enormous yellow pine tree, one of a grove of fif.ty
or more trees and is a fitting resting place for this pioneer Mason.
There is a se~timent among Masons of California that "this grave and
the tract of land on which it is located· and this 'wonderful grove of
yellow pine trees should be preserved :as the property of the Masons
of California. Because the matter had been tentatively handed dowu
to me by preceding Grand Masters, I began correspondence .early in
the year with Mrs. Hulsman, the owner of the land, and with Bro.

394

Jules Alexander of Susanville. By reason of this corr·espondence, and
through the good offices of Bro. Alexander, success has crowned my
efforts, and I am proud and pleased to report to you that Mrs. Hulsman
has deeded to the Grand Lodge of California the two acres of land
with the grove of yellow pine trees on which the grave is located. This
deed conveys to the Grand I,odge, free -0f all oharge, the two acres of
land, including the water right, and the only expense which Grand
Lodge has incurred in the deal is the survey of the site and the expense
of making and recording the deed, together with the cost of a certificate
of title. It is my recommendation now to this Grand Lodg·e that a
committee be appointed by the incoming Grand Master, the duties of
whic.h committee will be to properly care for the site, to fence it, and
to establish a memorial park, which will forever be a credit to Masonry
in California. I also recommend that a fund of not to exceed $500 be
appropriated for the use of this committee in making such a park.
I h.ave already expressed my personal appreciation to Mrs. Hulsman
for her generous gift and to Bro. Jules Alexander for his effective
work in the matter of the acquisition of the tract of land, and it is
my request that this appreciation be also extended by Grand Lodge.

Western Star Lodge
In connection with my interest in the matter of the Peter Lassen
grave and monument, I was greatly interested in my visit to the old
Masonic Temple and Lodge roori1 of Western Star Lodge No. 2. Here
have been accumulated, in a rather careless and desultory fashion,
records of Masonry from the foundation of our institution in California.
Western Star Lodge is in a very unsatisfactory condition by reason of
the desertion of the village by most of its former inhabitants. Most of
the membership of the Lodge, now numbering 94, are scattered over the
face of the earth. Several of them maintain their residences in Redding and go out to Shasta in order to make a quorum and to hold
the Lodge meetings. The original charter, brought by Peter Lassen
to this State· from Missouri, is a part of the property of the Lodge
and is preserved in an old safe in the building. The books and records
of Western Star Lodge are kept in a very unsatisfactory way, and
they should be preserved. Reference to the Tyler's register shows that
the Lodge is the Mecca for Masons from all parts of the United States
wh~, tr~velling north ·Or south on the ihighway between Oregon and
·California, make a detour in order to visit this old Masonic Temple.
The· Temple is and should be a shrine of Masonry in California.

The seeming complexity of the provisions governing Masonic trials
and the many decisions handed down during the past years governing
such procedure have been the cause of difficulties to Masters, Secretaries
and trial com.missioners of Lpdges, as well as to the Grand Lodge Committee on Appeals and Grievances. In order to simp.lify the procedure
and to bring all of the matter in relation to trials into one compact
form, our Worshipful Bro. Walter F. Haas, chairman of the Committee
on Appeals and Grievances, early in the year proffered his services in
the compilation and arrangement of all of the regulations, decisions
and forms governing Masonic trials. With the official sanction and
direction of the Grand Master, Bro. Haas, after several months of
diligent, arduous work, completed a manual which, by our direction,
was printed and distributed to the Masters of the State, and which,
in .a compact and compr:ehensive form, in plain, untechnical English,
portrayed Masonic trial procedure so that the lay members conducting
trials are now able to follow the same without confusion. \VorshipfuI
Bro. Haas, for. this very splendid work, has received the expressions
of gratitude and appreciation from the Grand Master, and I know that
he will have the hearty approbation of Grand Lodge.

: Physical· Requirements
Section 94 of our Constitution, relating to the physical qualifications
~f a candidate for the degrees of Masonry, is entirely unsatisfactory;

has been the basis for indecision and inquiry on the part of Masters and
brethren of the Lodges, and has been the cause of unending correspondence during this year. I have received hundreds of inquiries
asking for rulings and interpretations of Section 94 <luring the year,
to all of which I have invariably responded, as I must needs do, that
Section 94 is conclusive and means what it says, and that, according
to the interpretation of the Jurisprudence Committee, the Master of a
Lodge should, in the exercise of a wise discretion on the questions
of fact, decide for himself, and that each case should be <letermined on
its merits without fixing any hard and fast rules. But even this response
on the part of the Grand Master is not satisfactory and has resulted
in the most ridiculous nonconformity in Masonic Lodges. One Worshipful Master who receives this reply decides that a man with his
arm off at the left shoulder "conforms substantially to the requirements
of the several degrees." Another Worshipful Master, in the exercise
of a wise discretion, ·determines the question of fact for himself and
decides that an applicant with ihis arm off at the right shoulder "conforms substantially to the requirements of the severa1 degrees"; receives
the candidate's petition, elects him, and confers the degrees upon him.
The same Worshipful Master, again ex-ercising his wise discretion,
determines that a man who was injured by shrapnel during the war
and cannot bend his knee, at :rll, to kneel at the altar, conforms substantially to the requirements of the degrees. The same Wornhipful
Master, or another 'Worshipful Master, in the exercise of his wise
discretion, determines that a man who is so afflicted that he cannot
wear a hoodwink, conforms substantially to the several degrees and
receives and elects the candidate. The Worshipful Master of another
Lodge, perhaps in the same District, and at least not very . .far away,
decides that applicants similarly afflicted do not confol'm, and, in the
exercise of his wise discretion, rejects the petition.
.
.
It will readily be seen that there ir>' no uniformity in the operation
of this section of the Constitution. Your Grand Master believes that
there shoul·d be a resolution or ruling of Grand L-Odge which . wiU
provide this uniformity. The Grand Master has no power to i$iUe a
dispensation in this matter but I do not believe that it is a· matter
that should be wit:h the Grand Master. It is my belief that the regulation should be prnvided by Grand Lodge and should be sufficiently
plain and :oncise so that there would be no misunderstanding it by
the subordmate Lodges. Masonic µsage from time immemorial has
prescribed that a candidate for Masonry must be a "perfect youth,"
having no maim or defeet in his body that would deter him in serving
the art of his Master. But it is agreed that the ancient charge is too
restrictive and cannot apply in these later days. Nevertheless,. there
must be some restriction and some regulation, becau;e there has not

yet been provided any r·estriction or regulation that applies to the
discrimination of Masters of Lodges in this matter. · One Lodge in
California will receive any application from anyone, whether maimed
or halt or blind-another Lodge, whose Master exercises a different
kind of discrimination, will be characterized by having no man a member
of it who is maimed in mind or body. It is my belief that Section 94
should be amended, and I submit for the consideration of Grand Lodge
the following amendment to Section 94: "Section 94. No Lodge in
this jurisdiction shall receive an application * * * having no maim
or defect in his body that may render him ineligible to be a Mason."
That is, physical maims and defects should be considered on the basis
-Of his ability to receive, practice and impart freely and without artificial.
or other ai<l all the rites and ceremonies of ancient Cra.ft Masonry,
including the work in the Lodge room, and shall possess the mental
and physical ability to earn his living in his chosen occupation outside
the Lodge.

Fees for Dispensations to Hold Elections
Section 135 of our Constitution provides that the Master, Wardens,
Treasurer and Secretary of each Lodge shall be elected annually by
ballot at the stated meeting next preceding the anniversary of St. John
the Evangelist. Section 43 provides "the Grand Master, during the
interval between communication of Grand Lodge, may exercise all his
ex-ecutive powers defined in Section 9 except in the granting of charters.
By virtue of these, authority is given him, among other things, (2) to
grant dispensation for the election of an officer or officers at times
other than the regular period prescribed in Section 135 under regulations provided in Section 138." Section 138 provides the regulations
for issuing such dispensation. Section 39, d, requires that the Lodge
petitioning for a dispensation to hold an election other than that prescribed by Section 135 shall pay a fee of $10 for such dispensation.
While the purpose and spirit of this Section 39, d, are quite proper,
yet it so happens that practically the only Lodges ever petitioning for
such dispensation are those located in the mountain sections of the
State where it is i111possible for such Lodges many times to hold an
election on the date prescribed by the Constitution, and unfortunately,
too, such Lodges are the smaller Lodges of the State which cannot
afford very often to pay $10 for such dispensation. These Lodges are
only held together at this time by the over-exertion of the few remaining members who frequently find it a hardship to subscribe the $10
demanded by Grand Lodge for this dispensation. It is my recommendation th!lt Section 39 be amended by striking out all of the third paragraph
thereof.

Diamond Anniversaries
This has been a year for the celebration of the seventy-fifth
anniversary of several Masonic Lodges of this jurisdiction. Since the
celebration of its diamond anniversary by our Grand Lodge in Los
Angeles at the annual communication in 1924, the seventy-fifth anniversaries have been observed by appropriate celebrations, of California
Lodge No. 1, Western Star Lodge No. 2, Teh~ma Lodge No. 3, Benicia
Lodge No. 5, and before the end of this calendar year Tuolumne Lodge
No. 8, Corinthian Lodge No. 9 and San Jose Lodg·e No. 10 will have
reached their seventy-fifth milestone. It was my privilege to be able
to attend the seventy-fifth anniversary of California Lodge No. 1,
which was cdebrated on the site of the old Lodge room in the city of
San Francisco, and. which was made as realistic as possible by the
appearance at the opening of the Lodge of the officers attired in the
picturesque apparel of those early days. The furniture, lighting and
paraphernalia of the Lodge was made to correspond as nearly as possible
with those of the first days of Masonry in California.
Benicia Lodge No. 5, which was chartered in April of 1850, celebrated its seventy-fifth anniversary later in the year, and because of my
inability to attend, our Worshipful Bro. J o•hn Whicher, Grand Secretary,
represented the Grand Master and the Grand Lodge, and reported a
very splendid occasion.
At all of these anniversary celebrations, while there was an evident
desire to give honor to the Lodge, yet in every case did the membership
pay their full measure of resp·ect and homage to those good men and
true, whose vision made possible the org~nization of the Lodge; whose
courage and determination carried it on, when its administration was a
burden and a responsibility.
Dispensation to Reballot
Notwithstanding the action of many of my worshipful pr·edecessors
in refusing to grant dispensations for reballoting within a year upon
rejected candidates, there has seemed to be an ever-increasing desire
on the part of Lodges to petition for dispensation to reballot on such
rejected candidates. Innumerable requests have been received during
the year for such dispensation, and with but very few exceptions the
dispensations have been denied. We have taken the position that unless
a positive mistake has been made, evidenced by declaration on the
part of a brother who made such mistake, that dispensation should not
issue. We believe that this position is entirely cons'istent with tht
ancient charges and the law of Masonry. Mackie, in his Masonic

GRAND. LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

399

Jurisprudence, states that the right of a Lodge, expressed by unanimous
consent of all the brethren present, to judge of whom it shall admit
to its membership, is called an inherent privilege, and it is expressly
said that it is not subject to a dispensation. The reason assigned for
this is one that will suggest itself at once to any reflective mind, namely,
because the members are themselv·es the best judges of the particular
reasons for accepting or rejecting, and if an objectionable person is
thrust upon them contrary to their wishes, the harmony of the Lodg·e
may be· impaired or even its continuance hazarded. And, further on,
Mackie says: "So anxious is the law to preserve this independenc·e of
the ballot as the great safeguard of its purity that the Grand Lodge,
supreme on almost every other subject, 1has no power to interfere in
reference to the ballot for a candidate. And, notwithstanding, that an
injustice !llay have been done to an upright and excellent man by his
r·ejection, neither the Grand Lodge nor the Grand Master can afford
any redress, nor can any dispensation be granted for reversing the
decision of the Lodge."
Although that statement was written many, many years ago, it is
still sound doctrine and good enough for this Grand Master. My
action in refusing to grant thes·e dispensations is in concurrence with
the views expressed by Past Grand Master Bledsoe in 1915, and, also,
in accor·d with the sentiments of Past Grand Master Adams on the
same subject. To quote from the report of the Grand Lodge of
Nevada, the dispensation to re ballot should be a rare exception and
no longer the habit. Danger lurks in its use. Frequent use ·ends in
abuse, and, to say the least, it is a slipshod way of guarding the
portals of the Craft. Even in the case of an alleged mistake, the
Craft and not the p·etitioner should be given the benefit of the doubt, ·
for the petitioner has always another day ahead, and if possessed with
the makings of a good Mason, he can better afford to wait. A Lodge's
time-honored right to select its own material and the hallowed sacr-edness of the ballot should not be made the subject of dispensation nor
the whim of a Grand Master.
During the year, dispensations have been granted to ten Lodges to
reballot upon rejected candidates. But several times that number have
been denied, because Lodg·es could give no good and sufficient reason
wh:Y"a dispensation should be issued or that mistakes had been made
in the ballot.
Arrest of Charter
But once before in recent years has a Grand Master of this
jurisdiction aneste<l the charter of a regularly constituted Lodge.
A (;,r.an:d .Master refrains usually. from exercising this prerogative of
his office until ·every other effort to bring about order and harmony

PROCEEDINGS OF THliJ

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and obedience and submission has been exhausted. My attention was
directed to the situation existing in Yosemite Lodge No. 99 at Merced
early in the Y'ear.
For several years there had been unrest in the ranks of the membership. Unpleasant and un-Masonic differences of remote and r·ecent
occurrence had been reported to me. Old Past Masters, who were
not willing to admit that a newer and younger g·eneration was taking
its place in the sun, still endeavored to control the affairs of the
Lodge. The building of a new Temple, and the direction of its affairs,
aroused contentions in the membership. Political differences, irrigation
district rows which divided the community were permitted to be carried
into the Lodge, engendering strife and bitterness.
The Ku Klux Klan had injected its nefarious and baneful influence
into the Lodge. Petitioners for the degrees in Yosemite Lo<\ge were
being constantly blackballed. The annual election was pending. Klan
and anti-Klan politics were rife. As a result of the election the
Master was selected by a scant majority. The house was divided
against itself. Repeated inquiries brought replies of unsatisfactory
conditions. The matter was referred to Worshipful Brother William
W. Abbott, one of the most loyal, conscientious and honorable Masons
in this jurisdiction. He made a careful, diligent investigation, pronounced the case almost hopeless but urged that a visit from the
Grand Master might bring about a better understanding. Always ready
to restore peac·e and harmony the Grand Master went to Merced and
found the situation all that had been represented. Efforts were made
to get the contending influences together. The Master agreed to
renounce all connections with the Klan. Past Masters of the Lodge
agreed to meet the Master and his fri·ends half way. All gave me a
promise that they would thereafter act as became Masons, and with
the Constitution of the Grand Lodge hanging over their heads, with
warnings of the danger that threatened, Yosemite Lodge members were
given a time on probation. But the Grand Master had no sooner
departed than the back-biting and slander of the character assassins
were resumed. The promises were not kept. Masons of Merced and
particularly the officers and Past Masters did not keep faith with
the Grand Master. Accusations were hurled back and forth. We were
kept in close touch with the situation through W. Brother Abbott and
finally because the situation seemed impossible, becaus·e the Lodge
see.med no longer able to function as a Masonic institution, because
at the July stated meeting, the same old unwarranted tactics of rejecting every petitioner were resumed, and because it seemed useless and
unwis·e to trifle longer with Yosemite Lodge, on August 14, 1925,
I dispatched the following letter to Brother Charles William Dempsey,
Worshipful Master of the Lodge:

To Chas. William Dempsey, Master, and the Wardens and
Brethren of Yosemite Lodge No. 99, F. & A. M.

400

491

BR!lTHR!lN:

It appearing that the Lodge is and for many months past
has been guilty of violation and neglect of the ancient and
recognized usages of the Craft, in that a condition of lack of
harmony so necessary for the prop·er conduct of a Lodge of
Freemasons is prevalent; that contentions exist in the Lodge
and among the members thereof; that such contentions are
known to and discussed by citizens of the community in which
the Lodge is located ; that patient and continued effort on the
part of the Grand Master to affect a spirit of harmony among
the members have availed nothing.
' And it appearing that the good of Masonry requires that
the Lodge should cease its work and activities, it .is hereby
Ordered, that the charter of Yosemite Lodge No. 99,
F. & A. M., located at the city of Merned, be and the same
is hereby arrested and the work and business of the said
Yosemite Lodge is hereby suspended until the next annual
communication of our Grand Lodge.
It is further ordered that the charter of said Yosemite
Lodge be forthwith delivered into the custody of Worshipful
William W. Abbott, Inspector of the fifty-fifth Masonic District,
to be· by him transmitted to the Grand Secretary.
All moneys an<l property of said Lodge are hereby placed

(who is specifically exempted from this suspension), until the
further order of the Grand Master or Grand Lodge.
By order of David John Reese, Grand Master.

Dispensation Revoked
But while the arrest of a Lodge's charter has had to be directed,
a more serious and a far. more unpleasant duty has had to be performed.
By my order and direction the dispens;,1tion granted on December 18,
1924, to twenty-four Master Masons to form and open a Lodge in the
city of Los Angeles, to be known as and called Beacon of the West U. D.
was, on September 29, 1925, revoked. Beacon of the West Lodge was
a Masonic child of my own creation. The dispensation granted by me
provided that such dispensation was to continue until the annual communication of Grand Lodge, unless sooner revoked. It provided, too,
that Beacon of the West Lodge U. D. sh'ould in all respects conform to
the laws and regulations of Grand Lodge and that it should observe
the spirit no less than the letter of the law. This, Beacon o(the West
Lodge did not do, as is evidenced by the very careful and complete
investigation and report of W. Brother Charles P. Lyndall, Inspector
of the sixty-eighth Masonic District, who was appointed by me for the
purpose. Because of this report and becal\lse of the very serious disregard for Masonic law and custoin, I felt it my duty to revoke the
dispensation theretofore granted by me. My order directing said
revocation of dispensation is attached hereto and made a part of this
record, and all of the papers connected with the matter will be referred
to the proper committee for consideration.

To the Officers and Brethren, Bracon of the West Lodge U. D., .. ,

Three times this year have I had to resort to summoning Lodge
membership on account of alleged unMasonic conduct and violation of
Masonic laws. The first of these was in a Lodge which after its election
and before the qualification of its officers, was unable to function and in
which I reprimanded the Master and Master-elect, directed the removal
of all officers, ordered a new election, thereafter installed new officers,
and I am happy to state brought order out of chaos.
The second was in a Lodge, certain members of which participated
, in a drunken orgy on New Year's eve, disgraced themselves and their
Lodge. A summonsed meeting developed that these charges were in a
large, measure true, the offending members were reprimanded, and the
Lodge placed on probation.
And the third was in a large city Lodge, where the Master violated
the established laws of Masonry, where the summonsed meeting gave
proof of the charges and where a reprimand and probation resulted.
There have been a number of other violations of law and Masonic
custom reported to me during the year, some in direot protest which
could not be disregarded, some indirectly and therefore not demanding
attention. Due consideration has been given to all of these, however,
and an effort made to prove the sufficiency of the charges. Where the
offense could be corrected, I have felt it my duty to call it to the attention of the Lodge and its officers.
It seems passing strange that men who are qualified to direct the
affairs of a Masonic Lodge should permit such offenses as these to occur,
and yet I presume we must be charitable and charge the errors and
misconduct to the proverbial weakness and frailities of mankind.

DAVID J. REESE,

One of the fundamentals of our professions as Masons is resp!!Ct for
the law. The operation of a lottery, for instance, is not .only a transgression of a written legal and Masonic statute, but it is an offense
against the integrity of those who engage. in it. And while we as
individuals, may be knowingly or unknowingly guilty of infraction~ of
the law, yet when we as a Lodge violate any law we are making an
open proclamation to the world that we are not sincere in our· professions.

followed to accomplish these ends. The Grand Lodges of Massachusetts
and Pennsylvania hav·e done notable w.ork along these lines, for which
they are entitled to the thanks of the Craft at large. It is time the
Grand Lodge of California took the first steps to emulate them in their
inspiring example.

Grand Historian
The diamond anniversary of the Grand Lodge of California is now
a matter of history. We are verging on toward a century of Masonic
activity in California. Abel Stearns, the first regular Mason to become
a permanent resident, arrived in this state in 1848. During this period,
many of the most prominent and most useful citizens of the commonwealth have become Masons. Masonry, both through individual members and by direct activity, has figured large in that bewildering
development which makes up the history of California. Many phases
of that history can never be rightly appraised until these facts ar:e
disclosed, and the Grand Lodge of California will not be invested with
that full dignity, respect and honor which it is our duty not to withhold
from it until both its constituency and the citizens· at large are given
full, fair and authentic accounts of these activities.
Whether we consider the inspiration, the conquest, the beginning,
the ~.old excitement, the establishment of government, of education, of
chanty,. or the •essential business transportations, agricultural or other
enterprises, we find ever present an imposing Masonic element. Mention
. of a name here and ·there will serve to quick;en our interest and bring
this truth home to us. Kit Carson and George Yount, explorers, Commodore. Sloat and Colonel Stevenson (our first Grand Master), conquerers; the far-famed president of our first constitutional convention and
Myron Norton, the committeeman to whom was given the task of
formulating the constitution, Starr King and James King of William,
and other early figures of San Francisco; Lassen, Downey and Roop of
the mining region; Hodges, first Mayor of Los Angeles, Wilson, its
second Mayor; Derby, Ames, Robinson, Crossthwaite of San Diego,
and so on. But any mention of names here is really invidious because
it is rather in the manifold instances of the practice of Masoni~ virtues
by unnamed Masons on the trails, by Masons in the crude frontier
communities, that the glory of Masonry lies.
Thus far, absolutely no systematic effort has been made by the
Grand Lodge to take care of this important work. The burning of our
·early records in the San Francisco fire was a serious loss which should

The Festival was truly representative of the best and highest type
of manhood in the English-speaking world, and doubtless the effect of
the great gathering at St. Patrick's Cathedral and the dignity of the
services will serve the pnrpose--so much to be desired in Irelandof disabusing a portion of the public mind in that country of suspicions
and prejudices which prevail there. The Irish Times, in an editorial
comment, bravely and justly stated that "the celebration was an expression of the pride and gratitude of tens of thousands of Irishmen,
and of the good-will of the legion of fellow-craftsmen in other lands.
The term 'secret society' has a special significance in this country, and
ill-informed people have chosen to regard Irish Freemasonry as a 'secret
society' in the political and invidious sense. Again, there are bodies
of so-called Freemasons in Southern Europe whose activities are antiChristian and highly political, and Irish Freemasonry has suffered
through the myth that it has some association with them. We wish that
every man and woman in Ireland could be brought to read the text
of the Primate's sermon. Dr. d' Arey sets forth the main principles of
Freemasonry in plain and convincing words. The Masonry which is
practiced throughout the English-speaking world is not anti-Christian.
On the contrary, its foundation is a deep faith in God. It is hostile to
no church, and exhorts its members to be loyal to their several creeds.
It preaches obedience to the settled constitutions of States. The great
assembly in St. Patrick's Cathedral yesterday made prayer and asked
God to 'bless and direct the Governor-General of the Irish Free State
and the Governor of Northern Ireland, and those who bear rule under
them.' Finally, Freemasonry preaches charity in all things, and sets
an example in the perfect management and liberal maintenance of its
benevolent institutions. There is no religious intolerance in the Free
State, but misapprehensions, based on ignorance, survive in some minds.
If the present celebrations help to dispel that ignorance, they will have
done a good service to the caus·e of national peace and progress. Ireland, North and South, has no sons more patriotic, no citizens more
useful, than those who are enrolled as Masons."
Considering the programme seriatum, of course the thanksgiving
service in the great cathedral was the outstanding event of the Festival.
It is reported that two thousand five hundred Masons and one thousand
spectators not of the Craft attended. Before the service commenced, one
hundred and five girls and one hundred and one boys from the two
Masonic schools, with their teachers, marched into places reserved for
them. The brethren formed in the Lady Chapel, back of the chancel,
and the participants marched to the nave to the music of the organ.
The large choir headed the procession, singing that old hymn :

It may be of interest to note here that police regulations in Dublin
require all public meetings to close not later than 11 o'clock at night,
a practice which might be emulated in America with profit to the health
of our brethren who continue their banquets beyond that hour.
The Masonic Benevolent Institutions. Friday was devoted to a
visit to the Masonic schools. There are three Benevolent Institutions
conducted by the brethren of Ireland, all supported by voluntary contributions, with little help from Grand Lodge.

The Victoria Jubilee Masonic Annuity Fund
was founded in 1887 with the object of providing annuities for poor
brethren and widows, in their old age. Candidates must be at least
sixty years of age, or permanently disabled from earning · a livelihood.
The maximum amount of annuity to any one person is $200 per annum.
The Grand Master of California is a Vic'e President of this Fund, and
of the two schools for orphan children, and under the rules he is entitled to four votes for candidates for annuities, and five votes in each
of the schools. This came about in 1900, when Brother J . Holdbrook,
then Assistant Secretary of the Irish Funds, wrote to our Grand Master
Oscar Lawler that the unexpended balance of the contribution of the
Grand Lodge of Ireland to the Grand Lodge of California for the relief
of sufferers from the catastrophe of 1906, which had been refunded to
the Grand Lodge of Ireland, had been donated to the thl'ee Masonic
Irish charities, and that the Grand Master of California had been elected
a Vice President of those institu.tions. His voting is by a proxy held
by the Secretary at Dublin.

Masonic Female Orphan School
This institution, now located at Ballsbridge, near Dublin, was
founded in 1792, and is at the present time caring for one hundred and
eighty-two girls. Thirty-five past pupils are receiving grants for their
hig·her education, and forty-two non-pupils receive maintenance and
education grants. One hundred and five girls are housed at the school.
The curriculum includes English, Irish, French, literature, commercial
subjects,· mathematics, drawing, music, singing, needle work domestic
economy and gymnastics, and the teaching staff is composed of a head
mistress, a matron and twelve assistant class mistresses. The Board of
Governors is a large body, divided into committees on House, Education, Finance, Advisory, Ladies, and Apprentice Committee. These
committees meet at the school monthly, no two meeting at the same
time, and they pay t·he Home for their own meals-this in the way of
added contributions. The average cost per head for each resident pupil,
including lodging, clothing, education, maintenance, medical expenses
and upkeep of the house and grounds, is $325. The item of salaries
and wages amount to $8,000 a year. Twenty-one prizes have been
founded in various sums. As a sample, I quote two:
"The Shekleton prizes, five pounds ($25) yearly forever, founded by
the daughters of the late Robert William Shckleton, Deputy Grand
Master, by a donation of one hundred pounds. These prizes are awarded
after each annual examination to those pupils of the several classes
who have evinced the greatest amount of perserverance and industry in
all branches .of study during the year." Another, "to found a bursary
of six pounds ($30) yearly forever, for the benefit of the most necessitous and deserving pupil leaving the school in each year."
The girls, as you may judge from the photograph I hand you, are
well cared for, decently clad, and happy.
Masonic Orphan Boys' School
After luncheon with the girls, we visited the school for boys at
Richview, several miles from the school for girls. It is presided over
by Brother Jam es Moore, M. A., who has been Head Master since
1897. (As a compliment t.o his long service he was, on the 3d of
June, rewarded by being selected to receive the twenty-eighth degree
by the Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite.) One hundred and one
bright-faced boys are housed and schooled there, at a cost for maintenance and education of each resident pupil of $340 a year. They are
received at the age of nine and not over thirteen. The teaching staff
numbers twelve. The Board of Governors meets monthly at 9 a. m.
(note the hour), breakfast being previously served to them at the school

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

-at their expense. Twenty-three prizes have been founded by friends
of the school, some of them being for boys who enter as students in
some Irish university.
The total income for the three benevolent institutions last year was
$130,000, part being income from legacies, but the major part from
individual yearly donations of the brethren.
Dues in Dublin Lodges are generally four guineas a year ($20).
There are seventy-five Lodges in that city, the largest being No. 133,
with 300 members, and two hundred Lodges in Belfast.
When we consider that the entire membership of the six hundred
and fifty Lodges of the Jurisdiction does not exceed fifty thousand
Masons, many of them poor; that scores of formerly wealthy Masons
are now impoverished because of the wanton destruction of property
during the revolutionary war of some thr.ee and four years ago; that
Freemasonry is not looked upon with favor by a large percentage of
the people of Ireland, we and they may well be proud of their good
work in constructive Masonry. Their annuity fund and their two high_class schools, which rank with the best schools of the country, are only
the visible evidence of the serious and charitable work of our Irish brethren, but they are !vidence enough to prove their worth as men and
as Masons.

(X)(). In addition, orphan annuitants to the number of 221 receive some
$10,(X)() yearly. Special collections were taken in the Lodges of their
obedience in April of this year for the benefit of the Annuity Fund,
the receipts aggregating $24,000. At the same time their Orphan Fund
was increased over $13,000. Our brethren of Scotland take the view
that if a dependent child has one parent, assistance should be given to
the parent to help support and educate the child near its own home. In
the case of a full orphan, they try to provide full educational facilities
in some established school of high standing, so that no taint of institutionalism should ever attach to the child. They have several now
being educated in the best schools of Edinburgh-and that city is noted
as an educational center of the first rank. I am not unmindful of the
reputation of the people of Scotland for being "near" and "keerful,"
but I commend their policy of education for dependent children to
your thoughtful consideration.

Grand Lodge of Nevada
In June of this year a most courteous invitation was received from
M. W. Edward A. Ducker, Grand Master of Nevada, and from V. W.
Edward Vanderleith, Grand Secretary of that jurisdiction, to attend
the annual communication of the Grand Lodge to be held in Reno,
June 10, 11, 1925. N'evada is the state of our nativity and it was with
unusual pleasure and not a little satisfaction that we availed ourselves
of this opportunity. Your Grand Master was received most hospitably.
Our own Grand Lodge could not have made us more at home. Every
courtesy was extended. We were accorded the privileges of the floor
and as a climax to the recognitions and honors extended, the constitution of the Grand Lodge of Nevada was amen'ded by unanimous vote
to permit of the acceptance of honorary members and thereafter your
Grand Master was elected an honorary member with the title of Past
Grand Master. To be thus honored by the Masons of my native state
was especially gratifying and pleasant.
Possibly once before, but only once, has a Grand Master of California officially visited the Grand Lodge of Nevada. Nevada is our
Masonic offspring. Prior to 1865, the year of organization of its
Grand Lodge, the State of Nevada was under the jurisdiction of California ; Carson Lodge No. 1 was form!erly our No. 154; Virginia No.
3 was our No. 162; Amity No. 4 was our No. 163; Escurial No. 7
was our No. 171; Lander No. 8 was our No. 172, all of the jurisdiction
of California. Our two states are so close together, their interests in
the past and today, Masonically and otherwise, are so closely related
and of such mutual nature that we of California should iencourage ancl
carry on the most friendly and fraternal relations. I here make profound acknowledgment for honors extended to me, and I express the
hope that my visit may be the means of bringing about, and thus
cementing the ties that now exist, official fraternal visits each succeeding year when our respective Grand Lodges meet in annual communication.

Six Months' Inhibition·
There hav.e been some rumblings of discontent with the amend-·
ment to our laws, adopted in 1921, providing that· no l\faster l\fason
mq.y apply for membership in any of the coordinate bodies of Masonry;
the. prerequisite -0f which is that the petitioner be a ).faster Mason, for
at least six months; but whlen these rumblings are searched out it is
found, in every case, that some new Master Mason or his friends are:
very anxious that he shall take a shortcourse through the so-c;:alled
higher degrees to· the playground of Masonry. I am convinoed that
among the best legislation enacted in recent years is that providing for
this six months' inhibition. It has had its effect upon the Lodges of
this Jurisdiction and there can be no complaint among consistent, rightthinking Masons that the six months' inhibition works any hardship
upon anyone. \Ve can't make Masons too fast, but we are making
members too fast, and in the past we have conferred the three degrees
upon petitioners whose sole object and purpose was to. secure the
pret'equisites in order that they might wear the red fez of the Shrine..
There is some little contention among certain brethren that the Grand·
Lodge of California has no authority to make such a law, but I am:
confident that the Grand Lodge of California is still supreme in ·~it
matters of Masonic membership, and that thte laws which it has en-,
acted and which it will e!;lact are for the best interests of Masonry in .
this Jurisdktion.
There have been many inquiries as to the application of this six
months' inhibition provision in relation to the Masonic clubs of the ;
statle. Early in the year a letter was received from \Vorshipful Bro.
W. B. Ogden, Master of Hollywood Lodge No. 355, making inquiry as
to the application of Subdivision 13, Section 246, to the J'acific 2331
Club of Hollywood. The question was submitted to Most Worshipful
F. ::VL Angellotti, chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, and i.t
was :his opinion that Subdivision 13, Section 246, applied to aU Mas.onic
clubs, provided it is essential to admission to such club that one be a
Master Mason. · In his opinion, the chairman of the Jurispmdence
Committee stated. that the whole purpose of the change in our law.·
was to deter outsiders to some iextent at least from using a Masonic
Lodge simply. as a stepping stone to get into some other Masonic ,
organization; that it does not make any difference what kind of
organization it is, Masonic in character, a mere club, or otherwi~e, n~r
is it important whlether there be any formal initiation; it is the acquisi~
tion of membership that is meant; the word "initiation" is often >tscd
in such a sense and should be construed in that sense in the connection ,
which it is used in this subdivision. With this reply in hand, I promptly .
communicated with the ::Vfaster of Hollywood Lodge; and I ha\~e used

the same reply to members of other Masonic Lodges in this Jurisdiction who have made inquiry along the same lines.

Degrees by Courtesy
The provisions of our Constitution, Section 155, regarding' the
conferring of courtesy degrees for other jurisdictions recognized as

GRAND LODGE 01<' CALIFORNIA

423

regular by this Grand Lodge, are too well known to need any repetition
here. The three degrees of. Masonry can be conferred upon a candidate
of another jurisdiction only under written permission from the Grand
Master, and because this provision has been written into our Constitution, it has .been the occasion for many requests for courtesy degrees
during the year.
The todges of this jurisdiction have ·requested Lodges of other
jurisdictions to confer· degrees to the number stated as follows: First
degree, three; second degree, twenty-two; third degree, thirty. For
other jurisdictions, our Lodges have conferred the following: First
degree, nineteen; second degree,. one hundred ninety-one; third degree,
two hundred fifty.
Many requests have bl':en received in which it was desired that
we permit our Lodges to confer the first degree upon candidates who
are not in the Army or Navy service. These your Grand Master has
invariably declined to approve. We have taken the view that a candida.te electe.d fo receive the degr.ees of Masonry in another jurisdiction,
and· who, subsequently, removes to California before the first degree
has been conferred, should not be accorded privileges of our institution
by courtesy. · A Mason thus made could add nothing to the moral or
social strength of his Lodge, but would be merely another name on the
roster of members. He could not participate in any Lodge· activities,
he would not even know the form of the room in which his .Lodge
meets; his money, his fealty, his membership, would be in the old home
city, and he would be a drone in the great hive of nominal Masons.
The conferring of degrees upon such a candidate would really be unfair
to him and· subversive of the best interests of Masonry. On the other
hand, and in order to be entirely consistent, we. have positively denied
every petition from Lodges in our own jurisdiction that we request
Lodges in foreign jurisdictions to confer the three degrees of Masonry
upon candidates who have removed temporarily or permanently from
California to said foreign jurisdiction.

Past Masters' and Past Grand Masters' Jewels
There is no ruling or provision in our laws for a regulation or
prescribed jewel for the Past Master of a Lodge or for a Past Grand
Master of. Grand Lodge. Repeated inquiries have been made in this
respect by Masters and Inspectors and it would seem fitting and proper
to satisfy the demands and desires of Past Officers by adopting appropriate legislation. Mackey in his cyclopedia states that the jewel of a
Past Master in the United States is a pair of compasses extended to
sixty degrees on 'the fourth part of a circle with a sun in the center.

SrxTY-DAY PERIOD-WHEN Do:es IT START?
Burlingame Lodge requested interpretation of the provisions of
Section 101, as amended October 1924, with particular reference to
the date on which the sixty-day period starts.
"Section 101, as amended, provides: Application received
* * * if the report of the committee, or a majority thereof,
be favorable and no objection has been made by any member
of the Lodge, a secret ballot shall be had at once without any
postponement by the use of cubes and white balls: if any objection has been made no ballot shall be had unless such objec<tion
be withdrawn and unless withdrawn within sixty days such
objection shall have the effect of a rejection by ballot, and shall
be so reported to the Grand Secretary."
When a petition is received it is referred to a committee and the
committee report is received and presented to the Lodge at the next
stated meeting, at which time action is taken on the petition.
Under the amended provision of this section a brother may object
to a petition immediately after its reception or at any time in the
interim between ,the date of reception and the next stated meeting.
It is the duty of the Master of the Lodge to make a report on the
petition at the next st<tted meeting in any event, whether the committee
has reported fav.orably or unfavorably, or whether a brother, or brothers,
have made or presented an objection thereto. If such objection· be
made prior to the meeting at which the petition would be acted upon
in the regular procedure, then the Master must make such r-eport upon
the petition at such meeting. It will appear, therefore, that the sixty-

after the date when the Master makes report on such petition.

"Funds of a Lodge are trust funds. Necessarily, in keeping with
sound business practice, unexpen(Ied funds should be so employed as
to make some return. Funds in the possession of a fiduciary generally
must be invested with great precaution, and where there is not statutory
limitation, well recogniZed practice governs. It is within the province
of the Lodge to increase its dues but not within its province to make
any such segregation. This can 'be accomplished in regular order 'by
investing the surplus funds from time to time so long as the application
of the funds .in such manner would constitute a sound investment as
defined.''

Inspector William W. Abbott, of the Fifty-fifth Masonic District,

"In the year 1921 a petition was received by Turlock Lodge No. 395

After consultation with Most Worshipful Brother Francis. V.

given Insp·ector Abbott:
"Residence in California establishes the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge during such residence. While such jurisdiction tnaintains,.degrees
conferred beyond the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge without proper
permission will not be recognized by this Grand Lodge, and recognition
of anyone having received degrees under such circumstances is prohibited. Where all three degrees have been conferred in violation of
this right of jurisdiction it cannot be healed.
"There is only one course for such an individual and that is to
apply to be elected a member of the Lodge nearest his place of
residence."

6.

WITHDRAWAL OF CHARG!lS.

The Master of Visalia Lodge reported that after charges of
embezzlement had been preferred against a brother, after the Commissioners had been elected and before the trial had started the accused
had conferred with the accuser and the latter thereupon signified his
intention to withdraw ·the charges. Question was on the interpretation
<0f Section 195, because said section was not cle.ar and definite. Our
reply, based upon the opinion of :the Jurisprudence Committee member,
was as follows:
"\Vhere charges have been preferred against a brother and the
allegation of embezzlement is specified in support of the charge of
un-Masonic conduct, the Master is without authority to permit a
withdrawal of the charges because the specifications are criminal in
nature.
"The commission should proceed to a trial of the case, summoning the necessary witnesses.
"There is, as always, a reason for the rule. The Lodge is as
much interested as, if not more than, the brother preferring the
charges."

7.

\VITHDRAWAL OF APPLICATION.

An applicant for affiliation in Lompoc Lodge had been rejected by
objection after the committee had made a full and favorable report.
The applicant decided that he did not care to wait sixty days, and
asked to withdraw his application, the Master inquired as to rights
of applicant. My reply follows:
"The application for affiliation is governed by the law applicable
to application for degrees. (See Section 101 of the Constitution.)
The purpose to be subserved in prohibiting withdrawal after reception
of the petition is the same in a case of application for. affiliation as
it is in a case of application for degrees. It safeguards the integrity
of the Fraternity."

8.

MANN!iR or· VoTING.

San Joaquin Lodge desired ruling (1) on how a vote should be
taken in amending by-laws, (2) the number of, votes necessary to
adopt the amendment. Basing our opinion upon Decisions 472 and 473
of our Constitutions and Regulations we made answer as follows;

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

429

"If no motion is made to take the vote other than by show of
hands or viva voce, the Master· should order the vote to be taken in
the manner most usual in the conduct of business in the Lodge.
"Two-thirds of the members present are required to carry an
amendment to the by-laws. If there are 58 members present, 39 votes
are necessary. If 38 vote for the amendment, 13 against and 7 do not
vote, the amendment is carried, because the 7 who do not vate must be
assumed to acquiesce in the vote with the majority.
"Brethren who shirk their duty by casting blank ballots on any
proposition cannot complain of this ruling."

9.

NoT OF LAWFUL AGE:, R!lcrE:vF:s DE:GRE!ls.

Status: A petitioner in Point Lodge No. 503 represented that he
was 21 years of age; he was elected and received his degrees. Thereafter, it was discovered that he had not yet reached his majority, but
that his petition had been made because he had believed himself to be
of age and was innocent of wrong doing. Our reply to this inquiry
follows:
"If this candidate wilfully perjured himself in solemnly declaring
in his petition that he was at the date the petition was received by
your Lodge of the age of twenty-one years, charges should be preferred
against him and the trial commission should order him expelled. If,
however, it is made to appear to the satisfaction of the Master and the
brethren thait the i>etitioner honestly believed he was of lawful age at
the time of his application, I would take the view that he would be
deemed an irregular Mason made in a regular Lodge, and that he could
be 'healed' by having a petition presented after he became of lawful
age, and if it successfully passed the ballot, .that he be brought before
the altar and reobligated, which would constitute 'healing.'
"If the Lodge or the Master recdved the petition of one who was
not of lawful age, knowing that the petitioner was not telling the full
truth in his petition and knowing that he was not at the date of meeting
at which it was received of the age of twenity-one, the Grand Master
would be justified in arresting the charter of the Lodge.
"The Master, in this case, should make rigid inquiry and ascertain
definitely how and why this petitioner signed a petition ait a time when
he could not lawfully petition for the degrees-and the burden of
proof is upon the petitioner and not upon the Lodge."

Condusion
I

This, brethren, is the story .of my stewardship.- Thus, the duties
have been met and in the fashion described we together have tried to'
do the work. Much has been left undone. No doubt the things done
might have been done far better. But in the whole endeavor we have
been animated by one thought, one ambition, 'one desire, that which was
and is for the welfare and integrity of Masonry in the Grand Jurisdiction of California.
It has been our purpose to so represent Masonry, and to permit
such r.epresentation of it, that the world at large could in no way be
misled in its judgment of our institution by a lack of consonance and
harmony between professions and actual performance. It has been our
purpose, too, to safeguard and protect Masonry from misunderstanding
without-from indifference, apathy, prejudice and intolerance within.
I have tried to respond to every call, every duty, every obligation
devolving upon me. Where I have failed, my ow1; reflections have been
my reproach.

436

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The history of my year's service has already been dictated to Time's
stenographer, transcribed to the records of the Past, and the record
is about to be deposited and sealed in the arehives. I return the gavel
to you without any vain or idle regret, but happy in the thought that
it will soon reach the hands of a most worthy successor. I am grMeful for this exalted opportunity for service which you have afforded
me-a joyous service blessed with comradship whose fragrance shall
grow sweeter and sweeter as the years come and go.
The highest conception of Masonry is service. Every human
being has a claim upon our kind offices. Display and ostentation are
entirely foreign 10 the spirit of the Insti.tution. Every attempt to erect
a super-structure or to devise something wonderful upon which the
public might gaze, has been looked upon with disfavor. When the Great
Teacher with his three disciples, found their way to the mountain top
to commune with Moses and Elias, one of the emotional members of
the party proposed to erect three tabernacles. The Gr,eat Teacher
frowned upon the suggestion, and with his eyes directed to the valley,
led his disciples down the mountain side to the lowlands where the multitudes were, and began to heal the sick, relieve the distressed and
render his usual practical service. Brethren, our work is in the valley,
and I would have you press forward with earnestness and ze!d to the
prize of your high calling. Discouragement may come-ingratitude may
be in evidence on every side, even the heavens may seem dark and your
soul rent with agony, but these things are not lost.
And now may I close this address by reading to you that same
message which I have communicated to many of you over this great
jurisdiction this year; the paraphrase of the poem "Let me live in
the House by the Side of the Road."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

437

'Tis only a half truth the poet has sung,
Of the house by the side of the way;
Our Master had neither a h~use nor a home,
But He walked with ·the crowd day by day,
And I think when I read of the poet's desire,
That a house by the road would be good;
But service is found in its tenderest form,
When we walk with the crowd in the road.
So I say, let me walk with the men in the road,
Let me seek out the burdens that crush;
Let me speak a kind word of good cheer to the weak
Who are falling behind in the rush.
There are wounds to be healed, there are breaks we must mend.
There's a cup of cold water to give;
And the man in the road by the side of his friend
Is the man who has learned how to five.
Then tell me no more of the house by the road;
There"s only one place I can live :
It's there with the men who are ·toiling along
Who are needing the cheer I can give.
It is pleasant to live in the house by the way
And befriend, as the poet has said
But the Master is bidding us, "Bear ye their load,
For your rest waiteth yonder ahead."
I could not remain in the house by the road,
And watch as the toilers go on,
Their faces beclouded with pain and with sin,
So burdened their strength nearly gone.
I'll go to their side, I'll speak in giood cheer,
I'll help them to carry their load,
And I'll smile at the man in the house by the way
As I walk with the crowd in the road.
Out there in the road that goes by the house,
\Vhen the poet is singing his song,
I'll walk and I'll work, midst the heat of the day,
And I'll he! p falling brothers along ;
Too busy to live in the house by the way,
Too happy for such an abode,
And my heart sings its praise to the Master above
Who is helping me serve in the road.
