PROCLAMATION.
SIXTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE PUBLIC SCHOOLS \VEE:K
To the Masters, Wardens and Brethren of the Several Lodges in This
Jurisdiction:
The first proclamation instituting Public Schools Week in the
Masonic Lodges in California was designed to focus the attention of
the Craft on the crisis •that was then confronting the ·public school
system in America. That crisis is past, and 'the problem now uppermost in the minds of edueators and laymen is· how the publie schools
can best discharge 1he constantly increasing duties an:d ,responsibilities
imposed upon them by the people. In the last analysis, and: irrespective
of the efforts of educators, the solution of the problem will depend on
the existence· of an enlightened and informed public ·opinion with
respect to ·the aim and purposes of our public schools and the methods
adopted for their accomplishment.
Whether or not the conditions justify the cri;:icism to which our
public schools are being subjected can be known only by those who
are conversant with the facts. The primary objective of the sixth
annual observance of Public Schools Week will therefore .be, to inform
the public in general, and the parents of school children in particular,
of the real condition of our public schools .with specific reference to
certain matters that have been ·the subject of discussion and criticism,
such as "the curricula," "methods of instruction" and "the cost of
education."
The real benefit of the celebration of any anniversary is that it
directs the attention of a 'large number of people to the same thing
at the same time. With that idea in mind,.as Grand Master of Masons
in the jurisdiction of California,' I do therefore riow proclaim the week
commencing Monday, May 11, 1925, as "Public Schools Week" in the
Masonic Lodges in this jurisdiction; and I do most earnestly request
tha·t during that week there be held in the every community in California in which there exists a Masonic Lodge at least one public meeting
(and more, if practicable) through which the people of .that community
may be afforqed an opportunity to become informed and advised with
respect to 'the matters herein referred to:
The accompanying bulletin containiqg suggestions for arranging
and conducting meetings has been prepared by the committee by me
appointed for that purpose, and it is. my direction .that due heed be

Good Citizensh:p
Your committee is in hearty accord with all that the Grand Master
has said in reference to •this important subject. Masonry means good
citizenship and there should be no place for the law-breaker in our
Fraternity. Obedi.ence to law and support of constituted authority are
as essential to the welfare of the Craft as the observance of our
ancient landmarks and this matter is respectively referred to the
Committe·e on Policy and General Purposes and to the Committee on
Jurisprudence.
New Lodges
The question of new Lodges has for several years last past been
a troublesome one. After a careful consideration of the Grand Master's
observations in regard to this subject, your committee agrees with
him that smaller Lodges and more of them will afford a larger opportunity for future Masonic strength and for increasing the proper friendship and brotherly love that should exist among Masons. Searching
inquiry, however, should be made befor,e a dispensation is granted,
both as to the personnel of and the necessity for a new Lodge.

444

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

After dispensation be granted, careful supervision should be exercised, lest an undue desire to increase membership bring discredit to
the fair name of Frnemasonry in California and we respectfully refer
the several matters treated under this heading to the Committee on
General Policy and Purposes.

Extraneous Organizations
One of the most important subjects treat,ed by the Grand Master
is that of Extraneous Organizations, membership in which is based
upon the Masonic degrees. The Grand Master has clearly set forth
the evils resulting from the activities from these bodies and the discredit
such activities are bringing upon Masonry. He has pointed out how
Masons who are restrained, temperate and law abiding in thought,
speech and action while in the Lodge or engag.ed in Lodge work, yet
become reckless, lawless and inconsiderate while carrying on 1he
1lctivities of these side organizations. The public, observing the reckless
carrying on at many a convention or at many an affair preceding or
following a so-ealled "ceremonial" does not distinguish between such
organizations and our Masonic bodies and indiscriminately condemns
the Fraternity. ·
The Grand Master has spoken in no uncertain tone, the facts are
within our own knowledge and call for determined action. We shall
be false to our fine pretentions and principles, unworthy of the great
past of our Order and recreant to the trust resting upon us if we
do not end this intolerable condition. It may seem a difficult problem
and one from which we may feel inclined to shrink, but as we value
the future of our institution, as we value its effectiveness for continued
service, as we value the good opinion of the non-Masonic public, we
must act.
We therefore refer this problem to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes and to the Committee on Jurisprudenoe, earnestly
urging upon them to report some plan to this communication of Grand
Lodge for action.

t•eams. This degree •team work starting in a praiseworthy effort to
bring to the initiate the comfort and satisfaction of having the work
performed by his associates of a store, offioe or factory, it later developed to such a degree that work conferred by the Lodge officers only
is a rarity.
These teams are extending their work so greatly as to almost
supplant the Lodge in the interest of the members. Brethren who have

Dispensation to Reballot

Santa Barbara Earthquake
The Masons of Santa Barbara received a staggering blow by the
earthquake of June, 1925. Their beautiful Temple, completed and about
to be dedicated, was all but wreck!ed. Without the loss of time our
Grand Master, ever alert to relieve distress, hastened to Santa Barbara,
summoned the Finance Committee and appropriated $35,00).00 of the
funds of the Grand Lodge to repair the magnificent edifice. It was a
fine thing to do and demonstrates that our Masonry consists in performance as well as professions. We cannot too highly commend the
Grand Master in this splendid exemplification of true Masonic principles of relief and aid, and feel that Grand Lodge would be remiss
in its duty if it did not promptly ratify and confirm the a'Cts of our
Grand Master and the Finance Co_mmittee.
We therefore respectfully recommend that the acts of the Grand
Master and Finance Committee in appropriating $35,000.00 of the funds
of ,the Grand Lodge for the repair and reconstruction of the Santa
Barbara Masonic Temple be approved.

ANNUAL ORATION·
Grand Lodge then listened with rapt attention to the
Annual Oration of the Grand Orator, w.·. Robert B. Gaylord at the conclusion of which the representatives r·ose
to their feet. with rousing and enthusiastic applause. The
oration is full of meat, and the brother is justly entitled
to the encomiums of Grand Lodge. The full text of the
oration follows:
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge.'
"In Flanders fields the poppies blow
Between the crosses, row on row,
That mark our place ; and in the sky
The larks still bravely singing fly,
Scarce heard amidst the guns below.

We are the dead. Short days ago
We lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow,
Loved and were loved, and now we lie
In Flanders fields.
Take up our quarrel with the foe,
To you from falling hands we throw
The torch-be yours to hold it high;
If ye break faith with us who die,
We shall not sleep, though poppies grow
In Flanders fields."

Those voices still call to us from Flanders fields. They speak in
the words of Abraham Lincoln at the field of Gettysburg. They come
from the men who stormed the rock-ribbed defenses of New England;
from the Argonauts who crossed the plains; from the men who laid
deep the foundations of American institutions. They come from the
men who, in an earlier day, established the Anglo-Saxon principles of
individual rights and personal freedom which we still revere. They
come from that old race which, through the centuries, kept for us
the Book of the Law. They come from the martyrs who suffered at
Rome to vindicate their beliefs and to maintain their principles. They
come from all the men in all the ages who have worked and suffered
and endured to promote and to perpetuate civilization, morality and
the worship of God. '~If ye break faith with us who die, we shall not
sleep, though poppies grow in Flanders fields."
Those voices do not call to the American nation. They do not
call to the great religious organizations from whom we have received
and from whom the world expects so much. They do not call to the
Masonic Order, nor do they call to the Gr.and Lodge of Masons of
California. They call to the man, to the single, individual, isolated
man who sits in your chair this afternoon, or who speaks from this
platform; to the individual who is responsible for the progress, the
accomplishments, the sins, the ideals and the sentiments of a race, and
who can shift that responsibility to no other man or body of men.
Go home tonight and look in the mirror and you will see the government of the United States and the morality of a nation. Go home
tonight and look at your children-your own-their discipline and
training, the extent of their self-restraint and unselfishness and Godliness and love, and you will see the citizenship and the morality and
the religion of tomorrow.
Those voices call to the Masons, the individual Masons, of California; more than a hundred thousand men; upright, moral, intelligent,
clean men; the outstanding men in every communi•ty.
A hundred thousand men! There were sixty thousand who marched
with Sherman to the Sea; there were less than thirty thousand in Lee's
army when he surrendered at Appomattox; there was one regiment
of American troops and a few scattered units with Colonel McAlexander
at the second battle of the Marne who refused to obey the command
to retreat, and changed the tide of a great war. There are more
than a hundred thousand Masons in California alone!
There are approximately a million and a half of registered voters
in this State. Five hundred thousand of them will control any election
to office or any popular vote upon legislative or constitutional enactment. One in every five, almost one in every four, of those five hundred

450

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

thousand is a Mason-if we vote; and if you use male suffrage as a
basis, approximately one in every three, is a Mason.
How many active and despised abolitionists did it take in the
days when Garrison was mobbed through the streets of Boston-good,
old, moral, conservative Boston-how many despised abolitionists did it
take in those days to create the sentiment which wiped the curse of
slavery from the United States? There are more than a thousand men
in tpis very room, equally intelligent and able, and far more highly
regarded by their fellow men.
How many men does it take to form a bloc in Congress and
thwart the will of the American people? How many men does it take
in any time and in any cause, united, determined, courageous, to shake
the sentiment of the State or the Nation to its foundation? One man
led the Israelites from bondage and moulded the morality of a race
when he wrote the laws of Moses; one man broke the Boston police
strike, a very moderately successful lawyer, who is the President of
the United States, because he has the courage of his convictions; one
man can dominate the politics of a city, and often of a State; one man
can play a fiddle and a bridge will sway. One man sits in your chair
this afternoon, not responsible for the influence which he in fact exerts,
but responsible for the influence which he can exert, if he cares, and if
he dares.
In the days of the war the Four Minute man was told that there
were two elements, and only two elements, in a successful speech;
first, an idea, and then the sale of that idea to his audience; that he
must forget oratory and rhetoric, that he must forget himself and the
impression, good or bad, which he might create, that the welkin might
ring with applause when he finished; but that unless he sold the
goods-unless he created the market for Liberty bonds, or obtained the
Red Cross contribution, or engendered the sentiment which was his
aim, the speech was a failure. It is for that same reason that Lincoln's
Gettysburg address will be a classic as long as the English language is
known, while the rounded periods of the polished statesman from
Massachusetts who, for two long hours upon that same occasion held
his audience spellbound, are no longer even a memory. The tale of
the four-minute speech is the tale of human accomplishment; an idea,
and the sale of that idea to another man.
I have no new thoughts which I can offer to you this afternoon,
only my interpretation of ideas which are hoary with age; an interpretation which many of you have heard me give before; but the old
truths, if they be truth, endure. T'here is no greater force than Goel,
and he was old when time began; there is no more attractive quality
among men than common honesty, yet the Ten Commandments them-

selves condemn stealing and false witness; there is no stronger sentiment than mother love, yet doubtless even the brutes in pre-historic
ages possessed it. Nor, brethren, am I unmindful of the opportunity
of this occasion and of the responsibility which rests upon the man
who· speaks to you at such a time. It is an opportunity which will
not come to me again. It is one of the great opportunities which come
to any man; an audience of picked men, each of whom has been honored
by his Lodge, each of whom stands out in that Lodge and his community, each of whom is capable of influencing many others. The
speaker who could leave an idea with every man in the room-not a
passing impression nor a momentary enthusiasm; not necessarily the
same idea for 'each hearer; but the speaker who could leave a definite,
ooncrete idea, permanently sold to every man before he leaves the
room, might well give to his address the preparation of a life-time;
for by those implanted ideas passed on from man to man as such an
audience as this can pass them on, he could influence civic righteousness
and public and private morality throughout the State. What the
speaker is to Grand Lodge for the moment, each of us is in his own
community-the mouthpiece of Masonry. Masonry is not judged, as
the Grand Master has suggested to us, Masonry is not judged by
Lodges or temples; it is not judged by hospitals or homes or educational funds; its influence is not measured, nor is its scope determined,
by its teachings, by tlk lessor lights or even by its Great Light. Men
judge Masonry by Masons; and they judge Masons by their acts.

451

In any field of activity accomplishment demands courage. It takes
courage as well as attention to business to successfully handle a commercial transaction, and it takes courage as well as attention to business
to influence our fellow men and to make our contribution to human
uplift. In both cases the type of courage is the same-moral courage;
or, in a homelier phrase, the courage of a man's convictions. It was
that type of courage which carried Columbus across the sea, and it
required from him a higher type of courage to face the ridicule which
he met at home before he embarked than was required upon the
voyage to face the unknown perils which lay before him; a higher type
of courage than is demanded even of the man who faces cannon ball or
poison gas.

I imagine that for most of us it would require courage to take
the Great Light of Masonry from off the altar, to openly put it under
an arm and walk down the streets of San Francisco. I know it would
demand courage for most of us, to take that Book upon our knees and
read its pages as we travel to business in street-car or on ferry. That
particular thing may not be required, but the fact remains that the
thing, if it were necessary, would demand of most of us, as we are

452

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

453

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

constituted, some courage; it is also true that very few of us read
that Book as we should, and that the man who reads it the least, and
who needs it the most, is the man who would find it most difficult to
publicly display his interest in the volume. The man is an exception
who does not find it hard to discuss, or even to admit, his deepest
beliefs; who is not almost ashamed .of his sincerest religious convictions; and who does not find it hardest of all to emphasize the most
important phases of moral and physical welfare to those whom he
l'°v.es best of all, his own children. No man can do that better than
a father; no father can perform a worthier act; and every man in this
room admires and respects and is influenced by the other man who has
the courage of his convictions.
The day is surely coming, perhaps it has already come, when we,
as Masons, must squarely face the question what concrete influence we
are exerting in w'°rld affairs, in morality and in approach to. God ;
whether our Order with its growing membership, its increasing wealth
and its potential influence, justifies its existence; or whether, like so
many organizations political and social, which have gone before, it is
in danger of becoming too self-centered, too self-serving, too selfindulgent, to accomplish the purposes of God.
The greatest danger in the world today, political, social or moral,
is indolence. Indolent public sentiment, and ignorance which indolence
begat, permitted one world war and may permit another; only world
sentiment can create world peace, but moral indolence will not create
that sentiment. If there is corruption or incompetence in public office,
indolence and only indolence permits it. If young men fill our prisons,
if crime goes unpunis·hed, if respect for law becomes a lost virtue,
only the indolence of the men in this room, and of others like ourselves,
permits it. From what Pharisaical height do we condemn the Bolshevist who would abolish law, if we ourselves obey no law which thwarts
our own desires, or if we enforce no law whatever? If the religious
sentiment of a community wanes, if men instead '°f drawing nigh to
God, depart from Him as his chosen people so often did of old, what
but moral indolence is the cause, and whose is the indolence?
The other day there was a hue and cry throughout the nation at
the clanger of five to four decisions by the Supreme Court of the
United States. Men were appalled at the tremendous power vested in
one man by reason of a vote of five to four in that court, to thwart
the. will of the American people as expressed through representatives
in Congress. Did you happen to know, while that damor ·was at it~
height, or do you know today, that in one hundred and ,thirty-five
ye~rs of constitutional history in the United States, forty-eight Acts
of Congress and no more, forty-eight Acts of Congress have been held
unconstitutional by the Supreme Court? Did you happen to know

that .of those forty-eight Acts of Congress, only nine were held unconstitutional by a vote of five to four? Did you happen to know that of
those nine, only three were of more than passing importance? Do you
happen to know that of those three, one has since become the law
of the land by constitutional amendment; that the '°ther two of those
three Acts concerned only a single object, the regulation of child
labor in every community and hamlet of the nation by a central power
at Washington; and that today you <:annot find a corporal's guard. of
states which are willing to ratify a constitutional amendment granting
that authority to Congress? One subject matter in one hundred and
thirty-five years, and as to that one subject matter the people of the
United States today are unwilling to give the p'°wer to Congress 1
Upon that comparatively insignificant foundation rested all the clamor
which spread through the land, and because of that clamor, millions
of men were caused to distrust the greatest court upon the face of
the earth ; the only body under our system of gov1 ernment, which
stands as a bulwark for the rights of the individual citizen when
attacked by the unbridled license of a temporary majority who may
oppose him.
The point of the illustration is not the insignificance of the thing:
the point is that when the clamor was at its 'height, you and I did not
know the facts. Can you imagine such a condition as that existing
when the Colonies were struggling for their lives? Can you imagine
such a condition as that existing when the adoption of that same
Constitution was a matter of public debate? Can you imagine such a
condition existing in the days of the Civil War, when brother was
shedding the blood of brother, because of adherence or opposition
to the doctrine of States' rights? Political indolence!
What do you know today, wl1at does the average American citizen
know today of any of the great questions, d the facts of any great
question, before the Nation? What does he know of the facts r.egarding encroachment by bureaucracy? What does he know of the facts
which tend to increase the p'°wer of that bureaucracy? Does he know
whether it is a good thing or a bad thing? Does he know whether
it is wise to centralize power at Washington, and to clip the wings
of the States? Does he know the tendency of the day? Does he know
or has he an intelligent opinion, whether it is wise to substitute a pure
democracy, direct action by a temporary majority, for the representative
form of g,ovemrnent which is the genius of the American constitution?
For that matter, brethren, rloes he know the difference between a
republican and a democratic form of government? Political indolence!
When men fight for existence or for freedom, they prize the result,
and they survive. When men, or nations, or Masonic Lodges, loll in
easy affluence and indolence, they die.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

And what of moral indolence? What is our contribution to moral
uplift in the community and to the worship of God? Perhaps we go
to church; perhaps we seek some more congenial atmosphere. But
whether to church we go or at home we stay, what do' we do for the
God whose Book lies upon our altar? What is the religious contribution of a hundred thousand Masons in California, who bow the knee
to God, and praise Him with their lips? If our children are to worship
Him, and we hope they will, if they are to worship God, where shall
they learn of Him? Shall we send them to the church which some
other man has built, or which some other man supports; shall we
send them to Sunday school while we seek places which seem to us
more pleasant; or shall we point to them the example of some man,
some God-fearing man, some other man, who leads a better life than
we have the integrity or the courage or the willingness to live? We
teach our children morals and Masonry teaches us morality; but
morality is neither Masonry nor God. Mere morality has never built
a church or a school. It has never freed a slave or ennobled a woman
or lifted a drunkard from the gutter. It has never reformed a criminal
or saved a human life. It has never inspired a beautiful poem or a
noble deed. Something greater than morality sent a Father Dami('!n
to the leper isles, and history has yet to record the name of a man
or a woman who •has gone to the stake with the blessed name of
morality upon his lips.
For thousands of years men traversed the land by foot or beast
of burden, and the S•ea by oar or sail. Within a single cycle we have
conquered earth and air and water. We traverse the seas in palaces
propelled by steam, or dive beneath the waves. We have captured
the thunderbolt and rival its power. We speed through the air faster
than travelled the cannon ball in the days of '61. We talk for thousands
of miles with no means of communication other than ·the atmosphere
in which I speak to you. If responsibility comes with opportunity,
and opportunity with power, what responsibility rests upon the men
who, within a hundred years, possess the power to revolutionize the
physical world, and to annichilate habits of action and means of communication and transportation which previously have changed but little
since the days of Noah?
I do not know whither we are bound, nor do you. What the future
holds for the Order we revere and the land we love is known only to
God; but what that future shall be, rests not with Him, but with
ourselves. We do know that after the seed time cometh the harv~st,
and that as we sow we shall also reap. We do know that the same
God who sent the flood to sweep men from the earth, who brought
confusion at the Tower of Babel, who sent fire and brimstone upon
Sodom and Gomorrah, who, through the centuries sent His prophets

to His chosen p.eople, yet punished them when they sinned; we know
that that same God rules the universe today. We know that He is
not only the loving Father who sends His rain upon the just and
upon the unjust, but He is as well the jealous God who demands that
men shall lov'e and worship Him with all their hearts.
We know, too, that if we strive, however ineffectively, that if we
put the talent to the exchangers, though it be but one, that however
deeply we may sink in the depths of despair or degradation, always
there are beneath and about us the loving arms of Him who doeth
all things well, our Father's God. There is an old English '(loem
which tells a legend of Judas Iscariot, whose name was anathema.
You remember that there were those who arrested Christ, who placed
upon His brow the crown of .thorns, and spat upon His face. There
were the soldiers who crucified Him. There was the one that thrust
the spear into His side. There were those who persecuted Him
demanding His life and the freedom of a robber. There was Pontius
Pilate who sat in judgment upon Him, and washed his hands. All
of them pale into insignificance beside the figure of Judas, the ingrate;
the man who betrayed his Lord and Master, and who betrayed that
Master with a kiss. And at the erid he lay in the field of blood. And
the legend is that as he lay there in the field, the soul of Judas Iscariot
looked down upon the body in despair and sought to find some place
wherein to hide his disgrace from the eyes of men. He took the body
upon his back and wandered forth, hither and yon through the world,
seeking a place of hiding, but discovering none. He tried to bury
the body in the earth, but it could not be done. He cast it in the
stagnant pool, but it rose from the depths with glassy eyes staring
back at him. He sought to cast it in the torrent, but a thousand weird
faces drove him away. So he wandered on and on and on, always
seeking, but finding not. At last one night he saw in the distance a
gleam of light. With the body still upon his back he stumbled and
struggled toward it through the storm, and at last he came to the
open doorway of a lighted hall. Utterly exhausted, as he stood within
the circle of light, he cast the body upon the ground at his feet. And
then the poet says:

Suspensions and Restorations
At the risk of being rated a scold, I again call attention to the
unnecessary loss of membership by reason of suspensions for nonpayment of dues. For the year ended July 31 the chartered Lodges
reported 818 members as having been suspended and only 222 restored,
a net loss of nearly six hundred members, two-thirds of whom could
have been kept on the rolls if Masters, Secretaries and Committees on
Delinquent Members had exercised diligence and tact. It is not at all
creditable to a Lodge to show a large number of suspensions, and I
sincerely hope that for the current year our efficient Inspectors will
make a successful effort to improve this condition. Particular attention
is hereby called to Regulation 110, which makes it the duty of each
Lodge to have a Committee on Delinquent Members.

Charter of Ramona Lodge
On December 8, 1924, by order of the Grand Master, there was
indorsed on the back of the charter of Ramona Lodge No. 457, with
the signatures of the Grand Master and Grand Secretary, the following:
"Whereas, it appearing to· us that at the date of issuance of a
charter for Ramona Lodge No. 457, said Lodge was located in unincorporated territory adjacent to the city of Alhambra; that subsequent to
the date of said charter the city of Monterey Park was incorporated,
and that the said Ramona Lodge is and has been at all times since its
formation located within the territory embraced in the said city of
Monterey Park. Now, therefore, we ·do Order and Decree that Ramona
Lodge No. 457 has exclusive jurisdiction within the city of Monterey
Park until such time as another Lodge may be formed in said city,
and that it have no jurisdiction within the city of Alhambra."

Morning Session
Wednesday, October 14, 1925.
Grand Lodge was called on at 9 :30 o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.
The minutes of yesterday's sessions were read and approved.
The Grand Secretary reported, as required by the Constitution, that Pearl Harbor Lodge had failed to send in
its annual returns until two months after they were due,
and that therefore the Lodge was not entitled to representation. Whereupon it was moved and carried by unanimous vote that the Lodge be permitted to be represented,
and it appearing that Brother Alexander Paul Jones was
present as a duly-elected representative, he was accorded
a seat in Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON GRAND
. SECRETARY'S REPORT
To the 1vf.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee to which has been referred the Report of the
Grand Secretary begs leave to report as follows:
\Ve congratulate Brother John Whicher upon the completion of
his eighteenth year in the office of Grand Secretary and we congratulate
the Grand Lodge upon having had so capable, able and painstaking a
servant in that exacting office for almost a score of years.
The pr.esent report reflects the attention to detail, the comprehensive
thoroughness and the signal ability which has characterized his conduct
of the office throughout the entire term.
We observe from the report that there were on October 1, 1925,
115,517 Mast.er Masons, members in good standing in the Order, representing a net gain of 7344. We also note tha.t the declared policy of
the present administration for more and smaller Lodges has resulted
in 29 dispensations.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

495

The Grand Secretary again properly calls attention to the great
loss in membership from suspensions for non-payment of dues. Your
committee believes the criticisms of the Grand Secretary to be just
and that more car.e and diligence on the part of Secretaries of subordinate Lodges would materially reduce this discreditable showing.
Attention is properly called to the necessity for a Committee on
Delinquent l\fombers in ·the Lodge, and insistence upon it functioning.
The requests for recognition from the Independent Nationale Grand
Lodge of France and the Grand Orient of' the Argentine Republic
are referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Also the request for similar recognition from the Gran Logia
Valle de Mexico has already been referred ·to a special committee,
appointed by the Grand Master.
Your committee r.ecommends reference of the several sections of
the report as follows :
Duplicate charters: To the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Consolidation of Lodges: To the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Masonic Service Association: To the Finance Committee.
Representatives appointed: To the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Lodges under dispensation : To the Committee on Charters.
Charter of Ramona Lodge: To the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Life membership: To the Committee on By-Laws and Jurisprudence.
Special dispensations issued: To the Committee on Jurisprudence .
Amendments to by-laws: To the Committee on By-Laws.
Trial records: To the Committee on Appeals and Grievances.
Financial statement: To the Committee on Finance.
Fraternally submitted,

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit to you my eighteenth annual report as Grand
Lecturer, giving an account of my activities during the past year.
I have visited every district in the jurisdiction and many of the
districts several times by special request, holding both day and night
sessions. The Lodges are in a good healthy condition, and all <loin!!'
some degree work. Many of the Lodges each month have something
of a social or educational nature, a lecture, pictures of interest, or a
musical program. This all aids to stimulate interest, and tends greatly
to increase attendance. Many of the Masters in this manner have
achieved wonderful results, and have been amply repaid for the time
and energy spent in arranging these entertainments.
Many of the Lodges spend so much time in conferring four and
five degrees in an ev,ening that no time is left for social or educational
purposes. Nothing will diminish the attendance greater than for a
Lodge to confer the degrees upon more than two or three candidates
in an evening. I would recommend and urge that this Grand Lodge
adopt the rule that no Lodge shall confer the first or second degrees
upon more than three candidates at any meeting, nor more than one
third degree. I am of the opinion that when any Lodge has so many
candidates that it is necessary for them to confer four and five degrees,
it would be better to form another Lodge, and let the new Lodg,e do
some of the work.
At the session of the Grand Lodge ·of 1918, a Flag Ceremony was
introduced and adopted and made a part of the opening ceremony of
the Lodge. This is still in full force and effect. (Section 162 of
Decisions and Regulations.) I do not doubt in the least that many of
the brethren have felt that the Flag Ceremony was adopted at that
time as a war measure ,to teach and stimulate loyalty and patriotism,
and is therefore no longer of any importance. My belief is that not
alone in time of war, but in time of peace also, the sentiments of
loyalty and patriotism cannot be too deeply impressed upon the hearts
of all our citizens, particularly our brethren in Free Masonry.
The changes that were made in the ritual at the last communication
of the Grand Lodge have met with general commendation, and have
been put in pra-ctice with no difficulty whatsoever, with the most hearty
cooperation by the brethren everywhere,
It is gratifying to see that Lodges throughout the jurisdiction are
universally either building new Temples or remodelling their old
halls, and furnishing club rooms and social quarters. This to my

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

497

mind is one of the best forms of Masonic education, for it makes
for better fraternalism an<l brings the brethren in closer relationship
one with another. It also increases attendance at the meetin5s of
the Lodge. Possibly one of the most difficult problems among the
Lodges has been the old problem of non-attendance. A little earnest
effort and energy, however, seems to eventually solve most of these
ills complained of by the Master and brethren. Then they wonder why
this was not suggested before, and the Master comes to the realization,
much to his s,urprise, that after all he has had a pretty successful year.
I had the pleasure and privileg,e of many visits to Lodges with
the ~r:. w:. Grand Master, several of which have been to Lodges
that had never been visited before. These visits were greatly enjoyed
and appreciated, as manifested by the attention and attendance of the
. brethren. The sentiments and admonitions expressed by the Grand
Master were enthusiastically received, and I feel sure have sunk deep
into the hearts of all privileged to hear him.
I hav.e received reports from all the Inspectors and they give a
good account of the Lodges under their supervision. I desire to
express my sincere thanks to the Inspectors for the hearty cooperation
and assistance given to me by them at all times. Much credit is due
them for the results attainetl throughout the jurisdiction. I am grateful
to them for the service rendered.
'
There have heen thirty new Lodges formed this year. The greater
number of these are in the southern part of the State, which shows
the vast increase in population and the for.ming of many new communities in the Southland.
My thanks are due the
w:. Grand Secretary for the many
courtesies extended to me in his office. His council and advice is
always available, and most valuable and helpful in all matters.
There is not enough care given by the Masters of many Lodges
in the conducting of funerals. This is a most important ceremony
and one of the occasions that the Fraternity is before the public. This
ceremony is memorized by some of the Mas,ters, but whether it is or
not, the service should be at all times rendered in a dignHie<l and
impressive manner. The ~faster should have a practice meeting in
the ceremony with his officers if possible prior to the funeral, that all
may know what they are to do. The public judges largely by what
they see, and favorable impressions are created by well-conductec\ ·
funerals. The effect of the ceremony, if done hy competent officers,
is suhlime. If a Master does not feel competent to render the funeral
ceremony, he would far better request some Past Master to conduct
the service for him. I . know that all Masters desire to have this

v:.

ceremony performed impressivdy, which will not only reflect credit
on himself, but the Lodge.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF MASONIC HOMES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Following is the report of your Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1925, with
an account of work accomplished, together with a list of residents
in the two Homes as of 1st of September, 1925.
Pursuant to the requirement of the Constitution, the Board organized immediately after the close of Grand Lodge in 1924. The
Secretary certified the reappointment by the Grand Master of Samuel E.
Burke as a Trustee. The newly-installed Junior Grand Warden, Will
H. Fischer, together with the Deputy Grand Master and Senior Grand
\!Varden, and the holdover Trustees Charles M. Wollenberg, James B.
Gist, and Chas. Albert Adams, were present. Brother Wollenberg was
re-elected President, and Brother Gist was re-elected Vice President.

Responsibility of Lodges

brother-private schools and institutions; but if now we should admit to the privileges of the Masonic Home the children of wealthy or
well-to-do brethren, we would soon be compelied to abandon the
v·ery scheme for which the Home was by this Grand Lodge established, and enter upon an entirely new field of endeavor. That is to
say the Grand Lodge would be calied upon to establish a general
bo;rding school where children of members of the craft, rich and
poor, would be given the advantages usual to such institutions. This
course would necessarily involve the expenditure of vast sums of
money for the erection of buildings which would be required to
accommodate the influx of children from the homes of Masons, and
we would be entering upon a field foreign to the proper work of
Freemasonry. More than thi·s, a most disastrous social situation
would result, in that a condition of caste would inevitably foliow
that would soon destroy the sweet atmosphere of harmony and
democracy which now exists among our little ones, who now under
present regulations and our present policy are housed and schooled
as members of one family-all of them being on a level so far as
material wealth is concerned, and where no child can taunt another
that "My father is richer than yours."
We have steadily adhered to the principle that the Masonic Homes
of California are maintained for those of our brethren who have
become dependent upon the Lodges, for their wives, widows, mothers,
and children, and we believe that the brethren of the jurisdiction will
sustain us in this policy.

Your Trustees are embarrassed at times by being compelied to
deny applications for admission, although the widest latitude is accorded to all Lodges, consistent with what we conceive to be our
duty to the whole membership 'Of the jurisdiction. One distressing
case that was rejected was that of a Lodge which applied for the
admission of a member and his wife. Investigation by the Trustees
disclosed that the brother in whose behalf application was made had
received his Masonic degrees in the applicant Lodge two years before,
he being at that time 72 years old and had been suffering from a severe
affection of the heart for some seve11 years. Not only had the applicant been a member less than the three years required by the rules of
the Home (which might under proper circumstances be waived), but
it was apparent that the Lodge voluntarily assumed a risk which it
should not have attempted to pass to the whole fraternity. It was
the unanimous sentiment of the Board that the Lodge, and not the
Home, should assume the entire responsibility for the care of the
brother and his wife.
.
Again, we have had applications for the admission of children whose
surviving parent had ample funds to care for them, but who wanted
your Trustees to relieve them of their parental responsibility. A
particular case and fair sample of many, was that of a wealthy member of a California Lodge whose wife had died, leaving with the father
an eight-year-old daughter. This brother claimed he could not secure
the s·ervices of a competent housekeeper who would take the place of
the mother in the home-training and general care of the child, and
insistently offered to pay any sum which might be demanded if the
Trustees would admit the girl to the Home. His argument was
that while he could afford to pay for the maintenance and schooling of
his young daughter in any one of the numerous pay institutions in
the State, yet he believed the influence for good and the supervision
accorded the children in the Masonic Home was better than could
be found in other institutions; that the domestic and moral atmospher·e at our Home wa·s more nearly akin to a private home, and
therefore he claimed his child was entitled to participate in the privileges conceded to the children of poor parents, even though the
father was unfortunately possessed of considerable wealth.
Y onr Trustees, of course, are fully sensible of the problem of this
good brother and of his desire to accord to his child every moral
advantage which .love and parental responsibility would indicate.
And it is flattering to the members of this Board to know that their
conduct of our Home should make it a place for the proper care and
education of children which outrank•s-in the opinion of the wealthy

Viewpoint of a Resident at Decoto Home
There are more than two hundred residents at the Decato Home,
and when they are received we try to impress upon them that they
will be happy there, or not, as they please; that it is intended to be
a real home, where cheer and good will should prevail; where men
and women are expected to do their full share in adhering fairly
close to the Golden Rule, and even though they may be, as many
are, unable to. perform manual labor, they all can help to maintain
the real home atmosphere by being kind and considerate of their
feliows. And if some are unhappy at times, it is because of an unfortunate mental attitude.
We as well as Masters and Secr·etaries of Lodges, receive many
letters from residents at the Decato Home, some of them of a cheerful tone, and now and then one of complaint.
Some time ago one brother, soon after his admission, wrote to
the Secretary of his Lodge the following letter, which so nearly reflects conditions at the Home that we here present it:

502

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"Masonic Home, Decoto, Cal.
"Dear Sir and Brother :
"Will make an effort right now to fulfill the promise I made
you before leaving - - for the 'Masonic Home' and give you my impression of it.
"Have been here one month and a half today; have been observing, an attentive listener, as I mingled with the residents of the Home
and the Superintendent, also many and warm words of praise of both.
Without keeping any record by which I could give a correct percentage of each, I am confident that at least ninety per cent of the
people here are loyal to the Home and its management; if not, they
surely should be. The Home is beautiful, the superintendent, Mr.
Hartman, and Mrs. Richardson, the matron, are both doing all in
their power to make everyone here happy and contented.
"I am feeling much improved physically and hope no weaker mentally since coming here. My mind is at ease, no worry regarding the
future, sleep and rest well nights, report regularly for meals three
times a day. This we have to do or someone is sent to our rooms
to know why this is.
"I am not surprised at finding ·some unhappy people here. There
are some undoubtedly whose minds are diseased, the result of trouble,
possibly sickness or an unfortunate environment somewhere in the past.
All such should be treated kindly and with charity. Such i•s the policy
strictly adhered to by the management of the Home.
"Look over the residents of the Horne when all seated in the
dining room at meal time and note that there are not less than one
hundred and fifty white heads like myself. There is bound to be
some unhappy ones among them that many would call cranks.
"My sincere thanks to you, Brother - - , and the members of
Lodge for the assistance rendered me in securing admission to the
Home. Shall endeavor to prove myself worthy and ever grateful.
"Fraternally yours,

Improvements at Decoto
The buildings added last year, together with the increase in population, have made it necessary to add to our boiler capacity in order to
provide sufficient steam to properly heat the new buildings.
A contract has been entered into to furnish and install a new 200
H. P. Sterling boiler, for the sum of $13,258.00. Also two 6 x 4 x 6
\Vorthington Horizontal Duplex Boiler Feed Pumps at a cost of

$398.00.
To make room for this equipment in the power house, the laundry
is being moved to the basement of the Men's Building (new) where

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

503

there is being installed new and modern laundry machinery at a cost
of approximately $16,200.00
Further details of conditions at the Decoto Home will be found
in the report of the Superintendent.

Additional Building at Covina
At the Annual Conclave o~ the Grand Comrnandery Knights Templar of California, held at Pasadena in April, 1924, the sum of $10,000
was appropriated as the nucleus for a fund to build a hospital for the
children at the Covina Home. This gift was augmented at the
1925 conclave by an additional donation of stock of the Masonic
Temple Association of California of the par value of $40,000. Plans
for a hospital building are now being prepared, and as soon as the
Board can realize on the stock donated, building operations will be
commenced. The Trustees have acknowledged this gift and we suggest that Grand Lodge make further suitable acknowledgment.
The Administration building at the Covina Home, a part of which
comprises the dining room and kitchen, was built in 1916, when 56
children were ,domiciled there. The dining room was large enough to
accommodate twice that number, and the Trustees at the time did
not feel justified in expending money beyond that capacity. However,
the large influx of children in the year past-now numbering 163made imperative demands for a larger room and a larger kitchen,
as well as provision for the housing of the employes. Accordingly a
contract was let for the ·enlargement of the dining room, kitchen and
help's quarters, sufficient to accommodate the full capacity of the
Home. The work was sufficiently advanced in time to care for all
the children on their return from Camp Tucker September 10.
The above-mentioned work, together with remodeling the laundry,
a new ice plant, and new equipment, will ·entail an expense of approximately $95,000.00.
A new concrete road has been constructed through the grounds at
the Covina Home, and a modern sewage disposal plant completed.
Scholarships for Deserving Children
Your Trustees are endeavoring to provide educational facilities
for children after being graduated from high school, and are pleased
to be able to report that, while donations to the Student Loan Fund
are not as liberal as could be desired, yet no deserving child has been
discharged from the Home until after provision has been made for
schooling at some institution calculated to make him a useful and selfsustaining citizen.
Seven children are now participating in the Student Loan Fund.
This fund is used for the purpose of advancing money to our boys

New Buildings at Camp Tucker
· The children spent their · •summer vacation as usual at Camp
Tucker, on Balboa island, in the City of Newport. In previous years
the little folk and their attendants were housed in tents, which were
not satisfactory. Last spring our enterprising brother, Mervyn J. Newburg, Past Master of Phoenix Lodge No. 178, San Bernardino, who
is personally acquainted with and loved by all our children, undertook the ta>Sk of arousing interest and raising funds for the purpose
of providing permanent buildings suitable to an ideal camp life. Through
his untiring efforts and the whole-hearted co-operation of Lodges and
brethren in the southern part of the State, a splendid and comfortable
permanent camp has been established. Thirteen buildings have been
erected, comprising eight dormitories, a combined dining room and
kitchen one hundred and seventy feet long, a hospital, an assemblyroom building, two laundries, and one building for an office and living quarters for the Superintendent. The dormitories are equipped
with good beds, necessary hangers, and shower baths. One of the
dormitories is reserved for boys who have been graduated from the
Home and are now .gelf-supportjng and living in near-by cities. These
young men rightly look upon Mrs. Miller as "mother" and delight to
pass their week-end and holiday outings at the Home. In addition
to the buildings, cement walks were laid, sewers installed, trees p_lanted,
and Camp Tucker is now an ideal outing place for the children. The
cost of the improvements amounted to about $15,000. Appended to
this report is the Hst of donors, as submitted to the Board, to each
of whom written acknowledgment has been made.
Visit to Decoto H ome
Wednesday afternoon of this week will be devoted by you to a
visit to the Home at Decoto, and it is hoped that all of you and the
lady members of your families, will avail yourselves of this invitation
to see what has been accomplished for the comfort of the residents
there. Please bear in mind that each one of you is. a partner in t~is
enterprise, and that constructive criticism of the conduct of the
Home will be welcomed by the Trustees.
We recommend that the per capita tax for the Homes for the
current fiscal year be fixed at twenty-five cents, as usual, notwithstanding the increased cost of maintenance.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of Superintendent, Decoto Home
To the Board of Trustees, i\.fasonic Homes of California:
I herewith present for your oonsideration my sixteenth annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decoto, California,
for the year ending August 31, 1925.
The permanent improvements and repairs made for several years
past have enabled the management to render a higher standard of service in meeting the physical, mental and spiritual needs of the members
of .our large family and has resulted in improved methods of administration in the inter~ affairs of the Horne.
Ail the members ·of the Horne are encouraged to render some service in keeping with their strength and in their leisure hours to interest themselves in healthful and wholesome diversions for their general well-being.
Our new Assembly Hall with its splendidly equipped stage and
projection room has been a factor in promating entertainments of
various kinds which has enriched the social side of our family life.
The general conditions have shown a marked improvement during the past year due to the faithful efforts of the employes and
residents, all as far as possible contributing by personal example in
creating an atmosphere of peace and contentment in all the departments of the Home.
There are now at the Home 205 residents, 107 men and 98
women. During the year 52 persons have been admitted. Thirty
have passed away.
The general health of the Home has been good with the exception of those who are infirm and feeble owing :to advancing years.
There are now 32 members of the Home being cared for in the
hospital department, where they are receiving every care our physician
and nurses are able to give them.
Our water supply has been plentiful for household, garden, lawn,
fire and irrigating purposes.
The addition of the new buildings and the increased membership
of the Home have called for an enlargement of the facilities of the
laundry and power plant. A new laurtdry, equipped with modern machinery, is now being installed in the basement of the new men's
building, and plans made for an additional boiler, oil and water pumps,
to be placed in that part of the power plant formerly occupied by the
old laundry.
The greater part of the hill ranch has been leased either on shares
or cash rental. The orchards, hay fields, the chicken and hog ranch,
vegetable and berry gardens have given fair returns, the surplus being

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

521

sold in the San Francisco and local markets. A quantity of fruit has
been dried and stored for future use. Considerable work has been
done in beautifying the grounds of the Home, by the planting of vines,
shrubs and flower beds.
A number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare of the
Home by their labors in the carpenter and paint shops, picking fruit,
watering lawns, care of garage, library, kitchen, pantry, vegetable,
store and dining rooms and light chores.
The ladies of the Home have taken entire charge of the linen rooms
and attend to making, marking and mending of all household linen.
They also look after the care of their own rooms, also the halls, wash
rooms, reading and reception rooms in their departments.
There are 4200 volumes on the library shelves. Many magazines,
periodicals and daily papers are received, which are placed on the
tables of the library, men's club rooms and the ladies' reading room11.
Moving picture entertainments are given every Tht;irsday evening. Card parties on Tuesday evening. Song practice on Friday
evening. The usual services are held in the Assembly Hall on Sunday
afternoon, after which a few musical numbers are given by :the Home
orchestra.
Arrangements are made whereby the members of the family, a few
at a time, may visit nearby Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters. During the year many trips were made to Oakland, San Francisco and
towns in the vicinity of the Home.
During the year entertainments consisting of musicals, vaudeville
and moving pictures have been given by visiting friends, Ll!>dges and
members of Lodges with their ladies, all of which have been enjoyed and
appreciated by the members of the .Home.
The following is a list of those who have contributed to our enjoyment:
September 20. Oakland Lodge No. 88 gave a luncheoo in the
afternoon and an entertainment in the evening.
September 21. Members of Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 413, accompanied by their ladies, paid a visit to the family in the afternoon.

We are greatly indebted to Brother Ben Giroux of Oakland for
his kindness in furnishing moving picture entertainments on November
24, December 27, February 21, and July 4.
All holidays have been observed in an appropriate way. The specials were those which were held on New Year's Day, Lincoln's
Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Easter, Memorial Day, Fourth of
July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.
Grand Master David J. Reese and officers of the Grand Lodge
have made a number of visits to the Home, and during the year a
large number of visiting brethren have spent many pleasant hours
with us.
I desire to express my appreciation of the efficient and conscien.tious work on the part of the officers and employes, whose earnest
efforts have been a potent factor i~ maintaining a high stat!11ard of
service throughout their departments, and to thank the Board of Trustees for the kindly assistance given and the many acts of courtesy
received.
Fraternally submitted,
FRANK B. HARTMAN,

Report of Superintendent, Covina Home

To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes:
The past year has been a very busy but a very enjoyable one, and
the cooperation of the children and employes has brought results that
have made ,our Home nearer the real home and a very happy family.
We have had our problems like other families, but with this cooperation
it has been possible to solve each of them with greater satisfaction.
I wish I might mention to you each of the children and the employes,
but as that is impossible I will leave it by saying that I am truly indebted
to them for their cooperation during the past year.
The two new dormitories, which were completed last fall for the
older boys and the older girls, have added much to the comfort and
happiness of the children. The rooms have been very appropriately
furnished by the various Lodges and individuals. A list of the donors
will be found on another page, and I am sure they would feel amply
repaid if they could know how much the children are enjoying their
new rooms.
The new buildings have given the children a better opportunity to
do their studying at home, as before they were too crowded and could
not get away from interruptions of various kinds.
The sewing room in the new dormitory for girls has been especially
beneficial, inasmuch as it has created a greater desire in the girls to
make their 0 wn garments and they are showing much taste and skill.
The girls graduating from High School, as well as the girls from the

637

Grammar School, made their own commencement dresses this year, and
showed much originality as well as good taste.
A neW'. music room has relieved the congestion, enabling more
students to practice.
A club room in the basement of the boys' building, and a recreation
room in the basement of the girls' building, would be a valuable
addition.
The visitors who have come to the Home express admiration for
the Domestic Science Cottage and the office it performs in making
better homemakers and teaching the girls to assume certain housekeeping responsibilities which they delight in.
Six girls were graduated from High School this last year. One is
to enter N onnal School, two will take secretarial courses, one attend
the University at Berkeley, one a course in Commercial Art and one
returned to her relatives.
About 37 children will enter High School this year. Twelve boys
and six girls were graduated from the eighth grade last year. The
girl from the Home who has carried the banner for honor student in
the Covina High School for the past two years has added another year
to her record.
We appreciate the great interest among the children in their music
this past year, and to give yon an idea of the work that is being
accomplished I will refer to the report given by the Music Instructor,
Mrs. Ambos.
.
The health of the children has in the main been good, thanks
largely to the s:areful and skillful watchfulness of the medical men
who make frequent visits to the Home. Our thanks are particularly
due to Drs. W. P. and S. S. Magan, H. C. Barron and B .. M. Graybell
of Covina; Royal H. Crist of Los Angeles; and Dr. Edgar K. Shumaker,
eye, ear, nose and throat specialist Los Angeles. These gentlemen have
all won the hearts of the children and their services are highly appreciated by your Superintendent.
The dentists, too, have been generous, and under direction of Dr.
Ralph W. Russell the teeth of the little ones have been given every
necessary attention, without fee.
Sewing and mending, which are big items in the work of the
Home, have been helped by the good work of ladies from several of the
Chapters of the Eastern Star.
The children have been favored by moving picture shows regularly
once a month, the donor being Henry S. Orme Lodge No. 458. Others,
who have supplied the Home with moving pictures at times, are Wilshire
Lodge No. 445, Sunnyside Lodge No. 577, Elsinore Lodge No. 289,
Mount Olive Lodge No. 506, and also by Chester Conklin of University

PROCE.EDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge No. 394, Wm. F. Russell of the Two Thirty-three Club, J. A.
Lisy of the Mission theater at Glendora, and by the Balboa theater.
Our thanks are extended also to. members of Lodges at Covina,
Puente, Glendora, Baldwin Park, Azusa and San Dimas, who have
generously furnished automobiles and taken the children on numerous
outings; and particularly are we appreciative of the thoughtful and
generous Masons, from the Lodges just named, who transported the
children from the :Home to the summer camp, Camp Tucker, on
Balboa island.
The barbers have not been outdone by any in their services, and
we are pleased to acknowledge the work of the following ~fasons w~o
have attended to the tonsorial needs of the children : Lewis Rothstem
of Redlands Lodge No. 300, Upstart Willet of Kansas Lodge No. 194,
Barlow Gullet of New Mexico Lodge No. 22, Samuel David and several
assistants from Los Angeles.
Scout Master William Hoogendyke continues his good work with
our Boy Scouts.
Actuated by the spirit of love for our children, the ladies of the
Arema Club, O.E.S., of Manteca, have inaugurated a beautiful custom
during the year of sending to each child, to commemorate its birthday,
a gift and a letter. This custom is really unique in its originality and
creates in the child mind more of joy and happiness than any other
act could accomplish. A birthday is a big event in the life of a child,
and its celebration here by children who do not have the blessings of
family life, is a boon indeed.
A new radiola has been placed in the Assembly room by Doric
Lodge No. 216, San Francisco. It brings us all in .touch with the
events of the world and is much enjoyed.
The farm and orchard are cared for in the usual fine manner by
Mr. Gradler. His management of the orchard has been specially commended by the District Horticultural Commissioner.
Special holidays have been observed with appropriate music and
exercises : Easter Sunday was one of exceptional inspiration, as some
of the children attended the Sunrise service at Riverside and others
went to the Temple Club, returning in time to observe their own
Easter service at the Home, where they gave a musical program
befitting the solemnity and beauty of Easter Sunday. The floral decorations throughout the Home were beautiful.
In observing other holidays, I will mention Christmas as being
one of the joyous festivities, with the singing of carols, the Home
Christmas tree, and various entertainments given the children by the
different Lodges during the holiday season.

Camp Life

538

539

The children looked forward to the camp this season with great
expectation and were more than dt!lighted when they found so many
improvements for their comfort. The forethought of those who put
this project through makes it in every way an ideal spot in which to
spend their vacation, under the same care and supervision they experience at the Home in Covina, together with the added joy and freedom,
and the healthful sports and recreations, such as fishing, boating and
swimming, and all that goes to make up normal, healthful child
activities.
The social side is not neglected. The children are given entertainments of various kinds as well as outside trips, through the courtesy
of Masons and friends living near the camp. An occasional bonfire
is enjoyed by the children.
The spiritual side of the children is not overlooked, as the Sunday
service is carried on with the same. spirit as characterizes those at
the Home.
The competitive spirit is stimulated by different contests in aquatic
sports.
Those whose untiring efforts and interest in the welfare of the
children have supplied all the necessities and comforts, even to a
hospital, a well-equipped culinary department, a spacious airy dining
room, a large assembly hall (Harmony Hall) which furnishes a place
for reading and recreation at all times, and dormitories furnished with
comfortable beds. An outstanding feature of the camp is the commodious cement walk which nearly surrounds it. Trees and flowers
are being cultivated, which we hope may be added to in another year,
making it the beauty spot of Balboa.
We must not forget to mention the seven boats made by the boys
in ,the Sloid at the Home, supplying boats sufficient to obviate the
necessity for rental of boats as in previous years.
It is with justifiable pride that we point to this latest achievement
of the Masons for their wards. Their wisdom, generosity and vision
will extend into the future lives of these children, equipping and fortifying them to meet the world and to take with them the high ideals for
which their benefactors stand.
I cannot close this report without expressing my appreciation to
you, the Trustees, for your hearty support and cooperation, as well as
helpful advice on all matters pertaining to the Home. You have always
responded so cheerfully and willingly whenever I have called upon you,
and it is my earnest desire to faithfully and co11scicntious!y do my
part to carry 011 this great work which is so dear to the hearts of us all.
Respectfully submitted,
MAUDE E. MILLER, Superintel'!dent.

Report of Dentist
This is the report of my second year as chief of the dental staff
that is serving the children of the ·covina Home.
With the additional number admitted this year the total is 160
children. Last year there were 108, showing a decided increase and,
therefore, necessitating additional dental assistants.
The dentist in every case uses the material and kind of restoration
indicated, the same as he wot1ld in an "office pay patient." Each dentist
is particularly selected and takes pride and care in his work, never
considering time or cost, as the following report will show. Before
operating, each child is given a thorough prophylaxis to remove stains
and deposits and to note condition of surrounding tissues.
The items below show the work done in the past year :
Gold inlays and restorations ................................. .144
Gold fillings ................................................................ 18
Porcelain fillings ................................................... ,. ... 26
Amalgam (silver fillings) ...................................... Over 400
Extractions, deciduous ............................................ Over 200
A great amount of the credit for successful dental work upon the
children is due to the Covina staff, as without the perfect cooperation
of Mrs. Maude E. Miller and Mrs. S. Burgess, in reporting all cases
at once, it would be impossible to keep the work finished to date; also
the dose observance· of the House Mothers to the child's use of the
tooth brush is an indispensable aid.
The following is a correct list of the dentists who are doing the
dental work: Dr. Leo M. Boughman, Dr. C. M. Beebe, Dr. Rollie E.
Olson, Dr. A. E. Sanders, Dr. Jack C. Soister and Dr. Guy Van Buskirk.
Orthodontists-Dr. Fred E. Mcintosh, Dr. E. T. Black, Dr. Earl M.
Bronson.
Fraternally submitted,
RALPH w ARD Rt:SSELL, D.D.S.

Report of Music Depa.rtm.ent, Covina Home ·
In contributing this report of the musical activities during the past
seven months of the school year, of which I have had charge, I have
endeav,ored to outline the work accomplished. The following is the
teaching schedule, varying at times according to conditions, either less
or more as in cases of illness or extra work in preparing for programs:
Piano, 28 pupils ; voice, 8 pupils.
Private lessons: Piano, 1 lesson per week for each student, 30
minutes; voice, 1 lesson per week for each student, 30 minutes.

541

Practice periods cover half an hour each day per pupil, with personal supervision when possible.
Class lessons in Voice: 8 in class, 1 lesson per week, 40 minutes;

8 in class, 1 lesson per week, 3() minutes; 32 in class, 1 lesson per
week, 40 minutes.
One evening a week the entire school meets for the practice of
hymns for Sunday service and patriotic songs. We aim to have some
special number given by the children each Sunday morning.
Four programs have been given during this period at the Masonic
Club, Los Angeles; Lions Club, Covina; Masonic Temple, Covina.
These embraced vocal solos, duets, quartets, piano, violin, musical readings and recitations.
The work shows steady progress and in some instances remarkable
development.
It is the aim of this department to teach the children to know
music-not merely the performance thereof-giving them a knowledge
of the underlying principles, and, as in cases of real ability to fit them
for teaching. Great interest and love for the work is bein~ manifested
and in a majority of cases faithfulness to practice.
The year has bee!} gratifying in its results and it is the desire of
this department the coming season to cover more ground with a
general musical education, reaching as nearly as possible each child
in the Home.
The influence of music and of its application cannot be estimated
in its effects upon the physical, moral and spiritual well-being of the
child, aside from its artistic value, and is recognized as a vital factor
in education.
BELLE

w. AMBOS.

The report was adopted as read, except the recom~
mendation for a per capita tax of 25 cents for account
of maintenance, which was referred to the Committee on

Brother C. M. Wollenberg presented the following resolution:
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Commandery, Knights Templar, of California, having
generously donated the sum of $10,000 in cash and $40,000 par value
of stock of the Masonic Temple Association of California for the
erection of a hospital for the children of the Covina Home, and the
hospital being needed at this time; therefor-e be it
Resolved, that the Grand Lodge do purchase the said stock ( 4,000
shares), thus enabling the Trustees of the Masonic Homes to carry
out the purpose of th is munificent gift.

Referred to the Committee on Finance.
Brother Otis M. Carrington then sang, "So I May Worship Thee
Alone."

RE.PORT OF TRUSTEES U. C. MASONIC CLUB

w:.

To the M.'.
Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University
of California, Inc., submits herewith a brief report of the affairs and
activities carried on at that institution.
While one year ago, the board was able to report that th~
Masonic Club House was an accomplished fact and tliat all doubt
as to the use of the institution by the students at th<! State University had been dispelled by what had actually taken place in the
few weeks between the opening of college and meeting of Grand
Lodge, the real results to be accomplished among the students at
the University rested somewhat in surmise. The present report,
however, will constitute a survey of what has actually taken placl:!
during the year last past.
Although no actual daily count has been kept of the number of
students visiting the Club House, a fairly accurate estimate of
those entering its doors ·places the total attendance, from October
first of last year to the corresponding date of 1925, at approximately
eleven thousand. Our Masonic students at the University were not
slow to recognize the opportunity the Club House afforded for
the kind of association they so much desired, and which, for the
greater part, had been denied them because of inadequate facilities
at Berkeley. A resume of the various activities that are now func-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

568

569

PROCEEDINGS O:B' THE

tioning follows. These activities finance themselves and also absorb
the slight overhead expense resulting from formal functions.
The Masonic Club House Council, composed of a representative from each of the organizations meeting at or using the Club
House, is the central organization of the institution. Its work is
to co-ordinate activities and to initiate Club House affairs. It
serves, also, as a sort of clearing house for the proposals and plan$
for entertainment and service, and exercises a wholesome directio11
over all that is done in that line at the institution.
The Masonic Club of the University of California is composed
of Master Masons, either students or faculty members. Alumni
members may retain their membership. The purpose of this organization is to afford an opportunity to all Masons at the University
to become acquainted and foster a closer association among themselves. This is brought about by means of smokers, which are given
approximately once a month, when interesting speakers deal with
subjects of Masonic interest. Once each month, the Club holds a
joint dinner with Henry Morse Stephens Lodge. Its principal social
event is the dance given each semester. Last year the Club organized a team which exemplified the third degree in a number of
Lodges in the Bay District. The very marked proficiency and perfection of the work conferred by these young men and the warm
welcome they received in the various Lodges has led to a probable
continuance of the plan during this year.
Two years ago, a few women students at the University banded
together and founded the Women's Masonic Club, the purpose of
the organization being "to unite women from Masonic families and
make more possible the giving of assistance to relatives of Masons;
and to co-operate with the Masonic Club and the De Molay Club
in social and welfare activities." Weekly dances, fireside gatherings,
receptions and plays are among the varied types of social affairs
sponsored by this organization. The active membership consisb
of students in attendance at the University who are either sisters,
daughters, wives or mothers of Masons, and those whose Masonic
affiliations are more distant, but whose applications for membership have been favorably passed upon by other members. Among
the honorary members of this club is Mrs. W. W. Campbell, wife
of the President of the University. The Women's Masonic Club not
only unites women students with Masonic affiliations, but fosters
among them high ideals of service, friendship and loyalty to the
University.
The De Molay Club, founded during the early conception of
the Club House, is one of the most active of the organizations at

the University. Its activities appeal to the young fellows of De
Molay age. As evidente, note the following invitation sent out at
the opening of the present semester:
"WELCOME, DE MOLAYS! We want to meet each one of
you at our first smoker, Wednesday evening, August 26th, 8:00 p.m.,
at the Club House. Snappy speaker, eats, smokes and a good stunt.
"FROSH! At this time, we will give you the 'dope' about our
organization. Remember! This is a not a Chapter, but a Club for
De Malays. We offer you the social advantages of a Club and the
opportunity to meet Brother De Malays at the University.
"In addition, we have a SECOND DEGREE TEAM. Efforts
were started in this connection last semester, and this year our team
plans to make many trips. Are YOU interested?
"How about your membership, RIGHT NOW?"
The University Masonic Players' Club has been organized for
the purpose of giving those affiliated with the Club House an opportunity to use their dramatic and musical ability. This organization offers splendid training in music and dramatics. It has three
1livisions of work, any one of which is a worth-while activity-the
Glee Club, the orchestra and the Drama Division. Some very remarkable results have b.een accomplished by the members of this
organization.
The Ashlar Club was founded this year by a group of son~
of Masons, assisted by members of the Men's Masonic Club, and
has had a rapid growth, and con.siderable interest has been manifested in its work. One of its activities has been the getting together of a group of men who will live together in a large club house.
Henry Morse Stephens Lodge No. 541 is in reality a University
campus organization, its membership being composed of faculty
members, administrative officers and students. This Lodge has,
from the very first, maintained a deep interest in the Club House.
While it holds all its meetings in the Berkeley Masonic Temple, it
holds practically all its social functions in the Masonic Club House,
where it sponsors gatherings of Masons and fireside meetings. The
influence of this body of Masons in connection with our work at
the Club House cannot be over-estimated. In this organization, th~
younger men and women of the student body sec a concrete embodiment of the principles of Freemasonry. It has been very gratifying to your Board of Trustees to observe the very close relationship between this body of Master Masons, and the younger element
of the Masonic constituency at the University·.
