At the opening of the present college year, our students bega11
the publication of "U. C. Masonic Councilor," which is in the nature
of a bulletin of the activities carried on at the Club House. Fifteen
hundred copies of the paper are printed and circulated among the
Club House constituency. While this little publication was primarily
designed as a medium of notice of various activities carried on at
the Club House, it has served as a medium for a far more important
purpose. Witness two extracts from the August edition; the concluding paragraph of the De Molay column being as follows: "The
year has been a period of experimentation, one of building up 'goodwill,' and of creating embryo traditions. The members may look
back upon this time with well-deserved pride. Today we face another
year. We must not live upon our past. The future holds a world
of opportunity. STUDENTS! with the use of the Club House, a
trust was placed in· us by the Masons of California. Our institution
and its traditions are still in plastic form, and it is our duty and
privilege to make these traditions, as time goes by, worthy of the
original inspirations and of its realization thus far." The President
of the Masonic Club House Council closes his welcome to the new
students as follows: "To those of you who are just entering upon
your college career, we take the privilege of offering a word of
counsel. You are about to begin a unique experience, which will
last but four years. We ask you to make use of the facilities an,t
splendid opportunities available in this institution. Your primary
purpose is study. Remember! Whatever worth you will derive from
study is dependent upon yourselves and your individual effort.
Further, consider not the proximate value, but the future value of
your college work. In the words of Professor G. P. Adams: 'You
should obtain from college some world of intellectual and aesthetic
pleasure which you can keep for yourself during the remainder of
your life.' You will find a large field of collegiate activities. Choose
an activity in which you are interested, and give it your whole-

hearted endeavor. * * * 'College offers the greatest opportunity in
the world for. making friends, for developing ideals, for cultivating
a healthy body, for learning moral and physical control.'"
Just now much attention is being given to the social conditions
at American universities and colleges. There are those who would
have us believe that "the good old days" are things of the past,
never to return. Severe arraignment of student conduct is frequently
met with. Various reasons and explanations for the present situation are offered, and many theories are suggested as being the
proper medium for counteracting the so.-called "influences" which
have brought it all about. Without entering into a discussion oi
any of these explanations and theories, your Board of Trustees,
while not admitting that affairs are as bad as many. would have us
believe, feels that any institution which tends to bring about a
better condition and which nurtures the influence which will counteract the present conditions, whatever they may he, is well worthy of
the support of Master Masons, wherever located. The nearly eleven
thousand young people at the University of California are no different from the young people at any of our other educational institutions. Most of them are away from home and freed from the
influence of the family circle and paternal guidance. The social
environment in which they are thrown is entirely different from that
they were used to before entering the University. President Campbell of the University has said that "while the Club House is a
visible and concrete expression of the faith the Masonic fraternity
has in its students at the State University, and while the splendid
building is a monument to the generosity of the Order, the real
contribution the fraternity has made is to be found in the fact that
it supplies the restraining influence of the home to those young
men and young women who need it so much, and affords a wholesome opportunity for clean and uplifting social intercourse during
a period when every safeguard should be thrown about their
conduct."
After ·observing the practical working of the activities centering
in the Club House, Dr. Paul Cadman, Assistant Dean of Men, repeats the declaration that the influence of the Masonic activities on
the campus is one of the pronounced factors for good at the University. The approval of Dean Lucy Stebbins and of other administrative officers of the University is no less favorable than that of
the President.
Scarcely a <lay goes by at the Club House without bringing to
light some "human interest story" in connection with the students
at the University. A rare opportunity is offered the genial and
motherly hostess, Mrs. Sallie M. Pease, to bring sunshine into the

clouded prospects of the men and women who go to her with their
problems and troubles. The service rendered to the students at the
University is varied and interesting. It is at the opening of each
semester, and particularly iu relation to the enrolment of new students, that the ministrations of the office staff are most sought
after. The students need assistance in obtaining living accommodations, in arranging their courses of study and in preparing to make
their own way through college. The members of a volunteer group
of senior men and women, familiar with the various courses of
study at the University, are in frequent attendance at the Club House
during the opening days of the college to ass:st students of other
classes, particularly the freshman, with the problems of subjects,
hours and conflicts in the various departments.
A list of "places in Berkeley where room and board may be
obtained, confined largely to the homes of Masonic families and
Masonic boarding houses, is kept at the office. Every effort is made
to see that these places are proper, and that the environment for
the students, particularly the young women, is as it should be.
Every effort is also made to obtain work for those who arc in need
of it, and the number of students availing themselves of the opportunity to thus place themseh"es in position to work their way
through college is very large. Instances might be multiplied, but
a few will suffice, to show the character of the work the institution
does. A young woman from our Masonic home at Covina entered
the University. The transition from the protecting walls of the institution where she had been for some time under the direction of
a watchful and tender matron to the confusion and uncertainties oi
registration days at the University was most alarming to this
young woman. She felt she had been tum;;d adrift into the cold,
hard world. Everything was new and strange 1:0 her; but she had
been told to report at the Club House. There she found the same
interested attention and gentle influence that she had so long relied
upon at the Home. Mrs. Pease was able to locate her in proper
living quarters, to assist her in 'arranging her courses of. study and
to put her in position to assist in paying her way through the
University. Another young woman, who is making her way through
college by her own efforts, and assisting her dependent family by
"paying her board at home," found herself unable to go on. She
sought Mrs. Pease for counsel and advice, and her situation has
been so changed that she is continuing her work at the University.
The young men and young women take their troubles to Mrs.
Pease with almost the same freedom that they would approach
their own mothers. The influence of this good woman, whom we
were most fortunate in selecting as the hostess of the Club House,

573

is probably equal to that of the Dean of Women at the University.
The office staff has been efficient and in every way in sympathy with
the purposes for which the Club House is maintained. Miss Alice
E. Nelson, who has been our efficient financial secretary and bookkeeper for the last three years, Jeaves our service to complete her
senior studies at the University, in order to take up the business
career she has outlined for herself. Her work in the capacity noted
and as assistant to :Mrs. Pease has made this personal mention a
deserved recognition.

The action of Jewel Lodge No. 374 in taking its splendid symphony orchestra to Berkeley and giving a concert in ·the Club lfouse
for the students was a courtesy worthy of all emulation.
It is a matter of regret that the Board of Trustees has been
unable to reduce the indebtedness of the corporation during the
year. The unsecured promissory note to the First National Bank
in Berkeley for $17,500 remains unpaid. While many Lodges remitted the entire quota assumed hy them for the erection of the
Club House, the completion of the building seemed to mark the
end of all interest in the enterprise on the part of a large number of
Lodges throughout the state. Practically nothing has been received
from the Lodges since the last meeting of Grand Lodge. It was the
plan of your Board to launch some sort of a campaign, immediately
following the last communication of Grand Lodge, for the purpose
of wiping out the debt. After a careful survey of the situation by the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Trustees and a number of Grand Officers, and on advice of the
Grand Master, it was deemed unwise to undertake any such plan.
Efforts to collect a number of unpaid individual subscriptions have
proved futile. The amount is not very large, and probably represents
the normal shrinkage that follows the raising of funds by the plan
followed in this case.
The appropriation of $8,000 made by Grand Lodge for the
maintenance of the Club House one year ago has been carefully
and frugally used. When the books were closed on October first,
after the payment of all bills there remained the sum of $748.55.
About one-half of this sum represents the amount allocated to the
annual pro rata for the insurance on the Club House and furnishings apportioned on the basis of a three-year period. The books
of the corporation have been carefully checked and audited, as
appears from a complete financial statement furnished by the auditor
as of October first, which has been submitted to the Finance Committee. After a most careful checking of the necessary items of
expense and disbursements for the past year, the Board of Trustees
has adopted a budget for the next ensuing year of $10,192.44. The
increased amount over last year's budget is due almost wholly to
two sources of expense--taxes and necessary repairs of upkeep of
the building. The taxes one year ago were computed on the valuation of the building in its incomplete state, March first of last year.
The amount of taxes paid was comparatively small. This year, the
assessed valuation of the property is very high, owing to a so-called
"re-adjustment of local values," particularly by the Berkeley City
Assessor. Taxes for the fiscal year amount to $2407.30. Last year
the building was so new that very little repairs were necessary.
The amount during the next year will be larger. The bud;;et. as
prepared, has been also submitted to the Finance Committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK
To the M.' · W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Following is the report of the Committee on Public Schools \Veek.
Although at yottr request it is far more comprehensive than otherwise
it would have been, we believe that no good purpose would be served
in reporting in detail everything that was done by the committee. \Ve
have, however, as you directed, incorporated a brief resume of the
resuHs of the sixth annual observance of Public Schools \Veek as
disclosed by the reports received from the Lodges on blanks prepared
by the committee for that purpose; and we have reported such of the
proceedings of the committee as we believe might serve as a guide
for the future. In this connection, •the committee desires to express its
appreciation of the value of the data preserved by Bro. Irving Magnes,
the chairman of last year's committee, and to make acknowledgment
of the work done by him and his associates.
The organization of our committee was a somewhat anomalous
one. Although the twelve members constituted one committee, there
were two practically independent sections-one with hea<lq uarters in
San Francisco under the general chairman and the other meeting in
Los Angeles under Bro. Robert A. Odell as the local chairman. Immediately after the appointment of the committee the general chairman
met with the southern section in Los Angeles at which mee<ting a
general scheme or plan was outlined with the understanding that the
details thereof were to be administered by the •two sections functioning
independently in their respective localities.

To accompany the Proclamation of the Grand Master, the committee issued a bulletin containing suggestions for arranging and conducting meetings. This was prepared with great care and in such detail
as was believed would make it of valuable assistance to those charged
with arranging meetings. Not only did it furnish information with
respect to the desire of the Grand Master and the plans arranged by
the committee, but there were incorporated therein suggestions as to
the specific arrangements to be made for the meetings, and the methods
that might be employed to obtain publicity. So comprehensive was
this bulletin that it was the occasion of wonderment and surprise to
the committee when it developed that informa<tion was being requested
concerning· matters that had been therein fully explained. An investigation disclosed the fact that many of the Mas,ters had not received
their bulletins. These had been sent to the Secretaries in accordance
with the usual custom and because the addressograph in the Grand
Secretary's office contains the names of the Secretaries and not the
Masters; but they were addressed to "Inspectors, Masters and Members
of Committees Arranging Meetings," and it was of course assumed
that they would be promptly placed in the hands of (hose for whom
they were so evidently intended. A copy of this bulletin together with
copies of bulletins, annol1ncements and circular letters hereinafter
referred to is attached to this report and made a part hereof.
Following the bulletin there was issued a printed announcement
containing in concise form a statement of the origin, and the aims and
purposes, of Public Schools Week; and calling especial attention to
the fact that 1he meetings this year would be public, and that the
primary objective was to afford the public in general, and the parents
of school children in particular, an opportunity to become informed
and advised of the real condition of our public schools with specific
reference to certain phases of the public school system that had been
widely discussed and frequently criticized. This was designed for use
by organizations and individuals who might be willing to assist in
giving publicity to the meetings to be held in the various localities.
In addition to providing the Lodges with such a supply thereof as was
requested, copies were enclosed with all the letters sent out by the
General Committee to the State Organiza<tions to which reference will
be later made.

who not only would be conversant with the topics ,the Grand Master
desired discussed, but who could present the subject in such manner
as would prove interesting to a lay audience, a letter was prepared
and sent to about three hundred prospective speakers. The names
were selected from lists obtained from several sources and included

those of both educators and laymen. The body of this letter was
multigraphed, but each was individually addressed to the person for
whom it was intended and was personally signed. This was in accordance with the arrangement that had been made by the committee for
furnishing speakers. The plan, however, did not prove a success· not
we feel justified in saying, for lack of care in its preparati~n 0 ;
because of any inherent defects, but on account of circums'tances over

be avoided; and with respect to which we believe it is proper that a
further statement should be made.

The committee was not of course unaware of the difficulty that

The community referred to, it may be mentioned, was not the

purpose; and as would be naturally supposed, the meetings arranged
by th.em were in every sense unqualifiedly successful. If every Master
in the jurisdiction had had as clear an idea of the purpose of Public
Schools Week, there would probably have been no failures, and consequently no such excuse offered as appears in the report from one
Master, who complaining of the fact that out of a population of 7500
there were only 41 persons present, gave as the reason, "The people
here are entirely satisfied with our public schools and will not give
up an evening to the sort of program necessary in this case." Disregarding for the moment the fact that our program was not predicated
on the assumption tha•t there was any dissatisfaction with our schools,
it would seem that if the people of any community were indeed completely satisfied, the least they could do to evidence that satisfaction
would be •to lend their active support to Public Schools Week; because
it must be remembered that such work as we are doing means much
to the teachers and those charged with the administration of our
Public Schools. Here in California we are doing for them what school
men and women everywhere are ·eager to have done. The perennial
cry heard at National Education Meetings is that the public at large
seem blissfully unaware of the efforts that are being made for the
betterment of the schools, and that the only voices heard are of those
who cavil and complain.
As the direct result of Public Schools Week the meetings held
under the auspices, or arranged by, the Masons of California were
not the only meetings of that sort held during the week. More than
one Minister of the Gospel made his Sunday service practically a
Public School meeting; and because of the State-wide prominence of
the organization we feel it not inappropriate to mention by name the
Commonwealth Club of California. This organization had for its
speaker at the luncheon meeting held during Public Schools ·week,
Dr. Tully C. Knoles, who delivered a wonderfully interesting and
instructive address on "The Changing Concept of Education."

Mason may ardently proclaim his great regard for the public schools,
he is not inclined to attend a school meeting in preference to going to
a movie. Fortunate indeed was that Master who received from the

Your committee to whom was referred the communication of the

We have examined the records pertaining to Freemasonry in
Mexico on file in the office of the Grand Secretary, and have had the
benefit of personal interviews with Brother Ernest C. Forbes, who
made an investigation of conditions several years ago; of the report
of the M.". \.V.". Charles J\lhert Adams, Past Grand Master, who
visited Mexico in 1921; of the statement of William L. Vail, a memher
of one of the Lodges ohedient to the Grand Loclgc Vallee de Mexico;
together with a report of the so-called Texa~ Commission, as we~! as
other data.
It is impossible to make an intelligible report without adverting
to the schism of 1910, which marked the beginning of the present
unfortunate state of the Fraternity.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Prior to 1910 the Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico was iz1 fraternal
relations with our Grand Lodge, and consisted of some' thirty-two
Lodges, some of which were composed of Americans or Englishspeaking brethren, and others including only Mexicans and working
in the Spanish language. That year a dispute arose between the
Mexicans and the Americans over the adoption of a new constitution
and the election of the Grand Master, whereupon several of the
Mexican members withdrew from the Grand Lodge and organized the
body which is now asking for our recognition. Those who remained
continued to function as a Grand Lodge, the next year changed their
name to York Grand Lodge of Mexico, adopted English as the official
language, and have since been recognized by our Grand Lodge.

seceding brethren, urged by Past Grand Master Adams in his report
of September 30, 1921, that the Mexicans "had not become imbued
with that spirit of democracy which impels the Anglo-Saxons to
patiently submit to what we know as majority rule." But we recall
illustrious examples in the political history of our own country of
that same rebellious spirit and the unwillingness to submit to that
majority rule when it is considered unjust and oppressive. This is
not said in palliation of the conduct of the seceders, but merely to
emphasize the thought that intolerance is not confined to any particular
race of people.
After having given the matter our most careful consideration, we
have arrived at the conclusion that Mexico is entitled to have and
practice its Masonry in the language, and according to the ideas and
ideals of its citizens. It seems to us intolerable that a foreign element
should be permitted to usurp the rights and privileges of the citizens
of a nation and preclude them from admission into our universal
Fraternity, solely because their ideas do not conform to our own.
We are firmly of the opinion that one of the vital principles of
Masonry is patriotism, and that to encourage the citizenry of a country
to establish and maintain Masonic Lodges is to encourage and support
them in their patriotic devotion, that they may erect their government
upon a firmer foundation. This can only he done in the language of
the land, and we feel that we should be derelict in our duty if we
should fail now to recognize the right of our Mexican neighbors to
practice their Masonry, as we claim the right to practice ours, in their
own language and in their own way, so long as the ancient landmarks
of the Craft are observed.
With that end in view, we recommend that the Grand Lodge of
California extend its recognition to Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico
in accordance with its request.
F. v. K1tllSL!NG, P. G. M.,
DANA R. WJlLL!lR, P. G. M.,
BENJAMIN F. BL!lDSO!l, P. G. M.

Thus, there have existed in Mexico two Grand Lodges, one composed almost entirely of English-speaking members, and the other
largely Mexican, each claiming to be the legitimate successor of the
Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico and challenging the regularity of the
other body, the effect of which has been to disturb that peace and
harmony which should prevail among Masons.
Many of the underlying facts attending the schism of 1910 are
not obtainable, or at least the statements are so at variance with each
other that it is difficult to ascertain the truth.

In 1921 the Grand Lodge of Texas appointed a commission consisting of the Grand Master, M.". W.". Andrew L. Randell, and three
Past Grand Masters, who visited the city of Mexico, and held an
investigation, the result of which was that the commission proposed
that the two Grand Lodges should merge into one Grand Lodge.
According to the report of the commission, this recommendation was
accepted by the representatives of the two Grand Lodges, and the
Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico acted favorably upon it, but York
Grand Lodge refused to concur. The commission recommended to
the Grand Lodge of Texas that the Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico
be recognized, which recommendation was adopted, and Texas now
holds fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico.
The problem which confronts us now is not without its legal and
practical difficulties. We recognize York Grand Lodge, which claims
jurisdiction of the Federal District of Mexico and all unoccupied
territory of the Republic of Mexico. Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico,
which seeks our recognition, claims practically the same territory. It is
the policy of our Grand Lodge to recognize but one supreme Masonic
authority in any State or country. However, during the war we
deviated from this policy and extended recognition to two Grand Lodges
in France.
The practical side of the question is more momentous in its possible
results. We are not unmindful of the apparently just criticism of the

0RGANTZA'l'ION :

After receiving a communication from the Chairman outlining the
problems before the Committee, the two branches held meetings for
organization purposes :
The Northern Division has held six meetings as a body, together
with frequent informal conferences between the various members.
.The Southern Division has held a like number of meetings, together
with similar oonferences.
.
.
The Chairman has attended two meetings in Los Angeles and the
Vice-Chairman one in San Francisco.
The Committee determined at the outset that its work should be
the composite efforts of every member thereof and we are glad to
report that this idea has been pursued.
The Chairman Qf the Committee held a conference with Brother
A. L. Haywood, Editor-in-chief of the National Masonic Research
Society and of the "Buiolder." The Chairman acquired many valuable
ideas and suggestions from Brother Haywood and the Committee has
profited by them. The C-0mmittee expresses its gratitude to him for
his time and assistance, as also including his generous offer to assist
through his institution or personally at all times. It is the opinion
of the Committee that it cannot work too closely with Brother Haywood
and his society, because his work is identical with ours, only national.Jy.
The Committee is also indebted for correspondence and suggestions
foom Brother Sidney Morse, the Executive Director of New York's
Committee, as also the Committee of the State of Washington, and
acknowledgment is here made for the valuable suggestions and assistance received.
NAME:

The Committee has adopted the name "Eclucati~nal Committee."
This was done so as fo enable the work to be pursued along educational
lines not necess~rily confined to "Masonic education," using the term
"education" in its largest sense.
THE COMMITTEE'S IDEA OF ITS PURPOSE
AND FUNCTIONS
The Grand Master informed the Committee that he desired it to
adopt a plan of work; he indicated that the Committee would probably
be, in part at least, permanent in character, and that such plan as
might be 'approved by him and Grand Lodge would form the basis of
activity in future years.
The Committee, therefore, entered upon its work with the sole
idea of formulating such a plan, and with no intention of endeavoring
to put it into execution this year.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

597

The plan thus adopted by this Committee is annexed to and made
a part of this report and .is respectftllly submitted herewith for consideration of the Grand Lodge.
There are, however, certain Qbservations which must be made
concerning the plan. In order to obtain a cross-section of the view~
of members of the Craft generally, it was determined to visit as many
districts in the State as possible, and discuss the problems before. the
Committee.
MEETINGS THROUGHOUT THE STATE
Pursuant to such idea, the Committee by various of its members
has held meetings in ninety out of the. ninety-eight Inspectors' Districts
in the State, thus coming in contact with representatives of over. eighty
per cent of the Lodges, induding those in Hawaii, it being especially
fortunate that one of the Committee members, Major Overton, while
spending his vacation in Honolulu, took the necessary time to hold
meetings there. The eight districts not visited were only thQse in the
mQst remote sections of the State. So that the magnitude and scope
of the work of the Committee in holding these meetings may be
adequately comprehended and the beneficial results obtained therefrom
fully under·stood, it may be in order to say that approidmately fifty
meetings were held, each meeting consuming from two to three hours,
and the average attendance at each was about forty. Tims it will be
seen that the Committee has been in personal contact with almost two
thousand members of Lodges.
And what did we find! The members of the Committee holding
the meetings went with the avowed purpose, not to give information
but to obtain it; to inquire of those attending whether or not they
considered anything at all should be done along educational lines, and
if so, what. The attendance at these meetings included at least the
principal officers of each Lodge,, together with many others; in nearly
every instance the Inspectors were present and the response was most
enthusiastic and encouraging. The Committee member presiding made
it his business to "draw out" those in attendance and get a frank, open
statement from them of their ideas. Needless oo say, from the hundreds
of men thus approached there was a mass of ideas, all of which the
Committee has endeavored to digest.
The following statement is considered by the Committee little
short of remarkable :
\.Vith the exception of probably not more than ha! f a dozen contrary opinions, we found that there is a striking unanimity of ideas
and thoughts among the members of the Craft throughout the State.
They think alike; their desires are similar; their hopes almost identical.
It is, as stated, considered remarkable that throughout the length and

598

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

599

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

breadth of the State men of so diverse locations, occupations and
interests have of their own volition and without direction produced a
train of thought which is as though they had been previously coached
to answer all the same.
There can be but one explanati>on of this-they have all been
educated alike through the ritual and if any proof as to the efficacy
of the ritual were needed the result of this Committee's meetings
would, in the opinion of this Committee, furnish that proof.
OUR FINDINGS

1. It appeared to the Committee to be the practicallv unanimous
desire of the members of the C~aft that, as regards the ;itual, efforts
should be made to offer explanations and acceptable interpretations of
it; the word ritual here used as including also the various symbols.
The members feel that as fine and as splendid as is our ritual, still
there is something lacking-that it should be supplemented by authentic
approved explanations.
·
2. With respect to topics of general education, necessarily the
replies varied with the districts in which the meetings were held, but
here again diverse as the suggestions were, it was easy to detect a
similar train of thought, in that as to general subjects the desire was
for no one particular line; the brethren in the smallest community
professed as keen an interest in high commercial problems as did
those of the city in agricultural ones.
.3. The question of speakers was everywhere brought up; inasmuch
as the meetings were informal and frankness was urged, some enlightening ideas heretofore held by many but seldom expressed were put into
words. Naturally there was diffidence about making comments at first,
but as discussions continued, frankness took the place of this diffidence
and the real truth was announced. The Committee is in a similar
position but feels that in fairness to its duty, as indeed in equal fairness
to the many speakers themselves, the truth can be spoken. What are
the complaints? Speeches too long; subjects inappropriate; lack of
preparation; glittering generalities; high-sounding phrases; absence Qf
facts and information.
It is not to be concluded that the above represents the universal
opinion, because in the same breadth with the complaints came equal
approbation of many, many talks which had been presented. Indeed
there were many cases in which the good comments as well as the
reverse were made concerning different speeches by the same speaker.
The Committee feels that this problem is not difficult of solution;
that once it is brought home to the great number of good fellows who
have so generously given of their time and ability, that the members

are analyzing the quality Qf what is offered them, that the response
will be immediate to the end that only the best efforts will at all times
be put forth.
All the Lodges want speakers and are particularly .an:cious for
what might be termed "foreign talent." They feel that ~t ts one. of
the most effective methods of learning and at the same time offermg
an interesting evening. \Ve feel that if our speakers will heed the
comment which is above made, <mly, of course, in the most kindly
spirit and then permit us to impose upon their time to the extent of
visiti~g Lodges outside of their immediate community, that a long step
forward will have been taken with respect to this phase of our edm:ational work.
4 In most cases it was found that printed matter does not succeed.
For ;ome reason "they wont read." In the past there have admittedly
been pamphlets lssued by our Grand Masters and Committees and all
who read the pamphlets agreed that they were excellent and valuable,
and that if read would have had an extensive influence on the Craft;
but for some unexplainable reason they will not take the time to read.
The Committee feels that such printed matter as is offered must be
gotten up in such attractive form as to engage the attention ,of those
for whom it is meant.
5. The Committee believes that notwithstanding the fac~ that the
plan is to a large extent a unit, special atte?tion ,~houl~ ~e directed to
one topic appearing therein, namely, that entitled, Practicmg out of the
Lodge" under the sub-head, "Objects.'' It is felt that after we have
taught' the lessons as they are so well exemplified in the ritual, together
with supplementary explanations, special emphasis should be laid on
the use and application of the principles so taught outsi.de the '.our
walls of the Lodge. We feel that this point merits special mention i
that if the great question of "Practicing out of the Lodge" can be so
effectively impressed on the members as to instill in them a continuous
and increasing determination to actually practice the principles inculcated in their daily contacts, one of the cardinal objects of the Order
will have been attained.
Too much stress cannot be laid on the success of these meetings
and the enthusiasm displayed by those attending. They were glad to
have Grand Lodge confer with them; they were glad to be given an
opportunity to talk; and in every case "asked for more."
THE PLA:N' PRESENTED
The effort has been made to present a plan which can embrace
many factors along educational lines. Manifestly it cannot be all complete, and as time goes on additions and variati?ns must be made.
Equally manifest it is that it is one contemplatmg many years of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

600

601

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

activity and which must be gradually worked out. It is essentially
for "a new generation of Masons." If we have educated the present
108,000 members in California as far as we have through the present
ritual, it is thought that by the judicious use of educational efforts in
furtherance of the ritual, as also along general lines, the next 108,000
Masons made in California will be just that much further advan<:ed
over the present body. "Lack of interest" has been the doleful cry
for years. It is not supposed that the larger part of the present body
of members can be effectively aroused, but it is felt that if those hereafter to come in are given more information upon which to formulate
their ideas they will necessarily have a proporti>onately greater interest.
If, as in the opinion of the Committee above cited, the ritual has
proved its efficacy, it becomes apparent that the first effort should be
along similar lines; it is, therefore, the Committee's opinion that the
first work among the Lodges should be in furtherance of the ritual.
It is the unanimous opinion that just as the candidate was instructed
in the ritual as he went through, so should he be instructed in additional
elements with respect thereto as he goes through; that in addition to
what he now learns as prerequisite to his advancement, such further
information as may be adopted should be afforded him and should he
learn likewise as a prerequisite to his advancement Further, that this
identical proposition should also apply to the qualifications of officers
in order that the "teachers" of the Craft may indeed know what they
are teaching.
The Committee is working on the theory that if we make better
and more enlightened men as individuals the group of them will be
the same; hence we distinguish activity as to individuals rather than
as a body.
The Committee feels that we should have an Executive Director
who shall devDte all of his time to the work of the office and receive
an adequate salary. We feel that the selection of such a man will
probably be a difficult problem, inasmuch as he must possess sufficient
general as well as l\fasonic education.
The Chairman takes this opportunity to personally thank Brother
Lobdell, the Vice-Chairman, and each member of the Committee for
enthusiastic .co-operation in all of the work.
The Committee respectfully offers its thanks to Brother Reese, our
Grand Master, for his patient and valuable assistance at all times
rendered us.
RECOMMENDATIONS
The Committee recommends:
L That Section 27 of Article 7 of the Constitution be amended
to read as follows:

"The following standing committees shall he appointed by the
Grand Master at each annual communication, just before the close,
viz. : On finances, on accounts, on grievances, on correspondence,
on returns, on pay of members, on credentials, on :libraries, on
by-laws, on charter, on Grand Lodge week activities, to consist ,of
five members each; on general policy am! purposes, and on .jurisdiction, to consist of seven members each, and on education, to
consist of twelve members; the duties of which Committees shall
continue during the year thereafter, and shall cease at the close of
the next succeeding annual communication; provided, however, that
as to the members of the Committee on Education the term of
office shall be three years, excepting that the members of the
Committee appointed at the communication of 1925 shall so classify
themselves by lot that four of them shall go out of office at the
end of one year, four of them at the end of two years, and four
of them at the end of three years."
2. That Article 7 of the Constitution be amended by inserting
therein a new section, to be designated Section 32c, to read as follows:
"The Committee on Education shall consist of six members
from Northern California and six members from Southern California. It shall have general supervision of educational matters,
together with such powers as are necessarily incident thereto, and
the power to incur necessary expenses, not exceeding, however, th_e
annual appropriation of Grand Lodge to this Committee, all subject
to the approval of the Grand Master."
3. That Grand l,odgc adopt the accompanying plan for the Committee's work.
4. That Grand Lodge appropriate for the use of the Committee
the sum of Ten Thousand Dollars ($10,0CO).
Respectfully submitted,

Synopsis of Subjects· and Methods o.f Presentation
The following is the plan of action adopted by the Educational
Committee of the Grand Lodge of California
As is noted in the report, of which this plan is a part, it is not
intended to he all-comprehensive, but must he varied as the experience
of future years may demand.
It does, however, purport to he the frame-work for the Committee's
future work.
The plan is purposely set forth in skeleton form, as the Committee
realizes that time and experience, together with extensive effort, are
necessary to its full development.

of these various Boards of Relief was $30,235.60, or about 40 per cent
of the total expended for relief. This would seem wholly out of

Resolved, that the practice of appropriating a fixed amount for
expenses of the Grand Master be discontinued; that the Grand Master
be requested to submit statements of his actual official expenses to the
Grand Secretary from time to time, and that the Grand Treasurer be
authorized and directed to pay the same.

A permanent Board of Control should be appointed by the Grand
Master, to which all applications to form Boards of Relief or Employment Bureaus should be made, and which should investigate the needs
and make suitable recommendations to the Grand Master. Said Board
of Control should make a survey at the earliest possible time of the
present Boards and Employment Bureaus, and eliminate those found
unnecessary. They should evolve a system which should be the standard
for all Boards.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO
INVESTIGATE RELIEF WORK

Requests for reimbursement and monetary assistance, by Boards
of Relief and Employment Bureaus, should be made to said Board of
Control, which should make annual recommendations to the Finance
Committee for the necessary appropriations.

To the M. '. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee, appointed by the M.'. W.'. Grand Master to
investigate and report on Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus
throughout the State, has held regular meetings, and has gone into
the subject thoroughly.

We have sent out questionnaires, not alone to the Boards and
Bureaus of our own jurisdiction, but also throughout the country, and
have received answers which prompt our conclusions.
We find that there are many Boards of Relief in existence in our
jurisdiction which are wholly unnecessary, should never have been
started and should be eliminated. In carrying out the principles of
Masonry, they act more as a handicap than a help, excepting in the
larger centers. The expenses are wholly out of proportion to the
amount of relief, and the few cases could be easily han:lled by the
Masters of respective Lodges.
We find several Boards that have expended more for overhead
than for relief. One Board spent $1,994.01 for relief for the year, with
an overhead of $2,300.00. Another spent $1,045.38, with an overhead
of $1,612.22. We think also that when a Board has $120.00 expenses
for the year, and their total relief amounts to $300, said Board seems
superfluous.
There was expended, during the year 1923-24, by the Boards of
Relief in the various cities, according to their reports, $78,592.94; of
which Grand Lodge paid $14,854.64, besides donations_ to Employment
Bureaus of $3,400.00, making a total by this Grand Lodge of $18,254.64.
In addition to this, the total expenditures for running Employment
Jlnrcaus was $12,756.95. The total expenditures for overhead expenses

We, therefore, offer the following resolution, and recommend its
adoption:
"Resolved, that the Grand Master appoint a Board of Control for
Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus, consisting of five members,
one to serve three years, two to serve two years and two to serve one
year, and each Grand Master shall appoint the successors to those
whose terms expire, said successors to serve for a period of three years.
"That said Board of Control shall immediately take charge and
make rules and regulations, with a view to carrying into effect the
recommendations herein contained.
"That all necessary expenses of said Board of Control shall be
paid by the Grand Secretary, upon approval of the Grand Master."
Lours SuTTER, Chairman,
LEO BRUCK,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS

·.

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns has to report that returns from all
the Lodges of the jurisdiction were in before the opening of Grand
Lodge.
The number of members standing on t'he roll of the Grand Lodge
on July 31, 1925, is 115,517, making an increase of 7344 for the year.
This is slightly less than the increase for the pr·evious year. But we
should not worry over the matter. The quality may be just as goodor better-or worse. Time alone will tell.
If each Lodge will guard well its out·er door there need be no
concern over the quality of the material that is taken in. If only
good men and true are elected to become candidates, all is well.
Your committee is of the opinion that the standard of membership
is being maintained.

TO LIMIT THE NUMBER OF DEGREES

w:.

To the 11.J.".
Grand Lodge of California:
The committee having under consideration the report of the
v:. W.". Grand Lecturer begs to submit the following:
A perusal of the r·eport ·shows an undiminished degree of interest
and careful att~ntion to the welfare of our institution as evidenced by
his report and which is drawn from his intimate contact with the
Lodges throughout the jurisdiction.
\Ve commend to the Masters of Lodg·es the successful practice
reported, wherein many Lodges have induced greater attendance by
stressing the social features, particularly the custom of providing lectures, pictures of interest or musical programs at frequent intervals,
proving a welcome break in the degree work.
We particularly commend to the Grand Lodge the adoption of the
Grand Lecturer's recommendation limiting the conferring of degrees
to not more than three first or second degrees or not more than one
third degree, respectively, at any one meeting.
The reference to the non-observance of the Flag Ceremony at
stated meetings is most timely. Your committee recommends that
the Inspectors be required to see that the Lodges in their respective
distrids pay proper attention to this beautiful and patriotic ceremony.
Patriotism must be continuous to be patriotism.
Of great importance is his reference to the Funeral Ceremony
and the nec·essity of this ceremony being conducted in an intelligent,
dignilied manner; not only that proper respect be paid to the deceased,
hut that the general public in one of its few actual contacts with ~he
Masonic organization, be properly impressed with the dignity and deep
purpose of the Craft.
Your committee, in conclusion, desires to again voice the love and
regard in which the V.". W.". Grand Lecturer is universally and
deservedly •held by the Craft in this jurisdiction.

Jos. BLOCK,

As supplementary to the report of the special committee, Brother Block introduced the following proposed
amendment to the Constitution:
Sec. 115. No Lodge under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge
shall confer any degree of :Viasonry on Sunday, nor shall it confer
the first or second degrees upon more than three candidates at any one
meeting; nor shall it confer the third degree upon more than one
candidate at any one meeting; nor shall it confer more than one
degree upon any one candidat·e at any one meeting; nor shall it confer
either of the degrees upon more than one candidate at a time; nor
shall it confer more than three degrees in any one day.

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

To thf Jf.". //V.". Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which wa~ referred trial record
T\' o. 432, tried hy Justice Lodge No. 549, r'espectfully reports as follows:
The accused in the case was charged with un-Masonk comluct as
set forth in four specilications. The trial commission found him guilty
of the first, third and fourth specifications and sentenced him to expulsion. Appeal is taken by accused on the ground that the Master was

624

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

disqualified because accused wanted to call him as a witness on his
behalf.
Section 197 of the Constitution provides that a witness is disqualified
to preside as Master. At this trial the accused and the accuser were
each represented by able attorneys. The accuser was prepared to
proceed, having present many witnesses who had come from a distance
to be present at this trial. Not until the trial bad proceeded to the
taking of testimony did attorney for the accused inform the Master
that he desired to call him as a witness, and that as a witness he
would be disqualified to presid·e, and req•uested that the case be referred
to the Grand Master for transfer to another Lodge for trial. To this
procedure, attorney for the accuser strenuously objected. The Master
stated that he knew nothing to which he could testify pertaining to the
case and denied the request. The case proceeded, and after all other
witnesses had been heard, attorney for the accused called the Master
as a witness. Attorney for the accuser objected on the ground that
the right to call the Master had been waived by the accused by his
failure to have stated what he had expected to elicit by his questions
to the Master when he raised the point at the opening of the trial.
The Master refused to testify, whereupon, at the demand of attorney
for the accus·er, attorney for accused stated the questions he desired
to ask the Master.
Your cotnmittee cannot too strongly urge the necessity of strict
compliance with section 197 by Masters, and wherever there can be
any question as to disqualification the Master should refuse to preside. However, in this particular case your committee has carefully
examined the record and find that the Master presided with impartiality
and fairness bot:h to the accused and to the Fraternity. That there
was no showing made by the accused at the proper time to enable the
Master to determine whether or not he could act as a witness, and
when the questions were di·sclosed at the close of the trial, that attorney
for accused claimed he wished to ask the Master, it appears that they
were not directed to any issue in the case, but if they could ·have any
bearing at all, it would be only to show prejudice on the part of the
Master against the accused. The question of prejudices was not raised,
and if att0rney for accused had desired to raise it, he should have
proceed·ed on that ground.
The testimony in the case amply supports the charge and specifications and the penalty fixed is only commensurate with the seriousness
of the offense. Your committee therefore offers the following resolution
an<! moves its adoption:
Resolved, that the judgment and action of •the Lodge be and the
same are hereby affirmed.

Adopted.

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial r·ecord
N'o. 442 from Doric Lodge N'o. 216, beg·s leave to report as follows:
The trial commission found accused guilty as charged, and fixed
the pen~lty at expulsion. The ·evidence amply sustains the judgment
and action of the trial commission.
The accused appeals from the judgment on the ground of various
errors as to procedure and on the further ground that the trial Lodge
failed to obtain jurisdiction of the accus•ed by a proper service of
summons;
Your committee has carefully examined the entire case, includin-r
the evidence and is of the opinion that there is no error of any sor~
as to pleading, proc.edure or introductions of evidence that has resulted
in a mis·~arriage of justice. Your committee is further of the opinion
that sectwn 199 of the Constitution was fully complied with as to
service of summons and that the trial commission thereby obtained
for~sdiction to try the accused. The record shows that th•e place of
:es1dence of t~e accused was Oakland. The trial Lodge was located
m San Francisco. The accused residing without the jurisdiction of
the trial Lodge but within the State, and his r-esidence being known
proper service was obtained by the Secretary of the trial Locke forward~
ing by regist.ered mail to the accused at his address in Oakrand a copy
of t~e s~mmons together with a certified copy of the charge and
spec1ficat10ns. The fact the accused happened to be in Portland, Oregon'
at ~he. ti~e. of the ~ailing of the summons, does not deprive the Lodg~
of Jtmsd1chon obtamed by mailing the summons and copy of the charges
to a~cused at his residence in Oakland. It further appears that accused
received the papers served upon him by mail and at the request of an

· GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

626

627

attorney r·eceived a continuance of sixty days for the trial. We do
not consider that the continuance of sixty days added to the original
thirty days would constitute a ninety day service if such were required.
Service was not only properly obtained by mail, but it affirmatively
appears that no miscarriag,e of justice could have resulted by such
service in~smuch as the registered mail was received by accused.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the judgment of the trial commission covered by
trial record No. 442 of Doric Lodge No. 216 be and the same is

To the .i'.1.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California.:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
?( o. 425 from San Diego Lodge No. 35, begs l,eave to report as follows:
The trial commission found accused guilty upon the specification
in the charge and upon the charge of un-Masonic conduct and fixed
the penalty at expulsion. The specification charges that a•ccused, an
attorney-at-law, assisted a client to defraud creditors in a bankruptcy
case. A properly authenticated copy of the accusation, the findings of
fact. and conclusions of law, and the judgment in the matter of the
disbarment of the accused in the Superior Court of the State of
California in and for the county of San Di·ego No. 40178, was received
in evidence. In addition to the prima facie case thus established the
admissions of the accused are sufficient in themselves to sustain the
action .of the commission.
The charg·es herein were preferred by the Junior \Varden acting
without order of the Lodge or the Master. Accused appeals from the
judgment and urges that, inasmuch as disbarment of an attorney is
not the conviction of a crime the Junior Warden was acting' without
authority in bringing the charges her,ein under section 192 of the ·
Constitution. That section provides, "In the event of a final judgment
of conviction against a .'.\1ason in the State or Federal Courts of a
crime involving moral turpitude; it shall be the duty of the Junior
Warden of any Lodge having jurisdiction of such Mason to prder
charges against the Mason so convicted on account of the matters
·
involved in said conviction."
The question is not here involved as to whether or not in this
case it was mandatory on the Junior \Varden to have brought the::re
charges. The fact is that he did bring them as he or any other Mason
had a right to do.
The accused also urges on appeal that the final judgment record
of the State court is only admissabJ.e as prima fade evidence of the

guilt of the accused of bis acts and conduct when it is a record of a
crime involving moral turpitude and that inasmuch as the record introduced was of a disbarment proceeding it was not admissible.
Section 202 of the Constitution provides that "the records and
r,eporter's transcripts of testimony made in the courts of the land,
properly authenticated, may be allowed in evidence." There can therefore be no distinction between admissibility of a record of a final
judgment in a disbarment prooeeding containing findings of fact involving moral turpitude and of a record of a final judgment of conviction
of a crime involving moral turpitude.
Your committee is in accord with the penalty fixed by the trial
commission and therefore offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption :
Resolved, that the judgment and action in the case covered by trial
record No. 425, be, and the same are hereby affirmed.

Adopted.
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

No. 424, from San Diego Lodge No. 35, begs leav1e to report as
follows:
The trial commission found accused guilty upon the specification
in the charge and upon the charge of un-M.asonic conduct and fixed
the penalty of reprimand. The specification sets forth that accused,
an attorney-at-law, collected $610.54 of a client's money on January I,
1923, and failed to notify his client; that some 60 days after collection
the client met the accus~d and asked accused if he had collected the
money to which accused falsely repli·ed that he had, "just collected,"
the said sum of money, but had a pressing need of it to pay insurance
premiums and could not pay it over to the client; that he withheld
the money until June, 1923, he being unable to raise it before then.
The facts set forth in the specificaHon are established by aclmission in
evidence of the record made in the Sup•erior Court, properly authenticated, of facts ancl judgment finally determined where the issues of
fact found involve the same charge as in the Masonic trial. In addition
to the judgment roll of the State court the testimony of the client and
others including the accused is sufficient to sustain such a finding.
Jn view of the seriousness of the offense of which he is found guilty
under the specification your committee feels that the penalty fixed by
the trial commission is not adequate and therefore offers the following
resolution ·and moves its adoption:

To· tlie M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 415, from South San Francisco Lodge No. 212, begs leave to
report as follows:
The accused was charged with un-Masonic conduct under two
specifications. The certificate of the Secretary is to the effect that he
forwarded by mail, the summons and copy of the charges to the address
of accused in San Francisco, which is within the jurisdiction of the
Lodge. Had .the address of accused been without said jurisdiction,
such forwarding by mail would be deemed sufficient service, but if the
address of the accused be within the jurisdiction of the Lodge, section
199 of the Constitution requires that the summons and copy of the
charges shall be served personally by the Tyler or some other member
of the Lodge authorized by the Master for rhat purpose, or shall be
left at his ordinary residence or place of business. Service as certified
to, therefore, does not give the trial commission jurisdiction to proceed
· ·
·
with the trial.

Service is very essential to assure that justice be done the_ accused.
The result of this failure to follow out the mandatory provision of
the Constitution in this instance is that the trial proceeded without
the presence of rhe accused and he was expelled on October 2, 1924,
but did not receive the summons and copy of charges through the mail
until January, 1925, which was the first inforrnation the accused had
of the charges having been preferred.
Your committee is of the opinion that the judg111ent of the commission must be reversed and the sam_e remanded for a new trial on the
ground that jurisdiction was not obtained .in the manner provided by
our Constitution.
Your committee, therefore, . offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption :
Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by trial record
No. 415, be, and the same is herehy reversed, and the case remanded
for a new trial.

. Adopted.

629

To the M.". W.'. Grand Lodge of Califomia:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record·
No. 417, from Golden West Lodge No. 456, begs leave to report as
follows:
The accused was charged. with un-Masonic conduct as set forth
in twenty-five specifications. As related in the first of these specifications, "the Ancient Egyptian Order of Sciots is an organization in
which a prerequisite to membership is membership in the Masonic
Fraternity. That San Francisco Pyramid No. 1 is a subordinate
Pyramid of said Order. That from the 12th day of March, 1920, to
the 13th day of October, 1922, accused was Scribe of said San Francisco
Pyramid No. 1, which office of Scribe is equivalent to the office of
Secretary." After thus relating the status of the accused, the accuser
proceeds in this and the following eighteen specifications to allege facts
which, if found true, amount only to irregularities in the keeping and
footing of accounts of the Pyramid, by the accused, but in no instance
does a specification set forth facts that, if true, charg·e fraudulent
misappropriation of money or involve actions by the accused involving
moral turpitude. In many of these specifications, if the errors alleged
had been committed by accused even though in good faith, as is consistent with the charges, accused would be obligated to make up any
shortages that might result from his errors. Of these nineteen specifications the trial commission found the accused guilty of fourteen and not
guilty of five.
Three of the remaining specifications charge the. accused with
failure .as Scribe to obtain, preserve and safely keep vouchers as the
Sciot law requires.
The twenty-third specification alleges that accused "as Scribe of
said Pyramid had charge of all the records of the Pyramid, among
which was an invaluable book which was the minute book of the
original Boosters, being the name under which the Sciots were first
known. This original minute book was reclaimed from a garbage
dump in the Richmond District, San Francisco, California. That immediately prior to its reclamation from said garbage dump, said book
was in the custody and possession of said accused." On this specification the commission find accused "not guilty."

The twenty-fifth specification sets forth that the accused had been
expelled from the Sciots. "That one of the prerequisites to membership
in t•he Ancient Egyptian Order of Sciots, of which San Francisco
Pyramid No. 1, is a subordinate body, is membership in the Masonic
Fraternity. That the said expulsion of said accused from said Ancient
Egyptian Order of Sdots for said reasons tends to cast reflection

631

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CA'LIFORNIA

and odium upon the said Masonk Fraternity because of the fact that
it is commonly known that said Masonic membership is a prereqms1te
to membership in the Ancient Egyptian Order of Sciots." On these
specifications the commission find the accused guilty.
Your committee cannot concur with the conclusion of the trial
commission that expulsion of a member of the Sciots by that body,
even though such Sciot may chance to be a, Mason, tends to cast
reflection and odium 'Upon the Masonic Fraternity, and therefore your
committee concludes that said twenty-fifth specification states no act
of un-Masonic conduct on the part of the accused.
The twenty-fourth specification states that the attitude of the
accused, when confronted by authorized agents of the Pyramid with
said discrepancies, has been one of defiance, as for example, accused
wrote the following to the chairman of the Investigation Committee:
"As I stated before, all this was gone over with the Social and Outing
Committee before these excursions were ever run, and I question the
right of any committee appointed by the Toparch of another regime
to question the acts of a committee serving as the Social and Outing
Committee under a former Toparch."
Another example set forth is: "The minutes of the Social and
Outing Committee wiU show that I was given carte blanche in the
matter of the various excursions over which I had charge, and I still
maintain that the reports that I turned in to the committee were correct
and that the committee as well as the Toparch accepted them as such."
Your committee is of the opinion that no act of un-Masonic
conduct on the part of the accused is set forth in this twenty-fourth
specification. The stating of this specincation in the manner set forth
by accuser does, on the other hand, show that the accuser in these
charges is involving the Masonic Fraternity in a petty controversy
involving an organization in which Masonry has no interest.
There being no specification in the charge setting forth un-Masonic
conduct on the part of the accused, and no testimony in the record
sufficient to sustain a finding of un-Masonic conduct, your committee
is of the opinion that the judgment of the trial commission should be
reversed, and therefore offers the following resolution and moves the
adoption:

The record shows a judgment of suspension by the trial commission,
which penalty on review was raised to expulsion. The trial Lodge
(Downey No. 220) now by a vote of 40 to 2 recommends his restoration, but the petition is not supported by an affidavit or 'other showing
as to petitioner's present character or as to his conduct since the
trial. In view of this situation the petition must be denied.
Your committee therefore offers the following resoluti9!1, and
moves its adoption:
Resolved, that the petition of T. B. G. in case No. 240 for restoration be and the same is hereby denied.

Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by trial record
No. 417, be, and the same is hereby reversed.

Your committee, to whom had been referred trial record No. 421,

w:. Grand Lodge of California:
With reference to the matter of a brother suspended by Lodge
No. 498, and subsequently restored by said Lodge to all the rights and
privileges of Masonry, without said Lodge even sending the trial record
of the proceedings culminating in the suspension of the brother thus
restored, to the Grand Lodge for review, we beg to report as follows:
At a trial regularly had in such Lodge upon charges filed against
the accused, the accused was found guilty and sentenced to suspension.
No transcript of the record, as required by section 207 of the Constitution, was ever transmitted by the Lodge to the Grand Secretary. Said
section '207 provides, among other things, as follows: "In all appealed
cases, and in all cases of expulsion or suspension, whether appealea
or not, the Master s'hall cause the Secretary to prepare a transcript of
the record of trial, and immediately transmit it to the Grand Secretary,
together with in formation of the appeal intended, if any there be."
This was not done in the case in question. Without transmitting
of such record, the subordinate Lodge subsequently attempted by vote
to restore the accused to the rights and privileges of Masonry. Upon
the attention of the subordinate Lodge being called to the matter,
it claimed that the preparation of the transcript of the evidence would
be very expensive, and as no appeal was taken, regarded the transmission
of such record unnecessary. In this the trial Lodge was mistake~, as
the provisions of said section '207 are mandatory, for in all cases of
appeal, expulsion or suspension such record must be transmitted. This
requirement of the Constitution, in our opinion, has the force arid effect
of suspending the power of the subordinate Lodg,e to restore the suspended brother until after the Grand Lodge has passed on the matter.
Any other conclusion would necessarily result in the Grand Lodge
being deprived of its prerogative to review the case, reverse or modify
the verdict or change the penalty. This would be intolerable. Any
To the M.".

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

636

subordinate Lodge could otherwise set at defiance the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge in this respect. It could also result in the prevention
of the legal restoration of the accused, by simply denying him the
right of review, as he could not have the record reviewed, where no
transcript has been sent up. In the present instance a hardship may
be worked on the suspended brother, but as a fundamental principle of
Masonry is involved this cannot be taken into consideration. Much
greater harm to the Craft in general would result in taking any other
position. In our opinion the right of the subordinate Lodge to restore
a suspended brother is •held in abeyance until after action by the
Grand Lodge on the case. \Ve therefore conclude that the act of the
subordinate Lodge in attempting to restore the suspended brother
before adion in the case by the Grand Lodge is a nullity and that the
brother still stands suspended. Also that such suspended brother is
entitled to have his status determined as soon as possible. We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that subordinate Lodge No. 498, be and the same is
hereby directed and required to forthwith cause to be prepared and
sent to the Grand Secretary a full, true and complete transcript of the
case in question, including the testimony taken at the trial, for review
by the Grand Lodge, and that in the meantime the act of said subordinate Lodge in attempting to restore the suspended brother, be declared
a nullity and void.

Adopted.

w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
No. 418, from Redondo Lodge No. 328, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused, a Master Mason in good standing in Redondo Lodge,
was charged with un-Masonic conduct in fraudulently obtaining money
through the medium of forged contracts of sale, disposed of by the
accused to a Redondo bank. The accused was tried by a commission
elected by Redondo Lodge, was found guilty on this charge and specification, and was ordered to be expelled.
The minutes of the meeting of November 13, 1924, called for the
election of trial commissioners, do not show that the Master named
either the tinie or the place for the first meeting of the commissioners,
or that he directed the Secretary of the Lodge to prepare or issue
a summons directed to the accused, or to serve such summons, or to
furnish the accused with a copy of the charge, all as required by
section 198 of the Constitution. Apparently no summons was ever
issued, but in lieu of a summons and certificate of service, the Secretary,
at the trial held on December 15, 1924, produced a returned registered
letter, addressed to the last known address of the accused, and returned
by the postal authorities, marked "Moved, no address." The accused
was not present, and was not represented at the trial.
To the 111:.

638

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LOlJGE OE' CALIFORNIA

The issuance and service of a summons is jurisdictional; and
failnre to so issue and serve such summons can only he waived by
the voluntary appearance of the accused at the trial. Such waiver
was not had in this case.
Irrespective of the question of jurisdiction, the evidence is hearsay
and wholly insufficient to sustain t'he specification. The sole witness
for the prosecution testified that he could not swear that the accused
had forged the contracts in question, and there is no evidence that the
accused obtained money on the contracts knowing that they were
forged.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the finding and judgment of Redondo Lodge No. 328
in trial record No. 418 be and the same is 1hereby reversed and the
case remanded for a new trial.

Adopted.

VIOLATIONS OF LIQUOR LAWS
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, the members of the Masonic Fraternity, ever since the
days of George Washington, have always been loyal supporters of
the Constitution as well as in favor of the enforcement of law; and
Whereas, certain members of our ancient institution are commonly
reported to be violators of the eighteenth amendment to the Constitution, and the laws enacted for its enforcement; and
'Whereas, the President of the United States has called upon all
loyal citizens to support the eighteenth amendment and the laws enacted
for the enforcement thereof; now, therefore, be it
Resolved, that we unreservedly declare our allegiance to the Constitution of our country, and particularly to that part of it which has
to do with the prohibition of the sale and traffic in intoxicating liquor,
and we hereby pledge the members of this fraternal Order to the
observance of all laws which aim to suppress such traffic. And be it
further

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

641

Resolved, that it shall be the duty of the Junior Warden of a
Lod~e, wlien notified or advised that a member of the Lodge has been
convicted or plead guilty in any court of competent jurisdiction of the
offense of having violated, eit~er the state or national prohibition laws,
to procure a copy of such conviction and present it at the first meeting
of t?e Lo~ge, and thereupon it shall be the duty of the Lodge to expell
or mdefimtely suspend such member; and the failure of the Junior
Warden or the Lodge to act in accordance with this resolution shall
subject them to such discipline as the Grand Master may determine.

L. L. WHITSON.

To the M.'.
Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred certain observations and recommendations of the Grand Master,
respectfully reports thereon as follows :
I. Your committee is in en tine accord with opinion of the Grand
Master and commends his utterance on the subject of Good Citizenship.
Not the least of Masonry's splendid contributions to the advance of
civilization are its devotion to the cause of rdigious and political
liberty and its firm support of free governn1ent and the orderly administration of law. It is a truism to say that a good ,;..fason is a good
citizen. Our institution cannot support good government and constituted authority except through its members. Every good Mason
should be a bulwark against the forces clisintegratory and undermining
the fabric of our institutions through the flouting of our laws and
disobedience to constitttt~d authority. The words of the Grand Master
should be taken to heart by every Mason in California.
It seems to your committee that no new legislation is required
in the matter of the violation of laws. Transgressors against the laws
of the land or moral laws should be disciplined in accordance with the
provisions of the Masonic law, and the Grand Master has it within
his power to take proper and drastic action in those instances in which
the Lodges fail or neglect to perform their constitutional duty.

Approved.

Dispensation to Hold Elections
4. Your committee on Policy and General Purposes approves the
recommendation of the Grand Master that subdivision 3d of section 39
he stricken from the Constitution. This section provides that a fee
of $10.00 shall be charged for a dispensation to hold an election of an
officer or offi'cers at a time other than prescribed in section 135 of the
Constitution. It does not appear that any of the Lodges of. California
have failell to hold elections of officers at the time prescribed by the
Constitution because of any trivial reason, and that dispensations are
asked for only in those cases in which it was impossible· or impracticable
to hold the elections at the time fixed by law. We therefore recommend that subdivision 3 of section 39 of the Constitution be repealed.

The report was adopted, and subdivision 3d of section
39 of the Constitution was repealed by unanimous vote.

Boards of Relief
The report of the special committee appointed by the Grand Master
to investigate and report on Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus
states the startling fact Vhat the expenses of some of these organizations
are wholly out of proportion to the amount of relief extended, and
that some of them are entirely unnecessary and more of a handicap
than a help, and that several Boards expended more for overhead
than for relief. The r.eport instances a case where a Board spent
$1,994.01 for relief with an overhead expense of $2,300.00, while another
disbursed $1,045.38 with an overhead of $1,612.22. There is something
rv.dically wrong with a charitable organization where the expenses are
40 per cent of the amount expended for relief.
The special committee recommends the appointment by the Grand
Master of a· permanent Board of Control to exercise supervisory
power over Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus, standardize
their systems of doing business and to make recommendations to the
Grand Master and the Finance Committee respecting them and their
several demands and needs.
Your committee is loathe to recommend the setting up of new
committees, but in this instance it is apparent that some regulatory
power is needed, and it is too mudh to expect the Grand Master to
give his personal attention to the details of this branch of our relief
work.
Vie therefore recommend that such permanent ·Board of Control
be created and that the Jurisprudence Committee be directed to pr.epare
the necessary legislation to carry the report into effect.

Adopted.

Recognition of National Grand Lodge of France
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration requests for the recognition of foreign Grand Lodges
which have been presented at recent sessions of Grand Lodge and on
which, together with a request from the Grand Orient of the Argentine
Republic pr.esentecl at this commnnication, it hopes to make a full
and detailed report at the next annual communication.
Your committee has carefully considered the request for recognition received from the Grand Los·e Nationale lndependante et
Reguliere pour la France et les Colonies Francaises. It appears that
this Grand Lodge exercises jurisdiction over the thr-ee degrees of
symbolic Masonry, that it has eighteen working subordinate Lodges

646

PROCEEDINGR OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and a Lodge of Instruction and is based upon the practices and policy
of Masonry of the English-speaking world. Right Worshipful John
Whicher, Grand Secrdary, and the chairman of this committee, at
different times during the current year, had the pleasure of visiting
brethren and officers of the Grand Lodge under consideration, and
both wer·e impressed with a conviction that the Grand Lodge was
worthy of our recognition and fraternal regard.
In 1918 an extensive report on French Masonry was presented to
this Grand Lodge, and at that time recognition was withheld from
the said Grande Loge N ationale, the report stating that a long life
and greater .growth might justify the attention of the Masonic world
to this Grand Lodge. That growth has been accomplished, and that
Grand Lodge has justified the expectations of the English-speaking
Masonic world. In 1918 this Grand Lodg.e, actuated by a. generous
feeling of cordiality to the Masons who were our allies in the great
war in which we were then engaged, voting to recognize the Grand
Orient of France on oertain conditions precedent which have never
been performed, and we are not now in fraternal relationship with
the Grand Orient of France. The Grand Orient and said Grande Loge
Nationale occupy the same territorial jurisdiction.
Your committee respectfully recommends that this Grand Lodge
recognize the said Grande Loge Nationale and exchange representatives
therewith.
WM. RHODES HERVEY,
WILLIAM A. SHERMAN,
GEORGE F. RODDEN,
WILLIAM H. WASTE,
EUGENE E. ELKUS,
FRANK W. MrxT!lR,
