REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
Matter of Revocation of Dispensation
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
action of the M.".
Grand Master in the matter of the revocation
on September 29, 1925, of the dispensation authorizing •the forming and
opening of Beacon of the West Lodge of Los Angeles, which dispensation had been issued by him on December 18, 1924.

w:.

This Lodge had continued to function as a Lodgie from December,
1924, to the date of such "revocation," and the dispensation has been

686

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

returned to the Grand Secretary, with the by-laws, book of records,
etc., as required by siection 74 of our Constitution, together with a
petition and fee for a charter.
We are of opinion that under our Constitution the only power of
the Grand Master with relation to either a charter or dispensation that
has been issued, is that prescribed in the 7th subdivision of section 43
of the Constitution, viz.: "to arrest" the same for good reasons, and
"suspend the operations" of the Lodge until the next annual communication. This is the express wording of the provision specially applicable
to such a matter, and the words used seem to us to limit the powei:.
A dispensation issued by the Grand Master terminates upon the first
day of the month in which the next succeeding annual communication
is :holden (section 74, Constitution), and whether a continuation of the
dispensation shall be had for another year or a charter be issued, is
solely a question for the Grand Lodge (section 75, Constitution). The
language of •the 7th subdivision of section 43 is very explicit, and the
power of arrest and suspension of operations of the Lodge until the
next annual communication would appear to give every essential protection to Masonry.
All this is quite clear as to charters (see siections 130 and 132,
Constrtution), and the power of the Grand Master as to both charters
and dispensations as prescribed in section 43 is exactly the same, viz. :
"to arrest the chartier or dispensation of any Lodge, for good reasons
shown, and suspend the operations thereof until the next annual communication."
The right of the Grand Master to exercise all the executive powers
of the Grand Lodge between communications, prescribed by the first
sent•ence of section 43 of the Constitution, is necessarily limited as to
the subjects specially covered by the subdivisions of that section, by the
language of those subdivisions.
We attach no particular importance to the use of the word
"revoked" in the form pr•escribed for such a dispensation. It cannot
in any event operate as a modification of the provision specifying and
limiting the power of the Grand Master in subdivision 7 of section 43
of the Constitution, and must be read as synonymous with the word
"arrest" us•ed in said subdivision.
We are of opinion that the action of the Grand Master should be
taken simply as an arrest of the dispensation and a suspension of the
operations· of the Lodge.
As to the correctness of the action of the Grand Master in so
arresting the dispensation, we have made a painstaking examination of
the record. While the reports made to the Grand Master werie of
such a nature that we are satisfied he was justified in concluding that

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

687

for the protection of Masonry the operations of the Lodge should be
suspended, and was therefore fully justified in arresting the disp1ensation,
a most convincing showing has since been made to the effect that the
Lodge gave full consideration to the objections made by Masons who
were not members of •the Lodge, going even to the extent of appointing
a special Investigating Committee which made a full and 1elaborate
investigation; and that the members of the Lodge were fully satisfied
that none of the objections were wdl founded; and tha·t the applicant
was in all respects eligible to become a member of the Fraternity.
We are definitely of the opinion that the order of the Grand Master
had no other effect than to arrest the dispensation and suspend the
operations of the Lodge until October 1, 1925, the date of the termination of the dispensation, and that the question whether the petition for
a charter should be totally refused, or a continuanoe of the dispensation
until the next annual communication ordered, should be determined at
this communication. If no action is had at this communication the
Lodge cannot hereafter be reviv ed. We are disposed to feel, in 'view
of the showing now made, that this Lodge acted in good faith in this
particular matter, and that we should not now refuse to give it further
opportunity to demonstra·te its worth. At the same time we believe it
would be wise to defer the question of issuance of a charter to the next
annual communication and to continue the dispensation to such time.
If so c.ontinued it will of course always hie subject to arrest by the
Grand Master.
1

We therefore recommend that the views of this committee be
adopted as the views of this Grand Lodge, and that the dispiensation
heretofore issued be continued until the next annual communication.

The report and recommendation were adopted.

law of this jurisdiction and was considered and passed upon by this
Grand Lodge in its sessions of 1914 and 1916.
In 1916 Grand Master Burnett had this matter under consideratiOn
and stated as follows: "On a motion to amend the by-laws of a Lodge,
there being ten members present, five voted for it, three against it, and
two did not vote, the Master acting on the presumption that ail present
. and not voting are presumed to assent to the action taken (section 77(h)
of the Constitution) counted the two members not voting as those
voting in the affirmative, and therefore declared the amendment adopted.
It required a two-third vote to carry it. I hold that the amendment
was not carried, as the law requires a vote of two-thirds of those
present. This necessarily exacts actual participation in the ballot and
does not contemplate 'constructive voting.'"
We therefore recommend that the decision of the Grand Master
in response to the first question asked by the Master of San Joaquin
Lodge be affirmed, and that his decision in response to the second
question be reversed.

Definition of the Word "Orphan"
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

'Dhere has been submitted to this committee a recommendation
that the definition of the word orphan, as used in section 163 of the
Constitution be changed. The proposed definition is as follows: (1)
That the word "orphan" be defined as "the offspring of a Master Mason,
prior to the twenty-first birthday, after which time he ceases to have
any claim as a matter of right on the Masonic Fraternity; (2) That
the daughter of a Master :\1ason releases the Fraternity from obligation
upon her marriage."
That portion of the proposed law which has reference to males
is in accordance with the present law. While the second portion of
the proposed law does not, in terms, define a female orphan, it does
declare, that upon her marriage, a female ceases to ·have any claim
upon the Fra:ternity for assistance. Under its provision a :VIason's
daughter, no matter of what age, retains her claim for Masonic relief
so long as she remains single, while, on the other hand, such a person
who marries, forfeits such rights no matter what may happen to her
thereafter. As the law with respect to daughters of Masons now
stands, irrespective of her age or whether she is married or single,

Competition in Conferring Degrees
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:

The ruling of the Grand Master with respect to competition in
conferring degrees, which ruling was superinduced by a proposal to
hold a contest between various Lodges in San Francisco to determine
the degree of excellence attained in the ritual of the first degree, has
heen submitted to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
for consideration.
It appears from the evidence that elaborate plans had been laid to
hold a competition on a large scale; that the determination of the
result was to be intrusted to a selected jury, and that certain generous
members of the Craft had donated prizes for the successful contenders.
Reviewing the matter before it, your committee was deeply impressed
with the earnest zeal and ardent enthusiasm of the brethren who devoted
so much time and effort to perfecting the conditions under which the
contest was to be held. We realize full well that they were actuated
by a very laudable desire to stimulate interest in this very important
and oft-neglected degree. We believe, too, that they were justified in
the thought that their plan would result in a strenuous effort on the

6!}5

It must be apparent that at so momentous an event in his Masonic
life, a candidate should find himself enveloped in an atmosphere of
dignity, decorum and spirituality.

It is hardly conceivable that under conditions of contest, with
prizes as a reward, suc'h could be the result.
It would scarce be a matter of pleasure or pride for any one of
us if we, later, came to know that at our initial step in Masonry, we
had been but the central figure in a tournament.
Your committee therefore recommends that the ruling of the
Grand Master prohibiting competition in conference of degrees be
approv.ed.

Report adopted.
Investigating Committees
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California.:

After mature consideration, the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes finds itself unable to approve the recommendation of the
Grand Master that sections 99 and 100 of the Constitution should be
amended. The provision for secrecy respecting the identity of members
of investigating committees was written into our law to correct abuses
and to aid in securing a full and dependable report on petitioners. Only
on the basis of secrecy can detailed and faithful reports be received.
T·he so-called advisory committees referred to by the Grand Master
are excellent instruments for making careful investigations, and it lies
within the right and power of each Master to appoint such committees
if he so desires, to aid him and the Lodge in the performance of an
important Masonic duty. These advisory committ·ees, however, do not
supplant the committee required by the Constitution, but merely supplement its work; they usually assume the form of a personnel committee
which meets the petitioner and secures from him his account of himself
and his qualifications for membership. The Constitutional committee
goes farther afield to investigate reputation, sfanding, antecedents, moral
character, behavior, etc.
Your committee does not believe that sufficient reason exists for
requiring additional committees of investigation, and therefore recommends that. sections 99 and 100 of the Constitution be not amended.

Report adopted.

Physical Examination of Petitioners

w:. Grand Lodge of California:
'fihe Master and Wardens Association of Los Angeles propose a
resolution or law requiring an applicant for the degrees or for affiliation
to submit to a physical examinafi.on by a duly licensed physician as to
the physical condition of such applicant, and the reading to the Lodge
of such physician's report at the time of balloting on the petition or
application.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, after considera•tion of this matter, is of the opinion that in perhaps a few isolated
and exceptional instances, detriment has been occasioned to a Lodge by
reason of physical defects in a candidate which were unknown at the
time of his -election, but that no sufficient reason exists for the enactment
of the proposed legislation. It is a matter of great concern to a Lodge
to be advised of the general health and physical soundness of a petitioner
or applicant, and due care should always be exercised in these matte~s
by the Lodge. There is full authority and warrant in our law as 1t
now stands for a proper and full investigation of the physical condition
of petitioners and applicants. We, therefore, recommend that the proposal be not adopted.

Report adopted.
Educational Committee

w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The report of the Educational Committee and the observations and
recommendations of the Grand Master relative thereto have been
carefully considered by your committee, and with many misgivings and
some hesitation we respectfully recommend the adoption of the report.
The report 'of the committee is admirably conceived and intelligently
presented, and is far superior to any former plan ·or report on the
subject that has engaged the attention of this committee.
Our misgivings arise from a conviction that the demand for
Masonic education is not coupled with the will to pay the inexorable
price of knowledge-and our hesitation procee~s from our ~oubt th~t
the Masons of California want to pay a per capita tax to again experiment with an issue so doubtful of success.
For several years Grand Lodge has experimented in the field of
Masonic education without garnering any appreciable return ·for its
outlay of effort and money. The failure of accomplishment can not
be laid wholly at ·the door of Grand Lodge or its Education Committees.
It is undoubtedly true that a widespread demand exists for Masonic
To the M.".

697

instruction, but it is probably equally true that our members desire a
royal road to learning and expect to receive from entertainment that
which can only be won by application and mental toil. As the efforts
of the teacher must be seconded by the attention and industry of the
pupil in order to effectuate education, so the most scientific and painstaking planning and instruction of the Educational Committee can be
of real value only when the members of the Craft apply themselves
to the hard work of studying and thinking. If genuine Masonic
education is really wanted, our members must get it themselves-no
committee can give it to them. A committee can do no more than guide
and direct them.

Adopted.
Hawaiian Lodges

w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Master recommends a change of the Constitution •to
provide for the payment of additional moneys for the expenses of the
representatives of Lodges in the Territory of Hawaii. At the communication of this Grand Lodge in 1924, after consultation with the
representatives of the Hawaiian Lodges and a joint meeting of the
Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Finance,
it was recommended that the present Constitutional provision be adopted
to provide the payment of not to exceed the sum of $1,500.00 per year.
Under the law in force prior to 1924, the delegates from Hawaii received
no allowance from Grand Lodge for expenses.
The present law has been .in effect barely one year, and in view
of the limited time that has elapsed there has been scarce opportunity
to demonstrate the adequacy or equity of its provisions. After consultation with the Committee on Finance, we believe that the financial
demands at this session of Grand Lodge have been far in excess of its
income. Under these conditions, therefore, we believe it inopportune
to bring this matter at this time before Grand Lodge and feel 1hat it ·
should be deferred.
We, therefore, recommend that ·the matter be postponed for future
consideration.

Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes 1has considered
the report of the special committee appointed by the Grand Master to
examine into the request of the Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico for
recognition by this Grand Lodge, ·and begs to report that it does not
concur in the recommendation of the special committee.
In 1921, by authority of the Grand Master, Past Grand Master
Charles Albert Adams made a visit to Mexico and pursued an investigation of the Masonic conditions existing in that Republic and made
an exhaustive report to Grand Master Rodden, which is to be found
on pages 387 to 410 of the proceedings of 1921. The recommendations
of this report were approved by the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes and adopted by Grand Lodg,e and we have been in fraternal
relations with the York Grand Lodge of Mexico since the adoption of
said report. Your committee is informed and believes that no material
change has occurred in -the relationship between the two Grand Lodges
disputing jurisdiction in Mexico since the time of Past Grand Master
Adams' report and that the hope of this Grand Lodge expressed in its
resolntioi1 recognizing the York Grand Lodge that a solution might be
found for the problems confronting Ancient Craft Masonry in the
Republic of Mexico and that harmony might be restored, has not been
realized.

The recommendation of the special committee that this Grand Lodge
recognize the Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico raises qut:stions of
serious difficulty, for we are now in fraternal relationship with -the
York Grand Lodge, which has expelled a number of Masons who
now owe allegiance to the body proposed to be recognized and is not
in fraternal acc-ord or amity with the Grand Lodge Vallee de Mexico,
but on the other hand claims that Grand Body to be wHhout right and
not entitled to the recognition of itself or any other Masonic power.
No amity or concord exists between the two ·bodies, but each have
given very definite exhibition of resentments and ill-feeling.
It was long the policy of this Grand Lodge not to recognize two
Masonic powers occupying the same territorial jurisdiction. During
the war, and influenced by a commendable sentiment, the Grand Lodge
in a single case modified its long-standing rule and recognized two
bodies which were in amity and concord and in occupancy of the same
territory. If the report of the special committee is adopted, it means
an entire abrogation of the- long-established policy of this Grand Lodge
on the subject of ·recognitfon of foreign Masonic powers disputing the
same territory. Your committee is of the opinion that the policy should
not be abrogated and that this Grand Lodge should not proceed further
than in a proper case, and because of extraordinary circumstances,
to recognize two Masonic powers which by mutual consent and agreement occupy the same territorial jurisdiction. It is incongruous that
two Grand Lodges occupying the same •territory and refusing to
recognize. or fraternize with each other should both be recognized by
this Grand Lodge and that the members of such discordant bodies
should be recognized and received as regular in our Lodges when they
are regarded as irregular and clandestine at home and by a Grand
Lodge recognized by us.
Your committee is of the opinion tha·t the report of the special
committee above referred to should not be adopted so long as this
Grand Lodge continues fraternal relations with the York Grand Lodge
of Mexico. No resolution or other step looking >to the withdrawal of
recognition of the York Grand Lodge has been presented or has come
before this committee. Under these circumstances your committee
respectfully recommends that the recommendations contained in the
report of the special committee be not adopted.

Grand Lodge concurred in the recommendation.

Income from Endowment Fund
From the 1910 proceedings, we quote as foUows:
"That the sum received from Brother N eff's estate be entered as
the first donation and with the balance in the Permanent Improvement
Fund, making a total of $29,835.97, be placed in a fund to be known
as the Permanent Endowment Fund of the Masonic Home of California,
no part 'of which shaU hereafter be used for any purpose, only the
interest thereon to be used and that to go into the General Fund of
the Masonic Home."
On July 31, 1925, the Endowment Fund amounted to $464,291.62.
The interest on the Endowment Fund for the year ending 'on above
date was $15,359.42. It has been the ambition of a great many members
of Grand Lodge to see this Endowment Fund reach $1,000,000.00, and
we belie~e its creation and increase will influence many members of
the Craft to give to this fund, which in later years will in some
measure at least relieve the burden from the Lodges, in the matter
~f the maintenance of the Homes. Your committee is of the opinion
that none of the income from this fund should be used, until the fund
has reached the sum of $1,000,000.00.
We therefore offer the fo11owing resolution, and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that a11 inoome of whatsoever nature, received from the
Endowment Fund, be added thereto and become a part thereof, until
said Endowment Fund shall have reached $1,000.000.00.

Grand Lodge did not concur, and the resolution failed
of adoption.

Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley
Referring to the report of the Trustees of the Masonic clubhouse
at Berkeley, University of California: After a personal inspection by
your Finance Committee.. we see no way in which this institution
can be maintained without the annual support of this Grand Lodge.
The budget submitted to your committee calls for approximately
$10,000.00 annually and, after careful scrutiny, we have been unable to
suggest any material reductions in same. There is an item of $2,407.30
taxes, and an item of $1,050.00 interest, the Trustees at the present
time being in debt to the amount of $17,500.00.
We offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $10,000.00 be and is hereby appropriated
from the funds of this Grand Lodge, to maintain the Masonic clubhouse at Berkeley during the coming year, and, as this will be an
annual charge, it will be necessary to levy an additional tax for its
support; therefore, be it further resolved, that a per capita tax of

payable July 31, 1926, when other Grand Lodge dues are paid.

PROPOSAL FOR LARGER ROOM
Past Grand Master Henderson presented the following:
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
At the annual communication of 1904 I introduced a resolution to
provide for the erection of a new Masonic temple in San Francisco.
It is apparent to all that the present room in our temple is inadequate
to meet the requil"ements of Grand Lodge, and it is believed that an
enlarged room can be provided in this building. Therefore be it
ResQ)ved, that the incoming elected office.rs of Grand Lodg,e be
appointed a special committee empowered to confer and act in conjunction with other oodies and committees and arrangie for suitable
quarters within our own temple for the use of Grand Lodge, and to
that end that said committee is empowered to act.

Referred to the incoming Grand Master.

MEMORIAL SERVICES
The Grand Master called up the Grand Lodge and
formally advised the representatives of the death of Past
Grand Master George W. Hunter, following which solemn
memorial services were had. A helpful prayer was said
by the Grand Chaplain, followed by a feeling and eloquent
address by W .'. Jam es T. Fraser, a life-long friend and
neighbor of Judge Hunter.

The Grand Master caused to be read the following
telegram from Past Grand Master Louis A. W atres, President of the George Washington Memorial Association:
Scranton, Pennsylvania, October 9, 1925.
David J. Re,ese, Grand Master,
San Francisco.
The work of the George Washington Masonic N;1.tional Me111orial
Association of erecting at Alexandria, Virginia, a suitable memorial
temple to Washington the Mason, which in durability and ·beauty will
express the exultant and undying esteem of the three million Masons
in the United States for him in whose memory it shall stand through
the coming years, is progressing very satisfactorily. The charter of
the association is perpetual under the laws of Virginia. Every one of.
the forty-nine Masonic jurisdictions have contributed and are contributing to the work. The quota of each jurisdiction is as many
dollars as there are members. At this writing over one million eight
hundred thousand dollars have been paid in. By the February meeting
construction will have reached the cornice entirely around the temple.
It is most essential that money shall be received rapidly enough to
keep the work constantly going.
Your good jurisdiction, with 108,000 members, has paid in eighteen
thousand dollars, which includes the recent generous contribution of
your Grand Lodge. It would be a wonderful inspiration to our association and to all the brethren, as well as tci the advisory board composed
of Chief Justice Taft, General Leonard Wood, Governor Lowden,
Townsend Scudder, Governor Goldsborough, Senator Glass, Senator
Warren, Admiral Baird, Senator Chamberlain, if you would endorse
the project and make a definite recommendation to Grand Lodge, aad
if Grand Lodge would take such steps as shall fully inform the brethreh
of California of the far reach and deep significance of our mighty
movement.
The building of this temple is one of the greatest efforts ever put
forth in Masonry. It will be the rallying place for Masons not only
of the United States but eventually throughout the whole world. Under
its roof Masonic ideals will flourish. It will be more than a memorial
to Washington: It will be a monument to civil and religious liberty
and to a stablie and orderly government. Erected of enduring material,
our temple will stand through the ages. It will carry to generations
yet unborn and to those to whom we may seem an ancient race, the
message of human brotherhood. It will perpetuat'e the attributes of

713

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

712

self-denial, patriotism, love of country, and of fellow men which were
exemplified in the life and work of the great Mason, master builder of
our nation.

Referred to the Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ENDOWMENT
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
We, the members of your Endowment Committee of the Masonic
Homes of California, appointed by the Grand Master of the last Grand
Lodge, beg t~ rieport that this has been a year of education, and that
the results will not be apparent for some time to come. This is our
viewpoint, based on the fact that there ha~ been no drive or concerted
•effort, in the. various Lodges to increase the Endowmen~ Fund.
At the last annual communication there was distributed to each
representative present, a very beautiful and attractive booklet which
was prepared by our Junior Grand Warden, Brother \Vill H. Fischer,
for and on behalf of the Endowment Committee. It was the unanimous

714

GRAND LODGE OF CA.Ll~RNJA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

opinion of all the brethren present that a. sufficient number of these
bookl<ets should be printed so that every member of our Grand Jurisdiction could have a copy.
·
Immediately on the closing of the Grand Lodge, our committee
took the matter up with the Grand Master, and the copy to be placed
in the booklet, together with pictures of our Homes, were reviewed by
the elective Grand Lodge officers, and the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes. Some four months ago we received general approval,
and the booklet was printed and is now in the hands of the members
of the various subordinate Lodges.
No very general financial nesults have as yet been secured, but
undoubtedly many wills have been drawn giving liberal bequests to
the Homes, and your chairman has himself assisted in preparation of
five wills in which the Homes have been well remembered.
The activities of the Endowment Committee have not been particularly great, and all that can be acc~mplished (except by activity in the
various subordinare Lodges) has been done. We have prepared the
campaign of education; we have planted the seed as best we could in
the hearts of the brethren, and it is now for the wisdom of the Grand
Lodge to decide whether the committee should be continued. It seems
to your committee that except to appear as part of the general organization, there is nothing left that can be accomplished, unless it is the
desire of the Grand Lodge that a determined effort be QUt forth in
each Lodge to increase the Endowment Fund more ~. Thisreport is therefone submitted, awaiting your decision.

REPORT OF LIBRARY COMMITTEE
To the i';1.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Library, not having b~n apportioned the necessary funds wherewith to function, at the last session of Grand Lodge
held in the city of Los Angeles, regrets the necessity for such a report
as I am making-barren as it is of progress. toward the end so much
to be desired.
There were, however, extenuating drcumstances, and you will conceive t·heriefore that this portion of the report does not constitute a
complaint, but is rather an expression of regret, that circumstances
over which Grand Lodge seemingly had no control, should have intervened to hold up the establishment of a circulating library, for which
every preparation had been made.

MILEAGE FOR REPRESENTATIVES
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported back the
resolutions of the Grand Master proposing to repeal Regulation 221 and to amend sections 6, 41 and 57 of the Constitution, recommending the adoption of the resolutions,
and thereupon Regulation No. 221 was 1·epealed, and sections 6, 57 and stthdi vision 3<1 of section 41 were amended
hy unanimous vote to read as follows:
Sec. 6. At the close of each annual conmnrnication, the Grand
Treasurer shall pay to the offioers or to the representatives of each

718

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Lodge in the jurisdiction, the exact cost of transportation for one
person from the location of each Lodge in the jurisdiction to the place
of meeting of the Grand Lodge and back again, viz. :-an unlimited
first-class railroad fare, together with stage fare and cost of berth
in sleeper when require.cl, as ascertained by the approvied report of. the
Committee on Pay of Members, such report being his voucher therefor.
But no payment shall be allowed for the officers or representative of
any Lodge, the dues of which shall not have been paid in full, or which
shall be reported by thie Grand Secretary as having been delinquent in
the transmission of certificates of .the election and installation of ,the
officers of their respective Lodges, within the time prescribed by law.
No officer, or representative of a Lodge, shall receive such payment
in mone than one of those capacities, nor shall he receive it unless he
shall have been in attendance at such communication from the first to
the last day thereof, inclusive, unless excused by the Grand Lodge.
Sec. 41, 3d. For each Master Mason whose name is borne upon
their rolls at the date of the annual returns, such sum as the Grand
Lodge shall prescribe at each annual communication, which shall constitute a special fund to be denominated "T!hie Representative Fund."
And the Grand Lodge may levy, in addition to the above, such other
contributions as in its judgment may be required. Provided, nevertheliess, that no contribution of a~y sort, in the nature of a per capita tax,
shall be payable by a Lodge upon any Mason whose dues at the stated
meeting in July of the calendar year in which such tax would otherwise
be payable, shall have been remitted for the next preceding twelve
months' period, because of the inability of such Mason to pay such
dues. Each subordinate Lodge's annual report, in addition to any other
matter required, shall contain a list of the names of Masons whose
dues have been remitted, together with the cause of such remission,
as to whom non-payment of per capita tax contribution is to be had.
Sec. 57. It shall also be the duty of each Inspector in this j urisdiction to attend the Lodge of Instruction to be held by the Grand
Lecturer immediately before, during, or immediately following, each
annual communication of the Grand Lodge, and he shall be allowed
transportation from the Representative Fund in the same manner as is
allowed the officers or the representatives of the Lodges; provided that
he shall produce the certificate of the Grand Lecturer that he has
attended the Lodge of Instruction. No Inspector rece1vmg pay from
the Grand Lodge in any capacity, as a member or otherwise, shall
receive any pay as Inspector.

PRESENTATION TO GRAND MASTER
On behalf of Grand Lodge, Past Grand Master Samuel
E. Burke in an eloquent address presented · the retiring
Grand Master, for himself and Mrs. Reese, a beautiful
Chesterfield set. In his response Broth.er Reese said:
Most Worshipful Grand Alaster and Brethren of th(? Grand Lodge
of Calif ornia:
My heart overflows, my feelings and my sentiments arc overwhelmed, as I acknowledge this last expression of your esteem, your
love, your good will. My year of service iS ei:de<l, but my years of
usefulness, I hope, are but begun. To have served this Grand Lod'gc,
as I have been permitted to serve this year, has been a glorious privilege,
a wonderful experience. To have known you, \Vorshipful Sir, to have
associated with the Grand officers and Past Grand officers, to have come

722

PROCE)EDINGS OF THE

in contact with the able, honorable, conscientious members of the
Fraternity over this State has been a privilege which no man can fully
appreciate without having actually experienecd it. I am now released
from duty after twenty-eight consecmive years of active service, not
one week, one month, nor one year of whkh have I failed to respond
or answer the call for 1\1.;u;orllc action. The little mother, who was so
proud a year ago when I was honored by election to the highest office
in the gift of Masonry, and whose thoughts and whose hopes today
hang upon my .success in this position; my wife who has spared me
sacrificing home comfort and home interest that I might devote my
years aDid efforts to Masonry; my daughters who have been proud of
tbeif' father's preferment will welcome me home after more than a
quarter of a century's constant and consistent service to the cause of
Masonry. And I myself lay down my burden with feelings of relief
and satisfaction strangely mingled with regret and sadness.
To paraphrase the valedictory of that good man and Mason, Vice
President T'homas R. Marshall, I have ended my official Masonic life
as the presiding officer of this Grand Lodge of Masons. My retirement
does not mark my demotion to the ranks, for in truth, my brethren,
I never rose above them. I have given you all I have in my efforts to
discharge the duties of Grand Master. I may have failed, but I have
tried to keep the faith. As I have labored among you and for you,
I have come more and more to the belief that Masonic membership
is a privilege and a challenge to organized service for humanity. So
long as any organization has service for its watchword and purpose,
it can and may justify its existence, and Masonry will live as long
as it has an eye single to its teachings; it will die only· when its
principles and teachings are swallowed up and submerged by outside
attractions or distractions. Religions die because pdests mumble their
creeds, but have no faith in their Gods; governments fall .because statesmen shout aloud their shibboleths, but let friendly enemies pass the
ford.
But, my brethren, my race is run. It is not for me to even suggest
to you now. The time for that has pai;sed. For four long years have
I been with you; for one active, busy year have I served you. I come
to the end with a great feeling of re\i.ef. I am tired, oh so tired.
I come to the end with a feeling of heartfelt gratitude for the honors
you have copferred, for the pleasures you have given, for all those little
nameleas unremembered acts of charity wh'ich bave marked your friendship and your good will. ~ come to the end \Vith a feeling of sadness
and regret that I must retire from active association with the men with
whom I have so happily served during these long years.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

723

You have been good to me. The ·remembrance of your kindness
and your friendship will cheer every waning day, every waning year of
my life. I go, but you remain and, to paraphrase Marshall just a bit
further, I leave with the same inarticulate cry in my soul with which
I came to you-Masonry-good citizenship-toleration, morality, and
decency-service. To some, these have many meanings, but to me they
are the composite voice of all the good and wise and self-sacrificing
souls who compose our membership calling for that liberty which is
law-crowned; preaching that doctrine which seeks not its own, but the
common good, demanding from us unselfish and generous service in
behalf of our fellow men and fellow :\fasons. It is no new religion
we need. Our creed should be: One Lord, one faith, one baptismthe Lord of justice; the faith that under our form of government alone
democracy can permanently endure; the baptism of that spirit which
will not be content until no man is above the penalties and no man
beyond the protection of the law.
And, finally, my brethren, as I invoked the protection and guidance
of Almighty God, as I entered upon the duties of my ofike, so do I
now raise my voice in thankfulness and gratitude to Him for His help
during this trying year.
I thank you-and will you give me the privilege of quoting here,
as I have this year many times,
"l would like to give you the sunbeam
Or the twinkle of some bright star,
.Or the tiny piece of the golden fleece,
That clings to a cloud afar.
I would like to give you the essence
Of a myriad sun-kissed flowers,
Or the lilting song, as it flows along,
Of a brook, through shady bowers.
I would like to give you the dew drop
That sparkles at break of day;
And then at night, the eerie light,
That glistens the milky wayI would like to give you the power
That nothing can overthrow;
The power to smile and laugh the while
As journeying through life you go.
But these are mere faIJciful wishes;
I'll give you a God-speed instead,
And then I'll clasp your hand and you'll understand
All the things I've left unsaid.

To the Most WorshiPful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted
}.-fasons of California:
In the report herewith submitted by the Committee on Correspondence, we have reviewed the proceedings of all of the
Grand Lodges which have reached our desk. As this is the
first report submitted by this committee, we have refrained
from obtruding our personal opinions, confining our review to
the general subjects of Masonic importance discussed in the
reports of the various Grand Masters, and matters culled from
the printed proceedings which are of general interest to the
Craft.

Something more nearly approaching uniformity in rituals;
closer scrutiny by investigating committees of those asking
admission to the order ; a demand that there be inquiry as to
the conduct of Masons at conventions and semi-public affairs
held by organizations whose membership is predicated upon
Masonry; whole-hearted support and approval of the Order of
DeMolay; a healthy increase throughout the nation of Masonic
membership; a decided tendency toward toleration as it relates
to the membership of Masons in other organizations, coupled
with unmistakable warnings that strife must not be engendered
through religious creeds and racial dislikes-these are some of
the outstanding thoughts found in the messages of Grand
Masters whose reports in part are to be found here.
Some of the reports from the smallest states, where Masonry
ts numerically weakest, reflect, in the opinion of the reviewer,
a stauncher stand for the fundamentals of the Order, and per-

4

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

haps a better understanding of the structure upon which
Masonry is puilt than is found in the populous places. We
would do well to study the reports, not only for direct suggestions, but for those indirect and abstract ones which are sometimes more important. Canadian Brothers and those from the
storm-swept isles near us show a commendable brevity in
reports, at the same time containing much food for reflection.
Throughout the reports there is a loving overtone of respect
and admiration for those splendid leaders who have carried on
through the years and have laid down their emblems to enter
the Greater Grand Lodge in another and more beautiful Jurisdiction beyond this life.

The 104th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge convened
in the city of Montgomery, December 2nd, and continued in session
during December 3rd and 4th.
The commissions of the Grand Representatives of the Grand
Lodges of Idaho, Manitoba and Philippine Islands were revoked for
non-attendance· for three successive years.
Among the distinguished visitors present were M. \V. Brother Bert
S. Lee, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Missouri, and the Most
Puissant Grand Master of the General Grand Council of R. & S. M.
of the United States of America, who were introduced and accorded
a hearty welcome.
The Grand Master prefaced his address with the following sound
and practical advice for all Masons ;
"It is my judgment that the greatest hindrance to progress and to
the ~e_velopment of real brotherhood is that men from timidity or from
sttsp1c10n mduced by false rumor, or a natural inclination not to mix
with their fellows, remain strangers to each other. \Ve want to get
away from .al,I this, and let's begin now by touching elbows with all the
brethr·en, g_1vmg each other the handclasp of friendship and brotherly
reg~rd, tellmg each other who we are, and passing judgment on no one
until W·e know all the facts, or at least make inquiry to ascertain the
facts, from each viewpoint.

"Such an attitude wit.I obviate many misunderstandings and give us
that faith in human nature and in our ownselves that will add much to
the sum total of human happiness and our own peace of mind."
During the year, dispensations were granted for the organization
of 4 new Lodges; new or duplicate charters were issued to 3 Lodges;
dispensations to continue work, due to charters lost, destroyed by
fire, or otherwise, to 7 Lodges: dispensations to consolidate Lodges,
3; dispensations to change location of Lodges, 3.
During the year, the Grand Master was asked to accept a place
on the Board of Directors of the Alabama Educational Association.
These directors are selected from the heads of various institutions
of the State for the purpose of publicity work, that is, to impress
upon the people the necessity of better educational facilities and the
necessity of giving to· every child born and reared in Alabama a
chance.
The angel Death visited the official family of Grand Officers,
calling Brother Albert Leslie Reese, Junior Grand V.Tarden, whose
death occurred in the city of Birmingham, May 19, 1924. That
Death loves a shining mark was never more surely proven than in
the passing of Albert Leslie Reese. A young man just in his prime
of glorious manhood, with his sphere of influence constantly widening and his powers daily growing, he was cut down just at the time
of the beginning of his greatest usefulness to the Craft, to his
friends, to his community and to his State.
A pleasing feature of the session was a visit of the Lodges of the
Order of the Eastern Star, the party including the Grand Matron of
the Grand Chapter, Order of Eastern Star of Alabama, Mrs. Anne
Wynde Dillard, accompanied by Brother Oliver L. Stewart, Grand
Patron; Mrs. Julia Beauchamp, Associate Gra'nd Matron; Brother
Raymond E. Thomason, Associate Grand Patron; Mrs. Florence G.
Newsom, Grand Secretary; Mrs. Callie F. Tomlinson, Past Grand
Matron; and Mrs. Amy A. Carle, Past Grand Matron and General
Grand Adah of the General Grand Chapter 0. E. S. of the United
States of America, who were introduced to the Grand Lodge and
welcomed by the Grand Master.

The 19th .Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Alberta
was opened 111 Odd Fellows Hall in the Citv of ).fedicine Hat Province of Alberta, on Wednesday, June 11, l924.
'
The Grand Master recorded steady progress in all departments
of the work of the Fraternity during the past year. He stated, that

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

despite the reaction from the period of inflation, so noticeable in all
· activities of life, the general welfare of the Craft in Alberta has not
been seriously effected. The Grand Master took occasion to commend the Grand Secretary for his faithful work as secretary of the
Benevolent Committee, as it is upon him the work of personal
investigation so often falls, and such work demands unfailing
patience, tact and careful judgment. It was noted that the demands
of the Relief Fund are steadily increasing.
The Grand Master, during his year of office, visited every portion
of the Province. In his extended itinerary, he performed a useful
and important duty by bringing all brethren into closer touch with
each other and· with the Grand Lodge, its aims and advantages. His
first important duty when installed as Grand Master was to constitute and consecrate three lodges which had received their charters
at the last annual communication of the Grand Lodge, namely,
Hussar Lodge, Meridian Lodge and Kitscoty Lodge.
The Committee on the "Condition of Masonry" reported that
Masonry in the Province is making real progress, and that invariably
the Lodges were active, and with two exceptions, with bright prospects for the future.
The Committee called attention to the lack of attendance by the
membership at the regular meetings, and suggested that the Masters
should consider it as part of their duties to make the Lodge meetings sufficiently interesting to the members so that they would
consider their Lodge meeting an event not to be ignored or allowed
to be forgotten.
At a banquet served by the brethren of the City of Medicine Hat
Lodge, to those in attendance at the Grand Lodge, an address was
delivered by the M. W. Dr. J. W. McNeil!, Grand Master of the
Lodge of Saskatchewan, which is published in full in the proceedings.
The City of Edmonton was unanimously chosen as the place of
meeting for the next Annual Communication. The newly-elected
Grand Master is Horace P. Reid, Brother S. Y. Taylor being reelected Grand Secretary.

The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free· and Accepted
Masons of Arizona held its 42nd annual communication in the City

11

The Grand Master in his annual address stated that he had visited and spoken to every lodge within the jurisdiction. At all these
meetings banquets were served by members of the Eastern Star.
He had found Masonry in Arizona alive and awake, appreciative of
its privileges, conscious of its duty, loyal to its traditions and ready
and willing to meet and discharge its obligations.
The Grand Master attended the National Masonic Service Association meeting at \Vashington, and assisted in the laying of the
cornerstone of that magnificent memorial to George \Vashington
the Mason, now being erected by the Masonic Order on Shooter's
Hill, Alexandria, Virginia. In these ceremonies, the Grand Lodge
of Virginia was assisted by the Honorable Calvin Coolidge, president of the United States, and by William Howard Taft chief
justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
'
Directly closing the Grand Lodge at Prescott last year, the Grand
Master went to Tucson, where he instituted the Epes Randolph
Lodge No. 32. This lodge will be a lasting and living monumenno
the memory of that distinguished and exemplary Mason and man,
Col. Epes Randolph, who, during his life was a prominent figure in
railroad circles throughout Los Angeles, Arizona and Mexico.
During the year, the Grand Lodge also convened at \Vinslow,
. Ariz., for the purpose of laying the cornerstone of the Masonic Temple; Tucson, Ariz., for the purpose of laying the cornerstone of the
high school, and at Winslow, Ariz., for the purpose of dedicating
the new Masonic Temple.
During the year, the Grand Master issued a dispensation authorizing the brethren near the town of Bowie to open and form Bowie
Lodge U. D.
The Gi;:and Master, during his visitations, learned that a great
many lodges were holding interesting and profitable study club
meetings which were doing good work. He also recommended that
all lodges organize study clubs and devote at least one meeting a
month to this work.
The Grand Master approved of educational help for children of
Masons, and even went further, recommending help to any worthy
child, having the qualifications and will to acquire an education.
The report of committees showed that the committee on Educational Service had been especially active during the year. The committee reported that practically all the lodges were making use of
the material sent out, especially stressing the use of the bulletins of
the Masonic Service Association, mailing during the year the Short

Talk Bulletins issued by this organization, including "The Roll Call,"
"Our Public Schools," "Thf Spirit of Masonry," "Robert Burns,"
"Albert Pike," "The Book of Constitutions," "Warren G. Harding,"
"The Master's Peace," "The Rite of Restitution," "For the Good
of the Order," all of which are a part of the Association's program
for teaching a practical application of the lessons and symbolisms
of Free Masonry to every day life. This program covers the five
prominent principles taught in the degrees: religious liberty, equality
before the law, equality of opportunity, the dignity of labor, and
charity.
Otis James Baughn, Gila Valley Lodge No. 9, was elected Grand
Master; George James Roskruge, Tucson Lodge No. 4, re-elected
Grand Secretary.

The Grand Master expressed himself as disappointed with the
results obtained by Arizona from its connection with the Masonic
Service Association. He said:
"The tangible net results seem . to be negiligible. My letters to
officers of the Association have not even received the courtesy of an
answer. Nowher·e in this Jurisdiction have I found any stimulus in
Masonry as a result of such membership. Most of our Lodges seem
to have little or no idea as to the aims and purposes of the Association,
nor have I found any evidence to indicate that the brethren are getting
any good out of it whatever.
"That other Grand Jurisdictions are growing weary of contributing to the maintenance of the Association is shown by the fact that
the Grand Lodge of California, at its last annual communication, withdrew from membership therein. California will manage and finance
its own program of educational work among its subordinate Lodges,
believing that far better work and much better results will be obtained
thereby. In this connection it seems to me that if we develop our
study club idea, we can furnish the Craft something really worth whi.le
at much less expense."
During the year, two Past Grand Masters of the Jurisdiction
responded to the call of Death, Past Grand Master Fletcher Morris
Doan, who presided over the Grand Lodge in 1908, and Alexander
Gibson Oliver, Grand Master of the Grand Jurisdiction in 1891.
Including these two eminent Masons, a total of 74 members of the
constitutent, Lodges were called to the Great Beyond.
A notable visitation of the Grand Master was that of November
17th, when he met by appointment at Nogales, the Grand Master
and other Grand officers of the Pacific Grand Lodge of Mexico.
"Following the meeting across . the line, their Lodge was closed
and we all repaired to the hall of Nogales Lodge No. 11, where the
Lodge was dully opened. I was receiv·ed as Grand Master for my
official visit, and the Grand Master of the Pacific Grand Lodge properly received and introduced to the brethren. Here some other brief
addresses were delivered in further testimony of the high esteem in
which our brethren of the Pacific Lodge held us, as well as our own
expressions of good will and brotherhood toward them."
During the course of his address, the Grand Master took pains
to call attention to the fact that Masonry is not a religion, and
should not even be remotely so considered by the most ardent of its
members. Having been requested to contribute a statement as
Grand Master in furtherance of a "Go to Church" movement, he
took occasion to express the following:
"The church should be the soul of every community. A direct
reliance upon divine providence is utterly essential to the well being
of the individual, the family, the state and the nation. Yea, even the
hope of the world rests in the church. We have 'reformed' the Bible
out of our public schools and almost 'reformed' it out of some of our
churches. A sincere, whole-hearted return to the undimmed faith of
our forefathers is much to be desired.

The 43rd Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was held
in the Masonic Hall in the city of Phoenix on the 10th day of February, 1925.
The Grand Master's address deals with every phase of his work,
showing that his year has been one of activity, visiting every Lodge
in his Jurisdiction. For the benefit of our Eastern readers, we quote
in full his graphic description of the scenic beauties and wonders of
his state:
"Little do we realize brethren, what a wonderful State we live in.
With its sun-kissed valleys and majestic mountain range"S; its great
forests, tumbling waterfalls, indescribable in its beauty, might and
grandeur, and that greatest of all natural wonders, the Grand Canyon
of the Colorado River-when we view all these things brethren, the
heart of finit·e man is touched, and we realize, as never before, the
almighty omnipotence of the Great Architect of the Universe, at whose
creative fiat these, as well as all things else, were made. From the
snow-capped peaks of the San Francisco Mountains to the polka-dotted
shadows of the Sulphur Springs Valley; from Montezuma's Well and
that great outdoor mus·eum of natural history, the Petrified Forest,
to the turbid waters of the mighty Colorado River at Yuma; from the
matchless scenery of the new highway across the mountains into Clifton
to the ancient ruins of the Casa Grande; from the grandeur of the
Grand Canyon to the Mexican border-all this great wonderland, unspoiled in its God-given beauty, may be reached over roads which are
a delight to the traveler and tourist."

"As Grand Master of Arizona Masons, I would direct the attention of all Masons to the fact that Masonry is not a religion. It cannot take the place of the church. Its true mission in this regard is to
point, with never-failing accuracy, straight to the .door of the church.
Every Mason should be a regula.r communicant at some church."

held in the city of Tucson, commencing February 9, 1926.

The 83rd Communication of the M. \V. Grand Lodge of Arkansas
was held in the city of Little Rock on Tuesday, November 18, 1924.
Grand Master F. W. Harris's address indicated the thoughtful
Mason desiring to preserve the high standard of the Brotherhood.
In his opening remarks he said:
"\Ve congratulate ourselves that though the business interests of
Arkansas have suffer·ed by great depression during the past year, and
the minds of the people have been agitated by the industrial and political problems that nati.tra!:ly arise when our national election year
arrives, by strict adherence to the ancient landmarks, and the established usages of our profession, we avoid the storms which wreck
other societies and continue unabated our work of benevolence.
"We stand, therefore, on a platform broad enough and strong
enough to hold all good men; but let it be remembered that those who
come to us must come of their own accord and not by our solicitations. Our prospects are not proclaimed from the rostrum, pulpit,
housetops, or streets. but should be exemplified in our daily life and
conduct as taught by the Holy Bible the Great Light of Masonry.
Make it then the foundation of your council and your meditations."
The Grand Master made feeling reference to those whose lives
had ceased, and paid especial tribute to the R. W. Frank \V. Tucker,
Past Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas, who died at
his home in Little Rock on the 13th day of March, 1924; also the
R. \V. W. K. Dillendcr, District Deputy Grand Master, whose death
occurred in Dermoot, Ark.. on April 25th; also Past Grand Master

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

was opened in the Masonic Temple in the City of Vancouver, on
·Thursday, the 19th day of June, A. D. 1924.
The first 18 pages of the report was devoted to the records of
9 emergent communications of the Grand Lodge held during the
preceding year for the purpose of constituting lodges, the laying of
cornerstones and the dedication of lodge buildings.
Among the distinguished visitors present were Most Worshipful
Bro. James H. Bigg, P. G. M. of the Grand Lodge of Washington.
The Grand Lodge of British Columbia wastes no time in unnecessary preliminaries, and as soon as the opening ceremonies were over
the Grand Master, M. W. Bro. Chas. E. Tisdall, delivered his
address. The Grand Master spoke with pleasur.e of the increase in
the membership of 684 for the jurisdiction. During the year, 769
were raised to the degree of Master Mason. The estimated fund
and property of the lodges throughout the jurisdiction amounted
to $559,584.03. During the year, $12,920.11 was paid out in relief.
The Grand Master called attention to the desirability of greater
uniformity in the rituals of the order, and to the steadily increasing number of minor innovations that are being introduced in many
of the lodges.
In the matter of increased membership, the Grand Master in his
report says:
"The applicants- for membership apparently are fully the equal
of those already in the Order in respect to the moral worth and general good ·standing in the community. I have, however, repeatedly
drawn the attention of the constitutent lodges during my official visit
to the need of very close scrutiny to the class of material and also to
see that all candidates are properly instructed. All of us would like
to see our Order increase numerically, but not at the expense of quality. Our Order is g-enernlly becoming better organized, and thus is
able rriore thoroughly, year by year, to carry out the principles taught
in our charges and lectures in making Masonry a living power for
good.
"During my year of office, I have positively urged the members of
the Craft to carry the teachings of the lodge room into their daily
lives and to render community service wherever and whenever possible. I know of no better community work that can be given than time
devoted to the cause of education. I have long held the opinion that
technical education is much neglected, and would urge that interest in
public education by serving as scho.ol trustees or otherwise helping
along such work, is well worth the att-ention of members of the Craft
in their private capacity as citizens." ·
The Grand Master called attention to the fact that all over the
jurisdiction marked attention is being given to hospitals and expressed his satisfaction to know that in an overwhelming majority
of cases the Board of Directors consist largely of, members of the
Crafts.

He expressed his regret at the somewhat smaller attendance at
this session of the Grand Lodge, due to the fact that the Province
was in the midst of a Provincial election in which many of the
members of the Grand Lodge were either candidates or otherwise
active participants.
The Grand Master also called especial attention of the Standing
Committee on Finance to the constantly growing cost of the printing of the annual proceedings and suggested that either some of the
matter be eliminated or a smaller number be published.
It was the sorrowful duty of the Grand Master to report 19
dev.ths occurring among the membership of the Grand ·Lodge during the year, to whom a fraternal tribute was paid.
In the matter of the uniform form of ritual, the Grand Master
made the following pertinent remarks.
"I must again draw the attention of the members of the Grand
Lodge to the need of a more uniform form of ritual. Previous Grand
Ma:sters have brought this subj·ect repeatedly to the attention of the
Grand Lodge, but so far with no resui'tant action. The situation is
steadily getting worse. It would be bad enough if we had three authorized forms in use in the jurisdiction, but the three ar·e now being
rendered in three or four different ways."
During his term of office, the Grand Master made 60 monthly
visits to different parts of the jurisdiction, and by holding joint
meetings met some 80 lodges. One of his visits to the Northern
section of British Columbia resulted in his traveling 1935 miles
to make 5 official visits. This statement will enable our brethren
to grasp the magnitude of the territory in British Columbia, and
its sparse population in proportion to its area.
. The Grand Master closed his report with this worthwhile statement: "The imperative call comes today for a broader, deeper
and more practical application of the sublime truths and principles
of our Craft. Every Mason should carry this practical application
into civic, social and community life, this being the true spirit of
service to humanity."

The 69th annual communication was held in the City of Toronto,
July 16, A. D . .1924. The Grand Lodge was welcomed to Toronto
by His Worship, Mayor W. W. Heitz, Chief Magistrate of the City

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

of Toronto, who expressed the exceptional honor felt by the City hy
the Grand Lodge meeting for the second year in succession in that
city. The Mayor stated that the word "Toronto," which has come
down to us from the days when the red men were the sole occupants of the country, means "The place of meeting."
To the address of the Mayor the Grand Master responded,
briefly referring_ to the pleasant memory of the kind reception and
bountiful hospitality given to the Grand Lodge in 1923, and thanking the Mayor and the citizens for their warm-hearted greeting
and expressions of good will.
The Grand Master's report showed deep and earnest thought
with respect to Masonry, its ideals and prospects in the future and
the duty of the individual Mason during his lifetime with respect
thereto. "For the first time in many years," said the Grand Master,
"there are no notices of motions to be dealt with at this meeting;
in fact, our session should be characterized with alacrity and dispatch in the discussion of matters that may be presented to it."
During the year, warrants were issued to 12 lodges; and a dispensation granted for one new lodge.
Two special communications of the Grand Lodge were held for
the purpose of laying the cornerstone of the Masonic Temple at
Weston and the cornerstone of the U. E. Loyalist Memorial Building at Bellville.
During the year, the Grand Lodge distributed $100,000 to needy
dependents, and at least $50,000 more were distributed by the constituent: lodges. The attention of the lodges was directed to the
misunderstanding that is gaining ground that the Grand Lodge
should furnish all the funds for benevolences. "This is a mistaken
idea," said the Grand Master. "The grants made by the Grand
Lodge should be only supplementary, and the onus of providing for
our beneficiaries should fall on the constituent lodges."
The Grand Master commended the establishment of reading
rooms and libraries in connection with the Lodge quarters, where
the brain may drink deep at the fountain of knowledge that is to
be found in the various Masonic books and publications which can
be procured at moderate prices.
The Grand Master during the year visited 70 lodges. He also
participated in the laying of the cornerstone of the George Washington Memorial, which is being erected at a cost of $4,000,000.
"At this great gathering of Masons," the Grand Master said, "the
hospitality extended to the visitors and guests was unbounded, and
many firm and lasting international friendships were formed." The
•Grand Master advocated an extension of the inter-lodge meetings.
He said: "This is a custom which has grown with the years, one

19

· of which all should heartily approve. It creates an esprit de corps
among the officers, and it encourages them towards perfection in
their work; it gives an opportunity of making new acquaintances
and renewing old associations; it stimulates the attendance of mem- ·
hers and in many ways immeasurable benefits are derived."
He dealt severely with Masonic offenses, and said: "It is found
that there is too much leniency extended to Masons who were
guilty of criminal acts. This shows either a spirit of indifference
or a readiness to conceal or forgive crimes which should not b~
tolerated. The constitution is clear on the question of crime. A
Masonic trial should be inaugurated, and if the member is found
guilty, expulsion should follow."
He spoke highly of the splendid work being enjoyed by Masonic
bureaus where they have been established. "These bureaus act
as clearing houses for the different lodges in which the bureaus
are situated," he said. He suggested that bureaus be established in
all cities and towns where two or more lodges are established. In
closing his report, he said:
"During ~he three years of the post-war period a feverish anxiety
took posse~s10n ~f the young men of our province to join the Masonic
order. This desire was not confined to the province of Ontario but
~xtended throughout t~e Anglo-Saxon world: The popularity of
Masonry was reflected m the Lodges. They vied with each other in
making records for initiation. The records of 1922 and 1923 expose
the tragedy. In 1922, 1,158 members resilrned, and 957 were suspended
for non-payment of dues. Jn 1923, 1,202 resigned, and 1,005 were
suspended for. non-payment. These were chiefly members who joined
the Order durmg the boom years after the war. I can only repeat and
endorse what everyone of my predecessors in office has advocated
nam~ly-guard well t·he portals. Numbers are unimportant but th~
qual!tY of the membership is of vital importance to our Masonic
fabnc."
Both the Grand Master and the Secretary were re-elected.

an active public career, worthy of mention, one eminently fitting

not Masonic. The following excerpt from his address states the
attitude of the Grand Lodge fully:
"If this condition progresses to the point where the usefulness of
your Lodge should be impaired, the only remedy is to arrest the charter of the Lodge. I sincerely hope that it will not be necessary to do
this and it is the duty of every member of your Lodge to conduct him~
self in such a manner as not to create or encourage dissensions. With
Masons, the welfare of the Fraternity should be above all other considerations; and no one should be permitted to bring outside matters
. into the affairs of the Lodge.
"Neither the Grand Lodge of Colorado nor any of its constituent
Lodges will presume to dictate to the members of the Fraternity
whether or not they shall be associated with non-Masonic organizations; unless it later should develop that such non-Masonic organizations are attempting to interfer·e with the workings of the Craft.
"On the other hand, the Masonic Fraternity will not willingly. permit such non-Masonic organizations to attach themselves to the
Institution, particu:larly when such action leads to dissatisfaction,
dissension and confusion in the Fraternity."

The I 19th Annual Communication of the Most \Vorshipful Grand
Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Delaware, convened in the Masonic Temple, in the city of \Vilmington, on the
1st day of October, 1924. Grand Officers present, 14; Elected Past
Grand Officers, 46; Past Masters present, 137; representatives of
Lodges, 40; total representation, 237.
During the Masonic year 9 members of this Grand Lodge were
called by the Angel of Death to their reward.
During the year, 3 Emergent Communications of the Grand
Lodge were held for the purpose of laying the cornerstone of the
Newark public school, the Delaware Memorial Library on the
campus of the University of Delaware, and the Claymont School of
Wilmington. On each of these occasions the Grand Master used
the trowel used by him in the laying of the cornerstone of the
Washington Memorial, at Alexandria.
The Grand Master in his address reviewed the proceedings of
the annual meeting of the "Masonic Service Association of the
United States, held in Washington, on October 29 and 30, 1923."
We quote his findings:
"To my mind it is perfectly clear that an Association such as
this, is an imperative necessity if Masonry is to maintain its standard
as the leading Fraternity of the world. Delaware, the first to join the
Federation of States, should be the last to leave the Federation ·of
Masonry. It is claimed that the Association has made some mistakes,
has expended our Jive cents per member npon projects which could
Yery well have been omitted. Far be it from me to declare that perfection has been reached. To conceive and produce so large a program without a mistake would be as impossible as to conduct a world
war without a mistake. If we do not like some part of the program,
let us stay in where we have a part in shaping this policy to our
liking."

23

In his report, the Grand Master devoted considerable space to
the appointment of representatives to other Grand Jurisdictions.
Of California he said:
"For many years it has been the custom for this Grand Lodge to
exchange representatives with the majority of the other Grand Lodges
with whom we are in fraternal correspondence. A few of the Grand
Lodges do not do this. Among these was the Grand Lodge of California. In view of the fact that so many brethren of Delaware go to
California every year, both as temporary and as permanent residents,
it seemed to me that the present cordial relations existing between the
Masons of the two Jurisdictions should be promoted in every way
possible. I, therefore, proposed to M. W. Arthur S. Crites, Grand
Master of California, that an exchange of representatives be made,
and at the same time recommended for appointment from California to
Delaware, Past Master, Firman Thompson, of Hiram Lodge, No. 25,
Newark, who is at present residing at Sacramento. The proposal met
with a ready. and cordial response on the part of Grand Master Crites,
and the commission for the appointment of Bro. Thompson was
promptly prepared and forwarded."
The Grand Master reported that the new addition to the Masonic
Home, begun and dedicated during the term of his predecessors,
is now completed and occupied. At the last Annual Communication, a resolution was proposed, assessing the cost of the new addition against the constituted Lodges and giving them 3 years in
which to make payment. At the expiration of the first year, nearly
every Lodge had paid in excess of the first year's requirements, and
over half of the Lodges have paid in full. Out of a debt of $90,000,
only about one-tenth remains unpaid.
Among recommendations made by the Grand Master was an
appropriation of $200 at a Field Day Contingent Fund, for the purpose of covering deficits in the event of unfavorable weather, Over
2500 attended the Second Annual Masonic Field Day held at the
Masonic Home of Delaware, Friday, May 30, 1924 (Memorial Day).
The committee was embarassed by the. fact that the Grand Lodge
had issued instructions to hold a Field Day, but had made no appropriation for expenses. The Grand Master suggested that future
Field Days should be made afternoon affairs, as being ample for aU
benefits hoped for, and allowing Masons and their friends to attend
other Memorial Day exercises usually held in the morning.
Two questions for an official ruling came before the Grand
Master during the year:
No. 1 Can a Lodge as such attend divine service, in a denominational church, and call a meeting for that purpose, and if so, what
procedure should be followed?
Answer: Attending divine services in a denominational church
is not Masonic Labor, and it is therefore improper to open a Lodge

24

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE
REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

for that purpose, to wear the regalia of the Lodge, or to take its
paraphernalia. This, however, does not prevent individual Masons
from attending such services in a body.
No. 2. Is an applicant eligible to receive the Degree, who having been elected to membership in a Lodge, is subsequently found
to have an artificial foot?
Answer: \Vhen an applicant has been elected to receive the
Degree of Masonry, and by subsequent information it is learned
that he has an artificial foot, the election of the applicant is void;
he cannot be given the Degree, and his initiation fee must be
returned.
The Grand Master closed his address with the following sound
advice:
"To the Constituent Lodges, I leave this message: Keep up the
interest. Give the new members instructions for their labors. If
differences arise, endeavor to settle them for the best interest of
Masonry, and in a way that will leave no lasting scars.
. "To th<: Fraternity as a whole: Practice the teachings of Masonry
m yo~r da!ly conduct with your fellows. There is nothing wrong with
our ritual. There is nothing wrong with the institution itself. The
fault lies with the brother who is not and never was a Mason."
The Lodge closed with the election of Chas. D. Bird as Grand
Master.

The 114th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge F.
A. M., of the District of Columbia was held in the City of Washington, D. C., December 17 and 18, 1924.
Following the time-honored custom, the Grand Master in his
annual address presented briefly a review of the most important
events of the past year.
At the outset, he paused to pay tribute to those brethren, members of the Grand Lodge, including· 13 Past Masters, who had been
summoned from their earthly labors to the happiness and rewards
of the eternal life beyond the grave. He also paid touching tribute
to the dead of other jurisdictions whose distinguished services for
Masonry had won faithful atJ,d high places among their fellows.

25

The Grand Master reported the finances of the Lodges as being
in excellent condition. The consolidated returns showed that the
total receipts during the year amounted to $346,404.50 and compared
with $314,535.71 during the year 1923.
The visit of Sir Alfred Robbins, President of the Board of General Purposes of the Grand Lodge of England, and the party ac~
companying him, was made the occasion of many fraternal and social
functions during their stay in Washington. It is of general interest
that upon the return of this distinguished visitor to England, he
spoke in the most complimentary terms of his visits to the several
Grand Jurisdictions, the reception awarded him, and the numerous
activities and great achievements of American Masonry.
During the year, upon the petition of 26 brethren, the Grand
Master granted a dispensation to form a new Lodge to be designated at Brightwood Lodge.
During the year, the Grand Lodge was requested to lay the
cornerstones of a number of buildings, churches and lodge halls,
and the new law school of the George Washington University.
The Grand :\faster in his address highly commended the work
of "The Masters' Association;'' He said:
"One of the specially pleasing features· of the year has been the relations into which it was my privilege to enter with the Masters' Association. Even the most pronounced pessimist on the outlook of Masonry
would be transformed into an enthusiastic optimist if he were permitted
to see this splendid group of sincere men approach the duties and problems presented to the Association. No task was too har<l, no undertaking
too large, no sacrifice too great for them. Every request I made of the
Association was complied with cheerfully, promptly and efficiently, and
they administered the affairs of their respective lodges in a manner that
deserves the warmest commendation, which I here gladly give.
"Two events of which they had charge stand out as monuments to
their efficiency and ability to handle large tasks sucessfully. I refer to
the Annual Field Day for the benefit of the Masonic and Eastern Star
Home and the religious services held at Temple Heights on Sunday,
September 28, 1924. The proceeds kom Field Day will be far in excess
of the amount ever heretofore realized from this function, and this
gratifying result is due almost entirely to the zeal and inteHigence with
which the Association managed it.
"The religious services at Temple Heights on September 28 under
the auspices of the Masters' Association was one of the largest, if not
the largest, gathering of Ma sons amt their families ever seen in our
jurisdiction. The committee of the Association having this affair in
charge worked untiringly to secure this result, and the success achieved
tells its own story. Tt was an outstanding event in the annals of the
year and made a deep impression, not only on the brethren present, but
also upon President and Mrs. Coolidge, who were our guests on that
occasion."

burg is entirely clear of encumbrance. The majority of our Lodges are

In February, 1924, accompanied by Past Grand Master Ende!,
representing the Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons of Florida,
he attended the annual convention of the George Washington
Masonic National Memorial Association held in Alexandria, Va.
The program of the session included a visit to the Memor_ial building and surrounding grounds. The building at that time had progressed enough above the foundations to inspire one by its colossal
proportions and impress with its symmetry, beauty, and above all,
with its durability, for so far as possible it is constructed of indestructible materials which will stand an enduring monument throughout the countless ages.
On the question of "Prohibition" the1 Grand Master fearlessly
takes his stand in support of the Constitution of our Government.
He says:
"Although the Grand Lodge of Florida has legislated against the
traffic in liquor by its members, there has been no attempt to control

The Committee also directed attention to the apparent widespread carelessness or want of sufficient consideration on the part of
the Craft in balloting on petitions for the degree, as shown by the
fact that five applications were made to the Grand Master to re-open
dark ballots.
"In 1915 this Grand Lodge stated its position in such cases as
follows: 'While the discretion vested in the Grand Master in granting
dispensations cannot be reviewed by the Grand Lodge where the dispensation is within his power, yet your committee is of the opinion
that the question of re-opening a dark ballot is a very delicate one, and
in practice has been very sparingly exercised by our Grand Master.
This action was re-stated and re-affirmed by the Grand Lodge in 1919.'"

The following committee report is interesting: Your committee,
appoin"ted at the 1923 Grand Lodge, to consider the advisability of
placing a maximum number of members for Lodges, recommends
that no action be taken towards establishing a maximum number of
members permissible. This decision is reached after carefully digesting the Grand Master's remarks during the past year regarding
Lodges which cannot function on account of small membership.
We feel also that if a Lodge has built up such a reputation that
large numbers desire to join. that Lodge, such reputation having
been acquired Ly the exercise of the principles of Freemasonry, such
Lodge should not be penalized and prospective Masons should not
be deprived of joining the Lodge of their choice.
