The 57th Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge A. F. & A. M. of Idaho convened in Lewistown, Idaho, on the
9th day of September.
The Grand Master in his address stated that this was the first
time the Grand Lodge had been held at Lewistown. The Grand
Lodge of \Vashington chartered the Lewistown Lodge No. 10, the
first in Idaho, about 61 years ago. At that time Lewistown was
then an outfitting place for miners with a small and changing
population. It is now one of the most substantial and important
cities of Idaho.
Among the distinguished guests present from the adjoining sister
Grand Jurisdiction of Washington were: Robert C. McCroskey,
Most Worshipful Grand Master; Morton Gregory, Right \Vorshipful Deputy Grand Master, and Horace W. Tyler, Right Worshipful
Grand Secretary.
During the year, the Grand Master refused dispensations to the
request of two lodges to hold a regular meeting on a day other
than as provided in the by-laws; also to a lodge to hold meetings
for the conferring of degrees in a town within its jurisdiction, but

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

31

other than the town where the Lodge is located. He also refused
in several. cases to consent to the reception of petitions for the
degrees for candidates who were not physically able to conform
ritually to all the ceremonies of the initiation. He received several
requests for his approval to circularize lodges in the interest of
charitable and semi-public movements not connected with the Fraternity, all of which he refused.
In making his appointments on the Committee of Education, the
Grand Master said:
"You are familia,r with the excellent bulletins set out by the Chairman of this Committee. The expense has been negligible. The bulletins have done much to stimulate and maintain a desire for Masonic
knowledge. In a jurisdiction like ours, it is not practicabLe to have a
study club in each Lodge. The cost of an elaborate program would be
out of proportion to the benefits derived. The continuance of the work
carried on by this Committee seems the best solution of .the educational
work."
The Grand Master, in accord with a recommendation, appointed
a committee to investigate the conduct of Masons attending ceremonies of the Shrine, and certain other meetings.
The Grand Master in his recommendation stated that there is a
tendency in Masonic, as in other circles, to over-legislate. "Changes
are needed," he said, "to meet changing conditions, and I believe
the following will prove beneficial:
"!. Like my predecessor, I urge that steps be .taken to codify and
revise our laws. We require the officers to conform to and enforce the
law. But it is .difficult to find a law on many given points on the
present code and digest; and when found one may not be sure that it
has not l:\een amended.
"2. As it is the internal and not the external qualifications that
are essential in a Mason, I recommend that the Subordinate Lodge be
permitted to judge of the physical qualifications; provided that the
candidate must be able to substantially comply (without friendly
assistance) with the ceremonies of initiation; and illustrate or explain
the modes of recognition, and not be likely to become a charge on the
Lodge.
"3. I recommend that visitations be permitted by our brethren in
Lodges working under Grand Lodges that have been generally recognized by the Grand Lodges in this country, and that have not been
refused recognition by us; and that where there is no established
Grand Lodge, visitation be permitted in Lodges working under a Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite, recognized as regular by the
Southern Jurisdiction of th~ Scottish Rite in this country."
The Grand Master in his report stated that most of the lodges
within his jurisdiction were prosperous. Some were not as active
as they were a few years ago, he said, but when business conditions improved, we can look for r,enewed activity. In a few lodges
discord has arisen over feelings-pro and con-concerning the Ku

Klux Klan. "It is unfortunate," he said, "that feelings concerning
this, or any other non-Masonic organization, should ever come into
the lodge. Masonry has no connection with this, or any other
non-Masonic organization. For any Mason to pretend that there is
a connection is reprehensible, and cannot but be condemned."
The Committee on Education in this jurisdiction has provided for
the lodges a program and suggestion for holding a patriotic social
meeting on or about the birthday of Washington, with very gratifying results. Almost every lodge in the state reported a successful
and enjoyable meeting, and are practically unanimous in approving
the suggestion. of making it an annual event.
The Committee's report further stated.
"We feel that the cause of education is the greatest problem of .our
times, Masonically speaking. The best of our memb.ers have ~mt little
understanding of the fundamentals of our fraternity. It will make
better men of them-as well as more intelligent Masons~to have an
understanding of our laws and a comprehension of our literature and
its beautiful and inspiring teachings."
The afternoon of the second day of the session was occupied
entirely with the ceremonies of laying the cornerstone of the new
Science Hall at the University of Idaho, at Moscow. The entire
membership of the Grand Lodge was transported to Moscow by
automobiles, a distance of 40 miles. The ceremonies were largely
of the reminiscent and historical character, a striking feature of
which was an address by Ex-Governor Wm. McConnell, now nearing his 85th birthday, who was governor of the State when the
university was established, more than 30 years ago.
The Committee on the Grand Master's Address recommended
that a special committee be appointed by the incoming Grand Master
to work with the Grand Secretary to evolve a plan whereby lodge
dues may be fixed adequately to cover the running expenses of
such lodges, rather than depend upon fees through petitions to
cover deficits.
The history of the Orphans' Fund of the Grand Lodge of Idaho
is that of an institution of small beginning, slow but steady growth,
with a wholly creditable record of good accomplishments. This fund
was started at a session of the Grand Lodge in 1869, when Idaho
Masonry consisted of but seven lodges with a combined membership of 279. The fund has grown steadily until in 1923 it exceeded
$117,000. This principal at the present time is growing at the rate
of SO cents per member annually. As the membership is not far
below 10,000, $5000 per annum is being added to the principal of
this fund. It appears to be the purpose of this Grand Lodge to

The 85th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Illinois
was opened in the Eighth Street Theatre, in the city of Chicago, on
Tuesday, October 14, A. D. 1924, A. L. 5924, Grand Master Arthur
E. Wood presiding.
The Grand Lodge opened with prayer and devotions led by the
Grand Chaplain, Bro. R. Keene Rya.n, followed by the presentation
of the flag and singing of "America.''
The Grand Master presented his annual report, saying, in part:
"We must not forget that the usefulness and the perpetuity of our
beloved fraternity· do not depend upon the number we admit so
much as the character they sustain."
Addressing the \Vorshipful Masters present, he said:
"It is for you to require the strictest inquiry into the characters of
those who seek admission within our portals. We are not a reformatory institution. We require blocks purer than Parian marble for the
erection of our Mystic Temple. Let us, my brethren, take good material and finish it well."
Referring to the death of Bro. Daniel G. Fitzgerald, Past Grand
Master, at his home in Normal, April 24, 1924, the Grahd Master
said:
"No adequate biography can be given of so varied and useful a
life. He was born February 10, 1868, in Jefferson County, Illinois, thus
being in his fifty-seventh year at time of death. He was a Mason in
Ewing Lodge No. 705, thirty-one years ago. He served in almost
every position in his Lodge. Later he became District Deputy Grand
Master, member of the Board of Grand Examiners and held places of
responsibility on many committees of the Grand Lodge. In 1913
Brother Fitzgerald was elected without oppositiDn to the station of
Junior Grand \Varden. Be hecame Senior Grand Warden in 1915 .and
Deputy Grand Master in 1917. The unexpected death of Grand Master
Austin H. Scrogin on April 26, 1919, at once made him Grand Master.
"For the next two and one half years he served in this exalted
position. The exacting duties so suddenly thrust upon him, together

33

with the responsibilities incident to being President of the First National Bank at Normal, greatly impaired his health. At Bloomington,
exactly five years from the time >that he became Grand Master, the
Grand Lodge laid him to rest with the impressive funeral rites of the
Craft, conducted by P. G. M. Alexander H. Bell."
The Grand Master spoke of the laying of the cornerl!tone of
the George Washington Masonic N ationa1 Memorial as without
doubt the greatest gathering of prominent Masons which has ever
occurred in this country.
Commenting on the visit of Sir Alfred Robbins, P. G. Vv'., and
President of the Board of General Purposes of the United Grand
Lodge of England, he said:
"Brother Robbins came to the United States bearing with him a
message of good will from the Grand Master of England, and this
message was delivered to the Masons of Illinois through their Grand
Master at a dinner in honor of Brother Robbins given on the evening
of April 30. There were present at that dinner most of our Past
Grand Masters, Grand Lodge officers and other prominent Masons of
Illinois. Our Grand Jurisdiction felt highly honored at the opportunity
of greeting this distinguished brother from England."
In speaking of gambling, the Grand Master said that in view of
the questionable methods used by some lodges, and by organizations
that predicate their membership on Masonry, he promulgated on
January 2, 1924, the following edict:
"Brethren: It is my firm conviction that the practice of holding any raffle, circus or any form of chance or gaming for the use and
benefit of any Masonic lodge, and the use of punch boards for the distribution of prizes in connection wi.th and under the auspices of constitutent lodges or members thereof, is detrimental t-0 Masonry and not
in keeping with the principles of our great Fraterni.ty. Individual
Masons who participate in the activities as outlined above are liable to
Masonic discipline under Section No. 325 of the Grand Lodge By-Laws,
which is as follows : '325. All lodges and the members thereof are
striotly forbidden to give, or attempt to give, the aid or countenance of
Masonry to any raffie, lottery or gift enterprise.' If there is any one
thing that Masonry s>tands for, it is the upholding of the Common·
wealth, and I am sorry to say, many of the things being practiced today
are in direct violation of the law.
"Therefore, I, Arthur E. \V ood, Grand Master of Masons in the
State of Illinois, by virtue of the authority in me vested, do hereby
issue and promulgate this edict:
"From and after the date hereof, no lodge of Masons nor members
or members of any Masonic lodge shall engage in or have any part in
the conduct of any raffle, circus, or any form of chance or gambling.
Furthermore, no lodge of Masons nor any memher thereof, may use
or participate in the use of vunch boards. or similar devices, for the
distribution of prizes in connection with any enterprise conducted in the
name of Masonry, or directly or indirectly for the pecuniary benefit of
Masonry or any Masonic lodge, or any organization when membership
is composed solely of Masons ; neither shall any lodge of Masons, nor

34

REPORT ON COHHESPONDENCE

organization of Masons, accept any of the proceeds of any enterprise
as outlined in this edict."
In speaking of the annual dues, the Grand Master expressed
the conviction that the annual dues of a lodge should be fixed at a
sum adequate to cover fixed expenses, and strongly recommended to
each lodge a budget system in administering the financial affairs of
the lodge.

During the year the Grand Master received a number of communications asking him to officiate in the laying of cornerstones
on Sunday and that lodges be permitted to hold picnics on Sunday.
This was his answer:
"Masonry is the only order in the world that tries to hold this
day sacred. Masonic lodges are not permitted to assemble on Sunday, except to hold funeral services."
During the year, relief was extended through the Red Cross to

Jurisdiction.

"The action. of the Grand Master was based upon an act of the
Grand . Lodge found in the Proceedings of 1910, which provides that
it· is the duty of Subordinate Lodges to contribute to the relief of needy
Master Masons, their widows and orphans, to such an extent as the

"It is the opinion of ym1r Committee on Jurispr·udence that the
adult children of Master Masons are not the orphans of Masons in the
accepted term which is intended to refer to the minor children of a
Mason. Your Committee does not que;,tion that the children of a
Master Mason, regardless of their age, ar•t: entitled to the consideration of the Lodge of which the father was a member, but it is our
opinion that the question as t·o the worthiness of the cause, the obligation of the Lodge and the amount of Fraternal assistance to be expended, are matters which lie entirely within the province of the Lodge.
This opinion is substantia.ted bv many acts of the Grand Lod1<e as established by its previous declarations and is that the Grand Lodge has not
the power of controlling the charity of any Subordinate Lodge, and the
charity fund of 'each and every Lodge is under its own control.
"This declaration has been made on various occasions since .the year
1862, and was confirmed specifically in 1890. It is the opinion of your
Committee as an established principle, that the Grand Lodge nor the
Grand 2\fast•e;r has the right to require a Subordina,te Lodge to contribute relief in a case where the Lodge does not reasonably consider
the cause a worthy one, nor to require a Lodge to contribute a specific
amount of relief which the Lodge considers beyond its reasonable financial ability to pay. It has been the acoepted precedent and custom of
this Grand Lodge that the distribution of charity is a local matter pertaining to the Suhordinate Lodges and lies within the province of the
Subordinate Lod1<es. The Committee holds that every Lodge is obligated to pay its just obligations to its members and the~r dependents,

Masonic thought have been mentioned, but the great majority of our

During the year, the following rulings were rendered by the
Grand Master:
1. A lodge may properly accompany a member's remains to
the place of interment, regardless of jurisdictional boundary lines,
and there conduct the burial service. The Lodge must be opened
and closed according to regulations.
2. It is lawful for the Craft to lay the cornerstone of a building
to be erected by a Masonic body for Masonic purposes, even
though part of the same is to be used for renters.
3. Regardless of change in by-law raising or lowering the
amount, the fee in effect on date petition is received by Lodge
shall govern, no matter when the degrees may be conferred.

The 124th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was
held in Louisville, Kentucky, commencing on Tuesday, October
21, 1924.
In opening his address, the Grand Master said:
"While our membership has not increased during the past year as
much as it did during the war; however, we have had a very substantial, healthy growth. our roster showing at this report 72,603 members in 613 Lodges. The character of our membership is the most
important element of our strength, and to its purity we should apply our
zeal. Ours is a fraternity which emphasizes not the spectacular, but
the simple fundamental principles of a worthy life; a fraternity whose
mission is to build character in men, which will find its truest expressions in private and public morality, and which will exhibit in all human
relations the divine wisdom of life. My ambition for every Kentucky
Mason is that he may catch the real vision of Masonry; the vision of
service and usefulness."

"In viewing the above it should be borne in mind that the Trustees
are not duly installed officers of the Lodge, bound by their oath of office
to serve until their successors shall be elected and installed, but are
simply elected by ballot and automatically and without ceremony assume
their places on this Committee or Board.
"I replied that I was of the opinion that in case of resignation that
Section 24 of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge has no bearing on
this question. The Trustees are not officers of the Loclg·e in that sense,
but the Trustees are directors of a corporation, elected by the members
of the Lodge, who stand in the same position as stockholders. My
reply to the questions was as follows:
"1. The resignation of a member of the Board of Trustees should
be presented to the Chairman of the Board of Trustees, to be acted
upon by the Board.

its members : 'the vacancy in the Board of Dir·ectors shall be filled by
the Board, and the Director so appointed shall hold office until the next
annual election,' as provided by Section 551 of the Kentucky statut-es.
"4. The Lodge cannot accept the resignation of one of the Trustees,
and therefore it is not the duty of the Master to call an election for
tilling such vacancy.
"5. In my opinion, the whole matter is disposed of by the foregoing answers, but I may add that in case of vacancy by death or
r-esi!mation, the Board of Trustees as a Board of Directors are controlled by Section 551 of the Kentucky Statutes, and they alone can
accept a resignation and appoint the . successor until the next annual

During his term of office, the Grand Master rendered 56 rulings.
The following will be of general interest to the Craft:
"Under date of April 17, 1924, in reply to George Washington
Lodge No. 65, as to the authority of the Master, I ruled that the Worshipful Master of every Lodge is in sole charg•e of the affairs of the
Lodge during his term of office, and is responsible. directly to the
Grand Master and to the Grand Lodge. In an emergency, and with
assurance of said officers acting contrary to Masonic law and usage,
the Master may suspend any elective officer so acting until reviewed by
the Grand Master, who can order an election to fill the vacancy. The
appointive offic.er pro tern is responsible to the Worshipful Master durhis term of duty."
On account of the large number of descendants of French explorers living within the boundaries of the State, the spoken language is still a problem. The Grand Master closes his address with
the following recommendations:
"I further recommend that, as Louisiana is one of the constituent
States of the American Republic, and that, inasmuch as the English
languag:e is the official language of that Republic in which all the laws
are written, and all legal proceedings of every kind are had and transacted, and considering that the Masonic Fraternity is an integral part
of this Nation-not least in importance-it seems to me that the official
prooeedings of the Lodges in this Jurisdiction, in respect to language,
should conform to the usages and customs of the country. Therefore,
all their proceedings both spoken and written should be conducted in
the English tongue, and all of thei.r official records should be recorded
in that language.
"I appreciate as well as any man the love and veneration which
a person feels for his native country, or the nativ·e country of his
fathers. But when he comes to these United States of ours and becomes a citizen by choice, he is, or should be, an American in the full
sense of the term. I do not believe in hyphenates because a man is
either an American or not an American. It matters not whether he or
his ancestors came from Sunny Italy, from the vine-clad plains of
France, from the Vaterland of the late Kaiser, or the mountain;; of
Spain; he, or they, came her.e of their own f.ree choice, seeking to
better their conditions, and-in assuming citizenship here as a part and
parcel of that citizenship-they should also use the national tongue.
"For these reasons, with malice to none, and love to all, I suggest
that all Lodges in this state be required to conduct their Masonic proceedings, including ritualistic services, in the English language, and that
all their minutes and other records be written in that language."

this portion of the address was referred, made the following recommendation:

Mason for light. The face of every true Mason should be lifted

I can think which would better describe the attitude of every true

The 160th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was held
in Portland, on Tuesday, May 5th, 1925, continuing in session for
three days. There were present 262 delegates, representing 180 ·of
the 206 chartered lodges and 6 of the 9 living Past Grand Masters
were present.
The State of Maine has the proud distinction of standing first
o'f all the jurisdictions of the world in the proportion of Masons to
the population. In referring to this enviable position, the Grand
Master, in his address, makes fitting mention as follows:
"In 1863, M. W. Marquis F. King, then Grand Master, took pride
in stating that Maine with its · 19,466 Master Masons stood first in
all the jurisdictions of the world in the proportion of Masons to population. At that time, three per cent of the population of Maine were
Master Masons. Nevada stood second, with two and five-tenths per
cent; Vermont third, with two and one-half per cent; Connecticut
fourth, with two and three-quarter per cent; and New Hampshire
fifth, with two and one-quarter pe.r cent. Today, with our 42,981 Masons
fo. a poimlation of 768,000, we have the highest percentage in this
country, and probably in the world. Vermont comes second, w'ith a
percentage of five and two-tenths per cent; the District of Columbia
.third with four and eight-tenths per cent; New Hampshire fourth with
three and four-tenths per cent; while Nevada, originally •second in percentage, is 1iow fifth, with three and ninety-eight hundredths per cent.
"To gain and hold for more than forty years the distinction of having the highest percentage of Masons to population· of all the jurisdictions in the world is a source of satisfaction to this Grand Lodge.
"It has even ·greater interest in connection with the history and
traditions of our people. Such a percentage of Masons should have
had, and undoubtedly has had, great influence in shaping the character
of .our. citizenship. Men from Maine have always been noted.. for their
apility, integrity, sobriety, strength of character, and general reliability.
To hail from the State of Maine is a recommendation in itself. No
small part of this well-deserved repu'tation has been due to the influence
and teac;hings, the precepts and example of the many Mast·er Masons in

The following decisions made by the Grand Master during the
year may be of interest to the Craft:
"!. In answer to the question whether an application could be received from a man 63 years old who had lost one foot at the ankle,
but had an artificial foot, and will be able to give and receive all
signs necessary for Masonic .recognition, I stated, that in my opinion,
he was eligible for Masonry.
• "2. In response to a question whether a person who had an artificial
right foi:e arm and hand was eligible for the degrees, I replied as follows: 'It appears that this matter was settled in the Proceedings of
1923, page 416, and unless the candidate is able to receive and impart
all signs and tokens necessary for ;\fasonic information in each degree,
he is not eligible.' "
The Grand Master, in his address, asks the question, "Is Masonry
in Maine doing the amount of benevolent work which it should do?"
He proceeded to answer this question by reviewing: in a concise
way the charitable work being done by other jurisdictions. Many
states are maintaining Masonic homes, hospitals, orphan asylums and
schools. New York, with approximately 300,000 members, spends
annually for charitable purposes more than $350,000. Illinois, with
its 270,000 members, spends $130,000 per year in maintaining its
Masonic homes, besides doing other charitable work. Pennsylvania,
with about 200,000 Masons, maintains several homes and hospitals,
including one which accommodates over 700 guests and is the largest Masonic home in the world. It has more than $2,000,000 devoted
to benevolent purposes. To accomplish these results every initiate
in Pennsylvania has been required to contribute $20.00 for charity
in addition to the regular fee for the degrees. Last year this amount
was raised to $40.00 to be paid by each initiate. Compare this contribution with the minimum fee of $30.00 charged by most of our
lodges in Maine where often times the entire amount is spent for
running expenses of the lodge before the end of the year, leaving
nothing for charity. Ohio, with 187,000 members, already has a home
for over 200 guests, and is building a hospital to cost $700,000.
Indiana, with 120,000 Masons, spent last year nearly $100,000 in
running its home where over 300 guests are cared for. Georgia,
with 67,000 Masons, spends over $40,000 per year for charity. Alabama, with 50,000 members, cares for its adult dependents and
orphans at an annual expense of $65,000. Connecticut, with 41,000
members, spent in 1923 over $199,000 in charitable work. New Jersey, with 78,000, cares for its dependents at an annual expense of

51

over $65,000, and also provides adequate hospital facilities for the
sick. Kentucky, with 72,000 Masons, spends $75,000 per year for its
orphan children, and is raising a fund of $1,000,000 to provide a
home and hospital. Massachusetts has recently voted an annual
assessment of $2.00 per year, for each member, for charitable purposes. These instances show that Masonry in Maine is not doing
as much charitable work as other jurisdictions.
The M. W. Grand Master paid tender tribute to the memory of
Rev. John M. Bieler, Grand Chaplain, of North Berwick, who died
October 13, 1924. Brother Bieler was intensely interested in all
Masonic activities, and was regular in attendance at the Grand
Lodge.
Amendment to the Constitution:
. "Sec. 117. No lodge shall suspend or expel a member from the
rights of Masonry for non-payment of dues. The penalty of such delinquency shall be forfeiture or suspension of membership, and that
only after due trial, as in other Masonic misdemeanors.
"A brother suspended from membership for non-payment of dues
will be restored by the payment or remission of the amount due at
the time 'of his suspension at any time within five years after; but after
that time he can be restored only upon his application, and a unanimous
vote of the lodge, after payment of remission of the amount in arrears."

The Master's address was abounding in inspiring idealism, compassionate idealism for those in error, practical suggestions for the
welfare of the Craft, and above all else, breathing a proven sense of
gratitude and deb~ towards the Great Architect of the Universe,
foundation of all goodness.
Criticism was offered by the Grand Master of the wrong practic;e

The Grand Master commented against the wisdom of continuing

no Masonic standing during the refreshment hour. He stated that
these customs prevented freedom of speech and retarded development of the brethren. The Craft, he said, has sufficient resources
within itself, and opportunity should be given for its free expression.

fully justified the effort, eighteen to twenty essays being submitted

The 80th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Michigan was held at Flint, Michigan, May 27 and 28, 1924, A. L. 5924.
The Grand Master stated in his address that the Grand Lodge
had grown from a handful to about 140,000, and had nearly doubled
its membership within the past ten years, so that now the work consumes practically all the Grand Master's time."
The Grand Master reported the institution of six new Lodges,
the dedication of fourteen Masonic Temples, the laying of the cornerstones for two new Temples, a school house in Buena Vista
Township, Saginaw County, Board of Commerce building at Saginaw and a community church house for Rogers City.
The Grand Master attended many visitations and social functions,
one of the outstanding affairs being the Diamond Jubilee of all
Masonry in the Valley of Grand Rapids, held March 19, 1924. He
states that throughout his visits the interest of the officers and members of the various lodges in the finer things of Masonry has been
remarkable.
Pursuant to an order issued at the last Annual Communication
by Grand Master McKenzie, the Grand Master issued an order
"prohibiting the practice of holding fairs, circuses and bazaars, the
raffling of automobiles or any other commodity, and the use of punch
boards for the distribution of prizes in connection with and under
the auspices of the Constitutent Lodges." The Order further stated:
"Whenever a Masonic Lodge or a Mason participates in, or carries
on, one of these gambling devices they not only violate the law of the
State of Michigan, but violate the law of Masonry.
"Every Masonic Lodge carrying on these practices, and every )lfason
participating in these practices is guilty of un-Masonic conduct and
subject to discipline."
The Grand Master, in commenting, said:
"There are too many side issues which are bringing discredit upon
the Craft, which are leading our membership astray through exploitation of frivolous and undignified schemes; too many 'back to nature'
parties ; too many gambling devices in clubhouses and in connection
with so-called 'entertainment ; too much disorder and confusion, and
I believe the time has come for Grand Lodge to take some decided
action to curb the activities of these organizations which demand Masonic affiliation in order to acquire membership therein; and which
force Masonry to become an unwilling host.

"Masons who live in the memory of their fellows, are those who

to do to promote the welfare of thos·e about us, is the 1:est of service,

Speaking of the records of a Lodge, the Grand Master states:
"The records of a lodge are history. There may .come a time when
some indefatigable brother may want to write a history of the inception and continuance of every lodge in this jurisdiction. It may be
ordered by the Grand Lodge, as is the case today in many jurisdictions, and I believe the time has come for Michigan to have
its history written, for it has a very unique history, and I recommend
the appointment of a committee for this purpose." The address was
completed with the following significant words:
"The flag that floats over the Nation and that adorns our Lodge
rooms has in it every bit of emblem that was ever unfurled in the
_name of liberty. It has taken the tears of Israel, the conquests of
Alexander, the victory of Marathon, the campaigns of Caesar, the
ashes of Savonarola, the exile of Dante, the blood of William the
Silent, the daring of Martin Luther, the Magna Charta, the will of
Cromwell, the slaughter of the Huguenots, the landing of the Pilgrim

stars so bright.
"The principles of Masonry are of eternity. It has taken milleniums
to make it possible. Its potent seed was planted in the far-off soil of
the most archaic times, but it has taken the chemistry of the ages to
make it the blessing of this Twentieth Century."

The 72nd Annual Communication was held at St. Paul, January
21st and 22nd, with all the Grand officers present. During the season 255 Lodges were represented out of 298 on the roll.
The Grand Master's address is a valuable contribution to Masonic
thought, as regards our civic duties, and we quote the following:
"Masonry has, in my opinion, a very great and impending problem
before it, in our State and Country, to properly meet and surmount
the situation at present all too noticeable to any thinking red blooded
American Mason. Are we not too prone to be absorbed individually,
as well as collectively, in our own separate affairs, to the detriment
of the country?
''There are those conti.nually coming here, and too often those to
the manor born, openly endeavoring, nay boasting, of their desire to
overthrow our Republic (handed down to us by Washington and his
illustrious followers, through bloodshed and deprivations they endured,

leaving us the g.reatest heritage ever enjoyed by the gift of men). Do
we want to wake up and find ourselves in the condition that many of
the European Nations are in at this time; do we want or invite such
possibilities?
"Our conduct seems to imply •that we do invite it by our seeming
lack of thought and action. We daily note that the Judges of our

of those whom the court has power to return to the countries from

The proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Missouri for 1924 came
to our table in an excellent printed volume prefaced with a good picture of the Grand Master, Joseph S. Mcintyre of St. Louis, Mo.
This is followed by an interesting biographical sketch of true historical value. "Most Worshipful Brother Mcintyre is, first of all,
a Missourian. He was born in Andram County, near the city of
Mexico, April 4, 1871, in a house where his father was born, his
father being the first white child born in that county. He comes
from that rugged type of Missouri pioneer and farmer which has
made Missouri a wonderful state of opportunities; the rich experience gained from a boyhood spent on th.e farm, coupled with that
gained from long residence in one of our metropolitan cities, has
given to this brother a view of the world not accorded to the average man."
"Bro. McIntyre's life is a record of ceaseless activity in many
and varied spheres, and his splendid qualifications render him invaluable to many interests. His versatility, initiative and reliable
judgment are known to all of his Brethren and the manner in which

fiO

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

he took up the duties of Grand Master one year ago will not be
readily forgotten by those who were privileged to be present at his
installation."
The report shows conclusively that the administration of Brother
Mcintyre has been a busy one. His address deals with most of the
outstanding events of the year, the Grand Masters Conference, the
Washington Masonic Memorial, cornerstone laying, Flag Day observance, visitations, dedications, visit of the Grand Master of Virginia, visits to the Grand Lodges of Illinois and Michigan, receptions for Sir Alfred Robbins, the complimentary dinner given by
the St. Louis brethren, all show the various activities in which he
engaged. His work in promoting activity of the Masonic Service
Association in the state apparently has produced splendid results.
The Grand Master reported the death during the year of three
of Missouri's most illustrious Past Grand Masters, to-wit: Most
Worshipful Brother Clay C. Bigger, Most Worshipful Brother John
Rolph Parson and Most Worshipful Brother W. F. Kuhn.
The Grand Master also took occasion to approve the splendid
work being done by the DeMolay organization in Missouri and other
states. He characterized this organization as a movement for the
improvement and protection of the youth of the land and particularly approved of all that has be-en accomplished by it to date.
He also complimented the work being done by the Masonic
Service Association of Missouri under the able leadership of the
Committee composed of Ray V. Denslow, C. H. Briggs, Fred 0.
Wood, Arthur Mather, F. H. Littlefield, Geo. \V. Walker and John

equipped with approved facilities; providing a circulating library to
which all of the lodge had access, and outlining and furnishing
definite programs to be carried out by the local lodges on certain
national days or days of great moment in the history of Free
Masonry; and, lastly, the Committee has given to the Craft of Missouri for the first time what it designates as "The Missouri Grand
Lodge Bulletin," which is the official organ of the Masonic Service
Association of the Grand Lodge of Missouri.

rock upon which Freemasonry rests, and on which as long. as 1t rests
· we may well go on and be strong. But if we allow any interference
with that aspect of our faith; if we allow any departure from our, express belief in the truth that has been taught us at the altar of Freemasonry, we shall crumble, we shall pass; and shall deserve to crumble
and to pass as empires have done, when for the sake of temporary
glory they have parted with their soul in order to strengthen their body,
and both body and soul have perished in the process.
"A Mason can put aside his Masonic emblem; he can. leave th'!-t
behind with the Tyler of the Lodge; but he has to carry his M asomc
principles into his daily life, into his home life, into his .w.ork life,
into his business life and unless a man who 1s a Mason 1s a bett•er
man in his home life' in his relation of citizenship, and his daily contact with his fellow ~en, that man is not a true Mason. He is simply
a discredit to the great body to which he belongs, rather than one who
brings it any glory."

The 107th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was held
in the city of Jackson, on Tuesday, February 24th, 1925.
The officers of the Grand Lodge were welcomed to Jackson by
the Mayor of the city, Brother Walter A. Scott, and the governor

of Mississippi, Brother Henry L. Whitfield, and also by Mrs. Viola
E. Lake, Worthy Grand Matron, Eastern Star.
,. The Grand Master opened his address with a strong plea for law
~nforcement, handling "without gloves" the bootlegger and the individual patronizing him. He said:
"This question of peaceful relations and law enforcement has occupied the minds of politicians and general diplomats since the dawn of
history, and we cannot say that they have achieved signal success.
Now the world says we will give the brotherhood a trial at it. I was
greatly impress,ed with J. P. Alley's cartoon in the 'Commercial Appeal' a few weeks ago. He pictures a man with a package containing
a bottle of bootleg liquor under his arm. In the presence of his small
son he snaps his finger and says: 'A piffi,e for A law.' Years pass and
this man, ,old and decrepit, has perhaps long since seen the error of
his way but too late to recall his lost manhood. The son, now a man,
snaps his finger and says, 'A piffle for ALL law.' No, it is not more
laws, nor better laws that we need but a better regard for law. Some
writer has said 'I care not who makes the laws of a nation, if you
will let me write its songs.' We would not for a moment discount the
place and importance of music and harmony in shaping the destiny of
a nat~on, but WE would prefer to say 'I care not who makes the laws
of a nation (so long as they are good ,ones) if you will let me mold
the s'entiment and attitude of the people towards those laws.' What are
we as individuals doing to bring about the era of good will, peaceful
relations and proper respect for law?
"The man who buys and drinks bootleg liquors has no more respect
for law than the one who makes it and the one who sells it, and neither
·buyer nor seller can be a Mason, for Masonry teaches reverance for
and obedience to ALL law. An American Mason is one who beJi.eves
in the Holy Bible, the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution of
the United States, the public schools, and the supremacy of the law
over all other beliefs, creeds or edicts. And the purpose of Masonry
is to make men understand more perfectly their relationships and obligations to God and their fellow men that He may be glorified and that
manhood may be purified and magnified."
On May 3rd, 1924, the death occurred of Past Grand Master
Charles H. Blum. Brother Blum was born in the province of AlsaceLorraine on June 21st, 1856. He emigrated to America in the spring
of 1873, !anding in New York. In 1906 he was chosen Grand Master
of Mississippi Masons.
During the year, two Lodge Temples were destroyed by storm,
. Collins Lodge No. 458 and Summit Lodge No. 231. The Grand
Master called attention to the fact that each year several Lodges are
destroyed by fire or tornado and appeals were made to the Grand
Lodge for assistance. In many instances the statement is made that
no insurance was carried. Investigation revealed the fact that more
than 200 Lodges in this Jurisdiction carried no insurance.

The 60th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Ancient
Free and Accepted Masons of Montana opened in the Masonic
Temple in the city of Great Falls, at 9:30 a. m., August 20th, 1924,
and concluded its labors on Thursday, the 21st, at 6:30 p. m.
The Grand Master emphasizes the following suggestions:
"I recommend that from and after January 1st, 1925, all organizations exoepting regularly constituted Royal Arch Chapters, Commanderies of Knights Templar, Scottish Rite Bodies, Shrine Temples and
Chapters of the Eastern Star· be prohibited from meeting in the same
room occupied by what we term Blue Lodges.
"Great harm may be done to the Lodge by letting in poor material.
Great harm may be done to the candidat-e, if black-balled without proper
cause. I have heard that it is common in some Lodges, when a candidate has been rejected, for the friends of the petitioi1er to start an
immediate quest to attempt to ferret out who cast the black-ball. In
their search to learn the 'guilty party,' as they consider it, they suspect
everybody in the Lodge and make it generally disagreeable for many
innocent members.
"lt has come to my notice that some Lodg·es in this state have taken
it upon themselves to send !vlemorials and Petitions to our Representa- ·
tives in Congress either endorsing or objecting to certain measures
coming before that hody or submitting some measure to bring before
Congress.
"Eventually this action on the part of the Lodges will lead to political activities, the very thing which must not he. It is a very had
practice. If any Memorials or Petitions are sent to Congress, the
Grand Lodge should be responsible for them. I r·ecommend that this
Grand Lodge make a provision in our code, prohibiting lodges to petition Congress in any manner, shape or form.

"I realize that the teachings of Masonry are intended to make Masons
the highest class of citizens. If we follow the teachings as laid down
in our work we cannot be unworthy of the respect and esteem that is
due a gentleman and a citizen. I realize all men do not look at the
same thing and see it alike, and I do not understand how a man can
listen to our instructions and accept the work and in a short time forget them so as to become unprincipled enough to violate almost every
law of Masonry and of the country in which he liv•e.s. Yet we have
such cases. It is about as hard to get a man expelled from Masonry as
it is to get a jury to render a verdict to hang a woman. During my
year as Grand Master I have had mv attention called to members suspected of being bootleggers, whoremongers, cattle-rustlers; those who
will not pay their just debts, liars and horse-thieves. Thankfully, such
men are in the minority. I know that Masonry does not teach them to
do wrong. I think that much of this can be corrected bv work on the
part of investigating committees. \Ve have been too an:iious for numbers and dollars and not enough care exercised in the selecting of quality. On the other hand, I realize that within our ranks there are
thousands of men who are the salt of the earth, but why should they
be besmirched by the actions of the minority? Masonic ideals are of
the highest type and we must maintain them. Let us clean out from
our ranks the man who will not live the life that a Mascn should."

The Grand Secretary reported in detail on the Nebraska Masonic

total of 27 lqclges reported having no delinquent clues, 11 less than

Worshipful Brother Merrill B. Carman, Grand Orator, in his
address, spoke as follows:
"Masons should not only obey the law as individuals, but should
rally to the support of law enforcement everywhere and at all times.
This is an evidence of active Masonry. We must teach respect for law
to our children, both by pr>ecept and example. If our boys and girls of
this present clay are taught to obey the law there will be less need for
law enforcement a generation hence. Lawlessness and riots are not
born in a night; .they are the result of lack of obedience to discipline
in the home.
"I have heard men criticize the officers of the law when they themselves did not make their own children behave at the breakfast table.
The National President of the Parents and Teachers Association said
last fall in Lincoln that we are spending millions to educate our children in our schools, then after their school clays we spend a greater
amount on the same men and women in the enforcement of ·the law.
"The man who complains of the lawl·essness of the bank robber, of
the holdup man, or the crime of a cabinet officer, but himself under
cover of the darkness or some other hidden and secret way purchases
illicit liquor is iike the one of whom he complains, a dangerous citizen,
and when men lose their respect for law they arc too near anarchy to
he known as desirable citizens.
"I believe one thing needed in America is the return of the American Sabbath for American citizenship. Some folks act as if they would
like to foreignize our land, if we are to judge by the way the' Sabbath
of our fathers is desecrated."

Brother John R. Webster delivered the oration at the laying of
the cornerstone of the Masonic Home. He said, in part:
"The cornerstone represents the individual Mason. It was carefully selected, as aire all who gain admittance into our Order. It came
from the quarry a rough, uneven mass of rock, just as the applicant, a
Rough Ashlar, first knocks at the door of the Lodge. It has been subi•ected to chipping, grinding, pounding and surfacing, and as Entered
Apprentices, we were exhorted to make liberal use of the 'Common
Gavel' for the 'noble and glorious purpose of divesting our minds
and consciences of all vices and sup•e:rfluities of life; thereby fitting
us as living stones, for that spiritual building, that house not made
with hands, eternal in the heavens.' "
Through a resolution adopted, the Grand Lodge withdrew from

The portrait of Grand Master Edward A. Ducker prefaces this

The Grand Master's address is an interesting account of duties
well done, a splendid year of usefulness. Obedience to law was
one of the principal keynotes of this earnest address. He said:
"One of the great landmarks is respect for, and obedience to the
civil law and the government of the oountry where a Mason resides.
The landmark makes no distinction as to the kind or character of laws
that should be respected and obeyed. It embraces all laws. Respect
for and obedience to all the laws of our country, great .or small, popular
or unpopular, are therefore attributes of a true Mason. Any one who
disagrees with this disagrees with the supreme law of Masonry. Good

Following the opening of the Grand Lodge, California's own

Grand Master Reese, in acknowledging the honor conferred upon

"My heart is moved with deepest emotions this morning as I stand

have carried with me through all these long years, characterizes this

have been affected in many, many years.
"When our governor, Friend \V. Richardson, a brother Mason,
affixed his signature to the measure enacted by the recent legislature,
appropriating the splendid sum of $100,000 for a California building
at the Nevada exposition in 1926, he announced to the people of our
great state that he had approvt:d the appropriation and the bill in order
to oement more firmly the bonds of friendship and goodwill, of business
and social relations that have existed and should continue to exist between these two great sister states in this \Vestern World. He declared
that there was much in common between these two great "commonwealths, Nevada gold and silver had built and established California's
greatest industry, had endowed her colleges, had developed her greatest farms. California is and has be en the market for the remarkable
products of this remarkable state, and in every way there should be cooperation between them. He was prompted by the same spirit of

"While it was an honor and a pleasure, Most \Vorshipful Sir, to

will be met, hut its duty will be fulfilled only as far as its members

by our professions, we have catL<>cd the world to expect it to be. It is

The 135th Annual Communication was held at Free Mason's
Hall in the City of Concord, on Wednesday, May 21st, 1924. The
Grand Master in his address stated that the year had been bountiful
in the making of Masonic history, it having seen the laying of the
cornerstone of that great and wonderful memorial to Washington
"the Mason."
It has seen the Masonic Service Association, that body of men
made up of the strongest Masonic minds of the country, firmly
established in its headquarters at Washington, where it is carrying
on a wonderful work of instruction and education, ready to act as
the representative of the Masons of the United States in the event
of great calamity or in time of war.
In the jurisdiction of New Hampshire, a number of lodges are
making plans for the erection of new· buildings, and among the
more important are those at Manchester, Derry and Keene.
The Grand Master devoted considerable space to the \Vashington Memorial. This was particularly fitting, as the Grand Lodge
of the State of New Hampshire was, over a century ago, the first to
take action, declaring that the Free Masons of the country ought to

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

erect a Masonic Memorial to the memory and fame of their member,
George Washington. Nothing came of it, it is true, but it gave to
that jurisdiction a record that any of the states would be proud to
possess. These facts were the cause of many congratulations to the
Grand Master of New Hampshire at the ceremonies of the laying of
the cornerstone of this memorial on November 1, 1923.
In the large copper box of the cornerstone, the Grand Master
caused to be placed a plate of metal upon which had been deeply
inscribed the following:
"Grand Loclg·e of New Hampshire, A. F. & A. M. November 1,
A. L. 5923, A. D. 1923. The con~erstone, foundation and eight pillars
of the inner hall of this Memorial are of New Hampshire granite.
May it last as long as our hills."
The Grand Master, in closing his remarks upon this subject, says:
"I cannot dismiss this topic without giving to you the further information that this greatest of earth's memorials, to one of the greatest
men of all time, is to be wholly constructed of New Hampshire granite,
coming from what is known as the Reel Stone Quarry, located near our
village of Nor th Conway. This conclusion was reached at the annual
meeting of the Association, on February 22nd, 1924, held at Alexandria,
Va. We have every right to rejoice that the everlasting rock from
our own home hills has been chosen to typify the very heart and soul
of Free Masonry."
The Grand Master, in his report, severely criticized a too frequent use of the word "Mason." He said:
"1 dislike a public Masonic ball so advertised by large posters put
up in all the country round about, inviting everybody to attend, at
so much per couple. I have disliked to see athletics promot,ecl by a
Masonic baseball club, openly in competition for a season's playing with
other clubs. I dislike the tendency to form social organizations, within
our fraternity, with privileges only accorded to those who may pay
dues therein, giving to it as a part of its name the wore\ 'Masonic.'
But it is even astonishing, to me at least, that there are those who
look upon all the.se as keeping themselves well within the bounds of
propriety. I mention these things that they may be placed before
you. It shall not be said of me that I refrained from doing what
appears to be a duty."
The Committee on Jurisprudence fully sustained the Master
in this portion of his report. The Committee states:
"We view with great rnncern the tendency towards the promiscuous
use of the word 'Masonic' in connection with things and organizations,
for financial gain and arc heartily in accord with the views of the Most
\Vorshipful Grand Master.
"Your Committee are of the .opinion that such unwarranted use of
the word "Masonic" might at the same time prove a cause of contention among the Craft, and have a tendency to bring the Order into
disrepute and possible contempt. We, therefore, recommend the passage
of the following resolution:

"Resolved, That the use of the wore\ 'Masonic' is strictly prohibited
except in connection with those organizations decreed to be Masonic
from time to time by the Grand Lodge."
In the matter of the Masonic Home in New Hampshire, the
Grand Master stated that it was not meeting the needs of the lodges,
there being a large waiting list of applicants, because the rooms
have been kept filled to the limit. There is also no conveniences for
the care of those who need the treatment and the attention that our
hospital affords. In closing this portion of the report, he said:
"I will not be.lieve, until you so cleclare, that you want this condition to exist any longer. I believe that when you realize the situation,
yon will answer the call to what I feel is a Masonic duty, by ordering
the trustees of the Home to make such additions to the present building
as will make possible the fullest fraternal services in this great undertaking of ours and that in some way you will pay the cost."
The past year showed an increase in membership in the jurisdiction of 268. The Grim Reaper called 269 Masons during the year.
The Grand Master was re-elected for another term.

The 144th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free
& Accepted Masons of the State of New York was opened in the
Masonic Hall, city of New York, May 5th, 1925.
Considering the size of this jurisdiction, the Grand Master's
address is a most concise, business statement, devoid of rhetoric and
closes with the following admonition:
"Whatever strength and influence this Jurisdicfi.on may have, has
been attained by the attempts it has continuously made to discharge
its obligations to its own members, and answer to the calls for relief
in other jurisdictions; its endeavors to raise the standard of its membership, and at least keep pace with the general progress of civilization. 'Our duty to Masonry does not call for the impairment of our
initiative, lowering our standards, amending the Constitution, or surrendering any of the Landmarks, with the expectation that by so doing
we are serving humanity. On the other hand, let us maintain the integrity of our Institution from the diminishing attacks from without,
as well as the increasing attacks from within. The time will come. no
doubt. when ·our assistance will be needed elsewhere, and we shall
be better able to give it, and without injury to ourselves, if we keep
abreast of our obligations and are in entire accord at home."
During the year the Lodges of this state contributed over $240,000 as a portion of their quota to The George Washington Masonic
National Memorial Association, leaving only $60,000 to complete
their share.
Twelve printed pages of the Grand Master's address is devoted
to the review of correspondence and telegrams dealing with the
withdrawal of the Grand Jurisdiction from membership in the International 1fasonic Association. The Grand Master closes his remarks on this subject, thus:

The Grand Lodge convened in its 138th Annual Communication
in the hall of the Masonic Temple in the city of Raleigh on Tuesday
evening, January 20, 1925, there being present 38 representatives
from other Grand Jurisdictions.
During the year the Grim Reaper called from the official ranks
Joseph Franklin Rhem, Junior Grand Deacon, a Royal Mason, a
devoted physician and a faithful and true friend; also Walter Clark,
for many years the chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The Grand Master in his address referred to the completion of
the William J. Hicks Memorial Hospital, a magnificent building
now in use but not entirely paid for. It was recommended that the
balance due be assumed by the Grand Lodge, and that the same
be amortized by being distributed over a period of two or three
years.
The following commissions were issued as Grand Representatives of the Grand Lodge of North Carolina as near other Lodges:
United Grand Lodge of Queensville, R. W. Brother Jens Peter
Vilhelm Larson; Grand Lodge of Saskatchewan, R. W. Brother A.
M . Bell; Grand Lodge of New Zealand, R. W. Brother Frank Cargill Wade; Grand Lodge of New Hampshire, R. W. Brother William
G. Garmon.
Twelve special Communications were held during the year.
Among the recommendations offered by the Grand Master in his
address was the advisability of delegating some of the minor duties
of the Grand Master to the Deputy Grand Master; requiring the
latter officer to attend at the expense of the Grand Lodge, all board
and committee meetings of which the Grand Master is ex-officio
chairman. This suggestion was made to enable the deputy Grand
Master to become familiar with some of the duties of an office to
which in due time he may be advanced.
The Grand Master called attention to the fact that many of the
Masters of Subordinate Lodges were woefully ignorant of the laws
of the Grand Lodge. He said:
"vVhat we need are Masters .with a sufficient knowledge of our laws
to •enable them to apply and enforce them when necessary, and I recommend that no brother be installed as Master of a Lodge unless previous
to his installation he shall have certified to the Grand Master that he
has read the constitution of the Grand Lodge at least once.''

The Orphans' Friend and Masonic Journal, official organ of the
Grand Lodge of North Carolina, was published during the year at

The newly elected Grand Master is Leon Cash of WinstonSalem. This distinguished Mason was appointed Grand Sword
Bearer of the Grand Lodge in 1918 and has filled each station from
this to Grand Master. He has been an untiring worker in the fraternity, and by his devotion to the study of Masonry over a period
of 33 years is an authority on its laws and landmarks. As a member of the committee on Necrology for 15 years, his reports have
been one of the outstanding and impressive features of each Grand
Lodge session.

The 74th Annual Communication was held at Portland, Oregon,
June 11th, 12th and 13th, 1924. The Grand Lodge was called to
order by Grand Master George T. Cochran. During the roll call,
sustained applause greeted the calling of the name of the M. R.
Grand Chaplain and M. W. Honorable Past Grand Master J. R. M.
Bell, who returned thanks for the tribute. The Grand Master, in
his opening remarks, stated that ·the business of the Grand Lodge
had grown so great that the Grand Master must devote almost his
entire time to the duties of his office.
During the year the Grand Master issued 50 dispensations. Fifteen of them were for election and installation of officers; six for
the purpose of transacting certain business as special Communications; thirteen for holding meetings at some place other than the
regular meeting place or changing the meeting place from one hall
to another, and six being to confer degrees upon candidates without waiting the statutory time between the degrees.
During the year, regular petitions were filed of all conditions
complied with for instituting three lodges under dispensation,
namely, Veronia Lodge, Irvington Lodge and Westgate Lodge, the
two latter being in the city of Portl<r11d.
The Grand Master reported with pleasure that during the past
year the members of the Craftsmen's Club at the University of Oregon had secured a parcel of land and the same had been deeded
to the Grand Lodge. Following this, the contract was let for the
construction of the building and the cornerstone was laid by the
Grand Lodge on May 24, 1924. This is one of the first steps taken
toward recognition of Masonry in higher education in that state.
The Grand Master designated the week beginning November
11th, 1923, as Father and Son week, issuing the following pertinent
official circular:
"November 11th is preeminently a day to be observed by .the American people. It marks the anniversary of the close of· the great. war,
which required the spirit -of America as the leavening p<;>wer to. revive
the hope of the world.

The Grand Master handed down the following decision as to
whether or not an attorney appointed to prosecute a Masonic offense should be paid:
"A.-Jt is consistent with Masonic usages and landmarks for a
Lodge ~o employ a~ attorney for a money consideration to prosecute
one of its members m a Lodge trial.
"B.-It is consistent with Masonic usages and landmarks for a member who has been appointed either to prosecute or defend a brother
on a c~arge of un-Masonic conduct to ask pay for his services, but unless
there is an agreement at the time of the member's appointment as such
atto~ney by the Lodge .that he is to be paid for his services, then his
ser'.'1ces are to be considered as part of his duties in performina Masomc wo~k, and there is no contract or liability on the part of the Lodge
to P'.1Y him! and any payment would be a mere courtesy in recognition
of his services.
"C.-It is only proper to pay to such attorney as has a contract of
employment from the Lodg'e for a money consideration .
. "D.-It is not within the power of the Master of the Lodge to com11?1t the Lodge to the payment of an attorney fee, either in the prosecution or defense of ·one of its members in a Masonic trial."

At the March meeting the Grand Master made the following
statement relative to objectionable activities:
"Since assuming the duties of Grand ]\faster, numerous complaints
have been made regardin!;l' objectionable activities of various organizations which predicate their membership on ·Masonry. From investigations made covering the matters complained ·of, disclosures followed
which, to say the least, did not reflect credit UP<Jn the part of those in
interest, such as common gambling, objectionable advertising, indecent
shows, etc.
"These complaints involve the Shrine, the Tall Cedars, Grotto,
Tyrians, and Masonic Clubs. In two instances the chief excuse was
to raise money, while in another instance it was perhaps due to a lack
of money with which to provide a gootl clean program of amusement,
hence a cheap imitation on a low moral plane was staged.
"A Mason's good standing' in the Fraternity is always dependent
upon his obedience to the Rules, Regulations and Edicts of this Grand
Lodge, and it is quite clear that the Brethren responsible for the matters complained of are answerable as Masons for their conduct. It
would be unfair and unjust to place all -0utside organizations in one
gr-0up of offenders, hence our present inclination is to sit in judgment
upon each organization offending as a unit. I ask, therefore, and shall
confidently expect, to have the hearty cooperation of every member
of Grand Lod1<e, and especiallv each District Deputy, in seeing to it
that the activities of all organizations in his District which predicate
their membership on Masonry, shall be counselled and admonished
regarding this growing menace, with a view to eliminating such activities as will, if continued, bring discredit upon Masonry.
"This Grand Lodge can afford to take no other position, and we
have the unquestioned power necessary to forbid Masons owing allegiance to it. to join, or to require them to withdraw from such organ. izations as are conducted in such a way as to constitute a menace of our
Fraternity.
"Let us hope this note of warning will correct these evils forthwith,
and that no drastic action may he found necessary, but that Ma~ons
who ar•e members of these organizations will see to it that no offense
is committed against either the laws of the State or of this Grand
Lodge."

The Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, held its 13th Annual
Communication in the Masonic Temple, Manila, commencing on
Tuesday, January 27th, 1925. In opening his address, the Grand
Master said:
"I will begin by. informing you that •OUr Lodges have been very
active during the year and have done much constructive work for the
benefit of Masonry, the members of our great Institution, and humanity
·in gieneral. Their labors, ritualistic as well as otherwise, have been
exemplary both in and out of Lodge.
"Some of our Lodges situated in the more densely populated cities
and towns have this year been facing the same problems as the year
before, and it is with the greatest gratification that I can assure you
that they have confronted and worked out these problems without
doubt or vacillation and have given evidence of most commendable
wisdom, determination, and uprightness in this connection. I have
reference to the associations making use of emblems similar t·o or
closely resembling those of Masonry and to the clandestine Lodges.
"The stern resolution adopted by this Grand Lodge at its last annual communication resulted in the dissdution of bonds of friendship
that had stood the test of many years and untold vicissitudes. To our
great regret we lost some members who deemed it possible to maintain
clean and immaculate their honor, prestige and sworn allegiance r•emaining where they now are, at the cost of deserting our ranks. 'vVe
lost in numerical strength, but in compensation for our loss·es we have
now the certainty that those who have remained with us have the same
idea·s of duty and loyalty to our cause as we have."
During the year there were issued four dispensations for the
formation of new Lodges, two of which were in the City of Manila.
Under the caption of "Decisions Made," the Grand Master said:
"No great number of difficulti·es arose during the year in the various Lodges. The requests for advice and information were not numerous. Fortunately it was possible by clarifying the phraseology used in
the Constitution to explain away most of the difficulties. It was not
necessary to make any decisions which required official sanction. Our
Constitution has worked so well, and its provisions are so clear, that
if the same is followed in spirit and letter f.ew questions will ever be
asked. However, it is proper for the Lodges and members to ·seek advice on any question that may seem not clear to them, for thereby more
uniform procedure may result and frequently differences of opinion will
be lessened by early decisions on disputed points."

The Grand Lodge of Quebec held its 55th Annual Communication in the City of Montreal on the 11th day of February, 1925, with
73 Lodges represented. The address of the Grand Master sets forth
in a concise and orderly manner an account of his stewardship,
enabling the reader to obtain a ready grasp of all his official acts,
and a clear conception of the condition of Masonry within the Jurisdiction. The following quotations are worthy of consideration of
every faithful Mason:
"The temptation in Masonry is to ov,er-stress the form. There are
brethren who wear regalia and exhibit the ornaments who are void of
the Spirit of Masonry. There are excessive rituaHsts who will split
hairs over a word or accent, while all the while they are wholly unmindful of the Spirit enshrined in the form. Cases have been known
where "good men and true" have been barred from a lodge because
of some trifling difference in a password or a ,grip. This is surely to
caricature Masonry. Have we not all known brethren who were moved
by the highest and fulle,st Spirit of Masonry and yet were profoundly
unlettered in the use of forms? I want to ur~e, with what force I
may have, the paramonnt importance of the Spirit of Masonry, while

92

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCI~

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

at the same time giving to form its proper value. One sometimes hears
brethren express the desire that Masonry should ally itself to certain
movements in the social and political world. They would tie it to a
definite party of reform or seek to secure its support for some needed
cause. One can understand this desire, and in a measure sympathize
with it.
"We live in an age of Service Clubs-Societies that are pledged to
a well-defined effort of philanthropy. Men are asking: 'What is Masonry doing? Why does not your organization endorse some definitely
good work? Have you helped any institution or supported any beneficence?" Criticism is rife because Masonry has not backed any needful cause. It would, however, be fatal to the central principle of our
order if Masonry allied itself to any of the many forms of huinan
service. All societies are more or less partisan, and Masonry by its
very charter and character cannot identify itself with partisanship.
She stands for universal fellowship. and must eschew all partial causes,
even at the price of suspicion and misunderstanding. Masonry is a
Spirit, first, last and always. It is the Spirit of human friendship. It
rises above all sectional feelings, all racial differences. It has only one
doqma-the Fatherhood of God. Masonry is not a religion nor a
political society.
"She must refuse to identify herself with any Church, however
noble, or with any patriotic organization, however widespread. She
has often been accused of religious bias and :'.IJ ational prejudices becau,se of the weaknesses of her members, but in her real character she
cannot be sectarian or sectional. She stands not so much for tolerance
as for fraternity. She seeks to bind men of all races, creeds and
parties together. She is of all religions where God, the Great Creator
and Father, is rec'ognized. Any effort to identify her exclusively with
one form of religion or race would destroy her mrssion.
"Are you a Mason? That question, so frequently asked, demands
something more than being versed in ritual or in the exchange of secret
grips. If all you have to give in response to it is a whispered word or
a pressme of the fingers·, a sign or an offered jewel, then you have
learned little of what it means to be a Mason. For Masonry in its
deeper aspect is of the soul and mind. It is to see in your fellow-man,
whether he be learned or ignorant, whether he he. black or white,
whether he hails from West or East, a friend and brother, one whom
you can love and serv,e. The question you will a'sk him, if you be a
true Mason, is, not 'What is your creed?' but 'What is your need?'
You will see in him the rnme high aspiration and the same weaknesses
that you disco\er in yourself. The thought of ·exploiting him will
never darken yoursou!, the hope of claiming him for the highest will
radiate your heart and f!~sh your mind with promised victory. If you
have the spirit of Masonry you will be able to detect the. jewel of character under the most unattractive ugliness; you will recognize a brother
under the swarthiest skin. Being yourself fiHed with the Masonic
Spirit of Charity you will make excuses where others condemn: you
will love where others only admire, you will serve whiJ.e others talk."

On February 17, 1924, the Grand Master accepted an invitation
to attend the church service in connection with the l25th anniversary
of Mt. Vernon Lodge No. 4, held in the first public meeting house
of Providence, R. I. On this occasion, the Grand Chaplain, Rev.
Brother Edward Russell Evans, delivered a splendid oration on
Masonry. On February 22nd the celebration was brought to a conclusion with a banquet in the ball room of the Providence Biltmore
Hotel.
The Mt. Vernon Lodge has made a splendid growth during its
125 years of activity. The Grand Master expressed his regrets that
during his term of office no additional study clubs had been organize<l throughout the jurisdiction. "There is a desire on the part ot

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

many of our members," said the Grand Master, "to obtain by systematic methods more light on Masonry; a desire to learn more
about the symbols connected with our institution. To gratify this,"
continued the Grand Master, "I solicited the aid of nearly a score
of brethren whom I knew would command the attention of those
seeking knowledge along Masonic lines, but unfortunately none had
the time to spare. I, therefore, recommend that the incoming Grand
Master should appoint a committee to devise a method whereby any
Mason who is desirous of acquiring more knowledge of our institution may have the opportunity under the leadership of those best
qualified."
The Grand Master complimented the Grand Lecturer on his
efficient work, stating that under his untiring efforts ritualistic work
throughout the grand jurisdiction had materially improved.
The Grand Master heartily endorsed the organization of chapters
of the Order of DeMolay throughout the jurisdiction. "This Order,"
said the Grand Master, "composed of boys, sons of Master Masons
and their chums, is an extension in the right direction. The boys
of today are to be the citizens of tomorrow and Masons will be well
repaid for their interest in an organization that tends to make good
boys better boys and better citizens for the future."
The Grand Master stated that the growth of the Subordinate
Lodges during the past year had been very satisfactory, each Lodge
recording an increase of membership.
The Secretary also spoke of the membership in the Subordinate
Lodges, which showed an average membership of 425. He expressed a wish that more lodges might be instituted. Relative to
this matter, he said, "There is as much danger in an over growth
in a Subordinate Lodge as there is in a too small, conservative
membership. During my term, I have been convinced that the committees appointed for investigation in many instances do not fulfill
their duties and it seems to me that the time is not far distant when
lodges would do well to limit their membership."
Definite steps have been taken to erect a new temple iri Providence, the Masons of that city having outgrown their present quarters. This undertaking is being carried on by the A. A. S. R.
and Paledene Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S., more than $1,000,000 having been pledged to date.
The Grand Lecturer in his report stated that during the past
year 27 exemplifications had been held in the Masonic districts of
that Grand Lodge which had been under his direction and had been
witnessed by the Grand Lecturer or one of his assistants. "The
system of district exemplifications which became operative two
years ago has, during the past year proven to me," said the Grand

Lecturer, "as I believe it has to every officer in this jurisdiction, the
wisdom of the Grand Lodge iri adopting !?_uch a method."
Harold L. McAuslan, delegate to the convention of the Masonic
Service Association, submitted an extended report. In the course
of his report, be stated that the Committee on Relief of this Association asked that each Grand Lodge, either members or non-members of the Association, should be asked to voluntarily contribute an
amount equal to 5 cents per capita for the building of the American
School in Tokio, Japan, which was destroyed by the Japanese earthquake. The Committee felt that this would be a work of relief
which should stand out before the world as a monument to Masons.
The next matter in this report was the suggestion that a survey
be made of the United States to find out the conditions in the various jurisdictions regarding tuberculosis. It seems that some of the
jurisdictions are very hard put to relieve distress along this line,
particularly those in the Southwest, where a great number of the
brethren flock for relief. The Masonic Service Board, as a:ppointed
by the then present Grand Master, held seven meetings during the
year and directed its energies to carrying out the established educational and relief program inaugurated in previous years. This Board
has built the policy of continuity of purpose and perfection of
methods.
At the annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Rhode
Island, held in May, 1923, a special fund was established, to be
known as the Grand Lodge Educational Fund. This fund is credited
and maintained by an assessment of $1.00 per annum on each Master
Mason. The purpose of this fund is to provide scholarships to sons
or daughters of Master Masons. The fund is administered by a
Board of Trustees.
This jurisdiction mourns the death on February 14th, 1924, of the
Right Worshipful George Henry Holmes, who served the Grand
Lodge as Fifth District Deputy for the term following his appointment, on May 16th, 1898, and was a member of the Educational
Board, also a member of the Committee on Jurisprudence and the
representative to the Grand Lodge of Missouri and to the Grand
Lodge of England.

The 18th Annual Communication was convened in St. Paul's
Church, Prince Albert, on Wednesday, June 18th, 1924.
The Grand Master's report reflects the earnest Masonic spirit of
the Canadian brethren:
"The importance of the District Meetings and the interest in
those meetings appears to be growing. The influence would appear
to be entirely in the right direction. At nearly all the meetings an
earnest, intelligent desire was shown, to know more of the work
and the application of the symbolic meaning.
"It was demonstrated that Craft Masonry in Saskatchewan is a
live, vital organization, not only for the purpose of enrolling members, but to keep them intellectually interested, and also enthusiastic
for the ideals and for the purposes for which Craft Masonry stands.
The instruction given at those meetings by the Grand Secretary is
uniform and clear, and, to my mind, the result justifies the policy
adopted by a Grand Lodge and by predecessors in office. The work
done in almost every case, was done with a proficiency which would
only be attained by rigid adherence to our ancient practices."
