The Grand Master opened his address with an earnest appeal
for higher education of the masses. As this is a matter of the very
greatest importance, not only to Masonry, but to the Nation generally, we quote him in full:
"I have read a great deal of the doings of the Grand Lodges and
other Masonic Grand Bodies all over this fair land of ours, and the
outstanding thing toward which they have. directe~ their tho_u?ht
and effort is Education. Everywhere, there 1s planning and stnvmg
for a better and higher education for the masses as well as for the
Masons. We want our young men to become educated Ma~ons, but
if we educate the masses, we thereby take the longest possible step
toward accomplishing our desires. If the more than three million
Masons in this country of ours put their shoulders to the wheel of
the great educational movements that are being fostered throughout
the land we will soon be able to dispel the ignorance and superstition ~hich have so long held millions of our people in chains of
slavery and it will not be long before we can conquer man's greatest foe' error. \Vhen illiteracy has been banished from among our
people 'a higher Masonic education of our initiates will be the easiest
thing 'we have to accomplish. !his higher Mas?nic education is
greatly to be desired. Masonry 1s not the conferring of the several
degrees; a moral and spiritual edifice is to be erected.
"But alas how many of us stop, when the foundation is laid?
The wise ma'n puts a foundation under his house--it may be rough.
it must be strong. Then he encloses the building, embellishes it
with paneled wainscot and corbelled arches; he furnishes it completely before he can fully enjoy it. Why should we, as M~s.ons,
stop with the foundation? Why not enclose ?Ur _mor.al and sp1:1tual
building with the history of our order, embellish 1t with the philosophy of Masonry, make it comfortable with the poetry and imagery
that encrust our traditions. Then we can enter upon an enjoyment
of that part of Masonry that is now almost a closed book to the
great rank and file of our fraternity."
During the year death invaded the ranks of the Grand Officers,

The Grand Master in his address recommended that the Committee on "Fraternal Correspondence" be named hereafter "Committee on Fraternal Relations." In this particular he said:
"We list a Committee on 'Fraternal Correspondence' and charge
it with the duty of making a report on the Foreign Correspondent's
'Review of the Proceedings of Sister Jurisdictions.' This is not
work, it is a pleasure. I believe this committee should have some
work to do. I therefore, suggest that the name be changed to the
'Committee on' Fraternal Relations' and that to it be referred all
matters affecting our relations with other Grand Jurisdictions, and
that the Foreign Correspondent's 'Review' be made a part of the
Committee's· report."

"Experience shows," said the Grand Master, "that these men

find the law regarding various and sundry questions."

The Grand Secretary reported receipts from Lodges and other

The Masonic Fraternity in Tennessee during the past four years·
has been one of the most important factors in the elimination of
illiteracy throughout the state. The report of the Committee on
Education reads as follows:
"The inculcation of a system of education is in the very nature
of things, a slow process and yet the campaign of the Masonic Fraternity, begun less than four years ago, to educate its members and
the public generally as to the deplorable condition of our rural
school system, and the appalling percentage of illiteracy in Tennessee-has produced amazing results. The despised public school
now has friends on every side, and a strange and marvelous thing
has been brought to pass. A Governor of our State has had the
temerity to re<;ommend, as a matter of primary importance, a comprehensive educational program, which includes a term of eight
months for rural schools. More than that, he has dared to demand
drastic taxation on measures to put his plans into operation. Stranger
still, we have a legislature apparently in full sympathy with the position of the Chief Executive. Stranger than all, we find a citizenship
in our State thoroughly aroused and ready for the new era, and willing to pay almost any price to bring an equality of opportunity to
all the children of Tennessee.
"The members of this organization have had a large and important part in bringing iabout a sentiment for better education in
the State, but the struggle has just begun. The Government may
initiate and strongly urge reform, but the people must carry out the
program. The measures of taxation must receive the sympathetic
support of the citizenship if the ideals for which we stand pledged,
are realized.
Your Committee on Education earnestlv solicits an aggressive
support on the part of the Subordinate Organizations of this Grand
Body toward enlightening the people throughout the State concerning the importance of the movement for better education from the
rural schools. to the university."

The Grand Master, in his address, called attention to the decision
of the United States Circuit Court of Appeals in the case of United
States vs. Thompson and Bergera, upholding the decision of the
United States District Court in sentencing these two men convicted
of using the United States mails to defraud, to the United States
prison at Fort Leavenworth, where they are both now serving their
sentences. This ends the last chapter in this remarkable Masonic
fraud, which had its headquarters in the Jurisdiction of Utah.

The following report from the Committee of Jurisprudence relative to the attitude of the Masonic Fraternity in Utah towards the
Mormon church, will be of interest to Masons throughout the world:
"Whereas, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints,
commonly called the Mormon Church, is an organization, the teachings and regulations of which are incompatible with membership in
the Masonic Fraternity, therefore:
"Be It Resolved, That a member of the Church of Jesus Christ
of Latter Day Saints, commonly called the Mormon Church, is not
eligible to become a member of any Lodge, F. & A. M., in this state,
and membership in such Church shall be sufficient grounds for expulsion."

The 147th Annual Communication was held in the Masonic Temple, in the City of Richmond, February 10th and 11th, 1925.
The Grand Master opened his address in a spirit of patriotic
fervor as follows:
"Exultant claims of superiority and exceptional worth for our
order are but sounding brass and tinkling cymbals unless supported
by concrete evidence of efficient service to mankind in either a
moral or practical sense. Euphonious phrases alone never relieve
a widow's want, nor will high sounding platitudes stop the cravings

107

of a hungry man. Comfortable surroundings and wholesome social
intercourse stimulate interest in Lodge meetings, and should not be
discountenanced or discouraged in any Masonic community. This,
however, should not and. does not alter the fact that the relief of distress, the protection of the widow and orphan and the kind and sympathetic ministrations to those who have a just claim upon our
affections is the solvent and indisputable guarantee of our merit,
and the best assurance of posterity's favor.
"Indeed, it is by a strict adherence to, and an exemplification
of the world at large, and the eternal blessing of a just Providence.
I would not have you opine, my brethren, that I am charging you
with shortcomings or casting doubt upon the character of your
Masonry. Personal experience in the discharge of my official duties,
as well as extensive inquiry, convinces me that nowhere in all Masonry's varied field of activity can be found a more wholesome,
sacrificial devotion to its interests and righteous purposes, than is
today being exemplified in our revered and historic jurisdiction. A
great host is moving forward, armed with the spirit of benevolence,
willing and anxious to battle want and affliction within its ranks.
An intrepid fraternal legion has caught the vision which dutv and
service inspires, a wholesome, Godly aspiration for nobler things
in fraternal life. There is no want of zeal, no want of enthusiasm,
but an exultant, determined purpose of the most advanced and constructive character, and I congratulate vou upon this awakening,
this onward and uplifting spirit which will crown the present with
glorious achievement and go down to the future as a testimonial of
our fidelity to trust."
The devouring scythe of Time was not idle in the Jurisdiction
during the past year. \iV e note the death of the Past Master Thomas

The following decisions rendered by the Grand Master were of
general interest:
"That the secretary of a Lodge has no right to furnish a mailing
list of his members to anyone for other than Masonic purposes.
"That the trustees of a Lodge have no right to interfere with the
prerogatives of the Master, but when they have been vested with
special duties by a vote of the Lodge the Master cannot arbitrarily
change or interfere with those duties.

During the course of his address, the Grand Master touched a
little caustically on the character of some of the alleged Masonic
journals now published. He said:
"There are a number of Masonic journals in this country entirely
worthy of our approbation, and there are also others which do not
represent our conception of proper Masonic literature. In view of
this it behooves members to exercise prudence in subscribing to any
magazine or periodical until perfectly iamiliar with its policies and
the general nature of its contents. It is far better to read nothing
than to be poisoned by vicious tirades or appeals to passions as is
too often found in publications soliciting Masonic patronage or
claiming to represent Masonic ideals."

adjunct to the Crafts on its social s~de, and has always .been conducted in a manner that has met with the full approbat10n of the
Grand Lodge."
He also called attention to the fact that the Grand Lodge of
England had the first time in 200 years held a communication of the
Grand Lodge outside of the city of London; its September meeting
being held in St. George's Hall, Liverpool, and the number of qualified brethren who made application for tickets of admission was
3500, being 1000 in excess of the number the hall could accommodate, so an apportionment had to be made.
A quarterly communication of the Grand Lodge was held at
Bunbury in February, a few days in advance of the regular date,
owing to the visit of the fleet at Freemantle, which nece~sitated
many of the grand officers returning to Perth. The experiment of
holding a meeting in Bunbury was first tried five years ago and
proved to be such a success that it has been repeated. During that
period, the Craft has made great progress in this district, the membership increasing by nearly 50 per cent. The Grand Master urged
that all subjects of a political nature should be strictly excluded from
discussion at Masonic meetings as being in strict accordance with
long established :Masonic traditions. He said:
"It has loner been the proud boast of Free Masonry that it has
no politics, and that it does not interfere with th~ pojitical convictions of any of its members. On the contrary, 1t brings together
men who very often are otherwise kept apart by religion and politics.
On no account, therefore, must any attempt be made to bring the
Craft into the political arena, but this does not prevent a Free Mason
from taking an intelligent interest in the affairs of his country. He
cannot remain indifferent to what his country is doing, or what
le1.1:islation it is enacting. On the contrary, it is his duty to be well
informed so that he may do his part in maintaining those ideals for

The quarterly communication was held at Boulder, in August,
1923.

At this communication the Scottish District Grand Master, R. \V.
Brother E. C. Rosman, accompanied by his district grand officers,
was welcomed by the M. W. Grand Master and saluted in due form.
The Grand Master speaks of the Craft in Queensland as now
being thoroughly consolidated, and its position much strengthened
by the Lodges going together under their own state constitution,
and he expressed a hope that the day was not far distant ·when the
same happy condition of affairs would prevail in \Vestern Australia.
He said:
"It is a rather astonishing fact that our own state, which shows
such a united front on most questions affecting the well being of the
empire, should be unable to join its Masonic forces for the general
good of our old and cherished institutions. Although we have the
smallest population on the mainland of Australia, we have no less
than four distinct systems of Masonic government in operation, and

which Free Masonry stands, and which are the foundation of all
good government."
The Grand· Master stated that there seemed to be a growing
request for permission to initiate persons under the age of 21, and
during the last quarter he granted two dispensations for this purpose and deferred one. He stated that it was only in very exceptional cases that lads of 18 )'ears were fit and proper persons to be
admitted to the Craft, and that he intended to strictly limit the
issuance of dispensations for under age candidates in the future.
On Thursday, May 22, 1924, an annual communication of the
Grand Lodge was held in St. George's Hall, Perth. The Grand
Master's address contained a review of the history of the Grand
Lodge of Australia. The Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction was
established in 1900, the 33 lodges comprising it having an approximate mi:,mbership of Z.000, which has now been increased to 6,493,
the gain for the present year being 483. The year shows that an
overwhelming majority of the lodges have enjoyed an increase in
membership of over 100 with an average of 65 members per working
lodge, which seemed to the Grand Master to be of right size to
enable the brethren to get together, to learn each other's faults and
virtues, in fact, to know each other.
The chairman of the committee on Foreign Correspondence devotes nearly five pages to a review of the report of the Grand Lodge
of California. He gives considerable space to the address, "Masonry
in Its Relation to Citizenship," by the Grand Orator, Brother John
L. McNab.
In speaking of the perusual of the report of the trustees of the
Masonic Homes, the reviewer states:
"It makes one desirous to reach out and shake the hands of the
trustees. The care and attention lavished on the inmates of the
homes redounds to the credit of every California Mason. There are
two homes. One at Decoto for adults, where 88 men and women
are sheltered, and one at Covina for children, where 52 boys and 61
girls are cared for and educated. We confess to a certain antagonism
to the Order of the Eastern Star, but on reading the account of the
magnificent, noble work that Order is doing for the weak and helpless of those Homes, we respectfully raise our hat."

The 81st Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge was opened
in due form in the Scottish Rite Cathedral, city of Milwaukee, on
Tuesday, June 9th, 1925.
The Grand Lodge of \Visconsin certainly wastes no time in preliminaries but plunges at once into the business of the session. The
Grand Master's address is exceptionally brief and devoted almost
entirely to a detailed account of the principal events of his administration. He calls attention to the heavy death roll during the year,
637 Masons of Wisconsin having been summoned. None of the links
in the chain of the Grand Lodge Officers are missing. Of the Past
Grand Officers, who were prominent members of the Grand Lodge,
the following were called to their final reward:
Past Grand Master Jesse C. Bradley of Milwaukee; Past Senior
Grand \Varden Gruenewald of Oshkosh; Past Junior Grand Warden
John T. King of Madison.
During the year the Grand Master was called upon to preside at
nine Masonic trials.
The Grand Master referred to the matter in which Masonic
funerals were sometimes conducted in various lodges in \Visconsin.
He said:
"These services should be conducted in conformity to the Masonic Monitor of this Grand Lodge. It should be noted th~t the
Masonic services should be cof!Ipleted at the grave, the co.mm1tn:ent
made there and no services given there after the Masonic services
are complete. If other services are desired or given, they should be
before the Masonic service."
The Grand Master highly commended the work of Past Grand
Master Brother Aldro Jenks, Committee on Foreign Correspond~
cnce, a position that he has filled well and acceptab.ly for the past
28 years. Mr. Jenks is generally known and recognized among the
Masonic writers of the United States as one of the best of the Foreign Correspondents of the Grand Lodges of the country, and his
reports are always interesting and of great value to the Craft.
The Grand Master advised against the practice of Masonic chain
letters by Masons, recommending that all Masons receiving such
letters should immediately destroy them, and that after their arrival
home the members of the Grand Lodge should bring the matter up

It was fitting that the Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Wyoming, celebrating its Golden Jubilee should have been held at
Laramie, where fifty years ago the First Grand Lodge of that state
was organized. Laramie was then strictly a village, but it gradually
became one of the industrial centers of the state, and the mecca to
which high school students seeking higher education wended their
way.
Brother Albert W. McCollough, in delivering the address of welcome, said:
"It is fitting at a time like this that the Masonic institution,
which stands for the better and higher things of life and the development of the best in mankind, should meet here, and I hope that each
of you will thoroughly investigate conditions here anti at the university, and when you return home will have made up your minds
that your sons and daughters will be students at this great university."
Government oil royalties amounting to $1.713,798, have been allotted to the school districts of this state and an almost equal
amount to the road fund, which makes it possible for a large percentage of the country school districts to hold eight months of
school without levying a tax on the citizens of those districts.
The address of welcome was responded to by Brother Elwood
Anderson, Grand Lecturer.
The Grand Master's address was businesslike, and was devoted
almost entirely to a review of his official acts during the year.
Most Worshipful Brother Harlan L. Hart, Gram! Master of
Montana, was among the distinguished visitors at this Golden
Jubilee.

During the period of fifty years of the existence of this Grand
Lodge it has increased the number of lodges to 43, and the membership to about 7,000. During this period only in four instances
has a Grand Master served for more than one term, and in one instance it has occurred where the son of the Grand Master filled the
office his father held, and that was in the case of Frank A. Holliday,
who is the son of Jacob Kethro R. Holliday.
Among those who filled the honorable and responsible office as
Grand Secretary were Brothers John K. Jeffrey, William G. Town,
John H. Symons, Edgar P. Snow and William L. Kuikendall, the
latter being elected 20 times to that office. His first term was during the }:ear 1886, when he remained in office until his death, in the
year 1914.
Although one of the smallest states in population, Wyoming's
standing in the Masonic world is gratifying, and has been well
represented by members of the Craft at Washington. At the present time. the entire \Vyoming Congressional delegation is composed
of Masons.
\Vith a total percentage of thirty-five Masons to every one thousand of population, Wyoming ranks eighth in this respect in the
Nation.

"To those r1eaders who are not acquainted, nor have had any dealings with Latin-Americans, a great deal of the following will be incredible, whilst to those who do not know their temperament, it will
be easily understood. We have lived many years, side by side with our
Mexican neighbors and have worked, traded and studied with them,
and in what we are about to write we want it distinctly understood that
we do not attempt in any way to disparage the Mexican people. \Ve
find many very worthy Mexicans and we have many friends among
them, but we want to bring out the point that, between the Latin-American, and the Anglo-American there is a wide gulf r·egarcling their ways
of thinking and acting, and that harmony can best be preserved by each
being allowed to hold his independent views, and not try to coerce
1either side to accept the viewpoint of the other in Masonic affairs, but
allow each one to follow the ideals of his forefathers, and thus preserve peace and harmony, instead of trying to unite in an effort for
good, two absolute contradictory forces, and expect to have a successful, amicable community. Years of experience in all Latin America
have proved this cannot be clone. X ote the differ·ent Provincial Grand
Lodges established by the United Grand Lodge of England.
"The experience gained here bears out this argument. From the
time of the revolution in the Grand Lodge meeting in March, 1910,
when part of the Mexican brethren, not satisfied with the majority rule.
very unceremoniously left the Grand Lodge, and in June of the same
year, called a meeting of the Lodges represented by them. set up a new
Grand Lodge, and took the name of the 'Gran Logia Valle de Mexico.'
There has been no friction between the ::VIexican and foreign l\fasons.
In this rebellious movement there were 8 ::Vfexican Lodges, leaving 16
Emdish speaking and 2 Spanish speaking Lodges, with the Grand
Lodge, or in other words 18 per cent of the membership seceded, leaving· 82 per cent in the Grand Lodge. This 18 per cent in June took the
name of the Grand Lodge Valle de :vrexico, stating that all clone lw the
Grand Lodge in March was irregular, and that they were the Grand
Lodge. The following year, 1911, at the regular communication of t11e
legitimate Grand Lodge, the name was cham1;ed from Gran Logia Valle
de Mexico to 'The York Grand Lodge of :\Iexico, F. & A. ~I.'
"In this article we do not propose to touch on the different Grand
Lodges, except in so far as they have affected the Gran Logia Valle
de Mexico, and the York Grand Lodge.

had access to the works of Matoes, Chism and others and all translations from same are given in quotation marks."
Grand Master Herivel appears to have been an outstanding man
throughout Mexico. He was born in 1885 on the Channel Islands,
England, coming to Mexico in 1902 and starting work in the mining
line as a mine sampler, working up to his present position as assistant general manager of the Compania Esperanza, S. A., located at
El Oro in the State of Mexico. He is a member of the American
Institute of Mining and Metallurgical Engineers.

The proceedings of the York Grand Lodge of Mexico, containing the records of the 64th Annual Communication held in the City
of Mexico March 17th, 1924, and also those of a called communication for the purpose of dedicating the Masonic Hall, Caile
Republica de Cuba No. 75, is one of the most condensed proceedings
that has come to our desk during the year.
The greater portion of it is devoted to a review of Masonic history in Mexico by a Committee on Research. This review covers
fifty pages in the report, comprising six pages followed by an appendix. The Committee prefaces its report with the following:
"In preparing the following data on Masonry in Mexico, we have
had access to many and various documents, or histories and are struck
with the different versions and accounts of events that have taken place
during the last 100 years. There are no doubts in our minds that many
of these so-called histories, are full of misstatements and are so col-

Cecil C. Preston, P.G.M., chairman of the Committee on Foreign
Correspondence for the past ten years, made the following pertinent
reference to the small numerical growth of Masonry in Mexico:
"One reason why the York Grand Lodge of Mexico has been at a
numerical standstill for several years, is that the official language of
the York Grand Lodge is English. With the increased sphere of action
undertaken by the Mexican government. to implant a desirable degree
of education throughout the length and breadth of the land, and a corresponding increase in the number of schools and colleges imparting
some of the higher degrees of education, there is becoming available
as good Masonic timber a large army of bright intelligent young men,
who would gladly avail themselv,es of the moral advantages offered by
Freemasonry, if they could only understand the language in which our
ritual is written. In the opinion of the writer, the time is ripe for the
translation of our Ritual into the Spanish language, with a view of interesting the young manhood {)f this Republic in the teachings of our
Fraternity."
California in the report of the Committee on Correspondence is
given three full pages, with some pleasant bouquets thrown in.
The frontispiece of the report i~ a striking half tone of Grand
Master, M. A. Loevy, elected to serve the Grand Lodge of Mexico
for the year, 1925. Dr. Loevy was born in St. Louis, :Mo.. on August
31st, 1891. His parents were Dr. Adolph Loevy and Mrs. Caroline
Boehm Loevy of Prague, Austria, who came to the United States
in 1845. Dr. Loevy, following his arrival in the United States, in a
few years became a member of the St. Louis school board and. was
a member of the Board when the first high school was erected in
St. Louis, a few years later. He afterwards served as a doctor in
the U. S. service in the Civil War.
